questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the State Government after consultation with the State Pollution Control Board may declare any area as an:
questions.explanation: Section 19 empowers the State Government after consulting SPCB to declare any area as an air pollution control area.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(a) of the Air Act, 1981 (as amended by Amendment Act 47 of 1987), 'air pollutant' means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in the atmosphere in such concentration as may be or tend to be injurious to human beings or other living creatures or plants or property or environment, AND explicitly includes:
questions.explanation: The 1987 Amendment explicitly expanded Section 2(a) definition of air pollutant to include 'noise'.

questions.question_text: In Church of God (Full Gospel) in India v. K.K.R. Majestic Colony Welfare Association (2000) 7 SCC 282, the Supreme Court held regarding noise pollution from loudspeakers that:
options: Noise is not covered by Air Act
Noise is an air pollutant under Section 2(a) Air Act, and religious freedom under Article 25 does NOT include right to create noise pollution disturbing others
questions.explanation: Church of God (2000) held that no religion prescribes using loudspeakers/amplifiers to disturb public peace, and noise is an air pollutant under Section 2(a) of the Air Act.
questions.statute_or_case: Church of God (Full Gospel) in India v. K.K.R. Majestic Colony Welfare Assn. (2000) 7 SCC 282

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Air Act, 1981, no person shall, without the previous CONSENT of the State Board, establish or operate any industrial plant in an:
questions.explanation: Section 21 mandates prior SPCB consent before operating industrial plants in declared air pollution control areas.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31A of the Air Act, 1981 (inserted by 1987 Amendment), the Board has power to issue direct binding directions including:
options: The closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process, or stoppage/regulation of electricity, water or other services
questions.explanation: Section 31A gives statutory power to SPCB to issue closure and service disconnection orders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39D(1) of the Air Act, 1981 (as substituted by the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023, w.e.f. 1 April 2024), whoever fails to comply with the consent requirement of Section 21 (operating an industrial plant in an air pollution control area) is punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than:
options: One year and six months, but which may extend to six years and with fine
questions.explanation: Section 39D(1) retains this imprisonment scale for failure to obtain Section 21 consent; by contrast, contravention of Section 22 (discharge standards) or Section 31A directions is now only a civil penalty under the substituted Section 37.

questions.question_text: In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Delhi Vehicular Pollution / CNG Case 2002) 4 SCC 356, the Supreme Court issued directions under Air Act and Motor Vehicles Act for:
options: Phasing out diesel buses and converting Delhi's entire public transport bus fleet to Compressed Natural Gas (CNG)
questions.explanation: The CNG Delhi Case (2002) directed complete conversion of Delhi's public bus fleet to CNG to curb vehicular air pollution.
questions.statute_or_case: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (2002) 4 SCC 356

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the Air Act, 1981, the State Government, after consulting SPCB, may give instructions for ensuring standards for EMISSIONS FROM AUTOMOBILES to the authority in charge of:
options: Registration of motor vehicles under the Motor Vehicles Act
questions.explanation: Section 20 empowers State Govt to mandate vehicular emission compliance for vehicle registration.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of the Air Act, 1981, when an officer takes a sample of air or emission from a chimney/flue/duct, into how many parts is the sample divided in the presence of the occupier?
options: Two parts, sealed and marked by both officer and occupier
questions.explanation: Section 26 specifies sample splitting into 2 parts (one for State Air Lab and one for Central Air Lab if requested).

questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the Air Act, 1981, an appeal against an order of the State Board lies within 30 days to:
options: The Appellate Authority constituted by the State Government
questions.explanation: Section 31 provides for a 30-day appeal to an Appellate Authority constituted by the State Government, consisting of a single person or three persons as it thinks fit; Section 28 in fact deals with the State Air Laboratory.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43(1)(b) of the Air Act, 1981 (Citizen Suit Provision), a court can take cognizance of an offence on a complaint made by any person who has given notice of at least:
options: Sixty days in the prescribed manner to the Board
questions.explanation: Section 43(1)(b) enables citizen suits after 60 days prior notice to Pollution Board.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b) of the Air Act, 1981, 'air pollution' means the presence in the atmosphere of any:
questions.explanation: Section 2(b) defines air pollution as the presence of any air pollutant in the atmosphere.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(c) of the Air Act, 1981, 'approved appliance' means any equipment or gadget used for burning of fuel or controlling pollution approved by:
questions.explanation: Section 2(c) defines approved appliance as approved by SPCB.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(d) of the Air Act, 1981, 'approved fuel' means any fuel approved by:
options: The State Board for use in air pollution control areas
questions.explanation: Section 2(d) defines approved fuel as fuel approved by SPCB.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(1) of the Air Act, 1981, the main function of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) regarding air quality is to:
options: Improve the quality of air and prevent, control or abate air pollution in the country
questions.explanation: Section 16(1) specifies CPCB's primary air duty: improving air quality and controlling air pollution nationwide.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17(1)(g) of Air Act 1981, State Pollution Control Board is mandated to lay down standards for:
options: Emission of air pollutants into atmosphere from industrial plants and automobiles
questions.explanation: Section 17(1)(g) requires the State Board, in consultation with the Central Board, to lay down emission standards for industrial plants and automobiles.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(3) of Air Act 1981, the State Government after consulting SPCB can prohibit the use of fuel other than an approved fuel in:
questions.explanation: Section 19(3) lets the State Government, after consulting the State Board, prohibit the use of fuel other than an approved fuel in an air pollution control area.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(5) of Air Act 1981, if State Govt prohibits burning of any material (other than fuel) in air pollution control area, it prohibits:
options: Burning of material likely to cause air pollution (e.g. stubble/garbage burning)
questions.explanation: Section 19(5) lets the State Government prohibit the burning, in an air pollution control area, of material (other than fuel) likely to cause air pollution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of Air Act 1981, no person operating any industrial plant in air pollution control area shall discharge pollutants in excess of:
options: Standards laid down by the State Board under Section 17(1)(g)
questions.explanation: Section 22 prohibits discharge of air pollutants in excess of the standards laid down by the State Board under Section 17(1)(g).

questions.question_text: Under Section 22A(1) of Air Act 1981 (inserted 1987), SPCB can apply to which court for an injunction restraining apprehended air pollution?
options: Judicial Magistrate First Class or Metropolitan Magistrate
questions.explanation: Section 22A(1) lets a Board apply to a court not inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class for an order restraining apprehended emission in excess of standards.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(1) of Air Act 1981, where accidental emission of excess air pollutant occurs, who must be informed immediately?
options: The State Board and prescribed local executive authorities
questions.explanation: Section 23(1) obliges the person in charge of the premises to intimate the State Board and other prescribed authorities of an accidental excess emission.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24(1) of Air Act 1981, any officer empowered by SPCB has a right to enter and inspect any place for:
options: Examining control equipment, industrial plant or records
questions.explanation: Section 24(1) gives an empowered officer the right to enter and inspect any place to examine control equipment, industrial plants, or records for compliance.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of Air Act 1981, who may appoint Government Analysts to analyse samples of air or emission sent to a State Air Laboratory?
questions.explanation: Section 29(1) empowers the State Government to appoint Government Analysts, while Section 29(2) lets the State Board appoint Board Analysts with the State Government's approval; the Air Act has no separate "revisionary powers" provision.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of Air Act 1981, State Government may establish or specify one or more:
options: State Air Laboratories to analyze emission samples
questions.explanation: Section 28 empowers the State Government to establish or specify a State Air Laboratory to analyse samples of air or emission; Section 31 in fact deals with appeals.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38 of Air Act 1981 (as substituted in 2024), damaging, defacing or pulling down any notice or post put up by a Pollution Control Board attracts:
options: A civil penalty of not less than Rs. 10,000, extending up to Rs. 15 lakh
Imprisonment up to 3 months or fine up to Rs. 10,000 or both
questions.explanation: The 2024 amendment decriminalised the acts listed in Section 38(1), replacing imprisonment/fine with a civil penalty of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh imposed by the adjudicating officer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39D(4) of Air Act 1981 (the erstwhile Section 40 on offences by companies having been consolidated into this provision in 2024), where the imprisonable offence of failing to comply with Section 21 is committed by a COMPANY, who is vicariously liable?
options: Every person directly in charge of and responsible to the company for conduct of business, as well as the company
questions.explanation: The 2024 substitution removed the separate Sections 40 and 41 and moved corporate liability, for the imprisonable Section 21 offence, into Section 39D(4).

questions.question_text: Under Section 38A of Air Act 1981 (the erstwhile Section 41 on this subject having been omitted in 2024), where a contravention is committed by a Government Department, who is liable to the penalty?
options: The Head of the Department, liable to a penalty equal to one month's basic salary, unless he proves the contravention occurred without his knowledge or instructions
questions.explanation: Section 38A, as substituted in 2024, fixes a civil penalty of one month's basic salary on the Head of the Department (or a negligent officer), subject to a due-diligence/no-knowledge defence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 44 of Air Act 1981, members and officers of Pollution Control Boards performing functions under the Air Act are deemed to be:
options: Public servants within the meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code (corresponding to Section 2(28), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023)
questions.explanation: Section 44 deems Board members and officers to be public servants within the meaning of Section 21 IPC; Section 42 of the Act deals separately with protection of action taken in good faith.

questions.question_text: Under Section 46 of Air Act 1981, no Civil Court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which:
options: An Appellate Authority constituted under Section 28 is empowered to determine
questions.explanation: Section 46 bars civil courts from entertaining matters that an Appellate Authority under the Act is empowered to determine, and bars injunctions against action taken under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 52 of Air Act 1981, the provisions of the Air Act shall have effect:
options: Notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in any other enactment (save the Atomic Energy Act, 1962, as to radioactive air pollution)
questions.explanation: Section 52 gives the Air Act an overriding effect over any other inconsistent enactment, except that the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 continues to govern radioactive air pollution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(m) of Air Act 1981, 'occupier' in relation to any factory or premises means:
options: The person who has control over the affairs of the factory or premises, and, in relation to a substance, the person in possession of it
questions.explanation: Section 2(m) defines "occupier" as the person with control over the factory/premises' affairs, and, for a substance, the person in possession of it.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of Air Act 1981, in performance of its functions, every State Board is bound by directions issued by:
options: The Central Board and the State Government
questions.explanation: Section 18(1)(b) binds every State Board by written directions of the Central Board or the State Government, with disputes between the two referred to the Central Government.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of Air Act 1981, the report of a Government or Board analyst on an emission sample may be used in a proceeding under the Act as:
options: Evidence of the facts stated therein
questions.explanation: Section 30 lets an analyst's report be used as evidence of the facts stated therein; Section 25 in fact deals with the Board's power to obtain information from occupiers.

questions.question_text: In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Taj Trapezium Case 1997), emissions from coal-based foundries were causing damage to Taj Mahal marble by forming:
options: Acid rain (sulphur dioxide reacting with atmospheric moisture forming sulphuric acid)
questions.explanation: In the Taj Trapezium Case, sulphur dioxide from coal/coke-based industries reacted with atmospheric moisture to form sulphuric acid (acid rain), causing "marble cancer" (yellowing/corrosion) of the Taj Mahal.
questions.statute_or_case: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997) 2 SCC 353

questions.question_text: In Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991), the Supreme Court recognized that right to life under Article 21 includes right to enjoyment of:
questions.explanation: Subhash Kumar held that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to enjoyment of pollution-free water and air, enforceable through Article 32.
questions.statute_or_case: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) 1 SCC 598

questions.question_text: Under Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 (framed under EPA/Air Act), ambient air quality standards for noise in SILENCE ZONES during daytime (6am to 10pm) is capped at:
questions.explanation: The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 (framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986) cap ambient noise in silence zones at 50 dB(A) Leq by day and 40 dB(A) Leq by night.

questions.question_text: Under Noise Pollution Rules 2000, ambient noise limit in RESIDENTIAL areas during nighttime (10pm to 6am) is capped at:
questions.explanation: The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 cap night-time ambient noise in residential areas at 45 dB(A) Leq (55 dB(A) by day).

questions.question_text: Under Noise Pollution Rules 2000, loudspeakers or public address systems cannot be used at night (10pm to 6am) EXCEPT:
options: In closed premises (auditoria, conference rooms) or state-permitted cultural festivals up to 12 midnight (max 15 days/yr)
questions.explanation: Rule 5 of the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 permits loudspeaker use in closed premises, and allows the State Government to permit outdoor use between 10 pm and midnight on cultural/religious occasions, capped at 15 days a calendar year.
questions.statute_or_case: Rule 5, Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of Air Act 1981 (as substituted in 2024), contravention of any provision of the Act for which no specific penalty is otherwise provided attracts:
options: A civil penalty of not less than Rs. 10,000, extending up to Rs. 15 lakh, with an additional daily penalty for continuing default
1 year 6 months to 6 years imprisonment and fine
questions.explanation: Section 39, as substituted in 2024, sets a residuary civil penalty of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh, with an additional daily penalty of up to Rs. 10,000 for continuing contravention, replacing the earlier imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43(1) of Air Act 1981, no court inferior to which magistrate shall try any offence under the Air Act?
options: Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate First Class
questions.explanation: The concluding part of Section 43(1) bars any court inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class from trying an offence under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35 of the Advocates Act, 1961, which authority conducts disciplinary proceedings for professional misconduct against an advocate?
options: Disciplinary Committee of the State Bar Council
questions.explanation: Section 35 empowers the Disciplinary Committee of a State Bar Council to adjudicate complaints of professional or other misconduct against advocates.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the Advocates Act, 1961, there is only one class of persons entitled to practise the profession of law in India, namely:
questions.explanation: Section 29 enacted a unified legal profession in India consisting of a single class of practitioners called Advocates.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Advocates Act, 1961 (enforced in 2011), every advocate whose name is entered in the State roll shall be entitled as of right to practise throughout India in:
options: All Courts including Supreme Court, Tribunals, and any authority legally authorized to take evidence
questions.explanation: Section 30 guarantees the absolute right of enrolled advocates to practise before all courts, tribunals and authorities in India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, there shall be two classes of advocates, namely:
questions.explanation: Section 16(1) divides advocates into Senior Advocates and other Advocates.

questions.question_text: In Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court of India (2017) 9 SCC 766, the Supreme Court laid down comprehensive guidelines for:
options: Designation of Senior Advocates under Section 16(2) of Advocates Act
questions.explanation: Indira Jaising (2017) laid down comprehensive point-based criteria and guidelines for Senior Advocate designation.
questions.statute_or_case: Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court of India (2017) 9 SCC 766

questions.question_text: Under Section 24(1)(a) of the Advocates Act, 1961, a person is qualified to be admitted as an advocate on a State roll if he is a citizen of India and has completed the age of:
questions.explanation: Section 24(1)(a) mandates a minimum age of twenty-one years for enrollment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(1)(h) of the Advocates Act, 1961, which body is empowered to promote legal education and lay down standards of such education in consultation with Universities?
questions.explanation: Section 7(1)(h) vests regulation of legal education standards in the Bar Council of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, any person aggrieved by an order of the Disciplinary Committee of a State Bar Council may prefer an appeal within 60 days to the:
questions.explanation: Section 37 provides for an appeal to the Bar Council of India within 60 days.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38 of the Advocates Act, 1961, any person aggrieved by an order made by the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India may prefer an appeal within 60 days to the:
questions.explanation: Section 38 provides for a statutory appeal directly to the Supreme Court of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35(3) of the Advocates Act, 1961, the Disciplinary Committee of a State Bar Council after hearing the advocate may pass which orders?
options: Reprimand, suspend advocate from practice, or remove advocate's name from State roll
questions.explanation: Section 35(3) sets out statutory punishments for professional misconduct: reprimand, suspension, or removal from roll.

questions.question_text: Under BCI Rules framed under Section 49(1)(c), an advocate shall NOT act or plead in any matter in which he himself has a:
questions.explanation: BCI Rules prohibit an advocate from appearing in matters in which he has a pecuniary or personal interest.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Standards of Professional Conduct

questions.question_text: In Bar Council of India v. A.K. Balaji (2018), the Supreme Court held regarding foreign law firms that:
options: Foreign lawyers/firms cannot practice law in India on litigation/non-litigation side, but casual 'fly in and fly out' visits to advise clients on foreign law are permissible
Foreign lawyers can set up offices anywhere in India
Foreign lawyers are completely banned from entering India
Foreign lawyers can practice in High Courts
questions.explanation: A.K. Balaji (2018) affirmed foreign lawyers cannot set up law offices in India but permitted casual 'fly in fly out' visits for foreign law advice.

questions.question_text: In Ex-Capt. Harish Uppal v. Union of India (2003) 2 SCC 45, the Supreme Court held that lawyers have no right to go on strike or give a call for boycott of courts because:
options: It interferes with administration of justice and speedy trial of litigants
questions.explanation: Harish Uppal (2003) declared court boycotts and strikes by lawyers illegal and unethical.
questions.statute_or_case: Ex-Capt. Harish Uppal v. Union of India (2003) 2 SCC 45

questions.question_text: Under Section 45 of the Advocates Act, 1961, any person who practises in any court or before any authority without being entitled to practise under the Act shall be punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 45 penalizes unauthorized practice of law with imprisonment extending up to six months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33 of the Advocates Act, 1961, no person shall be entitled to practise in any court or before any authority unless he is:
options: Enrolled as an advocate under the Act
questions.explanation: Section 33 restricts legal practice exclusively to enrolled advocates.

questions.question_text: Section 3 of the Advocates Act, 1961 provides for the constitution of:
options: State Bar Councils (one for each State or group of States/Union territories named in the section)
A single all-India Bar Council only
A Bar Council for every district
Bar Associations attached to each High Court
questions.explanation: Section 3 constitutes State Bar Councils for the States and combinations of States/Union territories listed in it; the Bar Council of India is constituted separately under Section 4.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, the Bar Council of India includes as ex officio members:
options: The Chief Justice of India and the Law Minister
The Attorney-General of India and the Solicitor-General of India
The President of the Supreme Court Bar Association
One retired Supreme Court judge nominated by the President
questions.explanation: Section 4(1)(a) and (b) make the Attorney-General of India and the Solicitor-General of India ex officio members of the Bar Council of India.

questions.question_text: Under the Advocates Act, 1961, how is the Chairman of a State Bar Council chosen?
options: The Advocate-General of the State is Chairman ex officio
The senior-most High Court judge is Chairman
The State Government nominates the Chairman
The Chairman is elected by the Council from among its members under Section 3(3); the Advocate-General sits only as an ex officio member
questions.explanation: Section 3(3) provides for an elected Chairman and Vice-Chairman of each State Bar Council; the Advocate-General is only an ex officio member under Section 3(2)(a).

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, a primary function of a State Bar Council is to:
options: Lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates throughout India
Hear appeals from the disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India
Recognise universities whose law degree qualifies for enrolment
Admit persons as advocates on its roll and prepare and maintain that roll
questions.explanation: Section 6(1)(a) and (b) make admitting persons as advocates on the State roll and maintaining that roll functions of a State Bar Council; laying down conduct standards and recognising universities are functions of the Bar Council of India under Section 7.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(1)(b) of the Advocates Act, 1961, a main function of the Bar Council of India is to:
options: Lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates
Enrol individual advocates on a State roll
Issue certificates of enrolment to advocates
Try, in the first instance, complaints of misconduct against advocates on a State roll
questions.explanation: Section 7(1)(b) makes it a function of the Bar Council of India to lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates; enrolment and first-instance discipline are functions of the State Bar Council.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Advocates Act, 1961, what is the normal term of office of an elected member of a State Bar Council?
options: Three years from the date of election
Five years from the date of publication of the result of his election
Six years from the date of election
For the lifetime of the member
questions.explanation: Section 8 fixes the term of an elected member of a State Bar Council at five years from the date of publication of the election result, extendable by the Bar Council of India by up to six months if elections are not held.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, every State Bar Council must constitute which standing committees?
options: A disciplinary committee and a legal aid committee
A grievance committee and an audit committee
An executive committee and an enrolment committee
questions.explanation: Section 10(1) requires a State Bar Council to constitute an executive committee and an enrolment committee; disciplinary committees are constituted under Section 9.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the Advocates Act, 1961, every Bar Council is a body corporate having:
options: No power to hold immovable property
A tenure limited to five years
The status of a department of the State Government
Perpetual succession and a common seal, with power to acquire and hold property and to sue and be sued
questions.explanation: Section 5 makes every Bar Council a body corporate with perpetual succession, a common seal, and power to hold property, contract, sue and be sued.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(3) of the Advocates Act, 1961, Senior Advocates are subject to restrictions in the matter of their practice as prescribed by:
options: The Union Ministry of Law and Justice
questions.explanation: Section 16(3) provides that Senior Advocates shall, in the matter of their practice, be subject to such restrictions as the Bar Council of India may prescribe in the interests of the legal profession.

questions.question_text: Under the restrictions on Senior Advocates prescribed by the Bar Council of India (Section 16(3), Advocates Act, 1961), a Senior Advocate:
options: May file a Vakalatnama and act directly for any client
Shall not file a Vakalatnama or act, appear without an Advocate-on-Record (in the Supreme Court) or another advocate, or draft pleadings
May practise only in the Supreme Court
May not appear in any criminal matter
questions.explanation: The BCI restrictions on Senior Advocates bar them from filing a Vakalatnama or acting for a client, and from appearing without another advocate/Advocate-on-Record instructing them.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 16(3), Advocates Act, 1961; BCI Rules Part VI Chapter I

questions.question_text: Under Section 17(2) of the Advocates Act, 1961, the roll of advocates prepared and maintained by a State Bar Council consists of:
options: A single undivided list in alphabetical order
Three parts: Senior, Junior and Trainee advocates
Two parts: the first part containing the names of senior advocates and the second part the names of other advocates
questions.explanation: Section 17(2) provides that each State roll consists of two parts, the first for senior advocates and the second for other advocates. No person may be enrolled on the roll of more than one State Bar Council (Section 17(4)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of the Advocates Act, 1961, an advocate seeking transfer of his name from one State roll to another must apply to:
options: The State Bar Council on whose roll his name currently appears
The State Bar Council to whose roll he wishes to move
The High Court of the destination State
questions.explanation: Section 18 requires the application for transfer to be made to the Bar Council of India, which directs the removal and re-entry without any fee; seniority is retained under Section 18(2).

questions.question_text: Under Section 21(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, where two advocates have the same date of seniority, who ranks as senior?
options: The one who is senior in age
The one whose name comes first alphabetically
The one who paid the enrolment fee first
questions.explanation: Seniority normally runs from the date of enrolment (Section 17(3)(d)); Section 21(1) breaks a tie in favour of the advocate who is senior in age, and other seniority disputes are referred to the State Bar Council.

questions.question_text: Under the proviso to Section 24A(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, the disqualification for enrolment on account of a conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude ceases to have effect after:
options: Six months from the date of release
A period of two years has elapsed since his release or dismissal or removal
Five years from the date of conviction
The person turns 45 years of age
questions.explanation: The proviso to Section 24A(1) provides that the disqualification ceases after two years have elapsed since the person's release, dismissal or removal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24A(2) of the Advocates Act, 1961, the disqualification for enrolment under Section 24A(1) does NOT apply where the person, having been found guilty, was:
options: Dealt with under the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958
questions.explanation: Section 24A(2) exempts a person who, having been found guilty, is dealt with under the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 from the disqualification in Section 24A(1).

questions.question_text: Under Section 26(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, a State Bar Council refers every application for admission as an advocate to its:
questions.explanation: Section 26(1) requires every application for admission as an advocate to be referred to the enrolment committee of the State Bar Council, which disposes of it in the prescribed manner.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26A of the Advocates Act, 1961, a State Bar Council may remove from the State roll the name of any advocate who:
options: Is dead, or from whom a request to that effect has been received
Has not appeared in court for one year
Has failed to pay the annual Bar Council subscription
Has shifted his residence to another State
questions.explanation: Section 26A permits a State Bar Council to remove from its roll the name of an advocate who is dead or who has himself requested removal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the Advocates Act, 1961, rules made by a State Bar Council to carry out the purposes of Chapter III (admission and enrolment):
options: Take effect immediately on publication in the Official Gazette
Require the prior sanction of the High Court
Have no effect unless they have been approved by the Bar Council of India
Require ratification by the State Legislature
questions.explanation: Section 28(3) provides that no rule made by a State Bar Council under Chapter III has effect unless approved by the Bar Council of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 32 of the Advocates Act, 1961, can a court, authority or person permit a person not enrolled as an advocate to appear before it?
options: No, only enrolled advocates may ever appear
Yes, but only if the person is a law graduate
Yes, notwithstanding Chapter IV, in any particular case
Yes, but only with the prior permission of the Bar Council of India
questions.explanation: Section 32 allows any court, authority or person to permit a person not enrolled as an advocate to appear before it in any particular case.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, who may make rules laying down the conditions subject to which an advocate shall be permitted to practise in the High Court and courts subordinate to it?
questions.explanation: Section 34(1) empowers the High Court to make rules laying down the conditions subject to which an advocate shall be permitted to practise in the High Court and courts subordinate to it.

questions.question_text: In R.K. Anand v. Registrar, Delhi High Court (2009) 8 SCC 106, the Supreme Court held that a High Court, in exercise of its contempt jurisdiction, may:
options: Restrain an advocate found guilty of contempt from appearing before it for a specified period, this being distinct from the Bar Council's power to take away the right to practise
Permanently strike the advocate's name off the State roll
Impose an unlimited fine on the concerned Bar Council
Convert the contempt proceeding into a criminal trial for perjury
questions.explanation: R.K. Anand distinguished the "right to appear" in a court (which the court can regulate, including by debarring a contemnor advocate from appearing for a time) from the "right to practise", disciplinary control over which lies with the Bar Councils under the Advocates Act.
questions.statute_or_case: R.K. Anand v. Registrar, Delhi High Court (2009) 8 SCC 106

questions.question_text: In Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998) 4 SCC 409, the Constitution Bench held that while exercising its contempt power under Article 129, the Supreme Court:
options: May permanently disbar the contemnor advocate
Cannot suspend or revoke an advocate's licence to practise as a punishment for contempt, since that disciplinary jurisdiction is vested in the Bar Councils under the Advocates Act, 1961
May direct the Bar Council to enrol a person it has cleared
May impose the death penalty for aggravated contempt
questions.explanation: The Court held that punishing for contempt and taking away the right to practise are distinct; the latter falls within the exclusive statutory domain of the Bar Councils under the Advocates Act, so a contempt court cannot suspend an advocate's licence as punishment.
questions.statute_or_case: Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998) 4 SCC 409

questions.question_text: In V.C. Rangadurai v. D. Gopalan (1979) 1 SCC 308, the Supreme Court dealt with an advocate who deceived elderly clients about the limitation position of their case. It emphasised that disciplinary action under Section 35 is intended to:
options: Impose the maximum penalty in every proven case
Protect the public and preserve the purity and dignity of the legal profession, reformation being a relevant consideration
Transfer the matter to the criminal courts
questions.explanation: Rangadurai treated professional discipline as protective of the public and the profession rather than purely punitive, while still holding the advocate guilty of misconduct.
questions.statute_or_case: V.C. Rangadurai v. D. Gopalan (1979) 1 SCC 308

questions.question_text: In Hikmat Ali Khan v. Ishwar Prasad Arya (1997) 3 SCC 131, where an advocate assaulted his opponent in the courtroom with a knife and a pistol shot and was convicted under Section 307 IPC, the Supreme Court held that the appropriate punishment was:
options: Suspension from practice for three years
A fine payable to the Bar Council
Removal of his name from the roll of advocates
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court held that the misconduct was so grave that the advocate deserved to have his name removed from the State roll, rather than merely being suspended.
questions.statute_or_case: Hikmat Ali Khan v. Ishwar Prasad Arya (1997) 3 SCC 131

questions.question_text: In P.D. Gupta v. Ram Murti (1997) 7 SCC 147, an advocate bought a share of the disputed property from his client while the title litigation was pending. The Supreme Court held that this:
options: Amounted to professional misconduct and upheld his suspension from practice for one year
Was a purely private transaction outside the scope of Section 35
Was permissible because the client freely consented
Could only be dealt with by a civil suit for cancellation
questions.explanation: The Court held that an advocate purchasing disputed property from his own client during the litigation subverts the course of justice and is professional misconduct; the one-year suspension was upheld.
questions.statute_or_case: P.D. Gupta v. Ram Murti (1997) 7 SCC 147

questions.question_text: In Noratanmal Chouraria v. M.R. Murli (2004) 5 SCC 689, the Supreme Court held, on the scope of "misconduct" under Section 35 of the Advocates Act, 1961, that:
options: Only acts done while actually appearing in court can amount to misconduct
Misconduct is confined to acts also punishable as criminal offences
Misconduct covers conduct, whether in a professional or private capacity, that renders an advocate unfit to remain a member of the profession
A litigant-advocate can never be proceeded against for misconduct
questions.explanation: The Court held that misconduct is not limited to professional dealings; conduct even in a private capacity that shows the advocate to be unworthy of remaining in the profession can attract Section 35.
questions.statute_or_case: Noratanmal Chouraria v. M.R. Murli (2004) 5 SCC 689

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules (Part VI, Chapter II) on an advocate's duty to the Court, an advocate must:
options: Always accept the client's instructions to mislead the court if it helps the case
Maintain a respectful attitude towards the court, bearing in mind the dignity of the judicial office
Refuse to appear before any judge he has previously criticised
Decline to argue any point of law not raised in the pleadings
questions.explanation: The BCI Rules on duty to the court require an advocate to conduct himself with dignity and self-respect and to maintain a respectful attitude towards the court, bearing in mind the dignity of the judicial office.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Section I (Duty to the Court)

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules, may an advocate solicit work or advertise, whether directly or indirectly, by circulars, advertisements, touts, personal communications or interviews?
options: Yes, provided the fee charged is disclosed
Yes, in newspapers but not on television
No, solicitation and advertising are prohibited (an advocate may maintain only limited website information as permitted by the BCI)
questions.explanation: BCI Rule 36 (Part VI, Chapter II) prohibits an advocate from soliciting work or advertising; only limited, non-promotional website disclosure is permitted under the BCI's later relaxation.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Rule 36

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules, an advocate shall NOT:
options: Stipulate for a fee contingent on the results of litigation or agree to share the proceeds thereof
Charge different fees to different clients
Appear in a court in a city other than where he is enrolled
Accept more than one brief on the same day
questions.explanation: BCI Rule 20 prohibits an advocate from stipulating for a fee contingent on the results of litigation or agreeing to share in the proceeds of the litigation.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Rule 20

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules, an advocate who has advised a party in connection with a matter, drawn its pleadings, or acted for that party:
options: May later appear for the opposite party with the court's permission
May later appear for the opposite party after one year
May later appear for the opposite party if the first party gives oral consent
Shall not act, appear or plead for the opposite party in the same matter
questions.explanation: BCI Rule 33 bars an advocate who has advised or acted for a party in a matter from thereafter acting, appearing or pleading for the opposite party in the same matter.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Rule 33

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules, when an advocate receives money from a client for expenses or on account of fees, he is bound to:
options: Treat it as his own on receipt
Deposit it with the Bar Council
Return the entire amount if the case is lost
Keep proper accounts showing the amounts received and the expenses incurred, and furnish a copy to the client on demand
questions.explanation: The BCI Rules require an advocate to maintain accurate accounts of the client's money entrusted to him and to render an account to the client on demand or on the conclusion of the matter.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Rules 25-27

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules, an advocate shall NOT communicate or negotiate on the subject-matter of a controversy with a party who is represented by an advocate, EXCEPT:
options: When the other party is a public authority
After the first hearing in the case
When the communication is in writing
Through that party's advocate, or with that advocate's consent
questions.explanation: The BCI Rules bar an advocate from dealing directly with a represented opposite party on the subject-matter of the dispute except through or with the consent of that party's advocate.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Rule 37

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules on an advocate's duty to accept briefs, an advocate:
options: Is ordinarily bound to accept a brief in a court in which he professes to practise, at a fee consistent with his standing and the nature of the case, special circumstances apart
May refuse any brief without reason
Must accept every brief offered regardless of fee or conflict
May accept briefs only from clients introduced by another advocate
questions.explanation: BCI Rule 11 obliges an advocate to accept a brief in the courts where he practises, at a proper fee, unless there are special circumstances (such as a conflict of interest) justifying refusal.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Rule 11

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules, an advocate must wear the prescribed advocate's robes when appearing before a court, but he is NOT to wear them:
options: When he himself is a party to, or a witness in, the proceeding
When appearing in a trial court as opposed to an appellate court
When appearing in a matter listed after 4 p.m.
questions.explanation: The BCI Rules require an advocate to appear in the prescribed robes only in his professional capacity; he must not wear them when appearing as a litigant or witness in his own or another's case.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter IV (Form of dresses / robes)

questions.question_text: Under the BCI Rules, an advocate shall NOT, directly or indirectly (whether in his own name or another's), bid for or purchase property:
options: Sold in execution of a decree or order in a proceeding in which he was in any way professionally engaged
Located outside the district in which he practises
questions.explanation: BCI Rule 22 bars an advocate from bidding for or purchasing, in his own or another's name, property sold in execution of a decree or order in a proceeding in which he was professionally engaged.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Rule 22

questions.question_text: Under the Advocates' Welfare Fund Act, 2001, a welfare fund stamp of the prescribed value must be affixed on every:
options: Cause list published by the court
Copy of a judgment supplied to a party
Notice issued by the court to a witness
Vakalatnama filed by an advocate before a court, tribunal or other authority
questions.explanation: The Advocates' Welfare Fund Act, 2001 requires an advocate to affix a welfare fund stamp of the prescribed value on every vakalatnama filed by him; the proceeds go to the State Advocates' Welfare Fund.

questions.question_text: Under which provision of the Advocates Act, 1961 does the Bar Council of India draw its power to prescribe the form of dresses or robes to be worn by advocates?
questions.explanation: Section 49(1)(gg) empowers the Bar Council of India to make rules prescribing the form of dresses or robes to be worn by advocates, having regard to climatic conditions, when appearing before any court or tribunal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 42(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, the disciplinary committee of a Bar Council has the same powers as a civil court under the CPC in respect of:
options: Passing a decree for money against the advocate
Summoning and enforcing attendance of persons, requiring discovery and production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits
Attaching the advocate's property before judgment
questions.explanation: Section 42(1) vests the disciplinary committee with civil-court powers of summoning witnesses, compelling discovery and production of documents, receiving affidavit evidence, requisitioning public records and issuing commissions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 42(2) of the Advocates Act, 1961, all proceedings before a disciplinary committee of a Bar Council are deemed to be:
options: Administrative proceedings not subject to any penal law
Arbitration proceedings under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Judicial proceedings within the meaning of Sections 193 and 228 of the IPC (now Sections 229 and 267 of the BNS, 2023)
Executive inquiries with no evidentiary sanctity
questions.explanation: Section 42(2) deems proceedings before a disciplinary committee to be judicial proceedings within Sections 193 and 228 IPC (corresponding to Sections 229 and 267 BNS), and the committee to be a civil court for specified purposes.

questions.question_text: Under Section 36B(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961, if the disciplinary committee of a State Bar Council fails to conclude a disciplinary proceeding within one year from the date of receipt of the complaint (or initiation), the proceeding:
options: Abates and the complaint is treated as dismissed
Is remitted to the High Court
Continues before the State Bar Council with no consequence
Stands transferred to the Bar Council of India, which disposes of it as if it were withdrawn for inquiry under Section 36(2)
questions.explanation: Section 36B(1) requires disposal within one year, failing which the proceeding stands automatically transferred to the Bar Council of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 49A of the Advocates Act, 1961, who is empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of Chapters III and IV, including as to the qualifications for enrolment?
options: The Central Government (after consultation with the Bar Council of India)
questions.explanation: Section 49A confers on the Central Government the power to make rules for carrying out the purposes of Chapters III and IV, after consultation with the Bar Council of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 50 of the Advocates Act, 1961, which of the following earlier enactments was repealed?
options: The Legal Practitioners Act, 1879 (along with the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926 and other cognate enactments)
questions.explanation: Section 50 progressively repealed the enactments governing the old grades of legal practitioners, including the Legal Practitioners Act, 1879 and the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926.

questions.question_text: May an advocate on a State roll simultaneously hold a full-time salaried job (e.g. as a manager in a private company) while continuing to practise?
options: Yes, there is no restriction at all
Yes, provided the employer consents in writing

No; the BCI Rules bar an advocate from being a full-time salaried employee while he continues to practise, and require him to intimate the Bar Council and suspend practice for the duration of such employment
Yes, but only if the job is with a government department
questions.explanation: BCI Rules 47-49 (Part VI, Chapter II) prohibit an advocate from personally engaging in business or being a full-time salaried employee while practising; on taking such employment he must inform the Bar Council and cease to practise for that period.
questions.statute_or_case: BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter II, Rules 47-49

questions.question_text: "Pollution is a civil wrong. By its very nature, it is a tort committed against the community as a whole. A person, therefore, who is guilty of causing pollution, has to pay damages (compensation) for restoration of the environment. He has also to pay damages to those who have suffered loss on account of the act of the offender. Further, the offender can also be held liable to pay exemplary damages so that it may act as a deterrent for others not to cause pollution in any manner. However, the Court cannot impose any pollution fine in absence of any trial and finding of guilty under the relevant statutory provisions." This observation was made in :
options: M .C. Mehta v. Union of India
A .P. Pollution Control Board v. M.V. Nayudu

questions.question_text: The Seventh Schedule of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2015 Amendment) specifies categories of relationships which render a person ineligible to be appointed as an arbitrator due to:
options: Inherent conflict of interest and bias (de jure ineligibility under Sec 12(5))
questions.explanation: Section 12(5) read with Seventh Schedule renders persons with specified conflicts of interest ineligible de jure to be appointed as arbitrators (Perkins Eastman principle).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, "Arbitration" means any arbitration whether or not administered by a permanent:
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(a) defines arbitration including both institutional and ad hoc arbitrations.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(f) of the Arbitration Act 1996, an "International Commercial Arbitration" means an arbitration relating to disputes arising out of legal relationships, whether contractual or not, considered as commercial under law in force in India, where at least one of parties is:
options: An individual who is a national of, or habitually resident in, any country other than India
A body corporate incorporated in any country other than India
An association or body of individuals whose central management and control is exercised outside India
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(f) defines International Commercial Arbitration based on foreign nationality/incorporation/control.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(e) of the Arbitration Act 1996, in the case of arbitrations other than international commercial arbitration, "Court" means the Principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction in a district, and includes:
options: High Court in exercise of its ordinary original civil jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(e)(i) defines Court as Principal Civil District Court or High Court having original jurisdiction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(e)(ii) of the Arbitration Act 1996, in the case of International Commercial Arbitration, "Court" means exclusively the:
options: High Court having jurisdiction to decide questions forming subject-matter of arbitration
questions.explanation: For International Commercial Arbitration, Section 2(1)(e)(ii) designates the High Court exclusively as the "Court".

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Arbitration Act 1996, a party who knows that any provision of Part I from which parties may derogate, or any requirement under arbitration agreement, has not been complied with and yet proceeds with arbitration without stating objection without undue delay, shall be deemed to have:
questions.explanation: Section 4 enacts the statutory rule of Waiver of Right to Object.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the Arbitration Act 1996, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, in matters governed by Part I, no judicial authority shall intervene EXCEPT:
options: Where so provided in this Part
questions.explanation: Section 5 limits judicial intervention strictly to circumstances expressly provided under Part I.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, parties are free to determine the number of arbitrators, provided that such number shall NOT be an:
questions.explanation: Section 10(1) mandates that the number of arbitrators shall not be an even number.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996, failing any determination of number of arbitrators by parties, the arbitral tribunal shall consist of:
questions.explanation: Section 10(2) provides default rule: tribunal consists of a sole arbitrator.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11(2) & 11(3) of the Arbitration Act 1996, in an arbitration with three arbitrators, each party shall appoint one arbitrator, and the two appointed arbitrators shall appoint the third arbitrator who shall act as the:
questions.explanation: Section 11(3) designates the third arbitrator appointed by co-arbitrators as the Presiding Arbitrator.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11(6A) of the Arbitration Act 1996 (as examined in Duro Felguera v. Gangavaram Port Ltd), the Court while considering an application under Section 11 shall confine its examination strictly to the existence of an:
questions.explanation: Duro Felguera (2017) affirmed that Section 11 review is strictly confined to verifying existence of arbitration agreement.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, when a person is approached in connection with his possible appointment as an arbitrator, he shall disclose in writing any circumstances likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to his independence or impartiality, using the disclosure form in the:
questions.explanation: Section 12(1) mandates disclosure in accordance with the Sixth Schedule.

questions.question_text: The Fifth Schedule of the Arbitration Act 1996 contains guidelines for determining whether circumstances exist which give rise to justifiable doubts as to the:
options: Independence or Impartiality of an arbitrator
questions.explanation: Fifth Schedule lists grounds guiding challenge to independence or impartiality of arbitrators (based on IBA Guidelines).

questions.question_text: Under Section 12(3) of the Arbitration Act 1996, an arbitrator may be challenged ONLY if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his independence or impartiality, OR if he does not possess:
options: Qualifications agreed to by the parties
questions.explanation: Section 12(3) sets out statutory grounds for challenging an arbitrator.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996, a party who intends to challenge an arbitrator shall, within how many days after becoming aware of constitution of tribunal or grounds, send a written statement of reasons to arbitral tribunal?
questions.explanation: Section 13(2) prescribes 15 days deadline for submitting challenge to arbitral tribunal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(4) & 13(5) of the Arbitration Act 1996, if a challenge to an arbitrator is not successful before tribunal, tribunal shall continue proceedings and make award, and party challenging may make application for setting aside award under:
questions.explanation: Section 13(5) provides that rejected challenge to arbitrator can be raised as ground in Section 34 application against final award.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, the mandate of an arbitrator shall terminate if he becomes de jure or de facto unable to perform his functions or fails to act without undue delay. If controversy remains concerning termination, a party may apply to:
options: Court to decide on termination of mandate
questions.explanation: Section 14(2) empowers Court to decide on termination of arbitrator's mandate upon application.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996, where mandate of an arbitrator terminates, a substitute arbitrator shall be appointed according to:
options: The rules that were applicable to appointment of arbitrator being replaced
questions.explanation: Section 15(2) mandates appointing substitute arbitrator following same agreed procedure as original appointment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(1)(b) of the Arbitration Act 1996, a decision by arbitral tribunal that the contract is null and void shall NOT entail ipso jure the invalidity of the arbitration clause. This is the doctrine of:
questions.explanation: Section 16(1)(b) codifies doctrine of Separability treating arbitration agreement as independent of underlying contract.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996, a plea that the arbitral tribunal does not have jurisdiction shall be raised not later than:
questions.explanation: Section 16(2) requires jurisdictional plea to be raised at or before filing statement of defence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of the Arbitration Act 1996, parties shall be treated with equality and each party shall be given a:
options: Equal length of oral argument in minutes
Full opportunity to present his case (Equal treatment & Audi alteram partem)
questions.explanation: Section 18 mandates equal treatment and full opportunity for parties to present case.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, the arbitral tribunal shall NOT be bound by the:
options: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 or Indian Evidence Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Section 19(1) explicitly frees arbitral tribunals from strict rules of CPC and Evidence Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996, subject to Part I, parties are free to agree on procedure to be followed by arbitral tribunal. Failing such agreement, procedure shall be determined by the:
options: Arbitral tribunal in such manner as it considers appropriate
questions.explanation: Section 19(3) empowers tribunal to determine procedural rules in absence of party agreement.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, parties are free to agree on the place of arbitration. Failing agreement, place of arbitration shall be determined by arbitral tribunal having regard to circumstances of case. Distinguishing "Seat" vs "Venue" was resolved in:
options: BALCO v. Kaiser Aluminium & BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC
questions.explanation: BGS SGS Soma JV (2019) following BALCO affirmed that designation of place of arbitration ordinarily constitutes legal Seat.
questions.statute_or_case: BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC (2019)

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Arbitration Act 1996, unless otherwise agreed by parties, arbitral proceedings in respect of a particular dispute commence on the date on which a:
options: Request for that dispute to be referred to arbitration is received by respondent
questions.explanation: Section 21 fixes commencement date of arbitration as date request for arbitration is received by respondent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(4) of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2019 Amendment), statement of claim and defence shall be completed within a period of how many months from date arbitrator receives notice of appointment?
questions.explanation: Section 23(4) mandates completing pleadings within 6 months from notice of arbitrator appointment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, unless agreed otherwise by parties, arbitral tribunal shall decide whether to hold oral hearings for presentation of evidence or oral argument, or whether proceedings shall be conducted on basis of documents. Provided tribunal shall hold oral hearings on day-to-day basis and shall NOT grant adjournments WITHOUT:
options: Sufficient cause and recording reasons in writing
questions.explanation: Section 24(1) proviso mandates day-to-day oral hearings and restricts adjournments to cases of sufficient recorded cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25(a) of the Arbitration Act 1996, where without showing sufficient cause claimant fails to communicate statement of claim in accordance with Section 23(1), arbitral tribunal shall:
questions.explanation: Section 25(a) requires tribunal to terminate proceedings upon unexcused failure of claimant to file statement of claim.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25(b) of the Arbitration Act 1996, where respondent fails to communicate statement of defence, arbitral tribunal shall continue proceedings without treating such failure in itself as an admission of allegations, and may proceed to make award on:
questions.explanation: Section 25(b) provides that failure to file defense is not automatic admission; tribunal decides on evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of the Arbitration Act 1996, unless otherwise agreed by parties, arbitral tribunal may appoint one or more experts to report to it on specific issues to be determined by tribunal. Expert may be required to attend oral hearing where parties have opportunity to:
options: Cross-examine him and present expert witnesses on points at issue
Object to his appointment after report
questions.explanation: Section 26(2) grants parties right to cross-examine tribunal-appointed expert at hearing.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the Arbitration Act 1996, arbitral tribunal or a party with approval of tribunal may apply to Court for assistance in taking evidence. Court may execute request by issuing process to witnesses in same manner as in:
questions.explanation: Section 27 empowers courts to assist arbitral tribunal in issuing witness summons or commissions for evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act 1996, in an arbitration other than international commercial arbitration, arbitral tribunal shall decide dispute submitted to arbitration in accordance with the substantive law for time being in force in:
questions.explanation: Section 28(1)(a) mandates Indian substantive law for domestic arbitrations in India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996, arbitral tribunal shall decide ex aequo et bono or as amiable compositeur ONLY if the parties have:
options: Expressly authorized it to do so
questions.explanation: Section 28(2) restricts decisions based on equity/fairness (ex aequo et bono) strictly to cases expressly authorized by parties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28(3) of the Arbitration Act 1996, in all cases arbitral tribunal shall decide in accordance with terms of contract and shall take into account the:
options: Usages of the trade applicable to the transaction
questions.explanation: Section 28(3) requires tribunal to decide in terms of contract taking into account trade usages.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the Arbitration Act 1996, in arbitral proceedings with more than one arbitrator, any decision of arbitral tribunal shall be made by a:
questions.explanation: Section 29(1) enacts majority decision rule for multi-member tribunals.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29A(3) of the Arbitration Act 1996, parties may by consent extend the period specified in sub-section (1) for making arbitral award for a further period not exceeding:
questions.explanation: Section 29A(3) permits parties by mutual consent to extend time for award by up to 6 months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29A(4) of the Arbitration Act 1996, if award is not made within 12 months (or extended period), mandate of arbitrator shall terminate unless Court has extended period. If Court finds delay attributable to tribunal, Court may order reduction of arbitrator fee by up to:
questions.explanation: Section 29A(4) empowers Court to reduce arbitrator fees by up to 5% per month for inexcusable delay.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29B of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2015 Amendment), parties may agree to adopt Fast Track Procedure. Under fast track procedure, award shall be made within how many months from date arbitral tribunal enters upon reference?
questions.explanation: Section 29B mandates that fast track arbitration award shall be rendered within 6 months based on written pleadings without oral hearing unless requested.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act 1996, if during arbitral proceedings parties settle dispute, arbitral tribunal shall terminate proceedings and, if requested by parties and not objected to by tribunal, record settlement in form of an:
options: Arbitral award on agreed terms (Consent Award)
questions.explanation: Section 30 governs recording of settlement in form of an Arbitral Award on agreed terms.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, an arbitral award shall be made in writing and shall be signed by the members of the arbitral tribunal. In arbitral proceedings with more than one arbitrator, signatures of majority of members shall be sufficient provided:
options: Reason for any omitted signature is stated
questions.explanation: Section 31(2) permits majority signatures if reason for omitted signature is stated in award.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31(3) of the Arbitration Act 1996, arbitral award shall state the reasons upon which it is based UNLESS parties have agreed that no reasons are to be given, or award is an award on agreed terms under Section 30. A unreasoned award where reasons are required is:
options: Vitiated and liable to be set aside under Section 34
questions.explanation: Section 31(3) mandates reasoned awards unless agreed otherwise or consent award.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31(7)(a) of the Arbitration Act 1996, unless otherwise agreed by parties, where award is for payment of money, arbitral tribunal may include interest at such rate as it deems reasonable on whole or part of money for whole or part of period between date on which cause of action arose and date on which award is made. Post-award interest under Section 31(7)(b) (if not directed by award) carries interest at:
options: 2% per annum higher than current rate of interest prevalent on date of award
questions.explanation: 2015 Amendment to Section 31(7)(b) sets statutory post-award interest at 2% higher than prevailing market rate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31A of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2015 Amendment), the regime for Costs in arbitration enacts general rule that unsuccessful party will be ordered to pay costs of successful party. This is known as:
questions.explanation: Section 31A codifies "costs follow the event" granting legal and arbitral costs to prevailing party.

questions.question_text: Under Section 32 of the Arbitration Act 1996, arbitral proceedings shall be terminated by final arbitral award or by order of arbitral tribunal where claimant withdraws claim, or parties agree on termination, or tribunal finds continuation of proceedings has become:
questions.explanation: Section 32(2) lists grounds for termination of arbitral proceedings by tribunal order.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, within 30 days from receipt of arbitral award, a party with notice to other party may request arbitral tribunal to correct any computation errors, clerical or typographical errors, or give an interpretation of a specific point. Correction shall be made within:
questions.explanation: Section 33(1) provides 30 days for tribunal to correct clerical/computational errors in award.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33(4) of the Arbitration Act 1996, unless otherwise agreed by parties, a party with notice to other party may within 30 days of receipt of award request tribunal to make an additional arbitral award as to claims presented in arbitral proceedings but omitted from award. Additional award shall be made within:
questions.explanation: Section 33(5) allows 60 days for tribunal to issue additional award on omitted claims.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34(2A) of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2015 Amendment), an arbitral award arising out of arbitrations OTHER THAN international commercial arbitrations may also be set aside by Court if Court finds that award is vitiated by:
options: Patent Illegality appearing on the face of the award
questions.explanation: Section 34(2A) introduces Patent Illegality on face of award as ground for setting aside domestic awards (expressly excluding international awards).

questions.question_text: Under Section 34(2A) proviso of the Arbitration Act 1996, an award shall NOT be set aside on ground of Patent Illegality merely on the ground of an erroneous application of law or by:
questions.explanation: Section 34(2A) proviso explicitly bars courts from re-appreciating evidence under patent illegality ground.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34(4) of the Arbitration Act 1996, on receipt of an application under Section 34(1), Court may where appropriate and so requested by a party, adjourn proceedings for a period of time determined by it in order to give arbitral tribunal an opportunity to resume proceedings or take such action as will:
options: Eliminate the grounds for setting aside arbitral award
questions.explanation: Section 34(4) empowers Court to remit award back to tribunal to cure curable defects.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34(6) of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2015 Amendment), an application under Section 34 shall be disposed of expeditiously and in any event within a period of how long from date on which notice under sub-section (5) is served on other party?
questions.explanation: Section 34(6) mandates disposal of Section 34 challenge within 1 year from notice to opponent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 36(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996 (post-2015 Amendment), does filing of an application to set aside an arbitral award under Section 34 by itself render the award unenforceable (automatic stay)?
options: Yes, filing Section 34 automatically stays execution
No, filing Section 34 does NOT operate as automatic stay; court must grant specific order of stay upon separate application
Automatic stay applies for 6 months only
Automatic stay applies in international cases only
questions.explanation: 2015 Amendment to Section 36 abolished automatic stay; unconditional stay requires separate order upon terms.

questions.question_text: Under Section 36(3) proviso of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2021 Amendment), where Court is satisfied that a prima facie case is made out that arbitration agreement or contract which is basis of award, or making of award, was induced or effected by FRAUD or CORRUPTION, Court shall stay award:
options: Unconditionally pending disposal of Section 34 application
questions.explanation: 2021 Amendment proviso to Section 36(3) mandates unconditional stay where award is prima facie tainted by fraud/corruption.

questions.question_text: Under Section 42 of the Arbitration Act 1996, where with respect to an arbitration agreement any application under Part I has been made in a Court, that Court ALONE shall have jurisdiction over arbitral proceedings and all subsequent applications arising out of that agreement and arbitral proceedings shall be made in:
options: That Court and in no other Court
questions.explanation: Section 42 enacts rule of Exclusive Jurisdiction of the court first approached under Part I.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43 of the Arbitration Act 1996, the Limitation Act, 1963 shall apply to arbitrations as it applies to proceedings in Court. For purposes of Limitation Act, an arbitration shall be deemed to have commenced on date specified in:
options: Section 21 (date request for arbitration is received by respondent)
questions.explanation: Section 43(2) links commencement of arbitration for limitation purposes directly to Section 21 notice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 44 of the Arbitration Act 1996 (Part II Chapter I), a "Foreign Award" means an arbitral award on differences between persons arising out of legal relationships, whether contractual or not, considered as commercial under law in force in India, made in pursuance of an agreement in writing for arbitration to which the Convention set forth in the First Schedule applies. This is the:
questions.explanation: Part II Chapter I (Sec 44-52) governs enforcement of New York Convention Foreign Awards.

questions.question_text: Under Section 53 of the Arbitration Act 1996 (Part II Chapter II), a foreign award made in pursuance of an arbitration agreement to which the Convention set forth in the Second Schedule applies is a:
questions.explanation: Part II Chapter II (Sec 53-60) governs enforcement of Geneva Convention Foreign Awards.

questions.question_text: Under Section 48 of the Arbitration Act 1996, enforcement of a foreign New York Convention award may be refused at request of party against whom it is invoked ONLY if that party furnishes proof of grounds including incapacity of parties, lack of proper notice, or award dealing with dispute not contemplated, OR if court finds that subject matter cannot be settled by arbitration or enforcement is contrary to:
questions.explanation: Section 48 enumerates exhaustive grounds for refusing enforcement of a foreign award in India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 49 of the Arbitration Act 1996, where Court is satisfied that foreign award is enforceable under Part II Chapter I, the award shall be deemed to be a:
questions.explanation: Section 49 enacts that enforceable foreign awards operate directly as decrees of Indian courts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 50 of the Arbitration Act 1996, an appeal lies from an order of Court refusing to refer parties to arbitration under Section 45, or refusing to enforce a foreign award under Section 48. Does a second appeal lie from any order passed in appeal under Section 50?
options: Yes, Second Appeal lies to High Court
No second appeal lies (except Supreme Court Article 136 SLP)
questions.explanation: Section 50(2) explicitly bars second appeals from orders passed under Section 50.

questions.question_text: Under Section 67 of the Arbitration Act 1996, the Conciliator shall assist parties in an independent and impartial manner in their attempt to reach an amicable settlement of their dispute. The conciliator is guided by principles of objectivity, fairness and justice, giving consideration to:
options: Rights and obligations of parties, usages of trade, and circumstances surrounding dispute
questions.explanation: Section 67 defines role and functions of Conciliator in Part III.

questions.question_text: Under Section 75 of the Arbitration Act 1996, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, conciliator and parties shall keep CONFIDENTIAL all matters relating to conciliation proceedings. Confidentiality extends to settlement agreement EXCEPT where disclosure is necessary for:
questions.explanation: Section 75 enacts statutory confidentiality of conciliation proceedings and settlement agreements.

questions.question_text: Under Section 77 of the Arbitration Act 1996, parties shall NOT initiate during conciliation proceedings any arbitral or judicial proceedings in respect of a dispute that is subject-matter of conciliation proceedings, EXCEPT in so far as such proceedings are necessary for:
options: Preserving his rights (such as filing interim injunction or preventing limitation bar)
questions.explanation: Section 77 bars initiating court/arbitration proceedings during conciliation except to preserve legal rights.

questions.question_text: Under Section 80 of the Arbitration Act 1996, unless otherwise agreed by parties, the Conciliator shall NOT act as an arbitrator or as a representative or counsel of a party in any arbitral or judicial proceeding in respect of a dispute that is subject of conciliation, nor shall he be presented as a:
options: Witness by any party in such proceedings
questions.explanation: Section 80 bars conciliator from acting as arbitrator, counsel, or witness in subsequent proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 81 of the Arbitration Act 1996, in arbitral or judicial proceedings, parties shall NOT rely on or introduce as evidence views expressed or suggestions made by other party in respect of possible settlement, or admissions made, or proposals made by conciliator. This is the rule of:
options: Admissibility bar of conciliation evidence / Without Prejudice protection
questions.explanation: Section 81 renders all conciliation proposals, admissions and views strictly inadmissible in subsequent litigation/arbitration.

questions.question_text: Under Section 85 of the Arbitration Act 1996, the Arbitration Act 1940, the Arbitration (Protocol and Convention) Act 1937, and Foreign Awards (Recognition and Enforcement) Act 1961 are repealed. Proceedings commenced before 1996 Act came into force are governed by:
options: Old repealed Acts (unless parties agree 1996 Act applies)
questions.explanation: Section 85(2)(a) saves pending arbitrations commenced prior to 1996 Act under old repealed law.

questions.question_text: The Fourth Schedule of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2015 Amendment) sets out the model fee structure for arbitrators based on sum in dispute. Does the Fourth Schedule fee model apply to International Commercial Arbitrations?
options: No, Fourth Schedule does NOT apply to International Commercial Arbitrations
questions.explanation: Fourth Schedule model fee table applies to domestic court-appointed arbitrations, explicitly excluding International Commercial Arbitrations.
