questions.question_text: In Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd (2019), the Supreme Court held that a party who has an interest in the outcome of the dispute (such as a Managing Director or officer of a party) is disqualified from:
questions.explanation: Perkins Eastman (2019) held that a person ineligible under Section 12(5) cannot unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator.

questions.question_text: In TRF Ltd. v. Energo Engineering Projects Ltd. (2017), the Supreme Court held that once an arbitrator becomes ineligible by operation of law under Section 12(5), he cannot nominate another person as sole arbitrator because:
options: "Once an arbitrator's mandate terminates by law, he cannot nominate another" (Nemo dat quod non habet)
questions.explanation: TRF Ltd (2017) established that an ineligible managing director cannot nominate a substitute sole arbitrator.

questions.question_text: In Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (ONGC) v. Saw Pipes Ltd. (2003), the Supreme Court introduced which expanded ground under "Public Policy of India" for setting aside domestic awards?
questions.explanation: ONGC v. Saw Pipes (2003) added Patent Illegality as a ground of public policy, later statutory codified in Section 34(2A).

questions.question_text: In Associated Builders v. Delhi Development Authority (2015), the Supreme Court clarified that Public Policy of India under Section 34 includes fundamental policy of Indian law, interest of India, justice or morality, and:
options: Patent Illegality (if award goes to root of matter)
questions.explanation: Associated Builders (2015) comprehensively defined parameters of Public Policy and Patent Illegality in Section 34.

questions.question_text: In SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd. (2005), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that the function performed by Chief Justice/designate under Section 11 is a:
options: Judicial function (and not an administrative function)
questions.explanation: SBP & Co (2005) overruled Konkan Railway and held Section 11 power is a judicial function.

questions.question_text: In Chloro Controls India Pvt. Ltd. v. Severn Trent Water Purification Inc. (2013), the Supreme Court held that non-signatory group companies can be referred to arbitration under Section 45 if there is a clear intention to bind them in composite multi-party transactions. This is the doctrine of:
questions.explanation: Chloro Controls (2013) recognized Group of Companies Doctrine in international arbitration.

questions.question_text: In Cox and Kings Ltd. v. SAP India Pvt. Ltd. (2023), a 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the Group of Companies Doctrine in Indian arbitration, clarifying that non-signatories can be bound based on:
options: Mutual intention of parties, active participation in negotiation/performance, and single economic reality
questions.explanation: Cox and Kings (2023) 5-Judge Bench affirmed Group of Companies doctrine grounded in consent and participation.
questions.statute_or_case: Cox and Kings Ltd. v. SAP India (2023)

questions.question_text: In Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation (2021), a 3-Judge Bench of Supreme Court laid down a 4-fold test to determine Non-Arbitrability of disputes, holding disputes are non-arbitrable when they relate to actions in rem, affect third party rights, or relate to:
options: Inalienable sovereign functions of State or matters expressly reserved for specialized tribunals
questions.explanation: Vidya Drolia (2021) formulated 4-fold test for non-arbitrability (in rem actions, sovereign acts, statutory exclusions).

questions.question_text: In N.N. Global Mercantile Pvt. Ltd. v. Indo Unique Flame Ltd. (7-Judge Bench, 2023), a 7-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court reversed earlier 5-Judge ruling and held that an unstamped or insufficiently stamped agreement containing an arbitration clause:
options: Renders arbitration agreement null and void permanently
Does NOT render arbitration agreement void or unenforceable at Section 11 stage; stamping defects are curable before tribunal
questions.explanation: In Curative Petition re N.N. Global (7-Judge Bench Dec 2023), Supreme Court held unstamped agreements do not render arbitration clause void at Section 11 stage.
questions.statute_or_case: In Re Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements & Stamp Act (2023)

questions.question_text: Under Section 42A of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2019 Amendment), maintaining confidentiality of all arbitral proceedings is mandatory for arbitrator, arbitral institution and parties, EXCEPT where disclosure of award is necessary for purpose of:
questions.explanation: Section 42A mandates confidentiality across all arbitral proceedings except for enforcement of award.

questions.question_text: Under Section 42B of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by 2019 Amendment), no suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the arbitrator for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under the Act. This grants arbitrators:
options: Statutory Immunity from suit for acts done in good faith
questions.explanation: Section 42B confers statutory immunity on arbitrators for acts done in good faith.

questions.question_text: Under Part IA (Section 43B) of the Arbitration Act 1996 (inserted by the 2019 Amendment), which body was envisioned to promote and encourage ADR and accredit arbitral institutions in India?
questions.explanation: Part IA (Sec 43A-43M) inserted by 2019 Amendment establishes Arbitration Council of India (ACI).

questions.question_text: Under Section 37(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act 1996, an appeal lies against an order of Court refusing to refer parties to arbitration under:
questions.explanation: Section 37(1)(a) provides appeal against order refusing to refer parties to arbitration under Section 8.

questions.question_text: Under Section 37(2)(a) of the Arbitration Act 1996, an appeal lies to Court against an order of arbitral tribunal accepting plea referred to in Section 16(2) or 16(3) that tribunal:
options: Does not have jurisdiction or is exceeding scope of authority
questions.explanation: Section 37(2)(a) permits appeal against tribunal order accepting plea of no jurisdiction under Section 16.

questions.question_text: Under Section 37(2)(b) of the Arbitration Act 1996, an appeal lies to Court against an order of arbitral tribunal granting or refusing to grant an interim measure under:
questions.explanation: Section 37(2)(b) allows appeal against tribunal order granting/refusing interim measures under Section 17.

questions.question_text: In Government of India v. Vedanta Limited (2020), the Supreme Court held that the limitation period for filing an application to enforce a foreign award under Section 47/49 of Arbitration Act 1996 is governed by Article 137 of Limitation Act, 1963, which prescribes a period of:
options: 3 years from date right to apply accrues
questions.explanation: Vedanta (2020) settled that enforcement of foreign awards is governed by Article 137 Limitation Act (3 years).
questions.statute_or_case: Government of India v. Vedanta Ltd (2020)

questions.question_text: Under Section 30(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996, an arbitral award on agreed terms shall have the same status and effect as any other arbitral award on the merits of the case. It is enforceable under Section 36 as a:
questions.explanation: Section 30(2) enacts that a consent award has the status and enforceability of a regular arbitral award.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31(6) of the Arbitration Act 1996, arbitral tribunal may, at any time during arbitral proceedings, make an interim arbitral award on any matter with respect to which it might make a final arbitral award. An interim award is:
options: Challengeable under Section 34 and enforceable under Section 36
questions.explanation: Section 31(6) defines interim award which carries same legal status, challengeability and enforceability as final award.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, arbitral tribunal may fix amount of deposit or supplementary deposit as an advance for costs of arbitration. If one party fails to pay his share of deposit, the other party may pay that share; if both parties fail to pay, tribunal may:
options: Suspend or terminate the arbitral proceedings
questions.explanation: Section 38(2) empowers tribunal to suspend or terminate proceedings if advance deposit is not paid.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39(1) of the Arbitration Act 1996, subject to provisions of Section 39(2) and any provision to contrary in arbitration agreement, arbitral tribunal shall have a lien on the arbitral award for any unpaid costs of arbitration. If tribunal refuses to deliver award except on payment of costs, Court may on application order tribunal to deliver award on applicant depositing in Court:
options: The sum demanded by tribunal for consideration of Court
questions.explanation: Section 39 governs tribunal lien on award for costs and court procedure to release award upon deposit.

questions.question_text: Which Act received Presidential assent on 25th December, 2023 to consolidate and amend criminal offences in India, replacing the Indian Penal Code, 1860?
questions.explanation: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 45 of 2023) replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(f) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which new penal sanction has been introduced into Indian criminal jurisprudence?
questions.explanation: Section 4(f) introduces Community Service as a statutory non-custodial punishment for specified minor offences.

questions.question_text: Which Section of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 introduces a distinct statutory offence for Organised Crime committed by crime syndicates?
questions.explanation: Section 111 of BNS 2023 explicitly defines and penalizes Organised Crime, including syndicated unlawful activity, kidnapping, extortion, and land grabbing.

questions.question_text: Under Section 304 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which newly codified offence specifically targets sudden, quick, or forcible seizure of property from a person?
questions.explanation: Section 304 introduces Snatching as a distinct offence punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 69 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means (including false promise of employment or promotion, or marrying after suppressing identity) is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 69 penalizes sexual intercourse by deceitful means or false promise to marry with rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.

questions.question_text: Which Section of BNS 2023 replaces the erstwhile offence of Sedition (Section 124A IPC) with "Acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India"?
questions.explanation: Section 152 of BNS 2023 replaces IPC Sedition with an offence penalizing acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 103(2) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, when a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member shall be punished with:
options: Death or imprisonment for life, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 103(2) codifies penal sanctions against Mob Lynching, prescribing death or life imprisonment for all members of the group.

questions.question_text: Under Section 113 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which new offence has been explicitly defined to penalize acts threatening unity, integrity, security or sovereignty of India or striking terror?
questions.explanation: Section 113 defines and penalizes Terrorist Acts in general criminal law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 106(1) of BNS 2023, causing death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 106(1) increases punishment for rash or negligent act causing death to imprisonment up to 5 years (up from 2 years under Sec 304A IPC).

questions.question_text: Under Section 106(2) of BNS 2023, if a person causes death by rash and negligent driving and escapes without reporting it to a police officer or Magistrate soon after the incident (Hit and Run), he shall be punished with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 106(2) prescribes up to 10 years imprisonment and fine for Hit and Run driving cases.

questions.question_text: Under Section 64 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the minimum punishment for Rape shall be rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than:
questions.explanation: Section 64 provides that rape shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment of not less than 10 years, extending to life imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 70(1) of BNS 2023, where a woman is raped by one or more persons constituting a group (Gang Rape), each of those persons shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than:
questions.explanation: Section 70(1) mandates minimum 20 years rigorous imprisonment extending to life (remainder of natural life) for gang rape.

questions.question_text: Under Section 70(2) of BNS 2023, gang rape of a girl below how many years of age is punishable with imprisonment for life (remainder of natural life) or death?
questions.explanation: Section 70(2) prescribes death or life imprisonment (remainder of natural life) for gang rape of a girl below 18 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 112 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorized selling of tickets, or betting committed by a member of a group or syndicate is categorized as:
questions.explanation: Section 112 introduces Petty Organised Crime targeting street crimes, ticket scalping, and illegal betting.

questions.question_text: Under Section 303(1) of BNS 2023, Theft is defined as moving movable property out of the possession of any person without consent with dishonest intention. Punishment for first-time theft of property under Rs. 5,000 upon restoration may include:
questions.explanation: Section 303(2) proviso provides Community Service for first-time petty theft under Rs. 5,000 where property is returned.

questions.question_text: Under Section 308 of BNS 2023, intentionally putting any person in fear of injury and thereby dishonestly inducing him to deliver property is:
questions.explanation: Section 308 defines Extortion.

questions.question_text: Under Section 310 of BNS 2023, when five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit robbery, every person so committing is guilty of:
questions.explanation: Section 310 defines Dacoity requiring conjoint action by 5 or more persons.

questions.question_text: Under Section 316 of BNS 2023, dishonestly misappropriating property entrusted to a person or converting it to own use is defined as:
questions.explanation: Section 316 defines Criminal Breach of Trust.

questions.question_text: Under Section 318 of BNS 2023, deceiving any person and fraudulently or dishonestly inducing him to deliver property is defined as:
questions.explanation: Section 318 defines Cheating.

questions.question_text: Under Section 356 of BNS 2023, Defamation is punishable with simple imprisonment for a term up to 2 years, or fine, or both, or:
questions.explanation: Section 356(2) incorporates Community Service as an alternative punishment for defamation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38 of BNS 2023, the right of private defence of body extends to causing death in which situation?
options: An assault with intention of committing rape or gratifying unnatural lust
An assault with intention of kidnapping or abducting
An assault causing reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt
questions.explanation: Section 38 of BNS (corresponding to Sec 100 IPC) lists grounds where private defence of body extends to causing death.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45 of BNS 2023, a person abets the doing of a thing who instigates, engages in conspiracy, or intentionally aids the doing of that thing. Abetment of an offence in India from outside India is:
questions.explanation: BNS Section 48 covers abetment outside India of offences committed in India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 189 of BNS 2023, Unlawful Assembly is an assembly of how many or more persons with a common object to commit an offence or resist execution of law?
questions.explanation: Section 189 defines Unlawful Assembly requiring 5 or more persons.

questions.question_text: Under Section 191 of BNS 2023, whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly or any member thereof in prosecution of common object, every member is guilty of:
questions.explanation: Section 191 defines Rioting.

questions.question_text: Under Section 194 of BNS 2023, when two or more persons by fighting in a public place disturb public peace, they commit:
questions.explanation: Section 194 defines Affray.

questions.question_text: Under Section 336 of BNS 2023, Forgery is defined as making any false document or electronic record with intent to cause damage or injury to public or any person. Forgery of valuable security or Will is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 338 penalizes forgery of valuable security or Will with life imprisonment or up to 10 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 351 of BNS 2023, threatening another with injury to person, reputation or property with intent to cause alarm is defined as:
questions.explanation: Section 351 defines Criminal Intimidation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 115 of BNS 2023, voluntarily causing hurt to any person is punishable with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine. Voluntarily causing grievous hurt under Section 117 is punishable up to:
questions.explanation: Section 117 penalizes voluntarily causing grievous hurt with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 137 of BNS 2023, Kidnapping from lawful guardianship consists of taking or enticing a minor under how many years of age (if male or female) out of keeping of lawful guardian without consent?
options: 18 years for both male and female
questions.explanation: Under BNS Section 137(2), kidnapping from lawful guardianship applies to any minor under 18 years of age.

questions.question_text: Under Section 61 of BNS 2023, Criminal Conspiracy is defined as an agreement between two or more persons to do or cause to be done an illegal act or an act by illegal means. When the object is to commit a serious offence, punishment is the same as if:
questions.explanation: Section 61(2) provides that conspirator for major offences shall be punished in the same manner as if he had abetted the offence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of BNS 2023, nothing is an offence which is done by a child under how many years of age (doli incapax)?
questions.explanation: Section 20 enacts that nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age (absolute immunity).

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of BNS 2023, an act of a child above seven years of age and under how many years is not an offence if he has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge of the nature and consequences of his conduct?
questions.explanation: Section 21 extends qualified immunity to children between 7 and 12 years lacking maturity of understanding.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of BNS 2023, nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is wrong or contrary to law. This is the statutory rule of:
questions.explanation: Section 22 codifies legal insanity based on McNaghten's Rules.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of BNS 2023, involuntary intoxication is a defense if the thing which intoxicated the person was administered to him without his knowledge or:
questions.explanation: Section 23 provides defense for involuntary intoxication administered without knowledge or against will.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of BNS 2023, nothing is an offence merely by reason of any harm which it may cause, if done without criminal intention to prevent or avoid other harm to person or property (Necessity). This was famously examined in:
options: KM Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra
State of UP v. Ram Swarup
questions.explanation: R v. Dudley and Stephens (1884) examined limits of necessity in shipwreck cannibalism.

questions.question_text: Under Section 75 of BNS 2023, Sexual Harassment includes making unwelcome physical contact, demand for sexual favours, showing pornography, or making sexually coloured remarks. It is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 75 penalizes sexual harassment with rigorous imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.

questions.question_text: Under Section 77 of BNS 2023, watching, capturing or publishing the image of a woman engaging in a private act where she would usually expect not to be observed is the offence of:
questions.explanation: Section 77 defines and penalizes Voyeurism.

questions.question_text: Under Section 78 of BNS 2023, following a woman and contacting or attempting to contact her repeatedly despite clear indication of disinterest, or monitoring her internet/electronic communication is:
questions.explanation: Section 78 defines Stalking.

questions.question_text: Under Section 80 of BNS 2023, where the death of a woman is caused by burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage, and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty by husband or in-laws for dowry, it is:
questions.explanation: Section 80 defines Dowry Death punishable with imprisonment not less than 7 years extending to life.

questions.question_text: Under Section 85 of BNS 2023, husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to:
questions.explanation: Section 85 (re-enacting IPC 498A) penalizes marital cruelty with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 100 of BNS 2023, Culpable Homicide is causing death by doing an act with intention of causing death, or causing bodily injury likely to cause death, or with knowledge that act is likely to cause death. When culpable homicide is NOT murder, punishment under Section 105 is:
options: Imprisonment for life or imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 105 penalizes culpable homicide not amounting to murder with life imprisonment or up to 10 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 101 of BNS 2023, Culpable Homicide is Murder if the act by which death is caused is done with intention of causing death, or it satisfies exceptions like grave and sudden provocation. Murder under Section 103(1) is punishable with:
options: Death or imprisonment for life, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 103(1) prescribes death or life imprisonment for murder.

questions.question_text: Under Section 124 of BNS 2023, voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid or administering acid with intention of disfiguring or disabling any person is punishable with imprisonment not less than:
options: 10 years which may extend to life imprisonment, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 124 penalizes Acid Attacks with minimum 10 years up to life imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 147 of BNS 2023, waging or attempting to wage war against the Government of India is punishable with:
options: Death, or imprisonment for life, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 147 prescribes death or life imprisonment for waging war against Government of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 172 of BNS 2023, Bribery in elections consists of giving a gratification to any person with object of inducing him to exercise electoral right. Punishment for election bribery under Section 173 is imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 173 penalizes election bribery with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 196 of BNS 2023, promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or community is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: 3 years, or fine, or both (5 years if in place of worship)
questions.explanation: Section 196 penalizes promoting communal enmity with up to 3 years (or 5 years in place of worship).

questions.question_text: Under Section 227 of BNS 2023, giving false evidence or fabricating false evidence for use in any stage of a judicial proceeding is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 229 penalizes giving false evidence in judicial proceedings with up to 7 years imprisonment and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 270 of BNS 2023, Public Nuisance is defined as an act or omission which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or people in general. Punishment for public nuisance not otherwise punishable is fine up to:
questions.explanation: Section 292 penalizes general public nuisance not otherwise provided for with fine up to Rs. 1,000.

questions.question_text: Under Section 281 of BNS 2023, driving any vehicle or riding on any public way so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both
questions.explanation: Section 281 penalizes rash driving on public way with up to 6 months imprisonment or fine up to Rs. 1,000.

questions.question_text: Under Section 296 of BNS 2023, doing any obscene act in a public place, or singing/reciting obscene songs to annoyance of others is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 296 penalizes public obscenity with imprisonment up to 3 months or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 298 of BNS 2023, injuring or defiling a place of worship with intent to insult the religion of any class is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 298 penalizes defiling places of worship with up to 2 years imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 299 of BNS 2023, deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings of any class by insulting its religion or religious beliefs is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 299 penalizes outraging religious feelings with up to 3 years imprisonment or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 314 of BNS 2023, dishonest misappropriation of property is converting to own use any movable property dishonestly. Punishment under Section 314 is imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 314 penalizes dishonest misappropriation of property with up to 2 years imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 315 of BNS 2023, dishonest misappropriation of property belonging to a deceased person at time of his death by a person not entitled is punishable up to:
options: 3 years and fine (7 years if by clerk/servant)
questions.explanation: Section 315 penalizes misappropriation of deceased person's property with up to 3 years (7 years for clerk/servant).

questions.question_text: Under Section 317 of BNS 2023, receiving or retaining stolen property knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 317 penalizes receiving stolen property with up to 3 years imprisonment or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 324 of BNS 2023, Mischief is doing any act with intent to cause wrongful loss or damage to public or any person by destroying property. Punishment for simple mischief under Section 324(2) is imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 324(2) penalizes simple mischief with up to 6 months imprisonment or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 326 of BNS 2023, mischief by fire or explosive substance with intent to cause destruction of any building used as human dwelling or place of worship is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for life, or imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 326 penalizes arson of dwelling house with life imprisonment or up to 10 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 329 of BNS 2023, entering into or upon property in possession of another with intent to commit an offence or intimidate, insult or annoy is:
questions.explanation: Section 329 defines Criminal Trespass.

questions.question_text: Under Section 331 of BNS 2023, a person commits House-breaking who commits house-trespass by entering or quitting through any passage closed against entrance or by using force or climbing wall. House-breaking by night under Section 331(4) is punishable up to:
questions.explanation: Section 331(4) penalizes house-breaking by night with up to 3 years imprisonment and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 340 of BNS 2023, using as genuine a forged document or electronic record knowing it to be forged is punishable in the same manner as if he had:
questions.explanation: Section 340 equates punishment for using a forged document as genuine with forging the document itself.

questions.question_text: Under Section 341 of BNS 2023, making or possessing any seal, plate or instrument knowing it to be intended for committing forgery is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 341 penalizes making or possessing counterfeit seals or plates for forgery with up to 7 years imprisonment (or life where the intended forgery falls under Section 338).

questions.question_text: Under Section 352 of BNS 2023, intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 352 penalizes intentional insult provoking breach of peace with up to 2 years imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 79 of BNS 2023, uttering any word, making any sound or gesture, or exhibiting any object intending that such word or gesture shall be heard or seen by a woman to insult her modesty is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 79 (re-enacting IPC 509) penalizes insulting modesty of a woman with up to 3 years imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 353 of BNS 2023, making, publishing or circulating any statement, rumour or report with intent to cause mutiny in armed forces or cause fear/alarm to public is punishable up to:
questions.explanation: Section 353 penalizes statements creating public mischief or military mutiny with up to 3 years imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 108 of BNS 2023, if any person commits suicide, whoever abets the commission of such suicide shall be punished with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 108 penalizes abetment of suicide with up to 10 years imprisonment and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 109 of BNS 2023, Attempt to Murder is doing any act with such intention or knowledge that if by that act death were caused, he would be guilty of murder. It is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: 10 years and fine (or life imprisonment if hurt is caused)
questions.explanation: Section 109 penalizes attempt to murder with up to 10 years (or life imprisonment if hurt is caused).

questions.question_text: Under Section 110 of BNS 2023, Attempt to commit Culpable Homicide not amounting to murder is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: 3 years, or fine, or both (or up to 7 years if hurt is caused)
questions.explanation: Section 110 penalizes attempt to commit culpable homicide with up to 3 years (or 7 years if hurt is caused).

questions.question_text: Under Section 114 of BNS 2023, Hurt is defined as causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person. Grievous Hurt under Section 116 includes which of the following designated injuries?
options: Permanent privation of sight of either eye or hearing of either ear
Privation of any member or joint, or permanent disfiguration of head/face
questions.explanation: Section 116 enumerates 8 specific kinds of hurt designated as Grievous Hurt.

questions.question_text: Under Section 126 of BNS 2023, Wrongful Restraint is voluntarily obstructing any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed. It is punishable up to:
options: 1 month, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both
questions.explanation: Section 126 penalizes simple wrongful restraint with up to 1 month simple imprisonment or fine up to Rs. 5,000.

questions.question_text: Under Section 127 of BNS 2023, Wrongful Confinement is wrongfully restraining any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceeding beyond certain circumscribed limits. It is punishable up to:
options: 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both
questions.explanation: Section 127 penalizes simple wrongful confinement with up to 1 year imprisonment or fine up to Rs. 5,000.

questions.question_text: Under Section 129 of BNS 2023, intentionally using force to any person without that person's consent, in order to commit an offence, or intending or knowing it likely to cause injury, fear or annoyance, is:
questions.explanation: Section 129 defines Criminal Force (Section 128 defines "force").

questions.question_text: Under Section 130 of BNS 2023, making any gesture or preparation intending or knowing it likely that such gesture will cause any person present to apprehend that criminal force is about to be used is:
questions.explanation: Section 130 defines Assault.

questions.question_text: Under Section 132 of BNS 2023, assault or criminal force to deter a public servant from discharge of his official duty is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 132 penalizes assault or criminal force to deter a public servant with imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both.

questions.question_text: Under Section 140 of BNS 2023, Abduction is defined as compelling by force or inducing by deceitful means any person to go from any place. Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder under Section 140(1) is punishable with:
options: Death or imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years
questions.explanation: Section 140(1) penalizes kidnapping/abduction to murder with life imprisonment or death.

questions.question_text: Under Section 140(2) of BNS 2023, kidnapping or abducting a person and threatening to cause death or hurt in order to compel payment of a ransom is punishable with:
options: Death or imprisonment for life, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 140(2) penalizes kidnapping/abduction for ransom with death or imprisonment for life, and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 143 of BNS 2023, Trafficking of a person involves recruiting, transporting, harboring or receiving a person by means of threat, force, coercion or deception for exploitation. Trafficking of a minor is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for not less than:
options: 10 years, which may extend to life imprisonment, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 143(4) prescribes minimum 10 years up to life imprisonment for trafficking of a child.

questions.question_text: Under Section 139 of BNS 2023, kidnapping a child, or obtaining custody of a child not being its lawful guardian, so that the child may be used for begging is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than:
options: 10 years, extending to imprisonment for life, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 139(1) penalizes kidnapping or obtaining custody of a child for begging with rigorous imprisonment of not less than 10 years, extendable to imprisonment for life, and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 148 of BNS 2023, conspiring to wage war or attempting to collect arms with intention of waging war against Government of India is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for life, or imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 148 penalizes conspiracy to wage war with life imprisonment or up to 10 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 189(2) of BNS 2023, an assembly of five or more persons is an unlawful assembly if its common object is to overawe by criminal force the Central or State Government, or resist execution of any law, or commit any:
options: Mischief, criminal trespass, or other offence
questions.explanation: Section 189 lists common objects constituting unlawful assembly.

questions.question_text: Under Section 190 of BNS 2023, every member of an unlawful assembly at the time of committing of an offence in prosecution of common object is guilty of that offence. This embodies the principle of:
questions.explanation: Section 190 codifies constructive criminal liability of members of unlawful assembly.

questions.question_text: Under Section 198 of BNS 2023, a public servant who knowingly disobeys any direction of law as to the way in which he is to conduct himself as such public servant, intending to cause injury to any person, is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 198 penalizes public servant disobeying law to cause injury with up to 1 year imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 199 of BNS 2023, a public servant who knowingly disobeys direction of law requiring him to record information under Section 173 BNSS relating to sexual offences shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for not less than:
options: 6 months extending to 2 years, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 199 penalizes police failure to record FIR in sexual offences with 6 months to 2 years rigorous imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 209 of BNS 2023, failing to appear at the specified place and time as required by a proclamation published under Section 84 of the BNSS, 2023 is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both, or community service (up to 7 years if declared a proclaimed offender)
questions.explanation: Section 209 punishes non-appearance in response to a proclamation under Section 84 BNSS with up to 3 years, or fine, or both, or community service; up to 7 years if a declaration as a proclaimed offender has been made under Section 84(4).

questions.question_text: Under Section 221 of BNS 2023, intentionally obstructing any public servant in discharge of his public functions is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: 3 months, or fine up to Rs. 2,500, or both
questions.explanation: Section 221 penalizes obstructing public servant with up to 3 months imprisonment or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 223 of BNS 2023, disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant (such as curfew orders) causing danger to human life or health is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 2,500, or both
questions.explanation: Section 223 (re-enacting IPC 188) penalizes disobeying public orders causing danger with up to 6 months imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 238 of BNS 2023, causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen offender, is punishable if offence is punishable with death with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 238 penalizes destruction of evidence in capital cases with up to 7 years imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 253 of BNS 2023, harbouring an offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been ordered, if the offence is punishable with death, is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 253(a) penalizes harbouring an escaped or to-be-apprehended offender in a capital offence with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 274 of BNS 2023, adulterating food or drink intended for sale so as to make it noxious is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both
questions.explanation: Section 274 penalizes food adulteration with up to 6 months imprisonment or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 276 of BNS 2023, adulterating any drug or medical preparation in such manner as to lessen efficacy or change operation or make it noxious is punishable up to:
options: 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both
questions.explanation: Section 276 penalizes adulteration of drugs with imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both.

questions.question_text: Under Section 279 of BNS 2023, corrupting or fouling water of any public spring or reservoir so as to render it less fit for purpose is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both
questions.explanation: Section 279 penalizes fouling water of a public spring or reservoir with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both.

questions.question_text: Under Section 309 of BNS 2023, Theft is Robbery if in order to committing theft or carrying away property, offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death, hurt or wrongful restraint. Robbery on highway between sunset and sunrise is punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 309(4) increases robbery on the highway between sunset and sunrise to imprisonment up to 14 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 310(3) of BNS 2023, where one of five or more persons conjointly committing dacoity commits murder in so committing dacoity, every one of those persons is punishable with:
options: Death, or imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment not less than 10 years, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 310(3) penalizes dacoity with murder with death, imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment of not less than 10 years, and fine, for every member.

questions.question_text: Under Section 319 of BNS 2023, Cheating by Personation is cheating by pretending to be some other person, or knowingly substituting one person for another. It is punishable up to:
questions.explanation: Section 319 penalizes cheating by personation with up to 5 years imprisonment or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 336 of BNS 2023, making a false document or electronic record with intent to cause damage or injury to public or any person is Forgery. Forgery intended for the purpose of cheating (Section 336(3)) is punishable up to:
questions.explanation: Section 336(3) penalizes forgery intended to be used for cheating with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 349 of BNS 2023, selling, exposing or possessing for sale any goods bearing a counterfeit property mark is punishable with imprisonment up to:
questions.explanation: Section 349 penalizes property mark counterfeiting with up to 1 year imprisonment or fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 62 of BNS 2023, whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable by this Sanhita with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, and in such attempt does any act towards commission of offence, shall be punished where no express provision is made with:
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term provided for that offence
questions.explanation: Section 62 enacts general penal rule for attempts extending up to one-half of maximum sentence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of BNS 2023, the provisions of this Sanhita apply to any offence committed by any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India, and to any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) confers extra-territorial jurisdiction over Indian citizens and Indian registered vessels.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) of BNS 2023, BNS applies to any person in any place without and beyond India committing offence targeting any:
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) extends BNS extra-territorial jurisdiction to cyber offenses targeting Indian computer resources.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of BNS 2023, in calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life shall be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for how many years?
questions.explanation: Section 6 equates life imprisonment to 20 years for calculating fractional terms of punishment, unless otherwise provided.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(8) of BNS 2023, "Document" is defined as any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks, and includes electronic and digital records. This expanded definition explicitly incorporates:
questions.explanation: Section 2(8) modernizes the definition of Document to explicitly include electronic and digital records.

questions.question_text: Under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), within how many days must an electronic FIR (Zero FIR) be signed by the informant?
questions.explanation: Section 173(1) of BNSS 2023 provides that information given by electronic communication shall be taken on record by the police officer and signed within three days by the informant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 105 of BNSS 2023, what procedural mandate is required during police search and seizure operations at a crime scene?
options: Written approval from Judicial Magistrate prior to search
Presence of two Gazetted Officers during search
Mandatory audio-video electronic recording of search and seizure
Immediate live streaming to District Court
questions.explanation: Section 105 of BNSS 2023 mandates audio-video electronic recording of search and seizure operations, including preparation of list of seized items.

questions.question_text: Under Section 187 of BNSS 2023 (replacing Section 167 CrPC), police custody up to 15 days can be authorized by a Magistrate in whole or in parts during the first:
options: 40 days or 60 days depending on detention period
questions.explanation: Section 187 of BNSS 2023 permits 15-day police custody in parts across the first 40 or 60 days of the 60/90 days total detention period.

questions.question_text: Under Section 356 of BNSS 2023, what new procedure is provided for trial of a proclaimed offender who has absconded to evade trial?
options: Trial in absentia and pronouncement of judgment
Transfer of trial to High Court
questions.explanation: Section 356 of BNSS 2023 introduces Trial in Absentia for proclaimed offenders who fail to appear without reasonable cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 176(3) of BNSS 2023, forensic investigation by a Forensic Science Expert visiting crime scene is mandatory for offences punishable with imprisonment for:
questions.explanation: Section 176(3) mandates forensic team crime scene visits for offences punishable with 7 years or more.

questions.question_text: Under Section 173(3) of BNSS 2023, for offences punishable for 3 years or more but less than 7 years, police officer may conduct a preliminary enquiry before registering FIR within how many days?
questions.explanation: Section 173(3) allows a preliminary enquiry within 14 days with prior permission of an officer not below DSP rank.

questions.question_text: Under Section 230 of BNSS 2023, the Magistrate shall supply copies of police report and documents to accused within how many days from production or appearance?
questions.explanation: Section 230 mandates supplying police report and electronic documents to accused within 14 days.

questions.question_text: Under Section 258 of BNSS 2023, after hearing arguments in a sessions trial, the Judge shall give judgment within what period from completion of arguments?
options: 30 days, extendable to 45 days for reasons to be recorded in writing
questions.explanation: Section 258(1) requires the Judge to give judgment as soon as possible within 30 days of completion of arguments, extendable to 45 days for reasons recorded in writing.

questions.question_text: Under Section 479 of BNSS 2023, a first-time offender who has not been previously convicted shall be released on bail if he has undergone detention for what fraction of maximum imprisonment for that offence?
questions.explanation: Section 479(1) proviso relaxes undertrial bail threshold for first-time offenders to 1/3rd of maximum sentence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 530 of BNSS 2023, all trials, inquiries, proceedings, recording of evidence, examination of witnesses and judicial proceedings may be conducted through:
questions.explanation: Section 530 explicitly authorizes comprehensive use of electronic mode and video conferencing across all judicial proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35(3) of BNSS 2023, where arrest of a person is not required for an offence punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years, police officer shall issue a:
options: Notice of appearance directing him to appear before officer
questions.explanation: Section 35(3) makes notice of appearance mandatory where arrest is unnecessary for offences under 7 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35(7) of BNSS 2023, no arrest shall be made of a person who is infirm or above what age for offences punishable with imprisonment less than 3 years without prior permission of Officer not below DSP?
questions.explanation: Section 35(7) protects infirm persons and senior citizens above 60 years from arbitrary arrest for minor offences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 250 of BNSS 2023, an accused person in a warrant case instituted on police report may prefer an application for Discharge within how many days from supply of documents?
questions.explanation: Section 250 sets a 60-day deadline from date of supply of report under Section 230 for filing discharge application.

questions.question_text: Under Section 251 of BNSS 2023, if after discharge hearing the Magistrate is of opinion that there is ground for presuming accused committed offence, charge shall be framed within how many days from first hearing?
questions.explanation: Section 251(1) requires framing of charges within 60 days from the date of first hearing on charge.

questions.question_text: Under Section 193(3) of BNSS 2023, police report (chargesheet) must be completed within 60 days or 90 days as applicable, and progress report of investigation in rape cases shall be submitted to Magistrate within:
questions.explanation: Section 193(3) requires progress report in sexual offences investigation to be submitted within 60 days.

questions.question_text: Under Section 84 of BNSS 2023, if any court has reason to believe that a person against whom warrant is issued has absconded, court may publish a written proclamation requiring him to appear within not less than:
questions.explanation: Section 84 requires 30 days notice for proclamation of absconded person.

questions.question_text: Under Section 144 of BNSS 2023, a Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents empowers Magistrate of first class to order monthly allowance up to:
options: Such monthly rate as Magistrate thinks fit
questions.explanation: Under BNSS Section 144 (corresponding to 125 CrPC), no statutory ceiling is fixed; Magistrate orders such monthly rate as thinks fit.

questions.question_text: Under Section 163 of BNSS 2023 (replacing Section 144 CrPC), an order issued by Executive Magistrate in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger shall remain in force for not more than:
options: 1 month (extendable to 6 months by State Govt)
2 months (extendable to 6 months by State Govt)
questions.explanation: Section 163(4) limits initial emergency order duration to 2 months, extendable by State Government up to 6 months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 223 of BNSS 2023, a Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence upon a private complaint shall not take cognizance without giving the accused an opportunity of:
questions.explanation: Section 223 mandates giving opportunity of being heard to accused before taking cognizance on private complaint.

questions.question_text: Under Section 482 of BNSS 2023 (replacing Section 438 CrPC), an application for Anticipatory Bail can be made by a person apprehending arrest to the:
options: High Court or Court of Session
questions.explanation: Section 482 empowers High Court or Court of Session to grant direction for bail to person apprehending arrest.

questions.question_text: Under Section 528 of BNSS 2023 (replacing Section 482 CrPC), inherent powers to make such orders as necessary to give effect to any order or prevent abuse of process of court are preserved exclusively for the:
questions.explanation: Section 528 preserves the inherent powers of the High Court in criminal matters.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of BNSS 2023, a Court of Session may pass any sentence authorized by law, but any sentence of Death passed by a Sessions Judge shall be subject to confirmation by the:
questions.explanation: Section 22(2) read with Section 407 BNSS requires High Court confirmation before execution of a death sentence passed by a Sessions Judge.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of BNSS 2023, a Chief Judicial Magistrate may pass any sentence authorized by law except:
options: Sentence of death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term exceeding 7 years
questions.explanation: CJM can pass sentence up to 7 years imprisonment (cannot pass death, life, or >7 yrs).

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(2) of BNSS 2023, a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding:
options: 3 years, or fine up to Rs. 50,000, or both, or community service
questions.explanation: Section 23(2) allows a Magistrate of the first class to pass a sentence of imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine up to Rs. 50,000, or both, or community service.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(3) of BNSS 2023, a Judicial Magistrate of the Second Class may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding:
options: 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 10,000, or both, or community service
questions.explanation: Section 23(3) allows a Magistrate of the second class to pass a sentence of imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 10,000, or both, or community service.

questions.question_text: Under Section 289 of BNSS 2023 (Plea Bargaining), plea bargaining is available only for offences for which the maximum punishment of imprisonment does not exceed:
questions.explanation: Section 289 applies plea bargaining to offences other than those punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment exceeding 7 years, and excludes offences affecting the socio-economic condition of the country or committed against a woman or a child.

questions.question_text: Under Section 398 of BNSS 2023, every State Government shall prepare and notify a Witness Protection Scheme to ensure safety of witnesses. This makes witness protection:
questions.explanation: Section 398 statutorily mandates every State Government to formulate Witness Protection Scheme.

questions.question_text: Under Section 367 of BNSS 2023, where in the course of an inquiry or trial the Magistrate finds the accused to be of unsound mind and consequently incapable of making his defence, the Magistrate shall have the fact of unsoundness inquired into and may:
options: Postpone further proceedings and, if the accused is not dangerous, release him on bail on sufficient security being furnished for his proper care and to prevent injury
Immediately acquit the accused and close the case
Convict the accused and commit him directly to prison
Transfer the trial to the Court of Session for disposal
questions.explanation: Sections 367 and 368 of BNSS lay down the procedure where the accused is a person of unsound mind: the Court investigates the unsoundness, postpones the proceedings, and may release the accused on bail with security if he is not a danger, or otherwise detain him in safe custody.

questions.question_text: Under Section 419 of BNSS 2023, an appeal from an order of acquittal in a case instituted upon complaint can be filed by the complainant in the High Court only after obtaining:
options: Special Leave to Appeal from High Court
questions.explanation: Complainant appeal against acquittal requires Special Leave to Appeal under Section 419(4) BNSS.

questions.question_text: Under Section 514 of BNSS 2023, limitation for taking cognizance of an offence punishable with fine only is:
questions.explanation: Section 514(2)(a) sets a limitation of 6 months for offences punishable with fine only (Section 508 deals with proceedings in the wrong place).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(a) of BNSS 2023, "Bailable Offence" means an offence which is shown as bailable in the First Schedule, or which is made bailable by any other law. Any other offence is:
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(a) defines bailable and non-bailable offences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(g) of BNSS 2023, "Cognizable Offence" means an offence for which a police officer may, in accordance with the First Schedule or under any other law, arrest without:
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(g) defines Cognizable Offence as one where police may arrest without warrant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(y) of BNSS 2023, "Victim" means a person who has suffered any loss or injury caused by reason of the act or omission for which accused person has been charged, and the expression includes:
options: His or her guardian or legal heir
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(y) defines Victim broadly to include guardian or legal heir.

questions.question_text: Under Section 40 of BNSS 2023, any private person may arrest or cause to be arrested any person who in his presence commits a non-bailable and:
options: Cognizable offence, or any proclaimed offender
questions.explanation: Section 40 permits private arrest of persons committing non-bailable and cognizable offences in presence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of BNSS 2023, when any offence is committed in the presence of a Magistrate (Executive or Judicial) within his local jurisdiction, he may himself arrest or order any person to arrest the offender and may:
options: Try the case immediately without charge
Commit the offender to custody subject to bail provisions
questions.explanation: Section 41 empowers Magistrates to arrest for offences committed in their presence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 47 of BNSS 2023, every police officer or other person arresting any person without warrant shall forthwith communicate to him full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested, and where offence is bailable, that he is entitled to:
questions.explanation: Section 47 mandates informing arrested person of grounds of arrest and right to bail.

questions.question_text: Under Section 51 of BNSS 2023, examination of an arrested person by a registered medical practitioner at the request of a police officer not below sub-inspector rank is authorized when there are reasonable grounds for believing examination will afford evidence as to commission of offence. Examination of a female shall be conducted only by or under supervision of a:
questions.explanation: Section 51 requires medical examination of female arrested persons to be conducted by female practitioners.

questions.question_text: Under Section 184 of BNSS 2023, medical examination of a victim of rape or attempted rape shall be conducted by a registered medical practitioner in a hospital run by Government or local authority within how many hours of receiving information?
questions.explanation: Section 184(1) requires the woman to be sent for medical examination within 24 hours from the time of receiving information relating to the offence (Section 52 concerns examination of the person accused of rape).

questions.question_text: Under Section 58 of BNSS 2023, a police officer making an arrest without warrant shall take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction, or before the officer in charge of police station, within a period not exceeding how many hours (excluding journey time)?
questions.explanation: Section 58 enforces the constitutional 24-hour production mandate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 64 of BNSS 2023, Summons to an individual or corporate body may be served electronically by encrypted email or mobile messaging in such manner as prescribed by State Government. This introduces:
questions.explanation: Section 64 statutorily recognizes Electronic Service of Summons.

questions.question_text: Under Section 72 of BNSS 2023, every Warrant of Arrest issued by a Court under this Sanhita shall be in writing, signed by the presiding officer of such Court and bear the seal of the Court. A warrant of arrest remains in force until:
options: It is executed or cancelled by the Court which issued it
questions.explanation: Section 72(2) provides that an arrest warrant remains in force until executed or cancelled by issuing court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 88(3) of BNSS 2023, where a proclaimed person's attached property is at the disposal of the State Government, and within 2 years from the date of attachment he appears and proves that he did not abscond and had no notice of the proclamation, the property (or net sale proceeds) shall be:
options: Delivered to him after satisfying all costs incurred in consequence of the attachment
questions.explanation: Section 88(3) provides for restoration of the attached property, or the net proceeds of any sale, after deducting the costs of attachment, where the person appears within 2 years and proves he did not abscond.

questions.question_text: Under Section 107 of BNSS 2023, where a police officer making an investigation has reason to believe that any property is the proceeds of crime, he may, with the approval of the Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police, apply to the Court or Magistrate for:
options: Attachment of such property, and on conviction, its forfeiture
questions.explanation: Section 107 governs attachment, forfeiture and restoration of the proceeds of crime, including rateable distribution to affected persons.

questions.question_text: Under Section 94 of BNSS 2023, whenever any Court or officer in charge of police station considers that production of any document, device, or other thing is necessary for inquiry or trial, such court/officer may issue a:
options: Summons or written order to produce it
questions.explanation: Section 94 empowers courts and police to issue summons/order to produce documents or electronic devices.

questions.question_text: Under Section 185 of BNSS 2023, whenever a police officer making an investigation has reasonable grounds for believing that anything necessary for investigation may be found in any place within his police station limits, he may conduct search after recording grounds in the case diary. Copies of the record shall be sent to the nearest Magistrate:
options: Forthwith, and not later than 48 hours
questions.explanation: Section 185(5) requires copies of the search record to be sent to the nearest Magistrate forthwith, and in any case not later than 48 hours.

questions.question_text: Under Section 148 of BNSS 2023, an Executive Magistrate or officer in charge of police station may command any unlawful assembly to disperse. If upon being commanded assembly does not disperse, it may be dispersed by:
questions.explanation: Section 148 & 149 authorize use of civil force to disperse unlawful assembly.

questions.question_text: Under Section 170 of BNSS 2023, a police officer knowing of a design to commit any cognizable offence may arrest, without orders from a Magistrate and without a warrant, the person so designing, if it appears to officer that commission of offence cannot be otherwise prevented. Person arrested cannot be detained beyond:
questions.explanation: Section 170(2) limits preventive police detention to 24 hours max without Magistrate order.

questions.question_text: Under Section 175 of BNSS 2023, any officer in charge of a police station may, without order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case which a Court having jurisdiction over local area would have power to inquire into or try. No proceeding of police officer shall at any stage be called in question on ground that:
options: Case was one which officer was not empowered to investigate
questions.explanation: Section 175(2) protects police investigation from jurisdictional challenge.

questions.question_text: Under Section 180 of BNSS 2023, any police officer making an investigation may examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with facts and circumstances of case. Such person shall be bound to answer all questions relating to case put to him by such officer, OTHER THAN questions the answers to which would have a tendency to:
options: Expose him to a criminal charge, penalty or forfeiture (Protection against self-incrimination)
questions.explanation: Section 180(2) protects witnesses from answering self-incriminating questions during police examination.

questions.question_text: Under Section 181 of BNSS 2023, no statement made by any person to a police officer in the course of an investigation shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person making it. Such statement may be used at trial ONLY to:
options: Contradict such witness in manner provided by Section 148 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
questions.explanation: Section 181 restricts use of a police statement to contradicting the maker when called as a prosecution witness (Section 182 concerns the bar on inducement, threat or promise).

questions.question_text: Under Section 183 of BNSS 2023 (replacing Section 164 CrPC), any Judicial Magistrate may record any confession or statement made to him in the course of an investigation. Confession shall be recorded in manner prescribed and signed by person making it, and Magistrate shall append a memorandum stating:
options: That he explained that accused is not bound to make confession and that it may be used as evidence against him
questions.explanation: Section 183(4) mandates magisterial warning that confession is voluntary and can be used in evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 183(6) of BNSS 2023, in cases involving offences against women or children (sexual offences), statement of the victim shall be recorded by Judicial Magistrate as soon as information of commission of offence is brought to notice of police. Statement of victim with disability shall be recorded with assistance of:
options: An interpreter or special educator, and audio-video recorded
questions.explanation: Section 183(6) mandates special educator assistance and mandatory audio-video recording for disabled victims.

questions.question_text: Under Section 187(2) of BNSS 2023, total period of detention during investigation before filing chargesheet shall not exceed 90 days where investigation relates to an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for not less than:
questions.explanation: Section 187(2) sets 90-day chargesheet deadline for offences carrying death, life or 10+ years imprisonment (60 days for other offences).

questions.question_text: Under Section 187(3) of BNSS 2023, if investigation is not completed within 60 days or 90 days as applicable and accused is prepared to and does furnish bail, accused shall be released on bail. This is known as:
questions.explanation: Section 187(3) codifies indefeasible right to Default Bail / Statutory Bail upon expiry of chargesheet period.

questions.question_text: Under Section 189 of BNSS 2023, when an officer in charge of police station sees no sufficient ground for investigating a complaint, he shall not investigate and shall notify informant. In cases of offences punishable under 3 years, officer may decide not to investigate if:
options: Offence is not of serious nature and complainant agrees
questions.explanation: Section 189(1) proviso allows police to drop investigation in minor cases under 3 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 193(8) of BNSS 2023, nothing in Section 193 shall be deemed to preclude further investigation in respect of an offence after a report under sub-section (2) has been forwarded to Magistrate. Further investigation report submitted thereafter is called a:
questions.explanation: Section 193(8) authorizes submitting Supplementary Chargesheet after further investigation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 196 of BNSS 2023, where a person dies or disappears, or rape is alleged, while in the custody of the police or in any other custody authorised by the Magistrate or Court, an inquiry (in addition to the police investigation) shall be held by:
options: The Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed
questions.explanation: Section 196(2) makes a Magistrate's inquiry mandatory, in addition to the police investigation, into any death, disappearance or alleged rape occurring in police or other authorised custody.

questions.question_text: Under Section 197 of BNSS 2023, every offence shall ordinarily be inquired into and tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction:
questions.explanation: Section 197 lays down general rule of territorial jurisdiction: court where offence was committed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 203 of BNSS 2023, when an offence is committed whilst the person by or against whom, or the thing in respect of which, the offence is committed is in the course of performing a journey or voyage, the offence may be inquired into or tried by a Court through or into whose local jurisdiction:
options: The person or thing passed in the course of that journey
questions.explanation: Section 203 governs jurisdiction for offences committed during journey or voyage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 218 of BNSS 2023 (replacing Section 197 CrPC), when any person who is or was a Judge or Magistrate or a public servant not removable from office save by or with sanction of Government is accused of any offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting in discharge of official duty, no Court shall take cognizance without prior sanction of:
options: Central Government or State Government as applicable
questions.explanation: Section 218 requires prior government sanction for prosecuting public servants for acts done in official capacity.

questions.question_text: Under Section 218(1) proviso of BNSS 2023, sanction decision by Government on prosecution of public servant shall be communicated within how many days from date of receipt of proposal?
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Section 218(1), if the Government does not convey its decision within 120 days of receiving the request, the sanction is deemed to have been accorded.

questions.question_text: Under Section 227 of BNSS 2023, if in the opinion of a Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence there is sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall issue a Summons for attendance of accused in a summons-case, or a Warrant/Summons in a warrant-case. No summons or warrant shall be issued until a:
options: Chargesheet is approved by High Court
List of prosecution witnesses has been filed
questions.explanation: Section 227(2) bars issuing process against accused until list of prosecution witnesses is filed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 234 of BNSS 2023, every charge under this Sanhita shall state the offence with which the accused is charged, describing it by name given by law. If law gives no specific name, so much of definition must be stated as to give accused notice of matter. Charge must be written in:
questions.explanation: Section 234(6) requires charges to be written in the language of the Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 239 of BNSS 2023, any Court may alter or add to any charge at any time before judgment is pronounced. Every such alteration or addition shall be read and explained to the accused. This is the power of:
questions.explanation: Section 239 governs power of Court to alter or add to charges before judgment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 243 of BNSS 2023, for every distinct offence of which any person is accused there shall be a separate charge, and every such charge shall be tried separately, EXCEPT in cases of joinder of charges under Sections 244, 245, 246, and 247. Persons accused of same offence committed in course of same transaction may be:
questions.explanation: Section 246 allows joint trial of co-accused committing offences in same transaction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 249 of BNSS 2023, in a trial before a Court of Session, when accused appears or is brought before Court, prosecutor shall open case by describing charge against accused and stating by what evidence he proposes to prove guilt. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 249 defines opening case for prosecution in Sessions Trial.

questions.question_text: Under Section 250 of BNSS 2023, if upon considering record of case and documents, and after hearing accused and prosecution, the Judge considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding against accused, Judge shall:
options: Discharge the accused and record reasons for so doing
questions.explanation: Section 250 empowers Sessions Judge to discharge accused when no sufficient ground exists.

questions.question_text: Under Section 255 of BNSS 2023, if after taking all evidence for prosecution and examining accused, the Judge considers there is no evidence that accused committed offence, Judge shall record an order of:
questions.explanation: Section 255 provides for order of acquittal in Sessions Trial when no evidence exists against accused.

questions.question_text: Under Section 274 of BNSS 2023, in trial of a Summons-case by a Magistrate, when accused appears or is brought before Magistrate, particulars of offence of which he is accused shall be stated to him and he shall be asked whether he pleads guilty or has defense to make, but it shall NOT be necessary to:
questions.explanation: Section 274 dispenses with formal framing of charge in summons trial.

questions.question_text: Under Section 279 of BNSS 2023, where a summons-case has been instituted upon a complaint and the complainant fails to appear on the day fixed for the appearance of the accused, the Magistrate shall, after giving the complainant thirty days' time to be present:
options: Convict the accused for the offence charged
Commit the case to the Court of Session
Acquit the accused, unless he thinks it proper to adjourn the hearing
questions.explanation: Section 279(1) requires the Magistrate to acquit the accused on the complainant's non-appearance (after allowing 30 days), unless he thinks it proper to adjourn; the same applies where non-appearance is due to the complainant's death.

questions.question_text: Under Section 283 of BNSS 2023, a Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class may, for reasons recorded in writing, try in a summary way offences not punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term exceeding:
questions.explanation: Section 283(2) authorises the CJM or a first-class Magistrate to try summarily offences not punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment exceeding 3 years (Section 284 covers summary trial by a second-class Magistrate).

questions.question_text: Under Section 285 of BNSS 2023, in a Summary Trial, no sentence of imprisonment for a term exceeding how long shall be passed in case of any conviction under Summary Procedure?
questions.explanation: Section 285(2) provides that no sentence of imprisonment exceeding 3 months shall be passed on any conviction in a summary trial.

questions.question_text: Under Section 337 of BNSS 2023, a person who has once been tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction for an offence and convicted or acquitted of such offence shall not be liable to be tried again for same offence while conviction/acquittal remains in force. This is constitutional protection of:
options: Autrefois Acquit and Autrefois Convict (Double Jeopardy)
questions.explanation: Section 337 codifies Autrefois Acquit & Autrefois Convict under Article 20(2).

questions.question_text: Under Section 340 of BNSS 2023, any person accused of an offence before a Criminal Court, or against whom proceedings are instituted under this Sanhita, has a right to be defended by an:
questions.explanation: Section 340 guarantees fundamental right of legal defense by advocate of choice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 341 of BNSS 2023, where in a trial before Court of Session or Magistrate, accused is not represented by advocate and has not sufficient means to engage an advocate, Court shall assign an advocate for his defense at expense of the:
questions.explanation: Section 341 mandates legal aid at State expense for indigent accused.

questions.question_text: Under Section 343 of BNSS 2023, at any stage of investigation, inquiry or trial of an offence, Chief Judicial Magistrate or Magistrate of first class may tender a pardon to accomplice on condition of his making a full and true disclosure of whole circumstances. Person accepting tender of pardon is an:
questions.explanation: Section 343 governs tender of pardon to an accomplice (Approver).

questions.question_text: Under Section 351 of BNSS 2023 (replacing Section 313 CrPC), in every inquiry or trial for purpose of enabling accused personally to explain any circumstances appearing in evidence against him, Court shall question him generally on case after prosecution witnesses have been examined. Answers given by accused:
options: May be taken into consideration in such inquiry or trial
questions.explanation: Section 351 governs examination of accused without oath to enable personal explanation of evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 356(1) of BNSS 2023, where a person declared as a Proclaimed Offender under Section 84 has absconded to evade trial and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, Court shall after recording reasons proceed with trial in absentia after expiry of how many days from date of framing of charges?
questions.explanation: Section 356(1) provides 90-day grace period after charge framing before trial in absentia commences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 359 of BNSS 2023 (Compounding of Offences), offences specified in table under Section 359(1) may be compounded by persons mentioned in third column without permission of court, while offences under Section 359(2) may be compounded:
options: With permission of Court before which prosecution is pending
questions.explanation: Section 359 sets out compoundable offences with and without court permission.

questions.question_text: Under Section 359(8) of BNSS 2023, the compounding of an offence under Section 359 shall have the effect of an:
options: Acquittal of accused with whom offence has been compounded
questions.explanation: Section 359(8) enacts that compounding an offence operates as a full judicial acquittal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 392 of BNSS 2023, judgment in every trial in any Criminal Court of original jurisdiction shall be pronounced in open court immediately after termination of trial or at some subsequent time of which notice shall be given to parties.
