Judgment copy shall be uploaded on portal within:
questions.explanation: Section 392(1) mandates uploading copy of judgment on digital portal within 7 days.

questions.question_text: Under Section 395 of BNSS 2023, whenever a Court imposes sentence of fine or sentence of which fine forms a part, Court may order whole or part of fine recovered to be applied in defraying expenses of prosecution and in paying compensation for loss or injury caused to victim. This is:
options: Order to pay costs and victim compensation
questions.explanation: Section 395 empowers courts to award victim compensation out of fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 396 of BNSS 2023, every State Government in co-ordination with Central Government shall prepare a scheme for providing funds for purpose of compensation to victim or his dependents who have suffered loss or injury. This scheme is called:
questions.explanation: Section 396 mandates State Victim Compensation Schemes.

questions.question_text: Under Section 410 of BNSS 2023, where a case is submitted for confirmation of a death sentence and the High Court consists of two or more Judges, the confirmation of the sentence (or any new sentence or order) must be made and signed by at least:
options: Two Judges of the High Court
A single Judge of the High Court
A Full Bench of five Judges
questions.explanation: Section 410 requires the confirmation, new sentence or order to be made, passed and signed by at least two Judges where the Bench consists of two or more Judges.

questions.question_text: Under Section 415 of BNSS 2023, any person convicted on a trial held by a High Court in exercise of its extraordinary original criminal jurisdiction may appeal to the:
questions.explanation: Section 415 provides appeal from High Court original trial to Supreme Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 415(2) of BNSS 2023, any person convicted on a trial held by a Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge may appeal to the:
questions.explanation: Section 415(2) provides an appeal from a Sessions Court conviction to the High Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 415(3) of BNSS 2023, any person convicted on a trial held by a Magistrate of the first class or a CJM may appeal to the:
questions.explanation: Section 415(3) provides an appeal from a Judicial Magistrate's conviction to the Court of Session.

questions.question_text: Under Section 416 of BNSS 2023, where an accused has pleaded guilty and been convicted on such plea, no appeal lies (if convicted by the High Court), and if convicted by a Sessions Judge or Magistrate an appeal lies only as to:
options: The extent or legality of the sentence
questions.explanation: Section 416 bars an appeal on a plea of guilty, except (for convictions by a Sessions Judge or Magistrate) as to the extent or legality of the sentence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 438 of BNSS 2023, High Court or Sessions Judge may call for and examine record of any proceeding before any subordinate criminal court within its jurisdiction for purpose of satisfying itself as to correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 438 governs Revisionary powers of High Court and Sessions Judge.

questions.question_text: Under Section 438(2) of BNSS 2023, revisionary powers of High Court or Sessions Judge shall NOT be exercised in relation to any:
options: Interlocutory Order passed in any appeal, inquiry, trial or other proceeding
questions.explanation: Section 438(2) explicitly bars revision applications against Interlocutory Orders (Asian Resurfacing rule).

questions.question_text: Under Section 446 of BNSS 2023, whenever it is made to appear to Supreme Court that an order under this section is expedient for ends of justice, Supreme Court may order that any particular case or appeal be transferred from one High Court to another High Court or from a criminal court subordinate to one High Court to another criminal court subordinate to another High Court. This is:
options: Supreme Court power to transfer cases and appeals
questions.explanation: Section 446 governs inter-state case transfer powers of Supreme Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 447 of BNSS 2023, whenever it is made to appear to High Court that a fair and impartial inquiry or trial cannot be had in any subordinate criminal court, High Court may order transfer of case within its jurisdiction. This is:
options: High Court power to transfer cases
questions.explanation: Section 447 governs High Court case transfer powers within the State.

questions.question_text: Under Section 472 of BNSS 2023, appropriate Government may at any time without conditions or upon conditions suspend execution of sentence or remit whole or any part of punishment. Under Section 475, when a person is convicted of offence for which death is one of punishments, or sentence of life imprisonment is passed, sentence shall not be remitted or commuted below how many years of actual imprisonment?
questions.explanation: Section 475 (re-enacting Section 433A CrPC) mandates minimum 14 years actual imprisonment before life sentence remission/commutation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 478 of BNSS 2023, when any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by police officer, or appears before Court, and is prepared to give bail, such person shall be:
options: Released on bail as of right
Bailed only on High Court order
questions.explanation: Section 478 guarantees absolute statutory right to bail in bailable offences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 480 of BNSS 2023, when any person accused of non-bailable offence is arrested or detained, he may be released on bail by Court, BUT shall not be released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing he has been guilty of an offence punishable with:
questions.explanation: Section 480 restricts Magistrate bail in non-bailable offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 483 of BNSS 2023, High Court or Court of Session may direct that any person who has been released on bail under Chapter XXXIII be arrested and committed to custody. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 483 governs Cancellation of Bail.

questions.question_text: Under Section 497 of BNSS 2023, when any property regarding which an offence appears to have been committed is produced before Criminal Court during inquiry or trial, Court may make such order as thinks fit for proper custody pending conclusion of inquiry/trial. This is:
options: Order for custody and disposal of property pending trial (Interim Custody / Panchnama)
questions.explanation: Section 497 governs interim custody and disposal of property during trial (Sunderbhai Ambalal Desai principles).

questions.question_text: Under Section 514(2)(b) of BNSS 2023, limitation period for taking cognizance of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding 1 year is:
questions.explanation: Section 514(2)(b) prescribes a 1 year limitation for offences punishable with imprisonment up to 1 year.

questions.question_text: Under Section 514(2)(c) of BNSS 2023, limitation period for taking cognizance of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding 1 year but not exceeding 3 years is:
questions.explanation: Section 514(2)(c) prescribes a 3 year limitation for offences punishable with imprisonment exceeding 1 year but not exceeding 3 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 531 of BNSS 2023 (Repeal and Savings), the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is repealed. However, any appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending immediately before commencement of BNSS shall be disposed of in accordance with:
options: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (old CrPC as if BNSS had not come into force)
questions.explanation: Section 531(2)(a) saves pending criminal trials, inquiries, investigations and appeals to be completed under CrPC 1973.

questions.question_text: Which Act received Presidential assent on 25th December, 2023 to consolidate and provide general rules and principles of evidence for fair trial, replacing the Indian Evidence Act, 1872?
questions.explanation: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Act No. 47 of 2023) replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction, are relevant. This embodies which common law doctrine?
questions.explanation: Section 4 of BSA 2023 codifies the Rule of Res Gestae (facts forming part of the same transaction).

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of BSA 2023, any fact is relevant which shows or constitutes a motive or preparation for any fact in issue or relevant fact, or shows:
options: Previous or subsequent conduct of any party or agent
questions.explanation: Section 6 makes motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct of any party or agent relevant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of BSA 2023, anything said, done or written by any conspirator in reference to their common intention is a relevant fact against each of the persons believed to be so conspiring after:
options: Reasonable ground to believe that two or more persons have conspired together
questions.explanation: Section 8 makes acts and statements of co-conspirators admissible once reasonable ground exists to believe a conspiracy exists.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of BSA 2023, an Admission is defined as a statement, oral or documentary or contained in electronic form, which suggests any inference as to any fact in issue or relevant fact, made by:
options: Any person authorized by law or party under prescribed circumstances
questions.explanation: Section 15 defines Admission in civil and criminal proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of BSA 2023, no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence. This rule ensures protection against:
questions.explanation: Section 23(1) of BSA 2023 renders confessions to a police officer inadmissible against the accused (Section 22 deals with confessions caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise).

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(2) of BSA 2023 (Discovery Rule), when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence in police custody, so much of such information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered:
options: Can only be used against co-accused
questions.explanation: Section 23(2) incorporates the doctrine of discovery of physical evidence leading from information provided by accused in custody.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26(a) of BSA 2023, statements, written or verbal, of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, or who cannot be found, or who has become incapable of giving evidence, are relevant when the statement is made as to the cause of his death. This is known as:
questions.explanation: Section 26(a) codifies the statutory rule governing Dying Declarations.

questions.question_text: Under Section 61 of BSA 2023, an electronic or digital record shall have the same legal effect, validity and enforceability as any:
questions.explanation: Section 61 gives electronic and digital records equal status with traditional paper documents.

questions.question_text: Under Section 63 of BSA 2023, admissibility of electronic records produced by a computer system requires a certificate printed or signed by a person occupying a responsible official position, fulfilling conditions specified in:
questions.explanation: Section 63(4) mandates a electronic certificate for admitting computer prints, server logs, or digital evidence in court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 57 of BSA 2023, Primary Evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the court. Primary evidence includes electronic records where:
options: Extracted printout is submitted without certificate
Oral account of file contents is given
Photo copy of screen is taken
The electronic record is created or stored in multiple files in computer system
questions.explanation: Section 57 Explanation 4 treats original digital files and records stored across server locations as primary evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 58 of BSA 2023, Secondary Evidence includes certified copies, copies made from original by mechanical processes, counterparts of documents, and:
options: Oral accounts of contents of a document given by some person who has himself seen it
questions.explanation: Section 58 lists categories of admissible secondary evidence when primary evidence cannot be produced.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of BSA 2023, when the Court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law, science, art, or identity of handwriting, finger impressions, or digital signature, opinions of specially skilled persons are relevant facts. These persons are called:
questions.explanation: Section 39 defines Expert Opinions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 104 of BSA 2023, whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist. This responsibility is:
questions.explanation: Section 104 defines Burden of Proof.

questions.question_text: Under Section 105 of BSA 2023, the burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail if:
options: No evidence at all were given on either side
questions.explanation: Section 105 enacts the fundamental test for location of burden of proof.

questions.question_text: Under Section 121 of BSA 2023, when one person has, by his declaration, act or omission, intentionally caused or permitted another person to believe a thing to be true and to act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed to deny the truth of that thing. This is the doctrine of:
questions.explanation: Section 121 defines the rule of Estoppel.

questions.question_text: Under Section 138 of BSA 2023, an accomplice shall be a competent witness against an accused person, and a conviction is not illegal merely because it proceeds upon the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice. However, prudence requires:
questions.explanation: Section 138 read with the illustration (b) to Section 119 makes corroboration in material particulars a rule of judicial prudence when relying on accomplice evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 142 of BSA 2023, the examination of a witness by the party who calls him shall be called:
questions.explanation: Section 142 defines Examination-in-chief.

questions.question_text: Under Section 142 of BSA 2023, the examination of a witness by the adverse party shall be called:
questions.explanation: Section 142 defines Cross-examination.

questions.question_text: Under Section 146 of BSA 2023, any question suggesting the answer which the person putting it wishes or expects to receive is called a:
questions.explanation: Section 146(1) defines Leading Questions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 146 of BSA 2023, Leading Questions must NOT be asked in Examination-in-chief or Re-examination without permission of the Court, except:
options: As to matters which are introductory, or undisputed, or which have in opinion of Court been sufficiently proved
questions.explanation: Section 146 permits leading questions in examination-in-chief or re-examination, with the Court's permission, as to introductory or undisputed matters or matters already sufficiently proved.

questions.question_text: Under Section 146 of BSA 2023, Leading Questions may be asked in:
questions.explanation: Section 146 explicitly permits asking leading questions in cross-examination.

questions.question_text: Under Section 162 of BSA 2023, a witness may refresh his memory by referring to any writing made by himself at the time of the transaction concerning which he is questioned, or so soon afterwards that the court considers it likely that the transaction was fresh in his memory. This is called:
questions.explanation: Section 162 governs Refreshing Memory by witnesses.

questions.question_text: Under Section 117 of BSA 2023, when a married woman commits suicide within seven years from date of marriage and it is shown that her husband or relative subjected her to cruelty, court may presume that such suicide was abetted by husband/relative. This is a presumption of:
options: Abetment of suicide by married woman
questions.explanation: Section 117 provides statutory presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman.

questions.question_text: Under Section 118 of BSA 2023, when the question is whether a person has committed dowry death of a woman and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty for demand of dowry, court shall presume such person caused dowry death. This is a:
questions.explanation: Section 118 creates a mandatory presumption of law ("shall presume") for dowry death.

questions.question_text: Under Section 116 of BSA 2023, the birth of a child during valid wedlock, or within 280 days after dissolution (mother remaining unmarried), is conclusive proof of legitimacy unless it can be shown that:
options: The parties to marriage had no access to each other at any time when he could have been begotten
questions.explanation: Section 116 prescribes non-access as the sole legal ground to rebut conclusive proof of legitimacy.

questions.question_text: Under Section 111 of BSA 2023, when the question is whether a man is alive or dead, and it is proved that he has not been heard of for how many years by those who would naturally have heard of him if he had been alive, the burden of proving that he is alive shifts to the person who affirms it?
questions.explanation: Section 111 shifts the burden of proving a person is alive to the one asserting it, once he has not been heard of for 7 years (Section 110 covers the ordinary rule where he was known to be alive within 30 years).

questions.question_text: Under Section 131 of BSA 2023, no Magistrate or Police Officer shall be compelled to say whence he got any information as to the commission of any offence. This protects:
questions.explanation: Section 131 grants privilege against disclosing the source of information as to the commission of an offence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 128 of BSA 2023, communications during marriage between husband and wife are privileged and no person shall be compelled to disclose them unless:
options: Person who made it or representative-in-interest consents, or in suit between married persons
High Court orders in civil suit
questions.explanation: Section 128 protects communications made during marriage, except with the consent of the person who made it (or his representative-in-interest), or in suits between the married persons or prosecutions of one for a crime against the other.

questions.question_text: Under Section 132 of BSA 2023, no advocate shall at any time be permitted to disclose any communication made to him in the course and for the purpose of his employment by his client. This is the rule of:
questions.explanation: Section 132 codifies the professional (attorney-client) communications privilege.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(d) of BSA 2023, "Document" is defined as any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks, or by more than one of those means, intended to be used for recording that matter, and explicitly includes:
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(d) modernizes the definition of Document to explicitly include electronic and digital records.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(e) of BSA 2023, "Evidence" means and includes all statements which the Court permits or requires to be made before it by witnesses (oral evidence) and all documents including:
options: Electronic or digital records produced for the inspection of the Court (documentary evidence)
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(e) defines Evidence into Oral Evidence and Documentary Evidence (including digital records).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(h) of BSA 2023, whenever it is provided that the Court "May Presume" a fact, it may either regard such fact as proved, unless and until it is disproved, or may:
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(h) defines "May Presume" as a discretionary presumption of fact.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(l) of BSA 2023, whenever it is directed that the Court "Shall Presume" a fact, it shall regard such fact as proved, unless and until it is:
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(l) defines "Shall Presume" as a mandatory presumption of law subject to rebuttal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(b) of BSA 2023, when one fact is declared by this Adhiniyam to be "Conclusive Proof" of another, the Court shall, on proof of the one fact, regard the other as proved, and shall NOT allow evidence to be given for the purpose of:
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(b): "conclusive proof" bars any evidence aimed at disproving the presumed fact.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of BSA 2023, facts which are the occasion, cause or effect, immediate or otherwise, of relevant facts or facts in issue, or which constitute state of things under which they happened, are:
questions.explanation: Section 5 makes facts showing occasion, cause, or effect relevant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of BSA 2023, facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact, or which establish identity of any thing or person whose identity is relevant (Test Identification Parade), are:
questions.explanation: Section 7 makes explanatory facts and Test Identification Parades (TIP) relevant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of BSA 2023, facts not otherwise relevant are relevant if they are inconsistent with any fact in issue or relevant fact, or if by themselves or in connection with other facts they render existence/non-existence of any fact in issue highly probable or improbable. This is the plea of:
questions.explanation: Section 9 governs the defense of Alibi (being elsewhere at the time of crime).

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of BSA 2023, facts showing existence of any state of mind (such as intention, knowledge, good faith, negligence, rashness, ill-will or good-will) or state of body are relevant when:
options: The existence of any such state of mind or body is in issue or relevant
questions.explanation: Section 12 makes facts showing state of mind or body relevant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of BSA 2023, admissions are relevant and may be proved as against the person who makes them or his representative-in-interest, but they CANNOT be proved by or on behalf of person making them EXCEPT when:
options: It is of such a nature that if person making it were dead, it would be relevant between third persons under Section 26
Consists of statement of state of mind/body made at or about time when such state existed and accompanied by conduct
If it is relevant otherwise than as an admission
questions.explanation: Section 19 lists the statutory exceptions where a self-serving admission may be proved by the person making it.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of BSA 2023, in civil cases no admission is relevant if it is made either upon an express condition that evidence of it is not to be given, or under circumstances from which Court can infer parties agreed together that evidence of it should not be given. This protects:
questions.explanation: Section 21 protects "without prejudice" settlement communications in civil suits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of BSA 2023, a confession made by an accused person is irrelevant in a criminal proceeding if the making of the confession appears to the Court to have been caused by any:
options: Inducement, threat, coercion or promise proceeding from a person in authority
questions.explanation: Section 22 renders confessions caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise from a person in authority irrelevant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of BSA 2023, when more persons than one are being tried jointly for the same offence, and a confession made by one of such persons affecting himself and some other of such persons is proved, the Court:
options: Must convict co-accused on confession alone
May take into consideration such confession as against such other person as well as against person making it
questions.explanation: Section 24 permits the Court to take a co-accused's confession into consideration against the other person jointly tried, as well as against its maker.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26(b) of BSA 2023, a statement made by a person who cannot be called as witness is relevant when it was made in the ordinary course of business, and in particular when it consists of an entry or memorandum made by him in books kept in ordinary course of business or in:
questions.explanation: Section 26(b) makes business and professional routine entries of deceased/unavailable persons admissible.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26(c) of BSA 2023, a statement made by a person unavailable as witness is relevant when the statement is against the pecuniary or proprietary interest of the person making it, or when, if true, it would expose him to:
options: A criminal prosecution or to a suit for damages
questions.explanation: Section 26(c) makes declarations against pecuniary or proprietary interest admissible.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34 of BSA 2023, the existence of any judgment, order or decree which by law prevents any Court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial, is a relevant fact when the question is whether such Court ought to take cognizance or hold trial. This incorporates:
questions.explanation: Section 34 makes former judgments operating as Res Judicata relevant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35 of BSA 2023, a final judgment, order or decree of a competent Court in exercise of probate, matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction, which confers upon or takes away from any person any legal character, is conclusive proof of that legal character. This is a:
questions.explanation: Section 35 defines Judgments in Rem and their conclusive nature against the whole world.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of BSA 2023, when the Court has to form an opinion as to the person by whom any document was written or signed, the opinion of any person acquainted with the handwriting of the person by whom it is supposed to be written is:
questions.explanation: Section 41 makes opinion of person acquainted with handwriting relevant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41(2) of BSA 2023, when the Court has to form an opinion as to the electronic signature of any person, opinion of the Certifying Authority which issued the Electronic Signature Certificate is:
questions.explanation: Section 41(2) makes the opinion of the Certifying Authority which issued the Electronic Signature Certificate a relevant fact.

questions.question_text: Under Section 46 of BSA 2023, in civil cases, the fact that the character of any person concerned is such as to render probable or improbable any conduct imputed to him is:
questions.explanation: Section 46 enacts general rule that character evidence is irrelevant in civil suits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 47 of BSA 2023, in criminal proceedings, the fact that the person accused is of a good character is:
questions.explanation: Section 47 makes previous good character of accused in criminal cases relevant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 49 of BSA 2023, in criminal proceedings, the fact that the accused person has a bad character is irrelevant, UNLESS:
options: Evidence has been given that he has a good character, in which case it becomes relevant in reply
questions.explanation: Section 49 makes previous bad character irrelevant except in reply where evidence of good character has been given.

questions.question_text: Under Section 51 of BSA 2023, no fact of which the Court will take Judicial Notice need be:
questions.explanation: Section 51 enacts that facts judicially noticeable need not be proved by evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 52 of BSA 2023, the Court shall take Judicial Notice of all laws in force in territory of India, Articles of War, seals of courts, accession of Heads of State, and:
options: Geographical divisions and public festivals notified in Official Gazette
questions.explanation: Section 52 lists statutory matters of which Court must take Judicial Notice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 53 of BSA 2023, no fact need be proved in any proceeding which the parties thereto or their agents agree to admit at the hearing, or which by any rule of pleading in force they are deemed to have admitted. This is the rule of:
questions.explanation: Section 53 dispenses with formal proof of facts admitted by parties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 56 of BSA 2023, the contents of documents may be proved either by:
options: Primary evidence or by secondary evidence
questions.explanation: Section 56 provides that the contents of documents may be proved by primary or by secondary evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 59 of BSA 2023, documents must be proved by primary evidence EXCEPT in the cases hereinafter mentioned. This embodies the fundamental evidentiary rule known as the:
questions.explanation: Section 59 codifies the Best Evidence Rule requiring production of primary evidence, except in the cases in Section 60.

questions.question_text: Under Section 60 of BSA 2023, secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition or contents of a document when original is shown to be in possession of adverse party who fails to produce it after notice, or when original has been destroyed/lost, or when original is a:
questions.explanation: Section 60 lists statutory cases where secondary evidence is admissible (such as public documents).

questions.question_text: Under Section 67 of BSA 2023, if a document is required by law to be attested (such as a Will or Gift deed), it shall not be used as evidence until at least how many attesting witnesses have been called for purpose of proving execution, if alive and subject to court process?
questions.explanation: Section 67 requires calling at least one attesting witness to prove an attested document (Section 68 applies where no attesting witness can be found).

questions.question_text: Under Section 74 of BSA 2023, Public Documents include documents forming acts or records of acts of sovereign authority, official bodies, tribunals, legislative, executive and judicial officers of India or foreign country. All other documents are:
questions.explanation: Section 74 defines both public documents and, residually, private documents as all other documents.

questions.question_text: Under Section 78 of BSA 2023, the Court shall presume the genuine character of every document purporting to be a certificate, certified copy, or other document declared by law to be admissible as evidence of any particular fact, provided it is:
questions.explanation: Section 78 mandates a presumption as to the genuineness of certified copies and similar documents duly certified.

questions.question_text: Under Section 92 of BSA 2023, where any document proved or purporting to be how many years old is produced from custody which Court considers proper, Court may presume signature and every part of document is in handwriting of person by whom it purports to be written?
questions.explanation: Section 92 enacts the 30-year presumption for ancient documents produced from proper custody.

questions.question_text: Under Section 93 of BSA 2023, where any Electronic Record purporting or proved to be how many years old is produced from proper custody, Court may presume electronic signature was affixed by person by whom it purports to be affixed?
questions.explanation: Section 93 enacts the 5-year presumption as to electronic records produced from proper custody.

questions.question_text: Under Section 94 of BSA 2023, when terms of a contract, grant or disposition of property have been reduced to form of a document, no evidence shall be given in proof of terms EXCEPT the document itself or secondary evidence of its contents. This excludes:
options: Oral evidence of terms of document
questions.explanation: Section 94 excludes oral evidence to prove written terms of contracts, grants or dispositions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 95 of BSA 2023, when a contract, grant or disposition of property has been proved according to Section 94, no evidence of any oral agreement or statement shall be admitted as between parties for purpose of contradicting, varying, adding to, or subtracting from its terms. This is the:
questions.explanation: Section 95 codifies the Parol Evidence Rule excluding oral agreements to contradict written documents.

questions.question_text: Under Section 96 of BSA 2023, when language used in a document is on its face ambiguous or defective, evidence may NOT be given of facts which would show its meaning. Ambiguity apparent on face of document is:
questions.explanation: Section 96 excludes extrinsic evidence to explain Patent Ambiguity (ambiguity on face of document).

questions.question_text: Under Section 98 of BSA 2023, when language used in a document is plain in itself, but is unmeaning in reference to existing facts, evidence may be given to show that it was used in a peculiar sense. Ambiguity arising when applying plain language to facts is:
questions.explanation: Section 98 permits extrinsic evidence to clear up Latent Ambiguity (hidden ambiguity).

questions.question_text: Under Section 109 of BSA 2023, when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon:
questions.explanation: Section 109 places the burden of proving a fact especially within a person's knowledge upon that person.

questions.question_text: Under Section 108 of BSA 2023, when a person is accused of any offence, the burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing case within any General Exception in BNS (such as insanity, intoxication, self-defence) is upon:
options: The accused person, and Court shall presume absence of such circumstances
questions.explanation: Section 108 places burden of proving general exceptions strictly on accused.

questions.question_text: Under Section 116 of BSA 2023, the presumption of legitimacy of a child born during marriage or within 280 days after dissolution is a conclusive proof. In Dipanwita Roy v. Ronobroto Roy (2015), the Supreme Court held that a DNA test can be ordered only when:
options: Strong prima facie case of non-access is established and justice demands it
questions.explanation: Dipanwita Roy (2015) held DNA testing to rebut legitimacy presumption requires strong prima facie case of non-access.

questions.question_text: Under Section 124 of BSA 2023, all persons shall be competent to testify UNLESS Court considers they are prevented from understanding questions put to them or giving rational answers by reason of tender years, extreme old age, disease or unsoundness of mind. A child is a competent witness if he can:
options: Understand questions and give rational answers
questions.explanation: Section 124 enacts capacity to understand and give rational answers as sole test of witness competency.

questions.question_text: Under Section 125 of BSA 2023, a witness who is unable to speak (Dumb Witness) may give his evidence in any other manner in which he can make it intelligible, as by writing or by signs. Such evidence taken in open court shall be deemed to be:
questions.explanation: Section 125 explicitly treats written/sign evidence of dumb witness given in open court as Oral Evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 126 of BSA 2023, in all civil proceedings parties to suit and spouse of any party shall be competent witnesses. In criminal proceedings against any person, husband or wife of such person shall be:
questions.explanation: Section 126 makes spouse a competent witness in civil and criminal proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 127 of BSA 2023, no Judge or Magistrate shall, except upon special order of some Court to which he is subordinate, be compelled to answer any questions as to his own conduct in court as such Judge or Magistrate, or as to anything which came to his knowledge in court while acting as such. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 127 grants privilege to Judges and Magistrates regarding judicial acts in court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 129 of BSA 2023, no one shall be permitted to give any evidence derived from unpublished official records relating to any affairs of State, except with permission of the officer at the head of the department concerned. This is the privilege of:
options: State Secrets / Affairs of State Privilege
questions.explanation: Section 129 protects unpublished official records relating to affairs of State from disclosure without the permission of the head of department.

questions.question_text: Under Section 132 of BSA 2023, professional communications between advocate and client are privileged. Does this protection extend to communications made in furtherance of any ILLEGAL purpose, or any fact observed showing fraud/crime committed since employment?
options: No, protection does NOT extend to illegal purpose or crime/fraud observed during employment
questions.explanation: The proviso to Section 132 excludes communications made in furtherance of an illegal purpose, and facts showing a crime or fraud committed since the employment began, from the privilege.

questions.question_text: Under Section 134 of BSA 2023, no person shall be compelled to disclose to Court any confidential communication which has taken place between him and his legal professional adviser, unless:
options: He offers himself as a witness
questions.explanation: Section 134 protects the client's confidential communications with his legal adviser, unless he offers himself as a witness (in which case he may be compelled to disclose communications necessary to explain his evidence).

questions.question_text: Under Section 139 of BSA 2023, no particular number of witnesses shall in any case be required for the proof of any fact. This enacts that evidence is weighed by quality, not quantity, embodying the maxim:
options: Ponderantur testes, non numerantur (Evidence is weighed, not numbered)
questions.explanation: Section 139 codifies the principle that the quality of evidence matters, not the number of witnesses.

questions.question_text: Under Section 141 of BSA 2023, when either party proposes to give evidence of any fact, Judge may ask party proposing to give evidence in what manner alleged fact, if proved, would be relevant. Judge shall admit evidence if he thinks fact, if proved, would be relevant, and not otherwise. This is:
options: Judge's power to decide admissibility of evidence
questions.explanation: Section 141 vests authority in Judge to determine admissibility of evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 142 of BSA 2023, witnesses shall be first examined-in-chief, then (if adverse party so desires) cross-examined, then (if party calling him so desires) re-examined. The examination and cross-examination must relate to relevant facts, but cross-examination need NOT be confined to facts to which witness testified in his:
questions.explanation: Section 142(2) permits cross-examination to extend to any relevant facts beyond examination-in-chief.

questions.question_text: Under Section 144 of BSA 2023, a person summoned to produce a document does NOT become a witness by the mere fact that he produces it, and cannot be cross-examined UNLESS and until he is:
questions.explanation: Section 144 provides that producing a document on summons does not make the producer a witness or subject to cross-examination unless he is called as a witness.

questions.question_text: Under Section 145 of BSA 2023, witnesses to character may be cross-examined and:
questions.explanation: Section 145 allows cross-examination and re-examination of character witnesses.

questions.question_text: Under Section 148 of BSA 2023, a witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing or reduced into writing, and relevant to matters in question, without such writing being shown to him, OR being proved first. But if it is intended to contradict him by writing, his attention must, before the writing can be proved, be called to those parts of it which are to be used for the purpose of contradicting him. This is:
options: Cross-examination as to previous written statements
questions.explanation: Section 148 lays down the mandatory procedure for contradicting a witness with previous written statements.

questions.question_text: Under Section 149 of BSA 2023, when a witness is cross-examined, he may, in addition to questions hereinbefore referred to, be asked any questions which tend to test his veracity, discover who he is and his position in life, or shake his credit by injuring his:
questions.explanation: Section 149 specifies the questions lawful in cross-examination, including those testing veracity and shaking credit by injuring character.

questions.question_text: Under Section 151 of BSA 2023, if any question put to a witness in cross-examination relates to a matter not relevant to the suit except in so far as it affects the credit of the witness by injuring his character, the Court shall decide whether the witness shall be compelled to answer it. The Court may warn the witness that he is not obliged to answer if the imputation is:
options: Remote in time or of such a character that it would not affect the credibility of his evidence
questions.explanation: Section 151 empowers the Court to decide when a witness must answer credit-affecting questions, and to warn him that he need not answer where the imputation relates to matters remote in time or otherwise not affecting his credibility.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 152 and 153 of BSA 2023, a question in cross-examination that conveys an imputation against a witness ought not to be asked without reasonable grounds. If the Court is of opinion that such a question was asked by an advocate without reasonable grounds, it may report the circumstances to the:
options: High Court or other authority to which the advocate is subject in the exercise of his profession
questions.explanation: Section 152 bars questions conveying imputations without reasonable grounds; Section 153 allows the Court to report an advocate who does so to the High Court or other authority to which he is professionally subject.

questions.question_text: Under Section 154 of BSA 2023, the Court may forbid any questions or inquiries which it regards as indecent or scandalous, although such questions or inquiries may have some bearing on questions before the Court, UNLESS they relate to:
options: Facts in issue or matters necessary to be known in order to determine whether facts in issue existed
questions.explanation: Section 154 empowers the Court to forbid indecent or scandalous questions unless they relate to facts in issue or matters necessary to determine whether facts in issue existed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 155 of BSA 2023, the Court shall forbid any question which appears to it to be intended to insult or annoy, or which, though proper in itself, appears to the Court needlessly offensive in form. This protects witnesses against:
questions.explanation: Section 155 mandates court intervention against questions intended to insult or annoy, or needlessly offensive in form.

questions.question_text: Under Section 156 of BSA 2023, when a witness has been asked and has answered any question which is relevant to the inquiry only in so far as it tends to shake his credit by injuring his character, NO evidence shall be given to contradict him EXCEPT if he denies a previous conviction or is questioned to establish that he is biased. This is:
options: Exclusion of evidence to contradict answers to questions testing veracity
questions.explanation: Section 156 bars collateral evidence to contradict answers to credit-testing questions, except as to a denied previous conviction or to prove bias.

questions.question_text: Under Section 157 of BSA 2023, the Court may, in its discretion, permit the party who calls a witness to put any question to him which might be put in cross-examination by the adverse party. A witness so cross-examined by the party calling him is commonly termed a:
questions.explanation: Section 157 empowers the Court to permit the party calling a witness to cross-examine him (a "hostile witness").

questions.question_text: Under Section 158 of BSA 2023, the credit of a witness may be impeached by the adverse party, or by the party calling him with the consent of the Court, by evidence of persons who testify that they believe him unworthy of credit, or by proof that the witness has been bribed, or by proof of former statements inconsistent with any part of his evidence which is liable to be contradicted. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 158 lists the statutory modes of impeaching the credit of a witness.

questions.question_text: Under Section 160 of BSA 2023, in order to corroborate the testimony of a witness, any former statement made by such witness relating to the same fact, at or about the time when the fact took place, or before any authority legally competent to investigate the fact, may be proved. This is:
options: Corroboration of witness testimony by former statements
questions.explanation: Section 160 permits proving a witness's former statements to corroborate his later testimony as to the same fact.

questions.question_text: Under Section 164 of BSA 2023, an adverse party has a right to inspect any writing used by a witness under Section 162 to refresh his memory, and may cross-examine the witness thereupon. This ensures fairness in:
questions.explanation: Section 164 grants the adverse party the right to inspect any writing used to refresh memory under Section 162 and to cross-examine the witness on it.

questions.question_text: Under Section 168 of BSA 2023, the Judge may, in order to discover or to obtain proper proof of relevant facts, ask any question he pleases, in any form, at any time, of any witness, or of the parties, about any fact relevant or irrelevant, and may order production of any document or thing. Neither party shall be entitled to make any objection to such question or order, nor to cross-examine any witness upon any answer, without leave of the Court. This is:
options: Judge's Power to put questions or order production of evidence
questions.explanation: Section 168 (corresponding to the former Section 165 of the Evidence Act) confers plenary powers on the Judge to put questions and order production in order to discover the truth.

questions.question_text: Under Section 169 of BSA 2023, the improper admission or rejection of evidence shall NOT be ground of itself for a new trial or reversal of any decision in any case, if it appears to Court that independently of evidence objected to, there was sufficient evidence to justify decision, or that if rejected evidence had been received, it ought not to have varied decision. This is the rule of:
options: No new trial for improper admission or rejection of evidence
questions.explanation: Section 169 enacts that technical evidence errors do not invalidate decision if independent sufficient evidence exists.

questions.question_text: In Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014) and Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020), the Supreme Court affirmed that production of a Section 63(4) certificate (erstwhile 65B) for admissible electronic records is:
options: Mandatory condition precedent for secondary electronic evidence
questions.explanation: Arjun Panditrao (2020) settled that Section 63(4) certificate is mandatory for secondary electronic evidence.

questions.question_text: In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961), a Constitution Bench held that compelling an accused person to give specimen handwriting, signature, or thumb impressions does NOT violate protection against self-incrimination because specimen impressions are not:
options: "To be a witness" within Article 20(3) of Constitution
questions.explanation: Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) held taking specimen impressions is not "being a witness against oneself".
questions.statute_or_case: State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961)

questions.question_text: In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that involuntary administration of Narco-analysis, Polygraph test, and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP) on accused person violates:
options: Article 20(3) self-incrimination and Article 21 personal liberty
questions.explanation: Selvi (2010) declared involuntary narco-analysis and polygraph unconstitutional under Articles 20(3) and 21.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33 of BSA 2023, when a statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers, evidence shall be given of so much and no more of the statement as the Court considers necessary to a full understanding of its nature and effect. This is:
options: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation or document
questions.explanation: Section 33 governs the scope of evidence required when a statement forming part of a larger conversation, document or record is admitted.

questions.question_text: Under Section 170 of BSA 2023 (Repeal and Savings), the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 is repealed. However, any application, trial, inquiry, proceeding or appeal pending immediately before commencement of BSA shall be disposed of in accordance with:
options: Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (old Evidence Act as if BSA had not come into force)
questions.explanation: Section 170(2) saves pending trials, inquiries and proceedings to be disposed of under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

questions.question_text: The Companies Act, 2013:
options: Is Act No. 18 of 2013 and replaced the Companies Act, 1956; it received assent on 29 August 2013 and its provisions were brought into force in phases
questions.explanation: The 2013 Act introduced the one-person company, mandatory CSR, the class-action suit, the National Company Law Tribunal, and a stronger auditor and independent-director framework.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(62) of the Companies Act, 2013, a 'One Person Company' (OPC) is:
options: A company with only one director
A partnership converted into a company
A company which has only one person as a member
A company with one shareholder and one creditor
questions.explanation: An OPC is a private company; its memorandum must nominate a person who will become the member on the subscriber's death or incapacity.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 and Section 149 of the Companies Act, 2013, the minimum number of members and directors are:
options: A private company: 3 members and 3 directors
A public company: 2 members and 2 directors
A public company: 7 members and 3 directors; a private company: 2 members and 2 directors; an OPC: 1 member and 1 director
questions.explanation: The maximum number of members for a private company is 200 (excluding present and past employee-members); a public company has no upper limit. Every company must have at least one director resident in India.

questions.question_text: The principle that a company is a legal person distinct from its members, so that the company's property is not the members' property and the members are not liable for the company's debts, was established in:
options: Ashbury Railway Carriage Co. v. Riche (1875)
questions.explanation: Section 9 of the Companies Act, 2013 gives a registered company perpetual succession and the capacity to hold property and sue and be sued in its own name.

questions.question_text: Under the doctrine of 'lifting the corporate veil', a court will disregard the separate legal personality of a company where:
options: The corporate form is used to evade legal obligations, perpetrate fraud, defeat public policy, or as a mere facade concealing the true facts (and there are also statutory instances, such as fraudulent conduct of business under Section 339)
A company has only two members
questions.explanation: Indian courts have lifted the veil for tax evasion (CIT v. Sri Meenakshi Mills), enemy character (Daimler v. Continental Tyre) and to prevent fraud.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 and Section 5 of the Companies Act, 2013, the constitutional documents of a company are:
options: The prospectus and the annual return
The certificate of incorporation and the PAN card
The Memorandum of Association (stating the name, registered-office State, objects, liability and capital clauses) and the Articles of Association (containing the regulations for internal management)
The board report and the auditor's report
questions.explanation: The 2013 Act simplified the objects clause and, since the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015, abolished the requirement of a minimum paid-up capital.

questions.question_text: The doctrine that a person dealing with a company in good faith may assume that the internal procedural requirements of its articles have been complied with is:
options: The doctrine of indoor management (the rule in Royal British Bank v. Turquand)
questions.explanation: The Turquand rule protects outsiders; it does not apply where the outsider had knowledge of the irregularity, or where the circumstances were suspicious and put him on inquiry.

questions.question_text: Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, mandatory Corporate Social Responsibility applies to every company having, in the immediately preceding financial year:
options: A net worth of Rs 500 crore or more, or a turnover of Rs 1000 crore or more, or a net profit of Rs 5 crore or more — such a company must spend at least 2% of its average net profits of the three preceding financial years on CSR activities
A paid-up capital of Rs 1 crore
questions.explanation: Since the 2019/2021 amendments, unspent CSR amounts must be transferred to a specified fund (or, for ongoing projects, to a separate 'Unspent CSR Account'), and non-compliance attracts a monetary penalty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 149 of the Companies Act, 2013, an independent director:
options: Is any director who does not attend board meetings

Is a non-executive director who is a person of integrity with relevant expertise, and who (together with his relatives) has no material pecuniary relationship with the company; every listed public company must have at least one-third of its Board as independent directors
Is a director nominated by a bank
questions.explanation: An independent director holds office for a term of up to five consecutive years and may be re-appointed for one more term; Schedule IV prescribes a Code for Independent Directors.

questions.question_text: Under Section 149(1) proviso of the Companies Act, 2013, certain classes of companies must have at least one:
options: Woman director (listed companies and public companies with paid-up capital of Rs 100 crore or more, or turnover of Rs 300 crore or more)
questions.explanation: This gender-diversity requirement was one of the notable governance reforms of the 2013 Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(51) and Sections 203 of the Companies Act, 2013, 'key managerial personnel' (KMP) of a company include:
options: Only the chairman of the board

The chief executive officer or managing director or manager; the company secretary; the whole-time director; the chief financial officer; and such other officer (not more than one level below the directors) in whole-time employment as may be designated as KMP
questions.explanation: Every listed company and every other public company with a paid-up capital of Rs 10 crore or more must have whole-time KMP.

questions.question_text: Under Section 245 of the Companies Act, 2013, a 'class action suit' may be filed before the National Company Law Tribunal by:
options: A prescribed number of members or depositors (or any class of them), if they are of the opinion that the management or conduct of the affairs of the company is being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members or depositors
questions.explanation: The class-action remedy was introduced after the Satyam scandal to allow collective redress; banking companies are excluded.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, an application to the NCLT for relief against 'oppression and mismanagement' may be made where:
options: A member is dissatisfied with the dividend

The affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial or oppressive to any member or members, or prejudicial to public interest or to the interests of the company, or a material change in management has occurred that is likely to be prejudicial
questions.explanation: Sections 241-242 broadly correspond to Sections 397-398 of the 1956 Act; the qualifying threshold is generally 100 members or one-tenth of the members (or members holding one-tenth of the issued capital).

questions.question_text: Under Sections 408, 410 and 423 of the Companies Act, 2013, corporate disputes are adjudicated by:
options: The Company Law Board, which continues to function
The High Court in its ordinary original jurisdiction
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), with appeals to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), and a further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law within 60 days
questions.explanation: The NCLT/NCLAT (constitutionally upheld in Union of India v. R. Gandhi, 2010) replaced the Company Law Board, the BIFR and the company jurisdiction of the High Courts; Section 423 gives a further appeal to the Supreme Court within 60 days (extendable by 60 more days) on a question of law, and the NCLT is also the adjudicating authority under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.

questions.question_text: Under Section 179 read with Section 180 of the Companies Act, 2013, certain powers of the Board can be exercised only with the consent of the company by a special resolution, including:
options: Selling, leasing or otherwise disposing of the whole or substantially the whole of the undertaking; borrowing money exceeding the aggregate of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium; and contributing to charitable funds beyond the prescribed limit
questions.explanation: Section 180 restrictions (formerly Section 293 of the 1956 Act) now apply to all companies, not merely public companies.

questions.question_text: Under Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013, 'related party transactions' not in the ordinary course of business or not at arm's length require:
options: The prior approval of the Board by resolution and, for companies crossing the prescribed thresholds, the prior approval of the members by resolution (a related member cannot vote on such a resolution)
The approval of the Central Government in every case
Only disclosure in the annual return
questions.explanation: Section 177 requires the Audit Committee to approve or subsequently modify related-party transactions; contravention attracts penalties and, for a listed company, possible action for recovery.

questions.question_text: Under Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013, the mandatory rotation of auditors requires that a listed company (and prescribed classes of companies) shall not appoint or re-appoint:
options: Any auditor for more than one year

An individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm as auditor for more than two terms of five consecutive years (with a five-year cooling-off period thereafter)
An audit firm for more than 20 years
An auditor without Central Government approval
questions.explanation: Section 139(1) provides that an auditor is appointed for a term of five years, subject to ratification (ratification was removed by the 2017 amendment).

questions.question_text: Under Section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013, a person found guilty of 'fraud' involving an amount of at least Rs 10 lakh (or 1% of turnover, whichever is lower) is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for a term of not less than six months but which may extend to ten years, and fine of not less than the amount involved in the fraud, extending to three times that amount (minimum three years' imprisonment where the fraud involves public interest)
questions.explanation: Section 447 is the omnibus anti-fraud provision; the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) investigates serious corporate fraud under Sections 211 and 212.

questions.question_text: Under Section 164 of the Companies Act, 2013, a person is disqualified from being appointed as a director if, among other grounds:
options: He owns shares in a competitor
He is over 60 years of age
He has resigned from another company

He has not filed financial statements or annual returns for a continuous period of three financial years (for companies of which he is a director), or has failed to repay deposits/redeem debentures/pay declared dividends for one year or more
questions.explanation: Section 164(2) disqualifies such a director from re-appointment in that company and appointment in any other company for five years; Section 167 deals with vacation of office.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(20) and Section 3 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company comes into existence:
options: On registration by the Registrar of Companies, who issues a certificate of incorporation, which is conclusive evidence that the company is duly registered; the company acquires a Corporate Identity Number (CIN) from that date
On the signing of the memorandum by the subscribers
questions.explanation: A company limited by shares (other than an OPC or a company already carrying on business) must also file a declaration of commencement of business under Section 10A before it can commence business or exercise borrowing powers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 173 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company must hold:
options: The first Board meeting within 30 days of incorporation, and thereafter a minimum of four Board meetings each year, with not more than 120 days between two consecutive meetings
Board meetings only when the chairman calls them
questions.explanation: Participation in a Board meeting may be by video-conferencing or other audio-visual means (subject to certain restricted items); an OPC, small company, dormant company and start-up private company need hold only two Board meetings a year.

questions.question_text: Under Section 96 of the Companies Act, 2013, every company (other than a One Person Company) must hold an Annual General Meeting:
options: Within one month of the close of the financial year
Only in the year of incorporation
Within six months of the close of the financial year (the first AGM within nine months of the first financial year's close), and not more than fifteen months between two AGMs
questions.explanation: The Registrar may extend the time for holding an AGM (other than the first AGM) by up to three months for special reasons.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(85) of the Companies Act, 2013, a 'small company' (other than a public company) is one whose:
options: Registered office is in a rural area

Paid-up share capital does not exceed the prescribed limit (currently Rs 4 crore) and turnover does not exceed the prescribed limit (currently Rs 40 crore) — subject to exclusions for holding/subsidiary companies, Section 8 companies and companies governed by a special Act
questions.explanation: Small companies and OPCs enjoy several compliance relaxations (fewer board meetings, abridged directors' report, no cash-flow statement, lower penalties under Section 446B).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(87) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is a 'subsidiary' of another company (the holding company) if the holding company:
options: Controls the composition of its Board of Directors, or exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power either on its own or together with one or more of its subsidiary companies
Has a common director with it
questions.explanation: A company cannot, except as prescribed, have layers of subsidiaries beyond the prescribed number (two layers).

questions.question_text: Under Section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013, where a company proposes to increase its subscribed capital by issue of further shares, they must first be offered:
options: To the public by a fresh prospectus

To existing equity shareholders in proportion to their existing shareholding (a 'rights issue'), by a notice specifying the number of shares offered and a period of not less than 15 and not more than 30 days to accept
questions.explanation: Section 62 also permits an issue to employees under a scheme of employees' stock option (special resolution) and a preferential allotment to any persons (special resolution), subject to conditions.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 73 to 76 of the Companies Act, 2013, acceptance of deposits from the public:
options: Is freely permitted for all companies
Is completely prohibited for every company

Is permitted only for 'eligible companies' (certain public companies meeting net-worth/turnover thresholds) subject to conditions including credit rating and deposit insurance; a private company may accept deposits only from its members, subject to limits
questions.explanation: The deposit rules were tightened after several company failures; contravention attracts penalties and possible action under Section 447.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(68) and Section 2(71) of the Companies Act, 2013, the essential feature that distinguishes a private company from a public company is that a private company, by its articles:
options: Is exempt from filing financial statements
Restricts the right to transfer its shares, limits the number of members to 200, and prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities
questions.explanation: A subsidiary of a public company is deemed to be a public company even if its articles say otherwise.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company formed for promoting commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity or protection of the environment, which applies its profits only to promoting its objects and prohibits payment of dividends to members:
options: May be registered as a company with limited liability without the words 'Limited' or 'Private Limited' in its name, with a licence from the Central Government (Registrar)
Must be registered as a trust
Cannot be a company at all
questions.explanation: A Section 8 company (the successor to the Section 25 company of the 1956 Act) enjoys certain exemptions but its licence can be revoked for contravention.

questions.question_text: Under Section 447 read with Section 448 and Section 449 of the Companies Act, 2013, making a false statement in any return, report, certificate, financial statement or other document, knowing it to be false or omitting a material fact:
options: Is punishable as fraud under Section 447 (false statement), and giving false evidence in any examination or affidavit under the Act is punishable with imprisonment for three to seven years and fine up to ten lakh rupees
questions.explanation: These provisions underpin the integrity of corporate disclosures.

questions.question_text: Under the Constitution of India, which Article guarantees the right to constitutional remedies for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
questions.explanation: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the heart and soul of the Constitution.

questions.question_text: The doctrine of Basic Structure of the Indian Constitution was laid down by the Supreme Court in which landmark judgment?
options: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
questions.explanation: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), a 13-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot alter or destroy the basic structure of the Constitution under Article 368.
questions.statute_or_case: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Constitution of India prohibits discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth?
questions.explanation: Article 15(1) provides that the State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them.

questions.question_text: Under Article 21A of the Constitution of India, the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of which age group?
questions.explanation: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act 2002, mandates the State to provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years.

questions.question_text: Which writ is issued by a court to produce a person who is detained unlawfully, directing the detaining authority to present them before court?
questions.explanation: Habeas Corpus (literally "to have the body") is a writ issued to secure the release of a person unlawfully detained by state authority or private individual.

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Constitution of India abolished Untouchability and forbade its practice in any form?
questions.explanation: Article 17 explicitly abolishes "Untouchability" and declares its practice in any form to be an offence punishable in accordance with law.

questions.question_text: Under which Article of the Constitution is Part IVA containing Fundamental Duties incorporated, and by which Amendment Act?
questions.explanation: Part IVA and Article 51A were inserted into the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
questions.statute_or_case: Article 51A, Part IVA, Constitution of India

questions.question_text: Which provision of the Constitution provides for a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) throughout the territory of India?
questions.explanation: Article 44 in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) provides that the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India.

questions.question_text: Article 50 of the Directive Principles of State Policy directs the State to take steps regarding:
options: Separation of judiciary from the executive
questions.explanation: Article 50 directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

questions.question_text: Under Article 61 of the Constitution of India, what is the procedure for the impeachment of the President of India?
options: Initiated in Lok Sabha only by a simple majority
Initiated by the Supreme Court of India on reference by Prime Minister
Initiated in either House of Parliament by a charge signed by at least 1/4th members
Initiated in Rajya Sabha only by a 2/3rd majority of members present
questions.explanation: Article 61 provides that impeachment charges against the President may be initiated by either House of Parliament, provided notice is signed by at least one-fourth of the total membership.

questions.question_text: Under Article 72 of the Constitution of India, the President has power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment in which cases?
options: In all cases where punishment is by a Court Martial
In all cases where punishment is for an offence against a Union law
In all cases where sentence is a sentence of death
questions.explanation: Article 72 empowers the President to grant pardons in Court Martial cases, offences against Union laws, and all death sentence cases.

questions.question_text: Under Article 76 of the Constitution of India, who is appointed by the President as the highest law officer in India?
questions.explanation: Article 76 provides for the appointment of the Attorney-General for India by the President of India.

questions.question_text: Under Article 123 of the Constitution of India, the President has power to promulgate Ordinances when:
options: Both Houses of Parliament are in session
Except when both Houses of Parliament are in session and immediate action is required
The Supreme Court directs the Executive
questions.explanation: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament when immediate action is necessary.

questions.question_text: Under Article 143 of the Constitution of India, the President may consult the Supreme Court on questions of law or fact of public importance. This jurisdiction is known as:
questions.explanation: Article 143 confers Advisory Jurisdiction on the Supreme Court to give opinions upon reference by the President.

questions.question_text: Under Article 368 of the Constitution of India, Parliament may amend any provision of the Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down therein, subject to:
questions.explanation: Parliament's constituent power under Article 368 is limited by the Basic Structure Doctrine laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

questions.question_text: Under Article 110 of the Constitution of India, if any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, whose decision thereon shall be final?
options: Speaker of the House of the People (Lok Sabha)
Chairman of Council of States (Rajya Sabha)
questions.explanation: Article 110(3) enacts that if any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of Lok Sabha thereon shall be final.

questions.question_text: Under Article 129 of the Constitution of India, the Supreme Court of India shall be a:
options: Trial Court of First Instance for civil suits
Court of Record and shall have all powers including power to punish for contempt of itself
questions.explanation: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a Court of Record possessing power to punish for contempt of itself.

questions.question_text: Under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, the Supreme Court may in its discretion grant Special Leave to Appeal (SLP) from any judgment, decree, determination or order in any cause or matter passed by:
options: Any Court or Tribunal in the territory of India (except Court Martial)
questions.explanation: Article 136 confers extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal against decisions of any court/tribunal except military tribunals.

questions.question_text: Under Article 141 of the Constitution of India, the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be:
options: Subject to approval by Law Commission
Binding on all courts within the territory of India
questions.explanation: Article 141 enacts the constitutional rule of Precedent, making law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India.

questions.question_text: Under Article 148 of the Constitution of India, who is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal to audit all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India?
questions.explanation: Article 148 provides for the independent constitutional office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG).

questions.question_text: Under Article 165 of the Constitution of India, who is appointed by the Governor of each State as the highest law officer of the State?
questions.explanation: Article 165 provides for the appointment of the Advocate-General for the State by the Governor.

questions.question_text: Under Article 213 of the Constitution of India, the Governor of a State has power to promulgate Ordinances during recess of the State Legislature, which must be laid before the Legislature and ceases to operate after how many weeks from re-assembly?
questions.explanation: Article 213(2)(a) enacts that an Ordinance promulgated by a Governor shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the re-assembly of the Legislature.

questions.question_text: Under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, High Courts have power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for:
questions.explanation: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue directions or writs not only for Fundamental Rights but also for "any other purpose" (making its writ jurisdiction wider than Article 32).

questions.question_text: By which Constitutional Amendment Act was Part IX containing provisions for Panchayats (Articles 243 to 243O) inserted into the Constitution of India?
questions.explanation: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 inserted Part IX and the 11th Schedule establishing constitutional status for Panchayati Raj institutions.

questions.question_text: By which Constitutional Amendment Act was Part IXA containing provisions for Municipalities (Articles 243P to 243ZG) inserted into the Constitution of India?
questions.explanation: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 inserted Part IXA and the 12th Schedule governing Municipalities (Urban Local Bodies).

questions.question_text: Under Article 246 read with the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India, List III contains subject-matters on which both Parliament and State Legislatures have power to make laws. List III is named:
questions.explanation: The Seventh Schedule divides legislative powers into Union List (List I), State List (List II), and Concurrent List (List III).
questions.statute_or_case: Article 246, Seventh Schedule, Constitution of India

questions.question_text: Under Article 248 of the Constitution of India, who has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List (Residuary Powers)?
questions.explanation: Article 248 vests residuary powers of legislation exclusively in Parliament.

questions.question_text: Under Article 265 of the Constitution of India, no tax shall be levied or collected except by:
questions.explanation: Article 265 enacts the fundamental tax principle: "No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law".

questions.question_text: Under Article 280 of the Constitution of India, the President shall at the expiration of every fifth year constitute which body to recommend distribution of tax proceeds between Union and States?
questions.explanation: Article 280 provides for the quasi-judicial Finance Commission constituted every five years by the President.

questions.question_text: Under Article 300A of the Constitution of India, inserted by the 44th Amendment Act 1978, no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. Right to Property is currently a:
questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment Act 1978 deleted Right to Property from Part III (Article 31) and re-enacted it as a legal/constitutional right under Article 300A.
