questions.question_text: Under Article 312 of the Constitution of India, Parliament may create one or more All-India Services common to the Union and States if the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) passes a resolution supported by not less than:
options: 2/3rd majority of members present and voting
questions.explanation: Article 312 empowers Rajya Sabha by a 2/3rd majority resolution of members present and voting to authorize Parliament to create All-India Services.

questions.question_text: Under Article 315 of the Constitution of India, there shall be a Public Service Commission for the Union and a Public Service Commission for each:
questions.explanation: Article 315 provides for the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and State Public Service Commissions (SPSC).

questions.question_text: Under Article 324 of the Constitution of India, the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and conduct of all elections to Parliament and State Legislatures is vested in:
questions.explanation: Article 324 vests election management exclusively in the independent Election Commission of India.

questions.question_text: Under Article 352 of the Constitution of India, the President may proclaim a National Emergency if satisfied that a grave emergency exists threatening the security of India by:
options: War, external aggression or armed rebellion
questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment Act 1978 substituted "armed rebellion" for "internal disturbance" under Article 352.

questions.question_text: Under Article 356 of the Constitution of India, if the President on receipt of a report from the Governor of a State or otherwise is satisfied that governance cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution, he may issue a proclamation imposing:
questions.explanation: Article 356 governs President's Rule in a State upon failure of constitutional machinery.

questions.question_text: Under Article 360 of the Constitution of India, if the President is satisfied that financial stability or credit of India or any part of the territory is threatened, he may proclaim:
questions.explanation: Article 360 provides for Financial Emergency (which has never been declared in India so far).

questions.question_text: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court interpreted Article 21 to hold that procedure established by law depriving a person of personal liberty must be:
questions.explanation: In Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Supreme Court held that procedural law under Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable, incorporating substantive due process.
questions.statute_or_case: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)

questions.question_text: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) (Mandal Case), the Supreme Court upheld 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) subject to exclusion of the:
questions.explanation: Indra Sawhney (1992) capped total reservations at 50% and mandated exclusion of the "Creamy Layer" from OBC reservation benefits.
questions.statute_or_case: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Constitution guarantees Freedom of Speech and Expression, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)?
questions.explanation: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees to all citizens the right to freedom of speech and expression.

questions.question_text: Under Article 20(2) of the Constitution of India, no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. This is the doctrine of:
questions.explanation: Article 20(2) protects against Double Jeopardy.

questions.question_text: Under Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India, no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. This protects against:
questions.explanation: Article 20(3) protects an accused person against self-incrimination.

questions.question_text: Under Article 25 of the Constitution of India, freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion is subject to:
options: Public order, morality and health, and to other provisions of Part III
questions.explanation: Article 25(1) guarantees freedom of religion subject to public order, morality, health, and other Fundamental Rights.

questions.question_text: Under Article 30 of the Constitution of India, all minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to:
options: Establish and administer educational institutions of their choice
questions.explanation: Article 30(1) grants religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions.

questions.question_text: Under Article 39A of the Constitution of India, the State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall provide:
options: Free legal aid by suitable legislation or schemes
questions.explanation: Article 39A inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976 directs the State to provide free legal aid to ensure equal justice.

questions.question_text: Under Article 54 of the Constitution of India, the President is elected by members of an Electoral College consisting of:
options: All members of Parliament and State Assemblies including nominated members
Elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States (including Delhi and Puducherry)
Members of Lok Sabha and Governors only
questions.explanation: Article 54 specifies that the Electoral College for Presidential election comprises elected members of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies.

questions.question_text: Under Article 64 of the Constitution of India, the Vice-President of India shall be ex officio:
options: Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha)
questions.explanation: Article 64 enacts that the Vice-President shall be ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.

questions.question_text: Under Article 74(1) of the Constitution of India, there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, who shall in exercise of his functions:
options: Disregard the advice at his personal discretion
Refer all advice to Supreme Court
Act only on written approval of Speaker
Act in accordance with such advice (provided President may require reconsideration once)
questions.explanation: Article 74(1) as amended by 42nd & 44th Amendments binds the President to act in accordance with Council of Ministers' advice, with a single power to request reconsideration.

questions.question_text: Under Article 105 of the Constitution of India, members of Parliament enjoy freedom of speech in Parliament and immunity from court proceedings in respect of:
options: Anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof
questions.explanation: Article 105(2) grants absolute parliamentary immunity for speeches and votes within Parliament.

questions.question_text: In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) (NJAC Case), the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act and NJAC Act, restoring the:
questions.explanation: The 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down the NJAC Act as unconstitutional for violating judicial independence, restoring the Collegium System.

questions.question_text: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a 9-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court unanimously declared that the Right to Privacy is a Fundamental Right guaranteed under:
options: Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution
questions.explanation: In Puttaswamy (2017), the 9-judge Bench affirmed that Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21.
questions.statute_or_case: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)

questions.question_text: Which words were added to the Preamble of the Constitution of India by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976?
questions.explanation: The 42nd Amendment Act 1976 inserted the words "Socialist", "Secular", and "Integrity" into the Preamble.

questions.question_text: Under Article 1 of the Constitution of India, India, that is Bharat, shall be a:
questions.explanation: Article 1(1) declares that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.

questions.question_text: Under Article 3 of the Constitution of India, Parliament may by law form a new State, alter the area, boundaries or name of any State. Such a Bill can be introduced in Parliament only on the recommendation of the:
questions.explanation: Article 3 proviso mandates prior recommendation of the President before introducing a Bill for altering State boundaries or names.

questions.question_text: Under Article 12 of the Constitution of India, the definition of "the State" for Part III includes:
options: Government and Legislature of each of the States
All local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India
questions.explanation: Article 12 defines "State" broadly to include executive, legislative, local, and statutory authorities (including public sector instrumentalities under R.D. Shetty test).

questions.question_text: Under Article 13(2) of the Constitution of India, the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III. Any law made in contravention shall be:
options: Valid until challenged in High Court
Void to the extent of contravention
questions.explanation: Article 13(2) incorporates the rule of Judicial Review rendering unconstitutional laws void ab initio to the extent of inconsistency with Fundamental Rights.

questions.question_text: Under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India, the State may make provision for reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which in the opinion of the State is:
options: Not adequately represented in the services under the State
questions.explanation: Article 16(4) empowers the State to make reservations for backward classes not adequately represented in public employment.

questions.question_text: Under Article 22(2) of the Constitution of India, every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest Magistrate within a period of how many hours of such arrest?
questions.explanation: Article 22(2) guarantees production of an arrested person before a Magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey time.

questions.question_text: Under Article 23 of the Constitution of India, traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited. Any contravention shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law. This right is available against:
options: The State as well as private individuals
questions.explanation: Article 23 is a Fundamental Right enforceable against both State and private individuals (PUDR v. Union of India).

questions.question_text: Under Article 24 of the Constitution of India, no child below which age shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment?
questions.explanation: Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines or hazardous occupations.

questions.question_text: Under Article 31B of the Constitution of India, Acts and Regulations specified in which Schedule shall not be deemed to be void on the ground of inconsistency with Fundamental Rights?
questions.explanation: Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule were inserted by the 1st Constitutional Amendment 1951 to protect land reform laws from judicial review (subject to I.R. Coelho basic structure test after 24th April 1973).
questions.statute_or_case: Article 31B, Ninth Schedule, Constitution of India

questions.question_text: Under Article 53 of the Constitution of India, the executive power of the Union shall be vested in the:
questions.explanation: Article 53(1) vests the executive power of the Union in the President, to be exercised directly or through officers subordinate to him.

questions.question_text: Under Article 58 of the Constitution of India, what is the minimum age qualification for a person to be eligible for election as President of India?
questions.explanation: Article 58(1)(b) mandates that a candidate for President must have completed the age of thirty-five years.

questions.question_text: Under Article 60 of the Constitution of India, before entering upon his office, the President takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution. Who administers this oath?
options: Chief Justice of India (or senior-most Judge of Supreme Court)
questions.explanation: Article 60 enacts that the oath of office to the President is administered by the Chief Justice of India.

questions.question_text: Under Article 66 of the Constitution of India, the Vice-President is elected by members of an Electoral College consisting of:
options: Members of both Houses of Parliament (both elected and nominated)
Elected members of Parliament and State Assemblies
questions.explanation: Article 66(1) specifies that the Electoral College for Vice-President comprises all members of both Houses of Parliament.

questions.question_text: Under Article 75(3) of the Constitution of India, the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to:
options: The House of the People (Lok Sabha)
questions.explanation: Article 75(3) embodies the core principle of parliamentary democracy: collective responsibility of Cabinet to Lok Sabha.

questions.question_text: Under Article 78 of the Constitution of India, it shall be the duty of the Prime Minister to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to administration and proposals for legislation. This establishes:
options: Constitutional channel of communication between PM and President
questions.explanation: Article 78 defines the PM's duties to keep the President informed on Union administrative and legislative affairs.

questions.question_text: Under Article 80 of the Constitution of India, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) consists of how many members nominated by the President having special knowledge in literature, science, art and social service?
questions.explanation: Article 80(1)(a) empowers the President to nominate 12 members to Rajya Sabha for special contribution to literature, science, art, and social service.

questions.question_text: Under Article 84 of the Constitution of India, what is the minimum age qualification for a citizen to be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha)?
questions.explanation: Article 84(b) prescribes a minimum age of 30 years for Rajya Sabha membership (and 25 years for Lok Sabha).

questions.question_text: Under Article 85(1) of the Constitution of India, the President shall summon each House of Parliament such that how much period shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and first sitting in next session?
questions.explanation: Article 85(1) mandates that the maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament shall not exceed six months.

questions.question_text: Under Article 108 of the Constitution of India, if a Bill passed by one House is rejected by the other, the President may summon a Joint Sitting of both Houses. Who presides over the Joint Sitting?
questions.explanation: Under Article 118(4), the Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over a Joint Sitting of Parliament summoned under Article 108.

questions.question_text: Under Article 111 of the Constitution of India, when a Bill has been passed by both Houses of Parliament, it shall be presented to the President who may:
options: Return the Bill (if not a Money Bill) for reconsideration
questions.explanation: Article 111 specifies Presidential options regarding Bills passed by Parliament.

questions.question_text: Under Article 112 of the Constitution of India, the annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India laid before Parliament is constitutionally designated as:
questions.explanation: Article 112 terms the annual budget presented by Finance Minister as the "Annual Financial Statement".

questions.question_text: Under Article 124(2) of the Constitution of India, every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President and shall hold office until he attains the age of:
questions.explanation: Article 124(2) prescribes the retirement age for Supreme Court Judges as sixty-five years (whereas High Court Judges retire at 62 under Article 217).

questions.question_text: Under Article 131 of the Constitution of India, the Supreme Court has exclusive Original Jurisdiction in disputes between:
options: Government of India and one or more States
Government of India and any State on one side and one or more other States on the other
questions.explanation: Article 131 confers exclusive Original Jurisdiction on the Supreme Court for federal inter-governmental disputes.

questions.question_text: Under Article 137 of the Constitution of India, the Supreme Court shall have power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it. This is the power of:
questions.explanation: Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments subject to Parliamentary law and rules.

questions.question_text: Under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, the Supreme Court in exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter. This power was notably invoked in:
options: Ayodhya Title Suit & Bhopal Gas Leak settlements
questions.explanation: Article 142 gives plenary inherent power to the Supreme Court to do complete justice.

questions.question_text: Under Article 153 of the Constitution of India, there shall be a Governor for each State, provided that nothing shall prevent the appointment of the same person as Governor for:
questions.explanation: Article 153 proviso (inserted by 7th Amendment 1956) permits appointing the same person as Governor for two or more States.

questions.question_text: Under Article 161 of the Constitution of India, the Governor of a State has power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment for offences against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends, except:
options: Pardoning a death sentence (which is exclusive to the President under Article 72)
questions.explanation: While Governor can remit or commute death sentences, the power to grant full pardon for a death sentence rests with the President under Article 72.

questions.question_text: Under Article 169 of the Constitution of India, Parliament may by law provide for the abolition of the Legislative Council of a State having such a Council or for creation of such a Council if the Legislative Assembly of the State passes a resolution supported by:
options: Special majority (majority of total membership and not less than 2/3rd members present and voting)
questions.explanation: Article 169 requires a special majority resolution by the State Assembly to request Parliament to create or abolish a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad).

questions.question_text: Under Article 215 of the Constitution of India, every High Court shall be a:
options: Court of Record and shall have all powers including power to punish for contempt of itself
questions.explanation: Article 215 declares High Courts to be Courts of Record with contempt powers.

questions.question_text: Under Article 217 of the Constitution of India, a Judge of a High Court holds office until he attains the age of:
questions.explanation: Article 217(1) prescribes 62 years as the retirement age for High Court Judges (raised from 60 by 15th Amendment 1963).

questions.question_text: Under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, every High Court shall have superintendence over:
options: All courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction (except military tribunals)
questions.explanation: Article 227 confers power of judicial and administrative superintendence on High Courts over all subordinate courts and tribunals.

questions.question_text: Under Article 233 of the Constitution of India, appointments of persons to be, and the posting and promotion of, District Judges in any State shall be made by the:
options: Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Article 233 mandates Governor appointment of District Judges in consultation with the High Court.

questions.question_text: Under Article 262 of the Constitution of India, Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of waters of:
options: Any inter-State river or river valley
questions.explanation: Article 262 empowers Parliament to enact laws (such as Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956) barring Supreme Court jurisdiction in river water disputes.

questions.question_text: Under Article 279A of the Constitution of India, inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act 2016, who is the Chairperson of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council?
questions.explanation: Article 279A(2)(a) designates the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson of the GST Council.

questions.question_text: Under Article 311(2) of the Constitution of India, no civil servant shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank except after an inquiry in which he has been informed of charges and given a:
options: Reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges
questions.explanation: Article 311(2) guarantees constitutional protection against arbitrary dismissal of civil servants by requiring reasonable opportunity of hearing.

questions.question_text: Under Part XIVA inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976, Article 323A empowers Parliament to establish by law administrative tribunals for adjudication of disputes relating to recruitment and conditions of service of public servants. Landmark judgment upholding tribunal validity is:
options: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
questions.explanation: In L. Chandra Kumar (1997), Supreme Court held tribunal decisions subject to High Court judicial review under Article 226/227.

questions.question_text: Under Article 338 of the Constitution of India, which constitutional body is established to investigate and monitor all matters relating to safeguards provided for Scheduled Castes?
questions.explanation: Article 338 provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes.

questions.question_text: Under Article 338A of the Constitution of India, inserted by the 89th Amendment Act 2003, which distinct constitutional body was created for Scheduled Tribes?
questions.explanation: Article 338A created the separate National Commission for Scheduled Tribes.

questions.question_text: Under Article 343(1) of the Constitution of India, the official language of the Union shall be:
options: Hindi and English jointly for all times without law
questions.explanation: Article 343(1) prescribes Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union.

questions.question_text: Under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution of India (Anti-Defection Law), inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act 1985, who decides questions as to disqualification of a member of a House on ground of defection?
options: Chairman or Speaker of the respective House
questions.explanation: Paragraph 6 of the Tenth Schedule vests decision on anti-defection disqualification in the Speaker/Chairman of the House (subject to Kihoto Hollohan judicial review).

questions.question_text: In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court held that the Speaker/Chairman acting under the Tenth Schedule functions as a:
options: Tribunal and his decision is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 136
questions.explanation: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) held that Speaker's decisions under anti-defection law are subject to High Court/Supreme Court judicial review.

questions.question_text: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a 9-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 is:
options: Subject to judicial review and floor test is the only legal test to prove majority of Government
questions.explanation: S.R. Bommai (1994) established floor test as mandatory and brought Presidential proclamations under Article 356 under judicial review.
questions.statute_or_case: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)

questions.question_text: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar Case 2018), the Supreme Court held that passing Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill under Article 110 was valid by majority, but struck down Section 57 which allowed:
options: Private corporate entities to use Aadhaar for authentication
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court struck down Section 57 of Aadhaar Act allowing private entities to demand Aadhaar data.

questions.question_text: In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court decriminalized consensual homosexual acts between adults by reading down which section of IPC for violating Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21?
questions.explanation: Navtej Singh Johar (2018) struck down Section 377 IPC to the extent it criminalized consensual sexual acts between adults.
questions.statute_or_case: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)

questions.question_text: In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court struck down Section 497 of IPC (Adultery) as unconstitutional for violating Articles 14, 15 and 21 because it treated woman as:
questions.explanation: Joseph Shine (2018) struck down Adultery (Section 497 IPC) as manifest arbitrariness violating gender equality.
questions.statute_or_case: Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018)

questions.question_text: By which Constitutional Amendment Act was 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in education and public employment introduced (Articles 15(6) and 16(6))?
questions.explanation: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act 2019 introduced 10% EWS quota (upheld in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India 2022).

questions.question_text: Which Constitutional Amendment Act substituted "Goods and Services Tax Council" (Article 279A) and introduced nationwide GST under Article 246A?
questions.explanation: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act 2016 introduced Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India.

questions.question_text: Under Article 356 of the Constitution of India, a proclamation of President's Rule must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within how many months from the date of issue?
questions.explanation: Article 356(3) mandates that President's Rule proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of two months unless approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament.

questions.question_text: In Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) v. Union of India (2024), a 5-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court declared which scheme unconstitutional for violating the voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a)?
questions.explanation: In February 2024, the Supreme Court unanimously struck down the Electoral Bonds Scheme as unconstitutional under Article 19(1)(a).

questions.question_text: The Code on Wages, 2019 is:
questions.explanation: The Code on Wages received Presidential assent on 8 August 2019 and is Act No. 29 of 2019; it was the first of the four labour codes to be enacted.

questions.question_text: Under Section 69 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the Code subsumes and repeals which four earlier enactments?
options: The Factories Act, 1948; the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; the Trade Unions Act, 1926; and the Contract Labour Act, 1970
The Employees' Provident Funds Act, 1952; the ESI Act, 1948; the Gratuity Act, 1972; and the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961
The Payment of Wages Act, 1936; the Minimum Wages Act, 1948; the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965; and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976
Only the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 and the Payment of Wages Act, 1936
questions.explanation: Section 69(1) repeals the Payment of Wages Act 1936, the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act 1976, consolidating them into a single Code.

questions.question_text: A key change made by the Code on Wages, 2019 compared to the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is that:
options: Minimum wages are abolished for the unorganised sector
Only the Central Government may fix minimum wages
Minimum wages apply only to factories
Minimum wages now cover all employees in all employments, not merely the 'scheduled employments' notified under the old Act
questions.explanation: The Code universalises the statutory minimum wage: Section 5 prohibits any employer from paying any employee less than the notified minimum rate of wages, irrespective of sector or scheduled-employment status.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the 'floor wage' is:
options: Fixed by the Central Government taking into account the minimum living standards of a worker, below which no State's minimum wage may fall
The maximum wage an employer is required to pay
Fixed by each State independently with no central benchmark
The same as the bonus ceiling
questions.explanation: Section 9 introduces the concept of a nationally-set floor wage; minimum rates of wages fixed by the appropriate Government cannot be less than the floor wage, and existing higher minimum wages cannot be reduced. Different floor wages may be set for different geographical areas.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the Code on Wages, 2019, discrimination among employees on the ground of gender is prohibited in matters relating to wages:
options: By the same employer, in respect of the same work or work of a similar nature
Only where more than 100 workers are employed
Only in respect of recruitment, not wages
questions.explanation: Section 3 (which absorbs the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976) bars gender-based wage discrimination for same or similar work; Section 3(2) forbids reducing anyone's wages to comply and bars gender discrimination in recruitment except where women's employment is restricted by law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(y) of the Code on Wages, 2019, the term 'wages' includes basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance, but EXCLUDES:
options: Bonus, house rent allowance, conveyance allowance, overtime allowance, commission, gratuity and employer's provident-fund contribution
questions.explanation: Section 2(y) lists specific exclusions; a proviso caps the total of the excluded components at 50% (or a notified percentage) of total remuneration, adding any excess back into 'wages'.

questions.question_text: Under the first proviso to Section 2(y) of the Code on Wages, 2019, if the excluded components (bonus, HRA, etc.) exceed one-half of total remuneration:
options: The employer may ignore the excess entirely
The whole of the excluded components is added to wages
The amount in excess of one-half is deemed to be remuneration and is added back into 'wages'
questions.explanation: This 50% rule prevents employers from structuring salaries with a small 'basic' component to reduce statutory contributions (PF, gratuity, bonus) that are computed on 'wages'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(4) of the Code on Wages, 2019, the appropriate Government must review or revise minimum rates of wages ordinarily at intervals not exceeding:
questions.explanation: Section 8(4) fixes a maximum five-year cycle for revision of minimum wages, consistent with the old Minimum Wages Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(3) of the Code on Wages, 2019, where minimum wages are revised by the notification method, a revised notification comes into force (unless it provides otherwise) on the expiry of:
options: Three months from the date of its issue
questions.explanation: Section 8(3) provides a default three-month lead time; where the notification method is used, the concerned Advisory Board under Section 42 must also be consulted.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the Code on Wages, 2019, an employee who works beyond the normal working day is entitled to overtime wages at a rate not less than:
options: One and a half times the normal rate
Twice the normal rate of wages
questions.explanation: Section 14 sets the statutory overtime rate at a minimum of double the normal rate of wages.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the wage period fixed by an employer for any employee:
options: May be as long as one quarter
Is left entirely to the employee's choice
Must be daily, weekly, fortnightly or monthly, and in no case more than a month
questions.explanation: Section 16 caps the wage period at one month; Section 15 requires wages to be paid in coin, currency, cheque, bank credit or electronic mode.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of the Code on Wages, 2019, where an employee is removed, dismissed, retrenched or resigns, his wages must be paid within:
options: Two working days of his removal, dismissal, retrenchment or resignation
questions.explanation: Section 17 requires final wages on cessation of employment to be paid within two working days; for a monthly wage period, current wages are payable before the seventh day of the following month.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18(3) of the Code on Wages, 2019, the total amount of deductions from an employee's wages in any wage period must not exceed:
options: Seventy-five per cent of the wages
Fifty per cent of the wages
Twenty-five per cent of the wages
One hundred per cent of the wages
questions.explanation: Section 18(3) caps aggregate deductions at 50% of wages; only the purposes listed in Section 18(2) (fines, absence, damage/loss, house accommodation, recovery of advances, statutory levies, etc.) are permissible.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the total amount of fine that may be imposed on an employee in any one wage period must not exceed:
options: Ten per cent of the wages
Twenty per cent of the wages
Three per cent of the wages payable to him in respect of that wage period
One per cent of the wages
questions.explanation: Section 19 caps fines at 3% of the wage-period wages, bars fines on employees under 15 years, bars recovery by instalments or after 90 days, and requires prior Government approval of the list of finable acts and an opportunity to show cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(5) of the Code on Wages, 2019, no fine may be imposed on an employee who is under the age of:
questions.explanation: Section 19(5) prohibits fining any employee below 15 years of age.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26(1) of the Code on Wages, 2019, an employee who has put in at least 30 days' work in an accounting year is entitled to an annual minimum bonus of:
options: 8.33 per cent of the wages earned, or one hundred rupees, whichever is higher, whether or not the employer has any allocable surplus
20 per cent of wages in every case
Only such bonus as the employer chooses to declare
5 per cent of wages, subject to profits
questions.explanation: Section 26(1) guarantees a minimum bonus of 8.33% (or Rs 100) regardless of surplus; Section 26(3) caps the maximum bonus at 20% of wages where allocable surplus permits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the maximum bonus payable to an employee in an accounting year is:
options: Ten per cent of the wages
Twenty per cent of the wages earned in that accounting year
Fifty per cent of the wages
questions.explanation: Section 26(3) and 26(5) cap total bonus (including production/productivity-linked bonus) at 20% of the wages earned in the accounting year.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the Code on Wages, 2019, an employee is disqualified from receiving bonus if he is dismissed from service for:
options: Fraud; riotous or violent behaviour on the premises; theft, misappropriation or sabotage of establishment property; or conviction for sexual harassment
questions.explanation: Section 29 lists four specific grounds of dismissal that disqualify an employee from bonus, including the newly-added ground of conviction for sexual harassment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the 'allocable surplus' out of which bonus is paid is:
options: Always one hundred per cent of gross profit
Fixed at 8.33 per cent of turnover
Determined solely by the trade union
Sixty-seven per cent of the available surplus for a non-banking establishment, and sixty per cent for a banking company
questions.explanation: Section 31(1) sets allocable surplus at 67% of available surplus for non-banking establishments and 60% for banking companies; available surplus is computed under Section 33 after prior charges under Section 34.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of the Code on Wages, 2019, bonus must ordinarily be paid within:
options: Eight months from the close of the accounting year (extendable, but the total period cannot exceed two years)
One month from the close of the accounting year
questions.explanation: Section 39(1) requires payment of bonus by crediting the employee's bank account within eight months of the close of the accounting year, extendable for sufficient reasons up to a maximum aggregate of two years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the bonus chapter applies to every establishment in which:
options: Ten or more persons are employed
Twenty or more persons are employed, or were employed on any day during an accounting year
One hundred or more persons are employed
Any number of persons is employed
questions.explanation: Section 41(2) applies the bonus chapter to establishments with 20 or more employees; Section 41(1) exempts specified bodies such as the RBI, LIC and non-profit hospitals and educational institutions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 42 of the Code on Wages, 2019, in the Central Advisory Board and State Advisory Boards, the proportion of members who must be women is:
questions.explanation: Section 42(2) and 42(7) require that one-third of the members of the Central and State Advisory Boards be women; these Boards advise on minimum wages and on increasing employment opportunities for women.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the authority hearing a claim may, in addition to the claim determined, award compensation up to:
options: Twice the amount of the claim
The same amount as the claim
Fifty per cent of the claim
Ten times the amount of the claim determined
questions.explanation: Section 45(2) empowers the claims authority (an officer not below Gazetted rank) to award compensation of up to ten times the claim and to endeavour to decide the claim within three months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45(6) of the Code on Wages, 2019, an application for a claim must ordinarily be filed within:
options: Three years from the date on which the claim arises (condonable for sufficient cause)
questions.explanation: Section 45(6) prescribes a three-year limitation, extendable on sufficient cause; this is a significant expansion over the old 12-month period under the Payment of Wages Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 49 of the Code on Wages, 2019, an appeal against an order of the claims authority must be filed with the appellate authority within:
options: Ninety days from the date of the order (condonable for sufficient cause)
questions.explanation: Section 49(1) provides a 90-day appeal window; the appellate authority is an officer at least one rank higher than the claims authority and endeavours to decide the appeal within three months.

questions.question_text: Under the Code on Wages, 2019, the officer who inspects establishments is designated the:
options: Inspector-cum-Facilitator, with both an advisory role and an inspection role, subject to a web-based randomised inspection scheme
questions.explanation: Section 51 replaces the traditional 'Inspector' with an 'Inspector-cum-Facilitator' who advises employers and workers on compliance and inspects establishments under a notified, technology-enabled inspection scheme.

questions.question_text: Under Section 52 of the Code on Wages, 2019, a court may take cognizance of an offence under the Code only on a complaint made by:
options: The appropriate Government or an authorised officer, or an employee, or a registered Trade Union, or the Inspector-cum-Facilitator
questions.explanation: Section 52(1) lists who may complain; Section 52(2) bars any court inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class from trying offences under the Code.

questions.question_text: Under Section 54(1)(a) of the Code on Wages, 2019, an employer who pays an employee less than the amount due under the Code is punishable with:
options: Fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees
Imprisonment for not less than one year
Fine of exactly one lakh rupees and imprisonment
questions.explanation: Section 54(1)(a) prescribes a fine up to Rs 50,000 for underpayment; a repeat offence within five years attracts imprisonment up to three months or fine up to Rs 1 lakh or both.

questions.question_text: Under Section 54(3) of the Code on Wages, 2019, before initiating prosecution for certain contraventions, the Inspector-cum-Facilitator must:
options: Immediately file a complaint without notice
Give the employer an opportunity to comply through a written direction within a specified period (not for a repeat of the same violation within five years)
Obtain the sanction of the High Court
questions.explanation: Section 54(3) mandates a compliance opportunity before prosecution for first-time offences under Section 54(1)(c) and 54(2), shifting the enforcement approach from penal to facilitative.

questions.question_text: Under Section 56 of the Code on Wages, 2019, an offence not punishable with imprisonment only (or imprisonment and fine) may be compounded for:
options: The full maximum fine plus costs
Ten per cent of the maximum fine
A sum of fifty per cent of the maximum fine provided for the offence
questions.explanation: Section 56(1) allows compounding for 50% of the maximum fine; compounding is barred for a repeat offence within five years of an earlier compounded or convicted similar offence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 59 of the Code on Wages, 2019, where a claim is filed for non-payment or short payment of wages or bonus, or for unauthorised deductions:
options: The burden lies entirely on the employee
There is no burden of proof; the authority decides on affidavits
The trade union must prove non-payment
The burden to prove that the dues have been paid lies on the employer
questions.explanation: Section 59 places the burden of proving payment on the employer, recognising that wage and payment records are within the employer's control.

questions.question_text: Under Section 60 of the Code on Wages, 2019, an agreement by which an employee relinquishes his right to any amount or bonus due under the Code is:
options: Null and void in so far as it purports to remove or reduce the employer's liability
Valid if witnessed by a notary
questions.explanation: Section 60 bars contracting out of statutory wage and bonus entitlements; Section 61 gives the Code overriding effect over inconsistent awards, agreements, settlements or contracts of service.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(k) of the Code on Wages, 2019, the definition of 'employee' excludes:
options: An apprentice engaged under the Apprentices Act, 1961, and members of the Armed Forces of the Union
Anyone earning above Rs 21,000 per month
questions.explanation: Section 2(k) defines 'employee' widely to include skilled, semi-skilled, unskilled, manual, supervisory, managerial, administrative, technical and clerical staff, but excludes apprentices under the Apprentices Act and armed-forces personnel.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Code on Wages, 2019, in fixing minimum wages the appropriate Government must primarily take into account:
options: Only the profits of the employer
The skill of workers (unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled, highly-skilled) and/or the geographical area, and may additionally consider arduousness of work
questions.explanation: Section 6(6) requires the Government to base minimum-wage fixation primarily on skill category and geographical area, and permits additional weight for hazardous or arduous work.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the Code on Wages, 2019:
options: An employer may pay below the minimum wage with the employee's written consent
Minimum wages apply only to time-rated workers
Minimum wages are advisory, not mandatory
No employer shall pay to any employee wages less than the minimum rate of wages notified by the appropriate Government
questions.explanation: Section 5 is the core prohibition: payment below the notified minimum rate of wages is unlawful and cannot be waived by agreement (Section 60).

questions.question_text: Under Section 46 of the Code on Wages, 2019, a dispute about the fixation of, or eligibility for, bonus:
options: Is deemed to be an industrial dispute within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
Must be filed as a civil suit
Is decided by the Company Law Tribunal
questions.explanation: Section 46 routes bonus-quantum and eligibility disputes into the industrial-dispute machinery.

questions.question_text: Under Section 44 of the Code on Wages, 2019, amounts payable to an employee that cannot be paid because of his death or unknown whereabouts are:
options: Paid to the person nominated by him, or, in the absence of a valid nomination, deposited with the prescribed authority
questions.explanation: Section 44 provides for payment to the nominee or deposit with the prescribed authority, discharging the employer's liability once so paid or deposited.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the Code on Wages, 2019, an employee whose minimum wage is fixed by the day and who is required to work but is provided less than a full normal working day's work:
options: Is paid only for the hours actually worked in every case
Is entitled to wages as if he had worked a full normal working day (unless his own unwillingness caused the shortfall)
Is paid double for the shortfall
questions.explanation: Section 10 protects day-rated workers against loss of wages when the employer fails to provide a full day's work, subject to the proviso for the worker's own unwillingness.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45(3) of the Code on Wages, 2019, if an employer fails to pay the claim and compensation determined, the claims authority:
options: Files a fresh civil suit against the employer
Refers the matter to the police
Issues a certificate of recovery to the Collector or District Magistrate, who recovers the amount as arrears of land revenue
questions.explanation: Section 45(3) provides a summary revenue-recovery mechanism for enforcing wage and bonus claims.

questions.question_text: Under Section 61 of the Code on Wages, 2019, the provisions of the Code:
options: Have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in any other law or in any award, agreement, settlement or contract of service
Are subordinate to any collective settlement
Apply only where no contract of service exists
questions.explanation: Section 61 is the non-obstante clause giving the Code overriding effect over inconsistent instruments; Section 66 saves the MGNREGA, 2005 and the Coal Mines Provident Fund Act, 1948.

questions.question_text: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
options: Merely amended the Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Is Act No. 35 of 2019 and repealed and replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Applies only to goods, not services
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act (in force largely from 20 July 2020) repealed the 1986 Act and introduced the Central Consumer Protection Authority, product liability, mediation and e-commerce regulation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a 'consumer' does NOT include a person who:
options: Uses services with the approval of the person who hired them
Obtains goods for resale or for any commercial purpose (but the use of goods or services exclusively for earning a livelihood by means of self-employment is not a 'commercial purpose')
Buys goods through an online marketplace
questions.explanation: Section 2(7) expressly covers online and electronic transactions, but excludes purchases for resale or commercial purpose, with the self-employment/livelihood carve-out.

questions.question_text: A new concept introduced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (not present in the 1986 Act) is:
options: Product liability — the responsibility of a product manufacturer, service provider or seller to compensate for harm caused by a defective product
questions.explanation: Chapter VI (Sections 82-87) creates a statutory product-liability action; other new features include the CCPA, 'unfair contracts', endorser liability and mediation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) is established to:
options: Regulate matters relating to violation of consumer rights, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements which prejudice the public and consumers as a class
Fix the prices of essential commodities
questions.explanation: The CCPA is a class-action regulator with an Investigation Wing headed by a Director-General (Section 15); individual disputes go to the Consumer Commissions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the CCPA may, for a false or misleading advertisement, impose on a manufacturer or endorser a penalty which may extend to:
options: Ten lakh rupees (and up to fifty lakh rupees for every subsequent contravention), and may prohibit the endorser from endorsing that product or service for up to one year (three years for a subsequent contravention)
Nothing; the CCPA has no penalty power
questions.explanation: Section 21 gives the CCPA power to order discontinuation or modification of misleading advertisements and to penalise manufacturers, service providers, publishers and endorsers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 as amended by the 2021 Rules, the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has jurisdiction where the value of the consideration paid does not exceed:
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act originally set the District limit at Rs 1 crore; the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021 revised it to Rs 50 lakh, with the State Commission from Rs 50 lakh to Rs 2 crore and the National Commission above Rs 2 crore.

questions.question_text: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (as revised by the 2021 Rules), the pecuniary jurisdiction of the State Commission is:
options: Complaints exceeding one crore but not ten crore rupees
Only appeals, with no original jurisdiction
Complaints where the consideration paid exceeds fifty lakh rupees but does not exceed two crore rupees
questions.explanation: The State Commission also hears appeals against District Commission orders and complaints of unfair contracts within its pecuniary limit.

questions.question_text: A significant change to pecuniary jurisdiction made by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is that jurisdiction is now determined by:
options: The value of the consideration paid for the goods or services (not the value of goods/services plus the compensation claimed, as under the 1986 Act)
The place where the goods were manufactured
The turnover of the opposite party
questions.explanation: This shift, confirmed by the Supreme Court, generally reduces the value on which jurisdiction is computed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34(2) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a complaint may be instituted in a District Commission within whose jurisdiction:
options: Only the opposite party carries on business
The complainant resides or personally works for gain (in addition to the places where the opposite party resides or carries on business)
Only the registered office of the opposite party is located
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act adds the complainant's place of residence or work as a forum, a consumer-friendly change from the 1986 Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a consumer complaint:
options: Can only be filed in writing and in person
Must be filed by an advocate
May be filed in person or by electronic mode in the prescribed manner, and by a single complainant or by a recognised consumer association or by the Central/State Government
Can only be filed by the affected individual
questions.explanation: Section 35 permits electronic filing and representative complaints; a complaint can also be filed by one or more consumers on behalf of numerous consumers with the same interest.

questions.question_text: Under Section 37 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, at the first hearing after admission of a complaint (or later), the Commission may:
options: Refer the dispute to arbitration only
Dismiss the complaint if the parties are willing to talk
Do nothing; mediation is not available
Refer the dispute for settlement by mediation, where there exists an element of settlement acceptable to both parties
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act introduces a consumer-mediation mechanism (Sections 74-81), with consumer mediation cells attached to each Commission.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a consumer complaint should ordinarily be decided within:
options: Three months from the date of receipt of notice by the opposite party where the complaint does not require analysis or testing of commodities, and five months where it does
questions.explanation: Section 38(7) sets the 3-month / 5-month timelines for disposal, though these are widely treated as directory.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the reliefs a Consumer Commission may grant include:
options: Only a refund of the price

Removal of defects, replacement of goods, refund of price, payment of compensation (including for injury due to negligence), discontinuation of unfair or restrictive trade practices, withdrawal of hazardous goods, and punitive damages
Only an apology from the seller
questions.explanation: Section 39 gives a wide menu of reliefs, including punitive damages and compensation for loss or injury suffered due to negligence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, an appeal against an order of the District Commission lies to the State Commission within:
options: Thirty days, with a deposit capped at Rs 25,000
Forty-five days of the order, and the appellant (if directed to pay an amount) must deposit fifty per cent of that amount
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act requires a 50% pre-deposit of the awarded amount for the appeal (removing the Rs 25,000 cap that applied under the 1986 Act).

questions.question_text: Under Section 67 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, an appeal to the Supreme Court lies:
options: Against every order of every Consumer Commission
Only with the leave of the High Court
Never; the National Commission's orders are final
Against an order of the National Commission passed in the exercise of its original jurisdiction, within thirty days
questions.explanation: Section 67 restricts the Supreme Court appeal to National Commission orders in original jurisdiction; National Commission orders in appeal are challenged only under Article 227 / Article 136.

questions.question_text: Under Section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a consumer complaint must be filed within:
options: Two years from the date on which the cause of action arises (the Commission may condone delay for sufficient cause, after recording reasons)
Three years, as under the Limitation Act
questions.explanation: Section 69 carries forward the two-year limitation of the 1986 Act, with power to condone delay for sufficient cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 72 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a person who fails to comply with an order of a Consumer Commission is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for a term of one month to three years, or a fine of twenty-five thousand rupees to one lakh rupees, or both
A warning for the first default
questions.explanation: Section 71 makes Commission orders enforceable as decrees; Section 72 criminalises non-compliance.

questions.question_text: Under Section 84 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a product manufacturer is liable in a product-liability action if:
options: Only if the consumer proves negligence
Only if the product caused death

The product contains a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from manufacturing specifications, does not conform to an express warranty, or lacks adequate instructions or warnings — even if the manufacturer proves it was not negligent in making the warning or instruction
Never; only the seller is liable
questions.explanation: Section 84 lists the grounds; a manufacturer is liable on the warning/instruction ground regardless of proof of due care.

questions.question_text: Under Section 86 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a product seller (who is not the manufacturer) is liable in a product-liability action where, among other things:
options: The manufacturer is untraceable, and nothing more

He exercised substantial control over designing, testing, manufacturing, packaging or labelling; or altered or modified the product causing the harm; or failed to exercise reasonable care in assembling, inspecting or maintaining it; or sold a product knowing it was defective
questions.explanation: Section 86 sets a higher bar for seller liability than for manufacturer liability, generally requiring some element of control, alteration or knowledge.

questions.question_text: Under Section 87 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a product-liability action cannot be brought against a product seller where:
options: The product was misused, altered or modified at the time of the harm, or the harm was caused by a person over whom the seller had no control
The product was more than one year old
The consumer did not read the manual
questions.explanation: Section 87 also excludes liability for obvious dangers, or where the product was legally required to be sold only on prescription and adequate warnings were given to the prescriber.

questions.question_text: Under Section 89 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a manufacturer or service provider who causes a false or misleading advertisement prejudicial to consumers' interest is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment up to two years and fine up to ten lakh rupees (and, for a subsequent offence, imprisonment up to five years and fine up to fifty lakh rupees)
No punishment; only a CCPA direction
questions.explanation: Section 89 is the criminal offence for misleading advertisements, distinct from the CCPA's civil penalty power under Section 21.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(47) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, 'unfair trade practice' has been expanded to expressly include:
options: Only false representation about the standard of goods

Failure to issue a bill or cash memo, refusal to take back or withdraw defective goods or deficient services and to refund the consideration within the stipulated time, and disclosure of a consumer's personal information given in confidence (unless required by law or in public interest)
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act broadens 'unfair trade practice' beyond the 1986 list to cover billing, refund and data-privacy failures.

questions.question_text: Section 2(46) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 introduces the concept of an 'unfair contract', meaning a contract between a manufacturer/trader/service provider and a consumer that causes significant change in consumer rights, such as:
options: Any contract that is in writing
Any contract with an arbitration clause
Any contract above Rs 1 lakh in value

Requiring excessive security deposits, imposing a disproportionate penalty for breach, refusing early repayment of debts, terminating without reasonable cause, or unilaterally assigning the contract to the consumer's detriment
questions.explanation: Complaints against unfair contracts lie only to the State Commission or National Commission, not the District Commission.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(11) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, 'deficiency' in a service includes:
options: Any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature or manner of performance required to be maintained, and includes any act of negligence or omission that causes loss or injury, and deliberate withholding of relevant information
Only a total failure to perform the service
questions.explanation: The definition of 'deficiency' is expanded in the 2019 Act to expressly include negligence and withholding of information.

questions.question_text: Under Section 94 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Central Government may take measures to prevent unfair trade practices in:
options: E-commerce and direct selling (the basis for the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020)
questions.explanation: Section 94 empowers rules regulating e-commerce entities and direct sellers, including disclosure obligations and grievance-redressal mechanisms.

questions.question_text: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a celebrity or public figure who features in an advertisement (an 'endorser'):
options: Can never be held liable for an advertisement
Is liable only if he is also the manufacturer
May be penalised by the CCPA for a false or misleading advertisement, unless he has exercised due diligence to verify the veracity of the claims
Is liable only in a criminal court
questions.explanation: Endorser liability is a headline reform of the 2019 Act, with a due-diligence defence and a possible endorsement ban under Section 21.

questions.question_text: Under Section 100 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
options: The Act overrides all other consumer laws entirely
The Act applies only where no other remedy exists
The Act bars all civil suits
The provisions of the Act are in addition to and not in derogation of any other law for the time being in force
questions.explanation: Section 100 preserves a consumer's alternative remedies; the consumer forum is an additional, not exclusive, forum.

questions.question_text: Under Section 58 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (as revised by the 2021 Rules), the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has original jurisdiction over complaints where the consideration paid:
questions.explanation: The National Commission also hears appeals from State Commissions and exercises revisional jurisdiction; the 2021 Rules set its original pecuniary threshold at above Rs 2 crore.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(9) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, 'consumer rights' include:
options: The right to be protected against hazardous goods and services; the right to be informed; the right to be assured of access to a variety of goods at competitive prices; the right to be heard; the right to seek redressal; and the right to consumer awareness
Only the right to a refund
questions.explanation: Section 2(9) codifies the six basic consumer rights that the Consumer Protection Councils are to promote and protect.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a District Collector may, on a complaint or reference from the CCPA:
options: Inquire into or investigate complaints regarding violation of consumer rights or unfair trade practices and submit a report to the CCPA
questions.explanation: Section 16 gives the District Collector an investigative role feeding into CCPA action.

questions.question_text: Under Section 40 and Section 50 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the District and State Commissions have power to:
options: Review any order at any time for any reason
Review their own orders where there is an error apparent on the face of the record (a power the District Forum did not have under the 1986 Act)
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act confers a limited power of review on the District and State Commissions, in addition to the appeal remedy.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Civil Courts have jurisdiction to try:
options: All suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred
Service disputes of central employees exclusively
questions.explanation: Section 9 enacts that Civil Courts shall have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature unless expressly or impliedly barred.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of CPC, the doctrine of Res Subjudice mandates:
options: Transfer of suit to High Court
Stay of trial of subsequent suit where matter directly in issue is pending in previously instituted suit
questions.explanation: Section 10 bars the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted pending suit between same parties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the doctrine of Res Judicata prevents:
options: Filing a suit in a court lacking pecuniary jurisdiction
Executing decrees after expiry of 12 years
Re-agitating a matter directly and substantially in issue that has been finally decided between same parties
questions.explanation: Section 11 enacts the rule of Res Judicata, barring courts from trying any suit or issue in which the matter has been directly and substantially decided in a former suit between the same parties.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 16 to 20 of CPC governing the Place of Suing, suits for recovery of immoveable property shall be instituted in the Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction:
options: The subject-matter of property is situate
questions.explanation: Section 16 requires suits relating to immoveable property to be instituted where the property is situated.

questions.question_text: Under Section 80(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, no suit shall be instituted against the Government or against a public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done in his official capacity until expiration of how many months after notice in writing?
questions.explanation: Section 80(1) mandates 2 months prior written notice before instituting a suit against the Government or a public officer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 89 of CPC, where it appears to the court that there exist elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, the court shall formulate terms of settlement and refer the same for:
options: Arbitration, Conciliation, Judicial settlement including Lok Adalat, or Mediation
questions.explanation: Section 89 incorporates Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms into civil procedure.

questions.question_text: Under Section 100 of CPC, a Second Appeal lies to the High Court from any decree passed in appeal by a subordinate court if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a:
questions.explanation: Section 100 restricts Second Appeals strictly to cases involving a substantial question of law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 148A of CPC, any person claiming a right to appear before Court on hearing of an application expected to be made may lodge a Caveat. A Caveat remains in force for how many days from date of lodging?
questions.explanation: Section 148A(5) enacts that a Caveat shall remain in force for ninety days from the date it is lodged.

questions.question_text: Under Section 151 of CPC, nothing in the Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent:
options: Abuse of the process of the Court
questions.explanation: Section 151 preserves inherent powers of Civil Courts to ensure ends of justice and prevent abuse of court process.

questions.question_text: Under Order VII Rule 11 of CPC, a Plaint shall be rejected in which of the following cases?
options: Where it does not disclose a cause of action
Where relief claimed is undervalued and plaintiff fails to correct valuation
Where suit appears from statement in plaint to be barred by any law
questions.explanation: Order VII Rule 11 sets out statutory grounds for rejection of plaint.
questions.statute_or_case: Order VII Rule 11, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order VIII Rule 1 of CPC, the defendant shall present a Written Statement of his defense within how many days from the date of service of summons?
options: 30 days (extendable up to 90 days for reasons to be recorded)
questions.explanation: Order VIII Rule 1 requires written statement within 30 days, extendable up to 90 days maximum.
questions.statute_or_case: Order VIII Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order VI Rule 17 of CPC, the Court may at any stage of proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings, provided no application for amendment shall be allowed after trial has commenced unless court concludes that despite due diligence, party could not have raised matter before:
questions.explanation: Order VI Rule 17 proviso restricts post-trial amendment of pleadings unless due diligence is established.
questions.statute_or_case: Order VI Rule 17, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order IX Rule 13 of CPC, an ex-parte decree passed against a defendant can be set aside if defendant satisfies court that:
options: Summons was not duly served, or he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing
questions.explanation: Order IX Rule 13 provides grounds for setting aside an ex-parte decree upon showing non-service of summons or sufficient cause for absence.
questions.statute_or_case: Order IX Rule 13, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of CPC, Temporary Injunctions may be granted by court where property in dispute is in danger of being wasted, damaged, or alienated by any party, or to prevent:
options: Dispossession or injury to plaintiff in relation to property
questions.explanation: Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2 empower courts to issue temporary injunctions to preserve status quo and prevent injury.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(2) of CPC, "Decree" means formal expression of an adjudication which conclusively determines the rights of parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit. A decree may be:
questions.explanation: Section 2(2) defines Decree, specifying it may be either preliminary or final.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(9) of CPC, "Judgment" means:
options: Statement given by Judge on the grounds of a decree or order
questions.explanation: Section 2(9) defines Judgment as the statement given by Judge of the grounds of a decree or order.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(14) of CPC, "Order" means formal expression of any decision of a Civil Court which is not a:
questions.explanation: Section 2(14) defines Order as formal expression of any decision of a Civil Court which is not a decree.

questions.question_text: Under Section 114 read with Order XLVII of CPC, any person considering himself aggrieved by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred, may apply for a:
options: Review of judgment to the court which passed decree/order
questions.explanation: Section 114 & Order XLVII govern Review of judgment before the same court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 115 of CPC, the High Court may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any court subordinate to such High Court and in which no appeal lies thereto. This power is:
questions.explanation: Section 115 confers Revisionary jurisdiction on the High Court to correct jurisdictional errors.

questions.question_text: Under Section 113 read with Order XLVI of CPC, a subordinate court may state a case and refer the same for opinion of High Court where a question arises as to validity of an Act, Ordinance or Regulation. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 113 governs Reference to High Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 144 of CPC, where a decree or order is reversed or modified in appeal or revision, the court of first instance shall cause such restitution to be made as will place parties in position they would have occupied but for such decree. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 144 defines the rule of Restitution.

questions.question_text: Under Order I Rule 10(2) of CPC, Court may at any stage of proceedings order name of any party improperly joined as plaintiff or defendant to be struck out, or add any person who ought to have been joined. Such person is a:
questions.explanation: Order I Rule 10(2) empowers courts to add necessary or proper parties to enable complete adjudication.
questions.statute_or_case: Order I Rule 10, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order I Rule 8 of CPC, where there are numerous persons having the same interest in one suit, one or more such persons may with permission of Court sue or be sued on behalf of all. This is a:
questions.explanation: Order I Rule 8 governs Representative Suits.
questions.statute_or_case: Order I Rule 8, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXV of CPC, where two or more persons claim adversely to one another the same debt, sum of money or other property from another person who claims no interest therein other than charges/costs and is ready to pay to rightful claimant, he may file an:
questions.explanation: Order XXXV governs Interpleader Suits.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXV, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXVII of CPC, Summary Procedure applies to suits upon bills of exchange, hundis and promissory notes, or suits for recovery of debt/liquidated demand. In summary suit, defendant cannot defend suit unless he obtains:
options: Leave to defend from the Court
questions.explanation: Order XXXVII requires defendant to apply for leave to defend in summary suits.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXVII, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXVIII Rule 5 of CPC, Attachment before Judgment may be ordered by Court if defendant with intent to obstruct or delay execution of decree is about to dispose of whole or part of his:
questions.explanation: Order XXXVIII Rule 5 empowers attachment before judgment to prevent fraudulent disposal of property.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXVIII Rule 5, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XL Rule 1 of CPC, where it appears to Court to be just and convenient, Court may by order appoint a Receiver of any property, whether before or after decree. A Receiver is an officer of:
questions.explanation: Order XL Rule 1 provides for appointment of Receiver as an officer of the Court to manage property.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XL Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 34 of CPC, Court may award interest on principal sum adjudged from date of suit to date of decree, and further interest from date of decree to payment at rate not exceeding:
options: 6% per annum (or commercial rate for commercial transactions)
questions.explanation: Section 34 governs award of interest in civil suits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35A of CPC, where in any suit or proceeding any party objects to any claim or defense on ground that it is false or vexatious to knowledge of party, Court may award compensatory costs up to maximum of:
questions.explanation: Section 35A caps statutory compensatory costs for false or vexatious claims at Rs. 3,000.

questions.question_text: Under Order V Rule 1 of CPC, when a suit has been duly instituted, a Summons may be issued to the defendant to appear and answer the claim within how many days from date of service?
questions.explanation: Order V Rule 1 provides 30 days for appearance upon summons.
questions.statute_or_case: Order V Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(11) of CPC, "Legal Representative" means a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, and includes any person who intermeddles with the estate of the deceased, as well as where a party sues/is sued in representative character:
options: The person on whom estate devolves on death of party so suing/sued
questions.explanation: Section 2(11) defines Legal Representative broadly including intermeddlers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(12) of CPC, "Mesne Profits" of property means those profits which the person in wrongful possession of such property actually received or might with ordinary diligence have received therefrom, together with interest on such profits, BUT shall NOT include:
options: Profits due to improvements made by the person in wrongful possession
questions.explanation: Section 2(12) explicitly excludes profits resulting from improvements made by wrongful possessor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 Explanation IV of CPC, any matter which might and ought to have been made ground of defence or attack in a former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit. This is known as:
questions.explanation: Section 11 Explanation IV codifies Constructive Res Judicata.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 11 Explanation IV, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 Explanation VIII of CPC (inserted by 1976 Amendment), an issue heard and finally decided by a Court of limited jurisdiction competent to decide such issue shall operate as Res Judicata in a subsequent suit, notwithstanding that such court of limited jurisdiction was not competent to try:
options: Such subsequent suit or suit in which such issue has subsequently arisen
questions.explanation: Explanation VIII extends Res Judicata to decisions of courts of limited jurisdiction.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 11 Explanation VIII, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of CPC, a foreign judgment shall be conclusive as to any matter thereby directly adjudicated upon between same parties, EXCEPT when:
options: It has not been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction
It has not been given on merits of the case
It appears on face of proceedings to be founded on incorrect view of international law or refusal to recognize Indian law
questions.explanation: Section 13 lists 6 statutory exceptions when a foreign judgment is not conclusive in India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of CPC, every suit shall be instituted in the Court of the:
options: Lowest grade competent to try it
questions.explanation: Section 15 lays down pecuniary hierarchy requiring suits to be filed in court of lowest competent grade.
