questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of CPC, where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or to movable property, if the wrong was done within local limits of jurisdiction of one court and defendant resides or carries on business in jurisdiction of another court, suit may be instituted at option of plaintiff in:
questions.explanation: Section 19 gives plaintiff option to sue either where wrong was done or where defendant resides.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of CPC, subject to limitations aforesaid, every suit shall be instituted in a Court within local limits of whose jurisdiction the defendant (or each defendant) actually resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, OR where:
options: The cause of action, wholly or in part, arises
questions.explanation: Section 20(c) enacts general territorial jurisdiction where cause of action arises wholly or in part.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21(1) of CPC, no objection as to the place of suing (territorial jurisdiction) shall be allowed by any Appellate or Revisional Court unless such objection was taken in Court of first instance at earliest opportunity and before settlement of issues, AND unless there has been a consequent:
questions.explanation: Section 21 requires early objection AND consequent failure of justice to overturn decree for lack of territorial jurisdiction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of CPC, the High Court or District Court may at any stage of suit transfer any suit, appeal or proceeding pending before it for trial/disposal to any court subordinate to it, or withdraw any suit and try it itself. This is:
options: General power of transfer and withdrawal of suits
questions.explanation: Section 24 confers broad discretionary transfer powers on High Court and District Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of CPC, on application of any party, the Supreme Court may at any stage transfer any suit, appeal or other proceeding from a High Court or civil court in one State to a High Court or civil court in another State if satisfied that an order under this section is expedient for:
questions.explanation: Section 25 empowers Supreme Court to transfer civil suits inter-state for ends of justice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38 of CPC, a decree may be executed either by the Court which passed it, or by:
options: The Court to which it is sent for execution
questions.explanation: Section 38 provides execution of decree by issuing court or transferee court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 47 of CPC, all questions arising between parties to suit in which decree was passed, or their representatives, and relating to execution, discharge or satisfaction of decree, shall be determined by:
options: The Court executing the decree (and not by a separate suit)
questions.explanation: Section 47 bars a separate suit and mandates executing court to decide all execution questions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 51 of CPC, execution of a decree may be enforced by delivery of property, attachment and sale of property, arrest and detention in prison, by appointing a receiver, or in such other manner as nature of relief requires. Arrest and detention in civil prison for money decree requires:
options: Showing judgment-debtor has means to pay and refuses/neglects to pay (or committed dishonesty)
questions.explanation: Section 51 proviso (Jolly George Varghese v. Bank of Cochin) bars arrest for civil debt unless willful failure despite means is proved.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 51 proviso, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 60(1) of CPC, the following properties are EXEMPT from attachment and sale in execution of a decree:
options: Necessary wearing apparel, cooking vessels, beds of judgment-debtor and family
Tools of artisans, and implements of husbandry of an agriculturist
Salary to the extent of first Rs. 1,000 and two-thirds of the remainder in non-maintenance decrees
questions.explanation: Section 60(1) proviso enumerates statutory exemptions from attachment in execution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 75 of CPC, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, Court may issue a Commission to examine any person, to make a local investigation, to examine or adjust accounts, to make a partition, to hold scientific/investigative report, or to:
options: Sell property subject to speedy decay or perform ministerial act
questions.explanation: Section 75 lists statutory purposes for issuing Commissions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 80(2) of CPC, a suit to obtain an urgent or immediate relief against Government or public officer may be instituted with leave of Court without serving two months notice under Section 80(1). But Court shall NOT grant interim/ex-parte relief unless:
options: Government is given reasonable opportunity of showing cause
questions.explanation: Section 80(2) permits urgent suits against Government subject to notice of hearing before interim relief.

questions.question_text: Under Section 96(3) of CPC, NO appeal shall lie from a decree passed by the Court with the:
questions.explanation: Section 96(3) explicitly bars appeals against consent decrees.

questions.question_text: Under Section 96(4) of CPC, no appeal shall lie from a decree passed by a Court of Small Causes in a suit for recovery of money, except on a question of law, where value of subject-matter of original suit does not exceed:
questions.explanation: Section 96(4) bars appeals in small cause money suits under Rs. 10,000 unless on question of law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 104 read with Order XLIII Rule 1 of CPC, an appeal lies from specified orders such as an order under Section 35A (compensatory costs), Section 91/92, or Order XXXIX Rule 1 & 2 (injunctions). Does a second appeal lie from any order passed in appeal under Section 104?
options: Yes, Second Appeal lies to High Court
No second appeal lies from an order passed in appeal under Section 104
questions.explanation: Section 104(2) explicitly bars a second appeal from orders passed in appeal under Section 104.

questions.question_text: Under Section 148 of CPC, where any period is fixed or granted by Court for doing of any act prescribed or allowed by CPC, Court may in its discretion enlarge such period from time to time, even though period originally fixed has expired. Total enlargement period shall not exceed:
questions.explanation: Section 148 caps total enlargement of time by Court at 30 days in aggregate.

questions.question_text: Under Order I Rule 9 of CPC, no suit shall be defeated by reason of misjoinder or non-joinder of parties, and Court may deal with matter in controversy as regards rights of parties before it, EXCEPT in case of non-joinder of a:
questions.explanation: Order I Rule 9 proviso provides that non-joinder of a Necessary Party is fatal to suit.
questions.statute_or_case: Order I Rule 9 proviso, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order II Rule 2(1) of CPC, every suit shall include the whole of the claim which the plaintiff is entitled to make in respect of the cause of action. If a plaintiff intentionally omits to sue in respect of, or intentionally relinquishes, any portion of his claim, he:
options: May file fresh suit with court leave
Shall not afterwards sue in respect of the portion so omitted or relinquished
questions.explanation: Order II Rule 2 bars subsequent suit for omitted or relinquished portion of claim arising from same cause of action.
questions.statute_or_case: Order II Rule 2, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order II Rule 2(3) of CPC, a person entitled to more than one relief in respect of the same cause of action may sue for all or any of such reliefs. But if he omits, except with leave of Court, to sue for all such reliefs, he shall not afterwards sue for any relief so omitted. This is the rule of:
questions.explanation: Order II Rule 2(3) bars splitting of reliefs arising from same cause of action without court leave.
questions.statute_or_case: Order II Rule 2(3), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order VI Rule 1 of CPC, "Pleading" means:
questions.explanation: Order VI Rule 1 defines Pleading as Plaint or Written Statement.
questions.statute_or_case: Order VI Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order VI Rule 2 of CPC, every pleading shall contain, and contain only, a statement in concise form of material facts on which party relies for his claim or defense, BUT NOT the:
options: Evidence by which they are to be proved (Facta probanda vs Facta probantia)
questions.explanation: Order VI Rule 2 codifies rule that pleadings must state material facts (Facta probanda), not evidence (Facta probantia).
questions.statute_or_case: Order VI Rule 2, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order VI Rule 16 of CPC, the Court may at any stage of proceedings order to be struck out or amended any matter in any pleading which may be unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or which tends to prejudice/embarrass trial. This is power of:
questions.explanation: Order VI Rule 16 governs striking out scandalous, frivolous or vexatious pleadings.
questions.statute_or_case: Order VI Rule 16, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order VII Rule 10 of CPC, subject to provisions of Rule 10A, the plaint shall at any stage of suit be returned to be presented to the Court in which suit should have been instituted. This is:
options: Return of Plaint for lack of jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Order VII Rule 10 governs Return of Plaint to be presented in proper court.
questions.statute_or_case: Order VII Rule 10, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order VIII Rule 6 of CPC, where in a suit for recovery of money defendant claims to set-off against plaintiff's demand any ascertained sum of money legally recoverable by him from plaintiff, defendant may present written statement containing particulars of set-off. This is:
questions.explanation: Order VIII Rule 6 defines statutory Legal Set-off for ascertained money claims.
questions.statute_or_case: Order VIII Rule 6, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order VIII Rule 6A of CPC, a defendant in a suit may, in addition to his right of pleading a set-off, set up by way of counter-claim against claim of plaintiff any right or claim in respect of cause of action accruing to defendant against plaintiff. A Counter-claim has the same effect as a:
options: Cross-suit so as to enable Court to pronounce final judgment on both main claim and counter-claim
questions.explanation: Order VIII Rule 6A enacts Counter-claim treating it as an independent cross-suit.
questions.statute_or_case: Order VIII Rule 6A, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order IX Rule 8 of CPC, where defendant appears and plaintiff does not appear when suit is called on for hearing, Court shall make an order that suit be dismissed, UNLESS defendant admits claim or part thereof. Where suit is dismissed under Rule 8, plaintiff is barred from filing fresh suit on same cause of action under Order IX Rule 9, but may apply to:
options: Set aside dismissal order on showing sufficient cause
questions.explanation: Order IX Rule 9 allows application to set aside dismissal for default upon showing sufficient cause.
questions.statute_or_case: Order IX Rule 9, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order X Rule 1 of CPC, at first hearing of suit Court shall ascertain from each party or his pleading whether he admits or denies allegations of fact made in plaint or written statement. Under Rule 1A, Court shall direct parties to opt for:
questions.explanation: Order X Rule 1A mandates Court to direct parties to opt for ADR under Section 89 at first hearing.
questions.statute_or_case: Order X Rule 1A, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XI Rule 1 of CPC, in any suit plaintiff or defendant by leave of Court may deliver interrogatories in writing for examination of adverse parties. Interrogatories must relate to matters in question in suit. Interrogatories seeking discovery of facts are called:
questions.explanation: Order XI Rule 1 governs Discovery by Interrogatories.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XI Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XII Rule 6 of CPC, where admissions of fact have been made either in pleading or otherwise, whether orally or in writing, Court may at any stage of suit, on application or of its own motion, make such order or give such judgment as it may think fit having regard to such admissions. This is:
questions.explanation: Order XII Rule 6 empowers courts to pronounce Judgment on Admissions.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XII Rule 6, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XIV Rule 1 of CPC, Issues arise when a material proposition of fact or law is affirmed by one party and denied by the other. Issues are of two kinds: Issues of Fact and:
questions.explanation: Order XIV Rule 1 divides issues into Issues of Fact and Issues of Law.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XIV Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XIV Rule 2 of CPC, where issues both of law and of fact arise in same suit and Court is of opinion that case or any part may be disposed of on issue of law only, Court may try that issue first if it relates to jurisdiction of Court or a bar to suit created by any law. This is:
questions.explanation: Order XIV Rule 2 governs trial of Preliminary Issues of law.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XIV Rule 2, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XVII Rule 1 of CPC, Court may, if sufficient cause is shown, at any stage of suit grant time to parties and adjourn hearing of suit. But no such adjournment shall be granted more than how many times to a party during hearing of suit?
questions.explanation: Order XVII Rule 1 proviso limits adjournments to a maximum of three times per party during suit hearing.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XVII Rule 1 proviso, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXIII Rule 1(3) of CPC, where Court is satisfied that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect, or that there are sufficient grounds for allowing plaintiff to institute fresh suit, Court may grant plaintiff permission to withdraw suit with liberty to institute fresh suit. Withdrawing suit WITHOUT court permission bars:
options: Instituting fresh suit in respect of same subject-matter
questions.explanation: Order XXIII Rule 1(4) bars fresh suit on same subject-matter if withdrawn without court leave.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXIII Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXIII Rule 3 of CPC, where it is proved to satisfaction of Court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise in writing and signed by parties, Court shall order such agreement to be recorded and pass a:
questions.explanation: Order XXIII Rule 3 governs recording of lawful compromise and passing Compromise Decree.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXIII Rule 3, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXIII Rule 3A of CPC (inserted by 1976 Amendment), no suit shall lie to set aside a compromise decree on the ground that the compromise on which decree is based was:
questions.explanation: Order XXIII Rule 3A explicitly bars a separate suit to set aside a compromise decree on ground that compromise was not lawful.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXIII Rule 3A, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXII Rule 1 of CPC, every suit by a minor shall be instituted in his name by a person who in such suit shall be called the:
questions.explanation: Order XXXII Rule 1 requires minor plaintiff to sue through Next Friend.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXII Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXII Rule 3 of CPC, where defendant is a minor, Court on being satisfied of fact of minority shall appoint a proper person to be:
options: Guardian for the suit (Guardian ad litem)
questions.explanation: Order XXXII Rule 3 mandates appointing Guardian ad litem for minor defendant.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXII Rule 3, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXIII Rule 1 of CPC, a suit may be instituted by an Indigent Person (Pauper) who is not possessed of sufficient means (other than property exempt from execution) to pay fee prescribed by law for plaint. An indigent person is exempted from paying:
options: Court Fees at time of filing plaint
questions.explanation: Order XXXIII Rule 1 exempts indigent plaintiffs from paying upfront Court Fees.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXIII Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXVII Rule 3 of CPC, in a summary suit, defendant must enter appearance within 10 days from service of summons. Thereafter plaintiff serves summons for judgment, and defendant must apply for leave to defend within 10 days showing a bona fide defense. If leave to defend is refused:
options: Suit is transferred to High Court
Plaintiff shall be entitled to judgment forthwith
questions.explanation: Order XXXVII Rule 3(6) provides instant judgment for plaintiff if leave to defend is refused.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXVII Rule 3, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXIX Rule 3 of CPC, Court shall in all cases, before granting an injunction, direct notice of application to be given to opposite party, EXCEPT where it appears that object of granting injunction would be defeated by delay. Where ex-parte injunction is granted, Court shall make endeavor to finally dispose of application within:
options: 30 days from date on which injunction was granted
questions.explanation: Order XXXIX Rule 3A requires court to dispose of ex-parte injunction application within 30 days.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXIX Rule 3A, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of CPC, in case of disobedience of any injunction or breach of any terms on which injunction was granted, Court may order property of person guilty of disobedience to be attached, and may order such person to be detained in civil prison for a term not exceeding:
questions.explanation: Order XXXIX Rule 2A penalizes injunction breach with attachment of property and civil imprisonment up to 3 months.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXIX Rule 2A, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XLI Rule 5 of CPC, an appeal shall NOT operate as a stay of proceedings under a decree or order appealed from EXCEPT so far as Appellate Court may order. Mere filing of an appeal:
options: Does not operate as an automatic stay of execution of decree
questions.explanation: Order XLI Rule 5(1) establishes that filing appeal does not automatically stay execution of decree.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XLI Rule 5, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XLI Rule 22 of CPC, any respondent, though he may not have appealed from any part of decree, may not only support decree but may also state that finding against him in Court below ought to have been in his favor, or take any cross-objection to decree. This is:
questions.explanation: Order XLI Rule 22 governs filing of Cross-Objections by respondent in appeal.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XLI Rule 22, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XLI Rule 27 of CPC, parties to an appeal shall not be entitled to produce additional evidence in Appellate Court, EXCEPT where trial court improperly refused to admit evidence, or party establishes that despite due diligence evidence was not within knowledge, or Appellate Court requires document to enable it to pronounce judgment. This is:
options: Production of Additional Evidence in Appellate Court
questions.explanation: Order XLI Rule 27 sets out strict statutory exceptions allowing additional evidence in appeal.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XLI Rule 27, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXI Rule 22 of CPC, where an application for execution is made more than how many years after date of decree, executing court shall issue notice to person against whom execution is applied requiring him to show cause why decree should not be executed?
questions.explanation: Order XXI Rule 22 requires show cause notice for execution applications filed after 2 years from decree date.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXI Rule 22, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXI Rule 58 of CPC, where any claim is preferred to, or any objection is made to attachment of, any property attached in execution on ground that property is not liable to attachment, Court shall proceed to adjudicate upon claim/objection. Order made on such adjudication has same force as a:
questions.explanation: Order XXI Rule 58(4) provides that adjudication of claims to attached property has the force of a decree.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXI Rule 58, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXI Rule 90 of CPC, where any immovable property has been sold in execution of a decree, decree-holder or purchaser or person entitled to share may apply to Court to set aside sale on ground of a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting sale. Sale shall NOT be set aside unless applicant has sustained:
options: Substantial injury by reason of such irregularity or fraud
questions.explanation: Order XXI Rule 90 requires proof of substantial injury to set aside execution sale of immovable property.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXI Rule 90, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXI Rule 92 of CPC, where no application is made under Rules 89, 90 or 91, or where such application is made and disallowed, Court shall make an order confirming sale, and thereupon the sale shall become:
questions.explanation: Order XXI Rule 92 enacts that upon confirmation order, execution sale becomes absolute.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXI Rule 92, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXI Rule 95 of CPC, where property sold in execution is in occupancy of judgment-debtor or some person on his behalf, Court shall on application of purchaser order delivery to be made by putting purchaser in possession. Executing court issues a:
options: Sale Certificate under Order XXI Rule 94
questions.explanation: Order XXI Rule 94 mandates granting Sale Certificate to execution purchaser after sale becomes absolute.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXI Rule 94, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXI Rule 97 of CPC, where holder of decree for possession of immovable property or purchaser of any such property in execution is resisted or obstructed by any person in obtaining possession, he may make application to Court complaining of resistance/obstruction. This is:
options: Resistance / Obstruction to possession in execution
questions.explanation: Order XXI Rule 97 governs applications against resistance or obstruction to possession in execution.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXI Rule 97, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XXI Rule 101 of CPC, all questions (including questions relating to right, title or interest in property) arising between parties to application under Rule 97 or Rule 99 shall be determined by executing court and NOT by a:
questions.explanation: Order XXI Rule 101 bars separate suit and mandates executing court to decide all title questions in obstruction proceedings.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXI Rule 101, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 79 of CPC, in a suit by or against the Government, the authority to be named as plaintiff or defendant shall be, in case of suit by or against Central Government:
questions.explanation: Section 79(a) requires Union of India to be named as party in suits by/against Central Government.

questions.question_text: Under Section 79 of CPC, in a suit by or against a State Government, authority to be named as party is the:
questions.explanation: Section 79(b) requires the State to be named as "State of [Name]" in government suits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 88 of CPC read with Order XXXV, an Interpleader Suit cannot be instituted by an agent against his principal, or by a tenant against his landlord, for purpose of compelling them to interplead with any persons OTHER THAN persons claiming through:
questions.explanation: Order XXXV Rule 5 bars agents and tenants from filing interpleader suits against principals/landlords except where claims arise through them.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XXXV Rule 5, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 91 of CPC, in case of a public nuisance or other wrongful act affecting public, a suit for declaration and injunction or other relief may be instituted by Advocate-General, OR with leave of Court by:
options: Two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to them
questions.explanation: Section 91 permits representative suit for public nuisance by 2 or more persons with court leave without proving special damage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 92 of CPC, in case of alleged breach of express or constructive trust created for public purposes of a charitable or religious nature, a suit may be instituted by Advocate-General, OR with leave of Court by two or more persons having interest in trust. This governs:
options: Public Charities and Religious Trusts suits
questions.explanation: Section 92 governs representative suits relating to public charitable and religious trusts.

questions.question_text: Under Order V Rule 9 of CPC, summons may be served by delivering copy by proper officer of court, or by registered post ACKNOWLEDGMENT DUE, speed post, approved courier service, or by:
options: Electronic mail service or digital transmission as authorized by High Court rules
questions.explanation: Order V Rule 9 permits service of summons by electronic mail and digital transmission under High Court rules.
questions.statute_or_case: Order V Rule 9, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order V Rule 20 of CPC, where Court is satisfied that defendant is keeping out of the way to avoid service, or that for any other reason summons cannot be served in ordinary way, Court shall order summons to be served by affixing copy in conspicuous place in court-house and house where defendant resides, or by advertisement in local newspaper. This is:
questions.explanation: Order V Rule 20 governs Substituted Service of Summons.
questions.statute_or_case: Order V Rule 20, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XX Rule 12 of CPC, in a suit for recovery of possession of immovable property and for rent or mesne profits, Court may pass a preliminary decree directing an inquiry as to:
options: Mesne profits from institution of suit until delivery of possession or expiration of 3 years
questions.explanation: Order XX Rule 12 governs preliminary decrees for mesne profits inquiry.
questions.statute_or_case: Order XX Rule 12, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Order XX Rule 18 of CPC, where suit is for partition of immovable property, if decree relates to estate assessed to payment of revenue to Government, partition shall be made by:
options: The Collector or any gazetted officer subordinate to him
questions.explanation: Order XX Rule 18(1) requires revenue-paying estate partition to be conducted by the Collector (Section 54 CPC).
questions.statute_or_case: Order XX Rule 18 & Section 54, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

questions.question_text: Under Section 35B of CPC (inserted by 1976 Amendment), if on any date fixed for hearing of a suit or taking step, a party fails to take step or obtains adjournment, Court may order such party to pay to other party costs sufficient to reimburse reasonable expenses incurred. Payment of costs under Section 35B is a:
options: Condition precedent to further prosecution of suit or defense by such party
questions.explanation: Section 35B makes payment of delay costs a strict condition precedent for further prosecution/defense.

questions.question_text: In Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India (2005), the Supreme Court upheld validity of 1999 and 2002 CPC amendments and held that the 90-day time limit for filing Written Statement under Order VIII Rule 1 is:
options: Mandatory with zero exceptions in civil suits
Directory in exceptional cases, though ordinary limit is 90 days
questions.explanation: Salem Bar Association (2005) held 90-day WS deadline directory in ordinary civil suits (though mandatory in Commercial Courts).
questions.statute_or_case: Salem Advocate Bar Association v. UOI (2005)

questions.question_text: In Morgan Stanley Mutual Fund v. Kartick Das (1994), the Supreme Court laid down principles for grant of ex-parte ad-interim injunctions under Order XXXIX Rule 3, holding ex-parte injunctions should be granted only in:
options: Exceptional circumstances where irreparable loss would be caused by delay
questions.explanation: Morgan Stanley (1994) established guidelines restricting ex-parte ad-interim injunctions to exceptional urgent cases.
questions.statute_or_case: Morgan Stanley Mutual Fund v. Kartick Das (1994)

questions.question_text: Under Section 148A(2) of CPC, where a Caveat has been lodged under sub-section (1), the caveator shall serve a copy of caveat by registered post on person by whom application for injunction/order is expected to be made. Upon receiving application, Court shall serve notice on:
questions.explanation: Section 148A(3) mandates Court to give notice of application to the Caveator before passing interim orders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 153 of CPC, the Court may at any time, and on such terms as to costs or otherwise as it may think fit, amend any defect or error in any proceeding in a suit; and all necessary amendments shall be made for purpose of determining real question or issue raised. This is general power to amend:
questions.explanation: Section 153 confers general power to amend procedural defects or errors in proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright subsists in:
options: Ideas, procedures and methods of operation
Original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works; cinematograph films; and sound recordings
Any work, whether original or not
Only published works registered with the Copyright Office
questions.explanation: Copyright protects the expression, not the idea; it arises automatically on creation and registration under Sections 44-45 is optional (though useful as evidence).

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the first owner of the copyright in a work is:
options: Always the person who commissions the work

The author, except that where a work is made in the course of the author's employment under a contract of service for the purpose of publication in a newspaper/magazine (the proprietor, for that limited purpose), or as part of employment (the employer), or a Government work (the Government), or a work made for a public undertaking or an international organisation
questions.explanation: A commissioned photograph, painting, portrait, engraving or cinematograph film made for valuable consideration belongs to the person who commissioned it, absent agreement to the contrary.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the term of copyright in a published literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work is:
options: Sixty years from the date of first publication
The lifetime of the author only
The lifetime of the author plus sixty years, counted from the beginning of the calendar year following the year of the author's death (or, for joint authorship, the death of the author who dies last)
questions.explanation: The Copyright (Amendment) Act, 2012 brought photographs under Section 22 (life + 60) by omitting the separate Section 25.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 26 and 27 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the term of copyright in a cinematograph film and in a sound recording is:
options: Sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the year in which the film or sound recording is published
The lifetime of the producer plus sixty years
questions.explanation: Films, sound recordings, Government works, works of public undertakings and works of international organisations are all protected for 60 years from publication.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the exclusive right of the copyright owner of a literary work includes the right to:
options: Reproduce the work, issue copies to the public, perform it in public, make a cinematograph film or sound recording of it, make any translation or adaptation, and issue copies of a translation or adaptation
Only sell physical copies of the work
questions.explanation: Copyright is a bundle of exclusive rights; the specific rights differ for each class of work (Section 14(a)-(e)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 51 of the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright in a work is infringed when a person, without a licence:
options: Merely reads or listens to the work
Quotes a short passage with attribution for review

Does anything the exclusive right to do which is conferred on the owner, or permits a place to be used for a profit-making communication of the work to the public where it constitutes infringement, or imports infringing copies, or makes/sells/distributes infringing copies
Uses the work for private research
questions.explanation: Section 51 defines primary and secondary infringement; secondary infringement (dealing in infringing copies) requires knowledge or reason to believe.

questions.question_text: Under Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957, which of the following is NOT an infringement of copyright?
options: Making and selling pirated copies of a book
Broadcasting a film without a licence
Reproducing an entire textbook for a coaching class

Fair dealing with a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work (not being a computer programme) for private or personal use, including research; for criticism or review; and for reporting current events and current affairs, including a lecture delivered in public
questions.explanation: Section 52 lists numerous exceptions, including reproduction for judicial proceedings, use in education, making back-up copies of software, and reproduction of an Act or judgment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 57 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the 'special rights' (moral rights) of an author, which subsist independently of the assignment of copyright, are:
options: The right to claim authorship of the work (right of paternity), and the right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any distortion, mutilation, modification or other act in relation to the work which would be prejudicial to his honour or reputation (right of integrity)
The right to receive a fixed royalty in every case
The right to prevent any criticism of the work
The right to buy back the copyright at any time
questions.explanation: Moral rights are personal to the author and can be exercised even by the legal representatives of the author (Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India, 2005).

questions.question_text: Under Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957, a person who knowingly infringes or abets the infringement of copyright is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for a term of not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees
questions.explanation: Section 63 makes copyright infringement a criminal offence; Section 63A enhances the punishment for a second and subsequent conviction (minimum one year).

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of the Copyright Act, 1957, an assignment of copyright:
options: Need not specify the rights or duration

Is valid only if it is in writing signed by the assignor (or his authorised agent), identifies the work, specifies the rights assigned and the duration and territorial extent, and states the amount of royalty or other consideration; if the assignee does not exercise the rights within one year, the assignment is deemed to have lapsed unless otherwise stated
Is permanent and irrevocable in every case
questions.explanation: Where duration is not stated it is deemed to be five years, and where territorial extent is not stated it is presumed to extend within India.

questions.question_text: Under the provisos to Section 18 of the Copyright Act, 1957 (inserted in 2012), the author of a literary or musical work incorporated in a cinematograph film or sound recording:
options: Loses all rights once the work is used in a film
May assign the right to royalty to a music label
Has no right to any royalty

Retains the right to receive royalties for the use of the work in any form other than as part of the film/sound recording in a cinema hall, on an equal share basis with the assignee, and this right to royalty cannot be assigned except to the legal heirs or to a copyright society
questions.explanation: This reform (championed by lyricists and composers) ensures a continuing revenue stream to the underlying authors from downstream exploitation such as ringtones, streaming and radio.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the Copyright Act, 1957, a compulsory licence in respect of a published work may be granted where:
options: The owner has refused to republish or allow the republication of the work, or has refused to allow its communication to the public by broadcast (or in the case of a sound recording, to allow the work to be communicated), and the work is thereby withheld from the public
A competitor simply wishes to exploit the work
The work is more than ten years old
questions.explanation: Sections 31A-31D provide further compulsory and statutory licences: for unpublished/anonymous works, for the benefit of persons with disabilities, for cover versions of songs, and for broadcasting organisations.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31D of the Copyright Act, 1957 (inserted in 2012), any broadcasting organisation desirous of communicating a published literary or musical work and sound recording to the public:
options: May do so free of charge

May do so by giving prior notice and paying royalties to the copyright owner at the rate fixed by the Commercial Court (the function formerly performed by the Copyright Board/Appellate Board, before the IPAB's abolition by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021) — a 'statutory licence for broadcasting'
Must obtain a negotiated voluntary licence in every case
Is prohibited from broadcasting the work
questions.explanation: Section 31D creates a statutory licence so that broadcasters cannot be refused content, subject to payment of royalties; its applicability to internet streaming has been contested, and rate-fixing functions now vest in the Commercial Court following the IPAB's abolition.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(d) of the Copyright Act, 1957, in relation to a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, the 'author' is:
options: The person who causes the work to be created
questions.explanation: Section 2(d) also defines the author for each class of work: for a photograph, the person taking it; for a cinematograph film or sound recording, the producer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(3)(a) of the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright does not subsist in a cinematograph film if:
options: The film is over sixty years old
The film has not been certified by the CBFC
A substantial part of the film is an infringement of the copyright in any other work
questions.explanation: Section 13(3)(b) similarly denies copyright in a sound recording that infringes copyright in another work; Section 13(4) preserves the separate copyright in works incorporated in a film.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38, 38A and 38B of the Copyright Act, 1957 (as amended in 2012), a 'performer' (actor, singer, musician, dancer, etc.) has:
options: A performer's right subsisting for fifty years from the year of the performance, including exclusive rights of sound/visual recording, reproduction, broadcasting and making available, and moral rights of identification and integrity
No rights once the performance is recorded
Rights identical to and merged with the producer's rights
questions.explanation: Once a performer consents to the incorporation of the performance in a cinematograph film, he cannot object to the producer's enjoyment of the performer's rights, but retains a right to royalties for commercial use.

questions.question_text: Under Section 40 and the International Copyright Order, works of foreign nationals and works first published abroad:
options: Are protected in India as if they were Indian works, because India extends copyright protection to nationals of countries that are members of the Berne Convention, the Universal Copyright Convention and the TRIPS Agreement (WTO)
Are protected only if registered in India
Are protected for only ten years
questions.explanation: India follows the principle of national treatment for works originating in Convention countries.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 44 and 45 of the Copyright Act, 1957, registration of copyright:
options: Is compulsory before any protection arises
Is compulsory before an infringement suit can be filed
Is optional; copyright subsists automatically on creation of an original work, and the Register of Copyrights is only prima facie evidence of the particulars entered in it
Confers copyright that would not otherwise exist
questions.explanation: Indian courts have held that registration is not a pre-condition to maintaining an infringement action.

questions.question_text: Under Section 55 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the civil remedies available to a copyright owner for infringement are:
options: Injunction, damages, accounts and otherwise as are conferred by law for the infringement of a right (an innocent infringer who was unaware and had no reasonable ground to believe the work was copyrighted is liable only to an injunction and to an account of profits)
questions.explanation: Section 58 gives the owner a right to all infringing copies and plates ('conversion' remedy); the owner is treated as the owner of such copies.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the business of issuing or granting licences in respect of copyrighted works may be carried on only by:
options: A copyright society duly registered under the Act (such as IPRS for musical works or PPL for sound recordings), except that an owner may grant licences in his individual capacity consistent with his obligations as a member of a society
questions.explanation: Copyright societies are subject to registration (renewable every five years), member control and tariff-fixing oversight (Sections 33-36A).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(o) and Section 2(ffc) of the Copyright Act, 1957, a 'computer programme' is:
options: A set of instructions expressed in words, codes, schemes or in any other form (including a machine-readable medium), capable of causing a computer to perform a particular task or achieve a particular result — and it is treated as a 'literary work'
Not protected by copyright at all
questions.explanation: Software is protected as a literary work; the fair-dealing exception for private use does not extend to computer programmes, though back-up copies and interoperability reverse-engineering are permitted (Section 52(1)(aa)-(ad)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 65A and Section 65B of the Copyright Act, 1957 (inserted in 2012), it is an offence to:
options: Make a personal back-up of a lawfully purchased film
Lend a book to a friend
Circumvent an effective technological protection measure applied to protect copyright, or to knowingly remove or alter rights-management information, with the intention of infringing copyright
questions.explanation: Sections 65A-65B implement the WIPO Internet Treaties' obligations on anti-circumvention and rights-management information.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Copyright Act, 1957, a licence of copyright (as distinct from an assignment):
options: Must always be registered to be valid
Can only be granted by a copyright society
May be granted by the owner (or prospective owner) in writing signed by him or his authorised agent, and does not transfer ownership but only permits specified acts
questions.explanation: A licence may be exclusive or non-exclusive; an exclusive licensee has, to the extent of the licence, the same rights as an owner to sue for infringement.

questions.question_text: Under the Copyright Act, 1957, appeals from decisions of the Registrar of Copyrights and the erstwhile Copyright Board now lie to:
options: The High Court / Commercial Court, following the abolition of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 (the Copyright Board's functions had earlier been merged into the IPAB in 2017)
The Copyright Board, which continues to sit
questions.explanation: Tariff and licensing disputes and rectification of the register are now handled by the Commercial Court / High Court.
questions.statute_or_case: Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 (amending the Copyright Act, 1957)

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(y) of the Copyright Act, 1957, a 'work' means:
options: A literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work; a cinematograph film; or a sound recording
questions.explanation: These are the only categories of subject matter in which copyright can subsist under Indian law.

questions.question_text: The requirement of 'originality' for a literary work under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957 was authoritatively explained in Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak (2008), where the Supreme Court adopted:
options: The pure 'sweat of the brow' doctrine
The rule that facts can be copyrighted

The 'modicum of creativity' / 'flavour of minimum requirement of creativity' standard (a middle path between the 'sweat of the brow' doctrine and the higher US 'creativity' test), holding that copy-edited judgments with inputs of skill and judgment were original
The rule that no originality is required at all
questions.explanation: The Court held that mere labour in copying is not enough; some minimal degree of creativity or intellectual effort is required, though not novelty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 52(1)(za) of the Copyright Act, 1957, the performance or communication to the public of a literary, dramatic or musical work in the course of a bona fide religious ceremony:
options: Is an infringement unless a licence is obtained
Requires payment of royalties to a copyright society
Is permitted only in places of worship
Is not an infringement of copyright (and 'religious ceremony' includes a marriage procession and other social festivities associated with a marriage)
questions.explanation: This exception was clarified by a 2023 Government notice reiterating that no licence or royalty is required for music played at wedding functions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the Copyright Act, 1957:
options: No person is entitled to copyright or any similar right in any work otherwise than under and in accordance with the provisions of the Act (there is no common-law copyright in a published work in India)
Common-law copyright continues alongside the Act
Copyright may be claimed under general principles of equity
questions.explanation: Section 16 makes the Act the exclusive source of copyright, subject to the saving for the law of breach of trust or confidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(ff) of the Copyright Act, 1957, 'communication to the public' means:
options: Only a live public performance in a hall

Making any work or performance available for being seen or heard or otherwise enjoyed by the public directly or by any means of display or diffusion (whether simultaneously or at places and times chosen individually), regardless of whether any member of the public actually sees, hears or otherwise enjoys it
Sending a private copy to one person
questions.explanation: The definition is technology-neutral and expressly covers on-demand internet transmission ('at places and times chosen individually').

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the term of copyright in an anonymous or pseudonymous published literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work is:
options: The lifetime of the publisher plus sixty years

Sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the year of first publication (but if the author's identity is disclosed before that period expires, the term becomes life plus sixty years)
questions.explanation: Section 24 deals with posthumous works, and Section 29 provides that the terms in Chapter V are subject to Section 21 (relinquishment of copyright).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(i) of the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939, a woman married under Muslim law is entitled to obtain a decree for dissolution of marriage if the whereabouts of the husband have not been known for a period of:
questions.explanation: Section 2(i) provides a ground for decree of divorce if the whereabouts of the husband have not been known for 4 years.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2(i), Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(ii) of DMMA 1939, a married Muslim woman can seek dissolution of marriage if her husband has failed to provide maintenance for a period of:
questions.explanation: Section 2(ii) grants a statutory right of dissolution if the husband neglects or fails to maintain her for 2 years.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2(ii), Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939

questions.question_text: In the landmark judgment Yusuf v. Sowramma (1971), Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer held regarding Section 2(ii) of DMMA 1939 that:
options: Divorce can be granted only if husband's failure to maintain was wilful and without cause
Wife loses right if she earns an independent income
Maintenance ground applies only after 5 years
Failure to maintain for 2 years gives statutory right to divorce regardless of whether husband's failure was due to poverty, disability or wife's refusal
questions.explanation: Yusuf v. Sowramma affirmed the objective breakdown test under Section 2(ii), making failure to maintain for 2 years a strict ground.
questions.statute_or_case: A. Yousuf Rawther v. Sowramma, AIR 1971 Kerala 261

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(iii) of DMMA 1939, a married Muslim woman can seek dissolution of marriage if her husband has been sentenced to imprisonment for a period of:
questions.explanation: Section 2(iii) specifies a sentence of imprisonment for 7 years or upwards as a valid ground.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 proviso (a) of DMMA 1939, no decree shall be passed on the ground of husband's 7-year imprisonment UNTIL:
options: The husband completes 3 years in jail
The wife pays a security deposit
questions.explanation: Section 2 proviso (a) requires that sentence of imprisonment must become final before decree is passed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(iv) of DMMA 1939, a married Muslim woman can seek dissolution of marriage if the husband has failed to perform marital obligations without reasonable cause for a period of:
questions.explanation: Section 2(iv) specifies non-performance of marital obligations for 3 years as a ground.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2(iv), Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(v) & proviso (c) of DMMA 1939, where divorce is sought on ground of husband's impotency, what order shall the court pass on application by husband?
options: Order requiring husband to satisfy court within 1 year that he has ceased to be impotent
questions.explanation: Section 2 proviso (c) gives husband 1 year from court order to prove he has ceased to be impotent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(vi) of DMMA 1939, a woman can seek dissolution if her husband has been insane for a period of:
options: 2 years or is suffering from a virulent venereal disease
questions.explanation: Section 2(vi) provides insanity for 2 years or virulent venereal disease as a ground for dissolution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(vii) of DMMA 1939 ('Option of Puberty' or Khyar-ul-Bugh), a woman given in marriage before 15 years can repudiate the marriage BEFORE attaining 18 years, PROVIDED THAT:
options: The marriage has NOT been consummated
questions.explanation: Section 2(vii) proviso requires that the marriage must NOT have been consummated for Option of Puberty to be exercised.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(viii)(a) of DMMA 1939, cruelty includes habitually assaulting the wife or making her life miserable by cruelty of conduct:
options: Only if it results in grievous hurt
Only if witnessed by two male witnesses
Even if such conduct does NOT amount to physical ill-treatment
Only if medical report is attached
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(a) explicitly includes mental cruelty making life miserable even without physical violence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(viii)(f) of DMMA 1939, cruelty includes a scenario where the husband has more wives than one and:
options: Takes another wife without her written consent
Lives in a different house from second wife
Fails to buy gold for first wife
Does NOT treat her equitably in accordance with the injunctions of the Qoran
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(f) incorporates the Quranic mandate of equitable treatment among co-wives as statutory ground.

questions.question_text: In Itwari v. Asghari (1960) AIR All 684, the Allahabad High Court held that where a Muslim husband contracts a second marriage and seeks restitution of conjugal rights against first wife:
options: It raises a presumption of cruelty against first wife, and court will not compel her to live with him unless equitable treatment is proved
First wife must live with second wife unconditionally
First wife loses right to dower
questions.explanation: Itwari v. Asghari established that marrying a second wife without just cause constitutes cruelty against first wife.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 proviso (b) of DMMA 1939, a decree passed on ground (i) (husband's whereabouts unknown for 4 years) shall NOT take effect for:
options: One year from date of decree
Six months from the date of such decree (and if husband appears within 6 months and satisfies court he is ready for conjugal duties, decree is set aside)
questions.explanation: Section 2 proviso (b) suspends decree for 6 months allowing missing husband to appear and set aside decree.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of DMMA 1939, in a suit where husband's whereabouts are unknown for 4 years, who MUST be cited as parties to the suit even if they are NOT heirs?
options: Paternal uncle and brother of the husband
questions.explanation: Section 3 proviso mandates that paternal uncle and brother of husband must be cited as parties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 main clause of DMMA 1939, what is the effect of renunciation of Islam or conversion to another faith by a married Muslim woman on her marriage tie?
options: It renders marriage void ab initio
It transfers custody of children to husband automatically
It shall NOT by itself operate to dissolve her marriage tie
questions.explanation: Section 4 changed the uncodified traditional rule by enacting that woman's apostasy does NOT automatically dissolve marriage.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 4, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 second proviso of DMMA 1939, what is the EXCEPTION where a woman's conversion does lead to automatic dissolution?
options: A woman converted to Islam from another faith who re-embraces her former faith
A woman who converts to Hinduism
questions.explanation: Section 4 proviso 2 excludes re-conversion of a woman converted to Islam back to her original faith.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of DMMA 1939, does the dissolution of marriage under the Act affect a married Muslim woman's right to her dower (Mahr)?
options: No, nothing in the Act affects any right she may have under Muslim law to her dower or any part thereof
Yes, she forfeits all dower rights
questions.explanation: Section 5 expressly protects married woman's statutory and personal right to Mahr/dower upon dissolution.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 5, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Personal Law, what is 'Khula'?
options: Unilateral divorce pronounced 3 times by husband in one sitting
Divorce by judicial decree on ground of impotency
Divorce initiated by the wife with the consent of the husband, usually in exchange for financial consideration or giving up Mahr
questions.explanation: Khula is dissolution of marriage at the wife's instance with husband's consent for a consideration.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Personal Law, what is 'Mubarat'?
options: Divorce by mutual consent of both husband and wife where both desire separation
questions.explanation: Mubarat is divorce by mutual consent originating from a mutual aversion between both spouses.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Personal Law, what is 'Talaq-i-Tafweez' (Delegated Talaq)?
options: An arrangement where husband delegates his power to pronounce talaq to his wife or a third party, either absolutely or conditionally
questions.explanation: Talaq-i-Tafweez is a valid delegation of divorce power by husband to wife or third party.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Personal Law, what is 'Lian' (Imprecation)?
options: A ground for dissolution where husband falsely accuses wife of adultery, giving wife right to sue for dissolution
questions.explanation: Lian occurs when husband charges wife with adultery falsely; if unretracted, wife gets decree of dissolution under S. 2(ix).

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Personal Law, what is 'Ila'?
options: Comparing wife to prohibited female relative
A form of inchoate divorce where husband takes an oath not to have sexual intercourse with wife for 4 months or more
questions.explanation: Ila is a vow of celibacy/continence for 4 months; if kept, it operates as irrevocable divorce under traditional Sunni law.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Personal Law, what is 'Zihar'?
options: Where husband compares wife to a female relative within prohibited degrees of relationship (e.g. mother/sister)
questions.explanation: Zihar occurs when husband compares wife to his mother or sister; wife can refuse cohabitation until expiation (Kaffara) is done.

questions.question_text: In the landmark 5-Judge Constitution Bench decision Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) 9 SCC 1, the Supreme Court held Talaq-e-Biddat (Triple Talaq) to be:
options: Unconstitutional and void as being manifestly arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution
Voidable at option of wife within 30 days
questions.explanation: Shayara Bano (2017) set aside Talaq-e-Biddat as unconstitutional under Article 14.
questions.statute_or_case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) 9 SCC 1

questions.question_text: In Shamim Ara v. State of U.P. (2002) 7 SCC 518, the Supreme Court held that for a valid Talaq under Muslim law, it must be:
options: Pronounced in court in presence of Magistrate
For reasonable cause and preceded by an attempt at reconciliation between husband and wife by two arbitrators
questions.explanation: Shamim Ara established that talaq must be for reasonable cause and preceded by reconciliation efforts by 2 arbitrators.
questions.statute_or_case: Shamim Ara v. State of U.P. (2002) 7 SCC 518

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(viii)(b) of DMMA 1939, cruelty by husband includes associating with women of evil repute or leading:
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(b) makes leading an infamous life or associating with women of evil repute statutory cruelty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(viii)(c) of DMMA 1939, cruelty by husband includes attempting to force the wife to:
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(c) prohibits forcing wife to lead an immoral life under cruelty ground.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(viii)(d) of DMMA 1939, cruelty by husband includes disposing of wife's property OR:
options: Preventing her from exercising her legal rights over it
Buying property in his own name
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(d) protects wife's property rights against husband's illegal disposal/interference.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(viii)(e) of DMMA 1939, cruelty by husband includes obstructing the wife in:
options: The observance of her religious profession or practice
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(e) protects wife's freedom of religious practice against husband's obstruction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(ix) of DMMA 1939, a Muslim woman can seek dissolution on ANY OTHER ground recognized as valid for dissolution of marriages under:
questions.explanation: Section 2(ix) acts as a statutory saving clause incorporating all grounds recognized by Muslim personal law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(1) of the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939, the short title of the Act is:
options: The Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939
questions.explanation: Section 1(1) defines exact title of Act No. 8 of 1939.

questions.question_text: What was the word omitted from Section 2(vi) of DMMA 1939 by the Personal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 (Act 6 of 2019)?
questions.explanation: Act 6 of 2019 omitted 'leprosy or' from Section 2(vi) across personal laws to remove stigma against leprosy patients.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2(vi), DMMA 1939 (as amended by Act 6 of 2019)

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is 'Faskh'?
options: Unilateral divorce by wife without cause
Cancellation or dissolution of marriage by judicial decree of a Civil Court / Qazi on statutory or legal grounds
Automatic dissolution upon birth of child
questions.explanation: Faskh means judicial annulment/dissolution of marriage by court under DMMA 1939 or Shariat law.

questions.question_text: In Abdul Kadir v. Salima (1886) ILR 8 All 149, Justice Mahmood stated that under Muslim Law, marriage is:
options: A sacrament strictly binding in heaven
A civil contract, not a sacrament, having for its object the procreation and legalizing of children
questions.explanation: Justice Mahmood's famous dictum established that Muslim marriage is a civil contract.
questions.statute_or_case: Abdul Kadir v. Salima (1886) ILR 8 All 149

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, 'Mahr' (Dower) is defined as:
options: Dowry paid by wife's parents to husband
Gift given by bridegroom's father to bride's mother
A sum of money or other property which the wife is entitled to receive from husband in consideration of marriage
questions.explanation: Mahr is a statutory/contractual obligation of husband to wife in consideration of marriage.

questions.question_text: What are the two types of Mahr (Dower) under Muslim Law regarding time of payment?
options: Prompt Dower (Mu'ajjal) payable on demand, and Deferred Dower (Mu'wajjal) payable on dissolution of marriage or death
questions.explanation: Mahr is categorized into Prompt (payable immediately on demand) and Deferred (payable on dissolution/death).

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, if the husband fails to pay 'Prompt Dower' (Mu'ajjal) on demand, the wife has the legal right to:
options: Refuse cohabitation and live separately until prompt dower is paid
Adopt a child without his consent
questions.explanation: Non-payment of prompt dower gives wife complete defense to refuse cohabitation (Abdul Kadir v. Salima).

questions.question_text: In Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) 7 SCC 740, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 and held that maintenance:
options: Is limited strictly to iddat period expenses only
Must be reasonable and fair provision made WITHIN iddat period to cover wife's future lifetime (or until remarriage)
Is payable by Wakf Board in all cases
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi held that 1986 Act requires husband to make 'reasonable and fair provision' within iddat period for wife's entire future life unless remarried.
questions.statute_or_case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) 7 SCC 740

questions.question_text: Under Sunni Law, what are the three forms of Talaq-ul-Sunnat (approved modes of divorce by husband)?
questions.explanation: Talaq-ul-Sunnat consists of Ahsan (single pronouncement during tuhr followed by iddat abstinence) and Hasan (3 pronouncements in 3 consecutive tuhrs).

questions.question_text: What is 'Tuhr' in Muslim Marital Law?
options: The period of purity between two menstrual cycles
questions.explanation: Tuhr is the state of purity (non-menstruation) during which valid pronouncement of Talaq-ul-Sunnat must be made.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is the 'Iddat' period for a divorced woman who menstruates?
options: Three menstrual cycles (or 3 lunar months if not menstruating)
questions.explanation: Iddat for a divorced woman is 3 menstrual courses (or 3 months); for a widow it is 4 months and 10 days.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is the 'Iddat' period for a widow whose husband has died?
options: Four months and ten days (or until delivery if pregnant)
questions.explanation: Iddat of death for a widow is 4 months and 10 days.

questions.question_text: If a divorced Muslim woman is PREGNANT at the time of divorce, when does her Iddat period terminate?
options: Exactly after 3 months regardless of delivery
Upon delivery of the child or termination of pregnancy
questions.explanation: For a pregnant woman, iddat continues until delivery of the child.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939, can a Muslim woman seek divorce on ground (ii) (failure to maintain for 2 years) if her husband was in PRISON or POOR?
options: Yes, inability or poverty or imprisonment is NO defense under Section 2(ii)
No, poverty is a valid defense for husband
questions.explanation: Section 2(ii) failure to maintain is an absolute ground; husband's poverty or imprisonment does not excuse non-maintenance.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(vii), if a girl married under 15 years seeks to exercise Option of Puberty, who must she file the suit against?
options: Her husband in a Civil Court / Family Court before turning 18 years
questions.explanation: Option of Puberty under s. 2(vii) is exercised by filing a civil suit for dissolution before turning 18.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(viii)(a), does mental cruelty without physical violence entitle a Muslim wife to dissolution?
options: No, only verbal abuse certified by police is allowed
Yes, 'making her life miserable by cruelty of conduct even if not amounting to physical ill-treatment' is express statutory cruelty
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(a) explicitly includes mental cruelty making life miserable.

questions.question_text: In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (AIR 1985 SC 945), the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman unable to maintain herself is entitled to claim maintenance under:
options: Section 18 of Hindu Adoptions & Maintenance Act
Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
questions.explanation: Shah Bano (1985) held CrPC s. 125 is secular and applies to all divorced women including Muslims.
questions.statute_or_case: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum, AIR 1985 SC 945

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(i), if a husband vanishes and his whereabouts are unknown for 4 years, when does the court decree take FINAL EFFECT under proviso (b)?
options: Six months from the date of the decree (provided husband does not appear and offer conjugal performance)
questions.explanation: Proviso (b) delays final effect for 6 months to give missing husband a last chance to appear.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(a) of DMMA 1939, when a suit is filed under clause (i) for missing husband, the plaint MUST state:
options: The names and addresses of persons who would have been heirs of husband if he had died on date of filing plaint
questions.explanation: Section 3(a) requires listing hypothetical heirs in the plaint to ensure notice is served.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 Proviso 1 of DMMA 1939, if a Muslim woman converts to another religion, she:
options: Loses all right to sue in civil court
Forfeits her custody of children permanently
Remains entitled to obtain a decree for dissolution of marriage on any Section 2 ground
questions.explanation: Section 4 Proviso 1 saves woman's right to seek Section 2 grounds even after apostasy.

questions.question_text: What is 'Talaq-ahsan'?
options: Single pronouncement of talaq during a period of tuhr followed by abstinence from sexual intercourse during iddat
questions.explanation: Talaq-ahsan is considered the most approved (best) form of talaq under Islamic jurisprudence.

questions.question_text: What is 'Talaq-hasan'?
options: Three pronouncements made during 3 consecutive tuhrs (periods of purity) with no intercourse during any of those tuhrs
Instant triple talaq in one sitting
questions.explanation: Talaq-hasan is the 'good' approved form involving 3 successive pronouncements across 3 clean cycles.

questions.question_text: What was 'Talaq-e-Biddat' (Triple Talaq)?
options: Instant irrevocable divorce pronounced by husband three times in one sitting/sentence
questions.explanation: Talaq-e-Biddat was instant triple talaq declared unconstitutional in Shayara Bano.
questions.statute_or_case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)

questions.question_text: Under the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, pronouncing Talaq-e-Biddat (instant triple talaq) by a Muslim husband is:
options: Valid subject to fine of Rs. 1000
Void, illegal, and a cognizable & compoundable offence punishable up to 3 years imprisonment and fine
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act criminalized Talaq-e-Biddat with up to 3 years imprisonment.
questions.statute_or_case: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019

questions.question_text: Can a Muslim husband revoke a 'Talaq-ahsan' before the expiry of the Iddat period?
options: No, it is irrevocable immediately on pronouncement
Yes, Talaq-ahsan is revocable during iddat either explicitly by words or implicitly by cohabitation
questions.explanation: Talaq-ahsan remains revocable throughout the iddat period.

questions.question_text: When does a 'Talaq-ahsan' become IRREVOCABLE under Muslim Law?
options: Upon completion of the Iddat period without revocation
questions.explanation: Talaq-ahsan becomes final and irrevocable once the iddat period expires without cohabitation/revocation.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, if a husband retracts a false charge of adultery (Lian) made against his wife BEFORE evidence is closed in court:
options: The wife's suit for dissolution on ground of Lian may be dismissed by court if retraction is bona fide
questions.explanation: Bona fide retraction of Lian charge before trial conclusion extinguishes wife's Lian ground.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(vii), what is the maximum age limit for a woman to repudiate a child marriage under Option of Puberty?
options: Before attaining the age of 18 years
questions.explanation: Section 2(vii) strictly requires repudiation to take place before completing 18 years.

questions.question_text: If a Muslim wife repudiates her child marriage under Option of Puberty (s. 2(vii)), BUT consummation occurred WITH HER CONSENT after attaining puberty, what is the legal effect?
options: Option of puberty is lost because proviso requires marriage must NOT have been consummated
questions.explanation: Consummation post-puberty with consent destroys the statutory Option of Puberty under Section 2(vii) proviso.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, can a Muslim wife stipulate in her marriage contract (Nikahnama) that she shall have right to divorce herself if husband marries a second wife?
options: Yes, this is a valid Talaq-i-Tafweez (delegated divorce) condition permitted by law
No, marriage contract cannot contain divorce clauses
No, second marriage is absolute right of husband
Only if certified by High Court
questions.explanation: Stipulations in Nikahnama allowing wife to pronounce Talaq-i-Tafweez on second marriage are valid and enforceable.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(viii)(a), does 'habitual assault' require a minimum number of physical beatings?
options: No specific number; court evaluates whether husband's conduct shows a persistent pattern of physical violence or misery
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(a) leaves evaluation of persistent cruelty/assault to court's overall assessment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(iv) of DMMA 1939, 'marital obligations' include:
options: Only visiting wife's parents on festivals
Conjugal cohabitation, maintenance, affection, and protection
Only buying property in joint name
questions.explanation: Marital obligations encompass all standard conjugal duties expected in Muslim marriage.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(v), if husband was impotent at the time of marriage and continues to be so, who has the burden to prove impotency?
options: The wife initially, after which husband may apply for 1 year cure period under proviso (c)
questions.explanation: Wife must prove initial and continuing impotency; then husband gets 1 year period under proviso (c) if he applies.

questions.question_text: Does the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 apply to suits filed by a Muslim HUSBAND for divorce?
options: No, DMMA 1939 applies exclusively to suits for dissolution of marriage by WOMEN married under Muslim law
Yes, applies equally to husbands and wives
Yes, if filed in High Court
questions.explanation: The Preamble & Section 2 explicitly state DMMA 1939 applies to suits by women married under Muslim law.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, if a husband dies DURING the Iddat period of a REVOCABLE talaq, what is the wife's inheritance right?
options: She inherits from his estate as his widow because marriage tie was not completely severed during revocable iddat
questions.explanation: During revocable iddat, marital status persists for inheritance purposes if husband dies.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, if a husband pronounces an IRREVOCABLE talaq during his death-illness (Marz-ul-Mawt) to disinherit his wife:
options: Wife inherits only if sons agree
The wife is entitled to inherit from his estate if he dies before expiry of her iddat (Talaq-ul-Farr / Evasion Divorce rule)
questions.explanation: Talaq-ul-Farr doctrine prevents a dying husband from fraudulently disinheriting wife during death-illness.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(ii) of DMMA 1939, for how long must the failure/neglect to maintain persist before a suit can be filed?
questions.explanation: Section 2(ii) mandates a continuous 2-year failure to maintain.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(i) of DMMA 1939, for how long must the husband's whereabouts be unknown before a suit can be filed?
questions.explanation: Section 2(i) requires whereabouts unknown for 4 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(iv) of DMMA 1939, for how long must failure to perform marital obligations persist?
questions.explanation: Section 2(iv) requires failure to perform marital obligations for 3 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(vi) of DMMA 1939, for how long must the husband's insanity persist?
questions.explanation: Section 2(vi) requires insanity for a period of 2 years.

questions.question_text: What is the key distinction between 'Khula' and 'Mubarat' under Muslim Personal Law?
options: Khula is pronounced by husband; Mubarat by Qazi
Khula requires court decree; Mubarat does not
Khula applies only to Shia; Mubarat to Sunni
In Khula, desire for separation emanates from WIFE (who offers consideration); in Mubarat, desire for separation is MUTUAL from both spouses
questions.explanation: Khula originates from wife's initiative; Mubarat arises from mutual aversion of both spouses.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, can a Muslim wife waive her right to 'Deferred Dower' (Mu'wajjal) at the time of entering into a Khula agreement?
options: Yes, giving up or relinquishing Mahr is valid consideration for Khula
No, Mahr can never be waived
questions.explanation: Relinquishment of Mahr by wife is standard consideration for husband consenting to Khula.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of DMMA 1939, can a Muslim woman seek divorce if her husband is suffering from a 'virulent venereal disease'?
options: No, disease is not a ground
Only if disease was contracted before marriage
questions.explanation: Section 2(vi) explicitly includes suffering from a virulent venereal disease as a ground.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(iii) of DMMA 1939, if husband is sentenced to 7 years imprisonment, when can wife file the suit for dissolution?
options: After the sentence of imprisonment has become final (upon disposal of appeal/revision)
questions.explanation: Section 2 proviso (a) clarifies sentence must be final (appeal/revision concluded).

questions.question_text: In a suit under DMMA 1939 Section 2(i) (missing husband), if the missing husband appears in court 3 months AFTER decree is passed and satisfies court he is ready for conjugal duties:
options: Husband must pay Rs. 1 Lakh fine
The court SHALL set aside the decree under proviso (b), as 6 months have not elapsed
questions.explanation: Proviso (b) obliges court to set aside decree if husband appears within 6 months and offers conjugal performance.

questions.question_text: Does the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 apply to the Union Territory of Pondicherry?
options: Yes, extended by Act 26 of 1968, but does NOT apply to the 'Renoncants' of Pondicherry
questions.explanation: Section 1 footnote/proviso exempts the Renoncants of Pondicherry from DMMA 1939.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is the legal effect of a decree of dissolution passed by a Civil Court under DMMA 1939 on the marriage tie?
options: It operates as a revocable divorce for 1 year
It operates as an IRREVOCABLE divorce (Faskh) dissolving marriage immediately upon decree taking effect
It operates as judicial separation for 3 years
It has no legal effect until confirmed by Qazi
questions.explanation: A judicial decree under DMMA 1939 is an irrevocable judicial dissolution (Faskh).
