questions.question_text: If a married Muslim woman files a suit under DMMA 1939 alleging cruelty, and husband proves he struck her only once during a domestic quarrel:
options: Single strike automatically grants divorce without trial
Court evaluates whether conduct makes her life miserable under Section 2(viii)(a); habitual assault or cruel conduct is required
Suit must be transferred to Sessions Court
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(a) requires habitual assault or conduct making life miserable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(viii)(f) of DMMA 1939, if a Muslim husband has two wives and provides a luxurious house to one while neglecting the basic shelter of the other:
options: Husband can be jailed for 5 years
The neglected wife can seek dissolution of marriage for failure to treat her equitably under Quranic injunctions
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(f) grounds divorce on inequitable treatment among co-wives.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Personal Law, can a Muslim wife claim Mahr if the marriage is dissolved under DMMA 1939 BEFORE consummation?
options: Yes, she is entitled to half of the specified Mahr (or proper dower rules under Islamic law)
No, unconsummated marriage disentitles Mahr completely
questions.explanation: Under Muslim law, dissolution of unconsummated marriage entitles wife to half of specified Mahr under Section 5 DMMA.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of DMMA 1939, why must the paternal uncle and brother of a missing husband be cited as parties to the suit?
options: To ensure they have notice and opportunity to defend husband's interests or locate his whereabouts
questions.explanation: Section 3 proviso ensures close male agnates get notice to prevent fraudulent suits against missing men.

questions.question_text: What is 'Talaq-ul-Biddat' also known as in popular parlance?
questions.explanation: Talaq-ul-Biddat is the theological term for instant triple talaq.

questions.question_text: In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), which Bench strength of the Supreme Court rendered the decision setting aside Triple Talaq?
questions.explanation: Shayara Bano was decided by a 5-Judge Constitution Bench with a 3:2 majority.
questions.statute_or_case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, can a valid marriage be solemnized during the 'Iddat' period of a woman?
options: No, marriage during Iddat is Fasid (irregular) under Sunni law and Void under Shia law
questions.explanation: Marriage during iddat is prohibited; it is irregular (Fasid) in Sunni law and void (Batil) in Shia law.

questions.question_text: What are the three categories of marriage validity under Sunni (Hanafi) Law?
questions.explanation: Hanafi law classifies marriages into Sahih (valid), Fasid (irregular), and Batil (void).

questions.question_text: What is a 'Muta' marriage under Islamic Law?
options: A permanent marriage under Sunni law
A temporary marriage for a fixed period with specified Mahr, recognized under Shia (Ithna Ashari) Law
questions.explanation: Muta is a temporary marriage for a fixed duration valid only in Shia Ithna Ashari law.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, is 'Fasid' (irregular) marriage recognized as a distinct third category?
options: No, Shia law recognizes ONLY Sahih (Valid) and Batil (Void) marriages (no irregular category except temporary Muta)
questions.explanation: Shia law does not recognize Fasid (irregular) marriage as a middle category; a marriage is either Sahih or Batil.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(vii), if a minor girl is given in marriage by her FATHER, can she still exercise Option of Puberty?
options: Yes, DMMA 1939 explicitly allows Option of Puberty whether given in marriage by 'father or other guardian'
No, father's marriage cannot be repudiated under old law
questions.explanation: DMMA 1939 removed traditional distinction where father's marriage could not be repudiated; s. 2(vii) applies to father or guardian.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(viii)(d) of DMMA 1939, if a husband sells his wife's Stridhana/ornaments without her consent to pay his gambling debts:
options: Wife has no remedy under DMMA
Wife can seek decree of dissolution of marriage on ground of cruelty
questions.explanation: Section 2(viii)(d) makes disposing of wife's property or preventing her legal rights over it statutory cruelty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(i) of DMMA 1939, if husband's whereabouts are unknown for 4 years, who has the burden of proof in court?
options: The wife must prove that husband's whereabouts have not been known for 4 years to persons who would naturally have heard of him
questions.explanation: Plaint petitioner (wife) must establish 4-year absence without news.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of DMMA 1939, if a married Muslim woman renounces Islam and converts to Hinduism, does her marriage dissolve automatically on the date of conversion?
options: Yes, dissolves instantly on conversion date
Dissolves only if husband converts too
No, Section 4 enacts that conversion/renunciation shall NOT by itself operate to dissolve her marriage
questions.explanation: Section 4 main clause abolished automatic dissolution upon wife's apostasy/conversion.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 4, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 proviso 2 of DMMA 1939, Hindu woman A converts to Islam and marries Muslim man B. Later, A re-embraces Hinduism. What is the effect on her marriage tie with B?
options: Her marriage with B is automatically dissolved because proviso 2 exempts re-conversion to former faith
A must file suit under Section 2
A must pay compensation to B
questions.explanation: Section 4 proviso 2 provides that automatic dissolution rule still applies when a convert to Islam re-embraces former faith.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of DMMA 1939, if a Muslim woman obtains a decree of dissolution on ground of husband's cruelty, can she still recover her unpaid Deferred Dower?
options: No, obtaining divorce forfeits all dower
Yes, Section 5 explicitly preserves her right to dower or any part thereof
questions.explanation: Section 5 ensures dissolution under DMMA does not deprive woman of her Mahr.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is 'Kharch-i-Pandan'?
options: A personal allowance payable periodically by husband to wife under an ante-nuptial or post-nuptial agreement for her personal pin-money expenses
questions.explanation: Kharch-i-Pandan (betel-box expenses) is a recognized personal allowance under Muslim marriage contracts.

questions.question_text: What is the legal status of a marriage contracted by a minor under Muslim Law without guardian's consent?
options: Voidable at option of husband only
questions.explanation: Marriage of a minor lacking capacity and without valid guardian consent is void ab initio.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, if a husband agrees in writing to pay monthly maintenance to his wife living separately under a valid separation deed:
options: The agreement is valid, enforceable civil contract and not opposed to public policy
Agreement is void as opposed to public policy
Agreement is voidable by husband anytime
questions.explanation: Post-nuptial maintenance agreements for separate living on valid grounds are enforceable in civil law.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(ii), if a husband pays maintenance for 1 year 11 months, and then stops for 1 month before trial:
options: Ground (ii) is NOT satisfied because failure must be for a continuous period of full two years
questions.explanation: Section 2(ii) strictly requires full continuous 2-year period of non-maintenance.

questions.question_text: Under DMMA 1939 Section 2(iv), can a husband claim defense that he failed to perform marital obligations for 3 years due to 'reasonable cause' (e.g. valid job abroad where wife refused visa)?
options: No, liability is strict regardless of cause
Yes, Section 2(iv) explicitly uses the words 'without reasonable cause'; if reasonable cause exists, ground fails
questions.explanation: Section 2(iv) specifies failure 'without reasonable cause', so reasonable cause is a valid defense.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of DMMA 1939 (repealed in 1942), what section of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 was originally repealed?
questions.explanation: Section 6 of DMMA 1939 originally repealed Section 5 of Shariat Act 1937.

questions.question_text: What is the primary overarching object of the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 as set out in its Preamble?
options: To consolidate and clarify the provisions of Muslim law relating to suits for dissolution of marriage by women married under Muslim law and to remove doubts as to effect of renunciation of Islam
To introduce compulsory civil registration of Muslim marriages
To codify inheritance law for Muslim women
questions.explanation: The Preamble sets out the dual object of consolidating divorce grounds for women and resolving apostasy effects.
questions.statute_or_case: Preamble, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, giving or taking dowry is punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than:
options: Three years and fine of Rs. 5,000
Five years, and with fine not less than fifteen thousand rupees or the value of such dowry, whichever is more
One year and fine of Rs. 10,000
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) prescribes a minimum imprisonment of 5 years and fine not less than Rs. 15,000 or dowry value, whichever is higher.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, 'dowry' does NOT include which of the following?
options: Property given at the time of marriage
Valuable security given 1 year after marriage in connection with marriage
Dower or Mahr in the case of persons to whom the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) applies
Cash given by bride's father to bridegroom's father
questions.explanation: Section 2 explicitly excludes Mahr or Dower under Muslim Personal Law from the definition of dowry.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, property or valuable security given or agreed to be given constitutes dowry if given:
options: Only on the exact day of wedding
At or before or any time after the marriage in connection with the marriage of the parties
questions.explanation: Section 2 was amended in 1986 to cover property given at, before, or 'any time after the marriage'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, demanding dowry directly or indirectly from parents or relatives of a bride/bridegroom is punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than:
options: Six months, but which may extend to two years and fine up to ten thousand rupees
Five years and fine of Rs. 15,000
One month and fine of Rs. 500
Three years and fine of Rs. 50,000
questions.explanation: Section 4 prescribes minimum 6 months imprisonment (extending to 2 years) and fine up to Rs. 10,000 for demanding dowry.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4A of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, publishing or printing an advertisement offering share in property or money as consideration for marriage is punishable with imprisonment for not less than:
options: Six months, but which may extend to five years, or fine up to fifteen thousand rupees
questions.explanation: Section 4A imposes a total ban on marriage advertisements offering property/money share with min 6 months imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, any agreement for the giving or taking of dowry shall be:
questions.explanation: Section 5 renders any agreement for giving or taking dowry null and void ab initio.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1)(a) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, if dowry was received by a person other than the woman BEFORE marriage, that person must transfer it to the woman within:
options: Three months after the date of marriage
questions.explanation: Section 6(1)(a) mandates transferring pre-marriage dowry to the woman within 3 months after marriage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1)(c) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, if dowry was received when the woman was a MINOR, within what time limit after attaining 18 years must it be transferred to her?
options: Within three months after she has attained the age of eighteen years
questions.explanation: Section 6(1)(c) mandates transfer within 3 months of attaining 18 years of age.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3) proviso of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, if a woman dies within SEVEN YEARS of marriage otherwise than due to natural causes, to whom shall the dowry property held in trust be transferred if she has NO children?
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) proviso (a) directs that if she dies unnaturally within 7 years of marriage without children, property goes to her parents.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3) proviso (b) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, if a woman dies within seven years of marriage unnaturally leaving CHILDREN, to whom shall the dowry property be transferred?
options: To such children (held in trust for them pending transfer)
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) proviso (b) provides that if she leaves children, property is transferred to her children.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, failure to transfer dowry property to the woman or her heirs within the specified 3-month limit is punishable with imprisonment for not less than:
options: Six months up to two years, or with fine not less than five thousand rupees up to ten thousand rupees, or both
questions.explanation: Section 6(2) prescribes minimum 6 months imprisonment and fine between Rs. 5,000 and Rs. 10,000 for failing to transfer dowry property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(1)(a) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, no Court inferior to which magistrate shall try any offence under the Act?
options: Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class
Judicial Magistrate of the second class
questions.explanation: Section 7(1)(a) restricts trial jurisdiction to Metropolitan Magistrate or JMFC.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(1)(b) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, a court may take cognizance of an offence under the Act upon:
options: Its own knowledge, police report, complaint by aggrieved person/parent/relative, or complaint by a recognized welfare institution/organization
questions.explanation: Section 7(1)(b) provides wide locus standi including complaints by recognized social welfare organizations.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(2) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, does Chapter XXXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Limitation for taking cognizance) apply to offences under the Act?
options: No, nothing in Chapter XXXVI CrPC shall apply to offences punishable under this Act (no limitation period)
questions.explanation: Section 7(2) expressly excludes CrPC limitation periods for dowry offences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(3) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, a statement made by the person aggrieved by the offence in court:
options: Makes her an accomplice liable to equal punishment
Shall NOT subject such person to a prosecution under this Act
questions.explanation: Section 7(3) statutory immunity protects victims giving testimony from being prosecuted for 'giving' dowry.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 (as amended in 1986), every offence under the Act shall be:
options: Non-bailable but compoundable with court permission
questions.explanation: Section 8(2) explicitly mandates that all offences under the Act are non-bailable and non-compoundable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8A of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, where a person is prosecuted for taking, abetting, or demanding dowry under Section 3 or 4, the burden of proof is on:
options: The accused person to prove that he had NOT committed an offence
questions.explanation: Section 8A creates a statutory reverse burden of proof placing onus on the accused.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8B(4) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, the State Government may appoint an Advisory Board to assist Dowry Prohibition Officers consisting of not more than five social welfare workers, out of whom at least:
questions.explanation: Section 8B(4) requires that at least 2 out of max 5 members of Advisory Board must be women.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, presents given at marriage to the bride or bridegroom WITHOUT any demand are exempt from being treated as dowry PROVIDED THAT:
options: Given in presence of Police Officer
They are entered in a LIST maintained in accordance with Rules made under the Act, and (for bridegroom) are of customary nature not excessive in value
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) exempts voluntary customary presents if listed in compliance with the 1985 Rules.

questions.question_text: Under the Dowry Prohibition (Maintenance of Lists of Presents to the Bride and Bridegroom) Rules, 1985, the list of presents must be prepared at the time of marriage and MUST be signed by:
options: Both the bride and the bridegroom
questions.explanation: 1985 Rules mandate that the list of presents must be signed by both bride and bridegroom.

questions.question_text: What constitutes 'Dowry Death' under Section 80 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly Section 304B of IPC)?
options: Death occurring anytime within 10 years of marriage

Death of a woman caused by burns/bodily injury or occurring unnaturally within 7 years of marriage, shown that soon before death she was subjected to cruelty/harassment by husband or relative for dowry
Suicide occurring after 15 years of marriage
questions.explanation: Section 80 BNS / 304B IPC defines Dowry Death: unnatural death within 7 years of marriage with soon-before dowry cruelty.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum punishment prescribed for Dowry Death under Section 80(2) BNS 2023 (Section 304B(2) IPC)?
options: Imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life
questions.explanation: Section 80(2) BNS / 304B(2) IPC prescribes minimum 7 years imprisonment extending up to life imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 118 of Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (formerly Section 113B of Indian Evidence Act, 1872), when a person is accused of dowry death and it is shown that soon before death the woman was subjected to dowry cruelty:
options: The Court MAY presume at its discretion
The Court shall dismiss the case
Presumption applies only if written suicide note exists
The Court SHALL presume that such person had caused the dowry death (mandatory presumption of law)
questions.explanation: Section 118 BSA / 113B Evidence Act creates a mandatory statutory presumption ('shall presume').

questions.question_text: Under Section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly Section 498A of IPC), subjecting a married woman to cruelty by husband or relative of husband is punishable with imprisonment for a term up to:
options: Three years and shall also be liable to fine
questions.explanation: Section 85 BNS / Section 498A IPC prescribes up to 3 years imprisonment and fine for matrimonial cruelty.

questions.question_text: In Rajinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2015) 6 SCC 477, the Supreme Court clarified the expression 'soon before death' in Section 304B IPC / Section 80 BNS to mean:
options: A proximate and live link between the effect of cruelty and the death, NOT necessarily 'immediately before'
questions.explanation: Rajinder Singh (2015) held 'soon before' implies a live, proximate nexus between dowry harassment and death.
questions.statute_or_case: Rajinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2015) 6 SCC 477

questions.question_text: In the landmark judgment Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) 8 SCC 273, the Supreme Court issued mandatory directions regarding arrest under Section 498A IPC / Section 4 Dowry Prohibition Act to prevent:
options: Automatic and unnecessary arrests of husband and relatives without satisfying Section 41 CrPC requirements
questions.explanation: Arnesh Kumar (2014) laid down guidelines prohibiting routine automatic arrests under Section 498A / Dowry Act.
questions.statute_or_case: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) 8 SCC 273

questions.question_text: In Satvir Singh v. State of Punjab (2001) 8 SCC 633, the Supreme Court held that dowry demands made AFTER marriage fall under Section 2 of DPA 1961 if made:
options: In connection with the marriage of the parties
questions.explanation: Satvir Singh affirmed that post-marriage demands 'in connection with marriage' constitute dowry under Section 2.
questions.statute_or_case: Satvir Singh v. State of Punjab (2001)

questions.question_text: In Kamlesh Panjiyar v. State of Bihar (2005) 2 SCC 388, the Supreme Court held that a demand for money or property after marriage for starting a business or buying land:
options: Constitutes dowry demand if linked to or in connection with marriage
Is a simple commercial loan outside dowry law
Is legal if agreed by wife
Is punishable under Contract Act only
questions.explanation: Kamlesh Panjiyar held post-marriage demands for business/land connected with marriage constitute dowry.
questions.statute_or_case: Kamlesh Panjiyar v. State of Bihar (2005)

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(3) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, the Act came into force on:
questions.explanation: The Act was passed on 20th May 1961 and brought into force on 1st July 1961 by Central Government notification.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 Explanation II of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, 'valuable security' has the same meaning as in:
options: Section 5 of Transfer of Property Act
Section 30 of the Indian Penal Code (Section 2(31) of BNS 2023)
questions.explanation: Section 2 Explanation II adopts the definition of 'valuable security' from IPC Section 30.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) proviso of DPA 1961, can a court impose a sentence of imprisonment of LESS THAN 5 years for giving/taking dowry?
options: No, 5 years is mandatory with zero exceptions
Yes, on payment of double fine without recording reasons
Yes, for adequate and special reasons to be recorded in the judgment
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) proviso permits lesser sentence for adequate and special reasons recorded in writing.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 proviso of DPA 1961, can a court impose a sentence of imprisonment of LESS THAN 6 months for demanding dowry?
options: Yes, for adequate and special reasons to be mentioned in the judgment
No, 6 months is mandatory without exception
Yes, with permission of High Court only
Yes, if demand was made by phone
questions.explanation: Section 4 proviso permits court to reduce sentence below 6 months for special recorded reasons.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1)(b) of DPA 1961, if dowry was received AT THE TIME OF OR AFTER marriage by a third person, within what time limit must it be transferred to the woman?
options: Within three months after the date of its receipt
questions.explanation: Section 6(1)(b) requires transfer within 3 months of receipt date.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1) of DPA 1961, pending transfer of dowry property to the woman, the person holding it holds it as:
options: In trust for the benefit of the woman
questions.explanation: Section 6(1) explicitly creates a statutory trust holding property for woman's benefit.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3A) of DPA 1961, if a convicted person fails to obey court direction to transfer dowry property, how is the property value recovered?
options: By filing a civil execution suit
By selling his ancestral land in auction
An amount equal to the value of property may be recovered from him as if it were a fine imposed by Court
questions.explanation: Section 6(3A) enables recovery of property value as a criminal fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1) of DPA 1961, CrPC applies to offences under the Act as if they were cognizable offences FOR THE PURPOSES OF:
options: Arrest without warrant in all cases
questions.explanation: Section 8(1)(a) treats offences as cognizable specifically for investigation purposes.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8B(1) of DPA 1961, who appoints Dowry Prohibition Officers?
questions.explanation: Section 8B(1) empowers State Government to appoint Dowry Prohibition Officers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8B(3) of DPA 1961, the State Government may by notification confer upon a Dowry Prohibition Officer the powers of:
questions.explanation: Section 8B(3) allows State Govt to confer police officer powers on DPOs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of DPA 1961, who has rule-making power to prescribe the form and manner of list of presents?
questions.explanation: Section 9 empowers Central Government to make rules (including presents list rules).

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of DPA 1961, the State Government has rule-making power specifically regarding:
options: Additional functions and powers of Dowry Prohibition Officers under Section 8B
questions.explanation: Section 10 empowers State Government to make rules for DPO functions.

questions.question_text: Under Haryana State Amendment to Section 7 of DPA 1961 (Haryana Act 38 of 1976), no inquiry under the Act shall be made through a Police Officer below the rank of:
questions.explanation: Haryana State Amendment mandates inquiry by an officer not below DSP rank.

questions.question_text: Under Haryana State Amendment to Section 7 of DPA 1961, no court shall take cognizance of an offence EXCEPT on complaint made within a period of:
options: One year from the date of the marriage
questions.explanation: Haryana Amendment Section 7(b) prescribed a 1-year limitation from marriage date.

questions.question_text: Under Haryana State Amendment to Section 7(e) of DPA 1961, regarding police station inquiry:
options: Woman must attend police station within 24 hours
Inquiry must occur at High Court
Woman must be accompanied by 2 lawyers
No woman shall be called to a Police Station for the purpose of an enquiry regarding any offence under this Act
questions.explanation: Haryana s. 7(e) prohibits calling women to police stations for inquiry.

questions.question_text: In Kans Raj v. State of Punjab (2000) 5 SCC 207, the Supreme Court held regarding 'soon before death' in dowry death cases that:
options: It is a relative term dependent on facts of each case; there must be an unbroken continuous chain of cruelty for dowry leading to death
It means strictly within 24 hours of death
It means within 1 month of marriage
It requires written complaint before Magistrate prior to death
questions.explanation: Kans Raj (2000) clarified that 'soon before' requires an unbroken nexus between dowry harassment and unnatural death.
questions.statute_or_case: Kans Raj v. State of Punjab (2000) 5 SCC 207

questions.question_text: In Reema Aggarwal v. Anupam (2004) 3 SCC 199, the Supreme Court held regarding Section 498A IPC / Section 85 BNS that:
options: Strict proof of valid marriage ceremony is mandatory under Section 498A
A person who enters into a marriage contract can be prosecuted under Section 498A even if the validity of the marriage is disputed
Section 498A applies only to registered marriages
Section 498A applies to live-in partners only
questions.explanation: Reema Aggarwal (2004) held that 'husband' under S. 498A includes a person who enters into marriage relationship even if validity is contested.

questions.question_text: Under Section 117 of Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (formerly Section 113A of Evidence Act), when a married woman commits suicide within SEVEN YEARS of marriage and was subjected to cruelty by husband/relatives:
options: The Court shall dismiss the case
The Court MAY presume that such suicide had been abetted by her husband or relative
The Court transfers case to CBI
questions.explanation: Section 117 BSA / 113A Evidence Act creates a discretionary presumption ('may presume') for abetment of suicide within 7 years.

questions.question_text: What is the crucial statutory difference between Section 117 BSA (113A Evidence Act - Suicide presumption) and Section 118 BSA (113B Evidence Act - Dowry death presumption)?
options: Section 117 BSA is discretionary ('MAY presume'), whereas Section 118 BSA is mandatory ('SHALL presume')
questions.explanation: Abetment of suicide presumption is 'may presume' (discretionary), while dowry death presumption is 'shall presume' (mandatory).

questions.question_text: Under Section 86 BNS 2023 (corresponding to the Explanation to Section 498A IPC), 'cruelty' is defined as:
options: Any wilful conduct driving woman to suicide/injury OR harassment with a view to coercing her/relatives to meet unlawful demand for property
questions.explanation: Section 86 BNS (corresponding to the Explanation to Section 498A IPC) defines cruelty under two prongs: (a) grave injury/suicide drive, and (b) dowry harassment coercion.

questions.question_text: Can a woman's IN-LAWS (father-in-law, mother-in-law, sister-in-law) be prosecuted under Section 3 or 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 for demanding dowry?
options: No, only husband can be prosecuted
Yes, Section 4 applies to 'any person' who demands dowry directly or indirectly from parents or relatives of bride/groom
Only if they live in same house
questions.explanation: Section 4 explicitly covers 'any person' demanding dowry from parents/relatives.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) proviso of DPA 1961, for presents given to the BRIDEGROOM by bride's family to be exempt from being dowry, their value must:
options: Not be excessive having regard to the financial status of the person giving them
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) second proviso requires that bridegroom presents by bride's side must be customary and non-excessive relative to status.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(1) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, the Act applies to:
questions.explanation: Section 1(1) states the exact short title of Act No. 28 of 1961.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(2) of DPA 1961, the Act extends to:
questions.explanation: Section 1(2) extends the Act to the whole of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of DPA 1961, 'dowry' includes property given or agreed to be given by parents of either party to:
options: Either party to the marriage or to any other person
questions.explanation: Section 2(b) covers gifts to either party or to any other person.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of DPA 1961, abetting the giving or taking of dowry is:
options: Punishable with the exact same minimum punishment of 5 years imprisonment and fine as giving/taking dowry
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) places abettors of giving or taking dowry on par with principal offenders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4A(a) of DPA 1961, offering any share in property or business as consideration for marriage through an advertisement in which media is prohibited?
options: Newspaper, periodical, journal or any other media
questions.explanation: Section 4A(a) covers advertisements across all media platforms.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4A(b) of DPA 1961, printing, publishing, or circulating a marriage dowry advertisement is punishable with fine up to:
options: Fifteen thousand rupees (or min 6 months imprisonment extending to 5 years)
questions.explanation: Section 4A prescribes fine up to Rs. 15,000 for printing/publishing forbidden marriage advertisements.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1) of DPA 1961, if a mother-in-law receives dowry gold at the wedding, she holds it pending transfer to the bride as:
options: A trustee in trust for the benefit of the bride
questions.explanation: Section 6(1) mandates that any third person receiving dowry holds it in trust for the woman.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3) of DPA 1961, if a woman entitled to dowry property dies BEFORE receiving it (and dies naturally after 7 years of marriage), who can claim it?
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) main clause provides that upon her death, her heirs are entitled to claim it.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(1)(b)(ii) of DPA 1961, a recognized welfare institution or organization means a social welfare institution recognized by:
questions.explanation: Section 7(1) Explanation defines recognized welfare institution as recognized by Central or State Govt.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1)(b) of DPA 1961, CrPC applies as if offences were cognizable, EXCEPT for matters referred to in Section 42 CrPC and:
options: The arrest of a person without a warrant or without an order of a Magistrate
questions.explanation: Section 8(1)(b)(ii) limits cognizable status by excluding arrest without warrant/magistrate order.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8B(2)(a) of DPA 1961, a primary function of a Dowry Prohibition Officer is:
options: To see that the provisions of the Act are complied with
questions.explanation: Section 8B(2)(a) specifies ensuring compliance as a core function of DPO.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8B(2)(c) of DPA 1961, a Dowry Prohibition Officer has the function to:
options: Collect such evidence as may be necessary for the prosecution of persons committing offences under the Act
questions.explanation: Section 8B(2)(c) assigns evidence collection for prosecution to DPOs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(2)(a) of DPA 1961, Central Government rules can specify the form and manner in which the list of presents shall be maintained by:
questions.explanation: Section 9(2)(a) empowers Central Govt to rule on maintenance of presents list.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(3) of DPA 1961, rules made by Central Government must be laid before each House of Parliament for a total period of:
questions.explanation: Section 9(3) mandates laying rules before Parliament for 30 days.

questions.question_text: Under Haryana State Amendment to Section 3 of DPA 1961 (Haryana Act 38 of 1976), the fine for giving or taking dowry may extend to:
questions.explanation: Haryana s. 3 amendment substituted fine up to Rs. 5,000.

questions.question_text: Under Haryana State Amendment to Section 2 Explanation I of DPA 1961, presents made at marriage in cash, ornaments, clothes shall NOT be deemed dowry UNLESS made:
options: As consideration for the marriage of the said parties
questions.explanation: Haryana s. 2 Explanation I declared presents are not dowry unless given as marriage consideration.

questions.question_text: In Appasaheb v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 9 SCC 721, the Supreme Court held that a demand for money from wife's parents for urgent agricultural expenses or domestic stringency:
options: Did not amount to dowry demand as it was not in connection with marriage (distinguished in later decisions like Rajinder Singh)
questions.explanation: Appasaheb held urgent financial assistance demand was not dowry demand (later clarified in Rajinder Singh).
questions.statute_or_case: Appasaheb v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 9 SCC 721

questions.question_text: Under Rule 2 of the Dowry Prohibition (Maintenance of Lists of Presents) Rules, 1985, if the bride or bridegroom is unable to sign the list of presents, what must be done?
options: He or she may affix his or her thumb impression after list is read out to him/her
Magistrate must sign on their behalf
questions.explanation: 1985 Rules allow thumb impression after reading out list if party cannot sign.

questions.question_text: Under the 1985 Presents List Rules, what details MUST be included in the list of presents?
options: Brief description of present, approximate value, name of giver, and relationship of giver to bride/bridegroom
questions.explanation: Rule 2 requires description, value, giver's name, and relationship.

questions.question_text: Can a husband be prosecuted under Section 80 BNS 2023 (304B IPC) if the dowry death of his wife occurred 7 years and 1 day after marriage?
options: No, Section 80 BNS / 304B IPC strictly requires death occurring within SEVEN YEARS of marriage
questions.explanation: 7-year period from marriage is a strict statutory boundary for Section 80 BNS / 304B IPC.

questions.question_text: If a married woman dies an unnatural death AFTER 7 years of marriage due to dowry harassment, under which provision can the accused husband be prosecuted instead of Section 80 BNS / 304B IPC?
options: Cannot be prosecuted under any law
Section 85 BNS (Cruelty - 498A IPC) and Section 108 BNS (Abetment of Suicide - 306 IPC) or Section 103 BNS (Murder - 302 IPC)
questions.explanation: After 7 years, prosecution lies under general provisions of cruelty (s. 85 BNS), abetment of suicide (s. 108 BNS), or murder (s. 103 BNS).

questions.question_text: Under Section 85 BNS 2023 (498A IPC), is 'Cruelty' a continuing offence?
options: Yes, matrimonial cruelty involving persistent harassment is a continuing offence
No, limitation starts on wedding day
questions.explanation: Matrimonial cruelty under S. 85 BNS / 498A IPC is held to be a continuing offence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of DPA 1961, what is the minimum fine prescribed for giving or taking dowry?
options: Fifteen thousand rupees or the amount of the value of such dowry, whichever is MORE
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) specifies minimum fine of Rs. 15,000 or dowry value, whichever is higher.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of DPA 1961, what is the maximum fine prescribed for DEMANDING dowry?
questions.explanation: Section 4 specifies fine which may extend to Rs. 10,000 for demanding dowry.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4A of DPA 1961, what is the maximum fine prescribed for publishing a prohibited dowry advertisement?
questions.explanation: Section 4A specifies fine up to Rs. 15,000 for dowry advertisement offences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2) of DPA 1961, what is the minimum fine for failing to transfer dowry property to the woman/heirs within 3 months?
options: Five thousand rupees (extending to ten thousand rupees)
questions.explanation: Section 6(2) specifies minimum fine of Rs. 5,000 up to Rs. 10,000.

questions.question_text: If a father gives gold ornaments to his daughter at marriage voluntarily without any demand from groom's side, and enters them in a signed list under 1985 Rules, is he guilty under Section 3 for giving dowry?
options: Yes, giving gold is always illegal
No, Section 3(2)(a) expressly exempts un-demanded presents entered in a list maintained under the Rules
Guilty if gold value exceeds Rs. 10,000
questions.explanation: Section 3(2)(a) protects voluntary presents entered in the statutory list.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1) of DPA 1961, can a husband hold his wife's dowry property as HIS OWN personal property?
options: Yes, husband is absolute owner of wife's dowry
No, he holds it IN TRUST for the benefit of the woman and must transfer it to her within 3 months
questions.explanation: Section 6(1) makes husband/in-law a statutory trustee holding dowry for woman's benefit.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2) of DPA 1961, can an offence under the Dowry Prohibition Act be COMPOUNDED (settled out of court) by the parties?
options: Yes, on payment of Rs. 10,000 fine
No, offences under the Act are non-compoundable
questions.explanation: Section 8(2) explicitly enacts that offences under the Act are non-compoundable.

questions.question_text: Can a person accused under Section 4 for demanding dowry claim BAIL as a matter of right under Section 8(2) of DPA 1961?
options: No, Section 8(2) specifies that offences under the Act are NON-BAILABLE
Yes, if demand was under Rs. 5,000
questions.explanation: Section 8(2) as amended in 1986 made all offences under DPA non-bailable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8A of DPA 1961, when does the reverse burden of proof shift to the accused?
options: Once the prosecution establishes the essential facts of taking, abetting, or demanding dowry under Section 3 or 4
questions.explanation: Section 8A shifts burden of proof to accused once core prosecution facts under s. 3/4 are shown.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8B(2)(b) of DPA 1961, a Dowry Prohibition Officer has the statutory duty to prevent, as far as possible:
options: The taking or abetting the taking of, or the demanding of, dowry
questions.explanation: Section 8B(2)(b) mandates DPO to prevent taking, abetting, or demanding dowry.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8B(4) of DPA 1961, how many social welfare workers can be appointed to the Advisory Board for a DPO?
options: Not more than five social welfare workers (at least two women)
questions.explanation: Section 8B(4) caps Advisory Board members at 5, requiring at least 2 women.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3) proviso of DPA 1961, if a woman dies within 7 years of marriage unnaturally leaving NO children, to whom is dowry property transferred?
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) proviso (a) directs transfer to her parents if she dies childless within 7 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3A) of DPA 1961, if property value is recovered from an offender as a fine, to whom is it paid?
options: To the woman or, as the case may be, her heirs, parents or children
questions.explanation: Section 6(3A) specifies recovered fine amount is paid directly to the woman/heirs/parents/children.

questions.question_text: Under Section 80 BNS 2023 (304B IPC), does 'bodily injury' resulting in dowry death require marks of physical assault?
options: It includes burns or any bodily injury or death occurring otherwise than under normal circumstances
questions.explanation: Section 80 BNS covers burns, bodily injury, or death occurring otherwise than under normal circumstances.

questions.question_text: In Soni Devrajbhai Babubhai v. State of Gujarat (1991) 4 SCC 298, the Supreme Court held that Section 304B IPC (Dowry Death) enacted in 1986 cannot apply to offences committed before 1986 because of:
options: Article 20(1) of the Constitution (Protection against ex-post facto criminal laws)
questions.explanation: Soni Devrajbhai held Section 304B IPC cannot be applied retrospectively due to Art. 20(1) ex-post facto bar.
questions.statute_or_case: Soni Devrajbhai v. State of Gujarat (1991)

questions.question_text: Under Section 85 BNS 2023 (498A IPC), who can lodge an FIR / complaint for cruelty against husband?
options: The aggrieved woman or any person related to her by blood, marriage or adoption (or police officer)
questions.explanation: Section 85 BNS / 498A IPC & CrPC s. 198A allow complaints by woman or her blood/marriage relatives.

questions.question_text: What is the key element distinguishing Section 80 BNS (304B IPC - Dowry Death) from Section 108 BNS (306 IPC - Abetment of Suicide)?
options: Section 80 BNS specifically requires proof of dowry cruelty 'soon before death' and death within 7 years, creating a mandatory presumption under Section 118 BSA
Section 80 BNS applies only to males
Section 108 BNS applies only to rich people
questions.explanation: Section 80 BNS is a specific offence requiring dowry harassment nexus with 7-year unnatural death and mandatory presumption.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of DPA 1961, if groom's father demands Rs. 5 Lakhs cash 2 days BEFORE wedding as a condition for solemnizing marriage, this demand is:
options: An illegal demand for dowry punishable under Section 4 of DPA 1961
questions.explanation: Demanding cash as condition for marriage is a classic illegal dowry demand under Section 4.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1) of DPA 1961, if dowry is received by groom's father, within what period must he transfer it to the bride if received at the wedding?
options: Within three months after the date of its receipt
questions.explanation: Section 6(1)(b) requires transfer within 3 months of receipt date.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(1)(c) of DPA 1961, a Judicial Magistrate 1st Class trying a dowry offence is empowered to:
options: Pass any sentence authorized by the Act on any person convicted
Impose fine up to Rs. 1,000 only
Refer all cases to High Court for sentencing
questions.explanation: Section 7(1)(c) explicitly authorizes JMFC/Metropolitan Magistrate to pass any sentence permitted by the Act (including 5+ years).

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1) of DPA 1961, for what purpose is the Code of Criminal Procedure applied as if offences were cognizable?
options: For arrest without warrant without magistrate order
For the purposes of investigation of such offences
questions.explanation: Section 8(1)(a) specifies investigation purpose.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10(1) of DPA 1961, State Government rules made under the Act must be laid before:
questions.explanation: Section 10(3) requires laying state rules before State Legislature.

questions.question_text: Can an agreement to give dowry be enforced in a Civil Court to recover unpaid promised dowry cash?
options: Yes, if written on stamp paper
No, Section 5 of DPA 1961 declares any agreement for giving/taking dowry to be VOID
questions.explanation: Section 5 renders dowry agreements void ab initio; no civil suit lies to enforce them.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2)(b) of DPA 1961, presents given at marriage to the BRIDEGROOM are exempt from dowry provided they are entered in a list AND:
options: Given without any demand, are of customary nature, and value is not excessive having regard to financial status of giver
questions.explanation: Section 3(2)(b) proviso sets out non-demand, customary nature, and non-excessive value conditions.

questions.question_text: What is the main statutory objective of the 1986 Amendment (Act 43 of 1986) to the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961?
options: To legalize dowry up to Rs. 50,000
To stringently enhance minimum punishments (min 5 yrs for s.3), introduce Section 4A advertisement ban, Section 8A burden of proof, Section 8B DPOs, and insert Section 304B IPC Dowry Death
questions.explanation: The 1986 Amendment comprehensive reform strengthened penalties, burden of proof, DPOs, and inserted IPC 304B.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8B(2)(a) & (b) of DPA 1961, Dowry Prohibition Officers are mandated to collect evidence for prosecution AND to prevent:
options: Taking, abetting taking, or demanding of dowry
questions.explanation: Section 8B(2)(b) tasks DPOs with preventive action against taking, abetting, or demanding dowry.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3) proviso (a) of DPA 1961, if a married woman dies unnaturally within 7 years of marriage leaving NO children, her parents receive her dowry property held in trust. If parents are also dead, who receives it?
options: Her legal heirs under applicable personal law
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) provides property passes to her heirs if parents/children are not available.

questions.question_text: What is the primary overarching object of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 as stated in its Preamble?
options: To prohibit the giving or taking of dowry
To enforce compulsory registration of marriages
questions.explanation: The Preamble states DPA 1961 is 'An Act to prohibit the giving or taking of dowry'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Central Government has power to take all such measures as it deems necessary for:
options: Protecting and improving the quality of the environment and preventing, controlling and abating environmental pollution
questions.explanation: Section 3 enacts general powers of the Central Government to protect environment, enacted following the 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy.

questions.question_text: Under what constitutional provision was The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 enacted by Parliament to implement decisions of the 1972 Stockholm United Nations Conference?
options: Article 253 of the Constitution of India (Legislation for giving effect to international agreements)
questions.explanation: The EPA 1986 was enacted under Article 253 to implement 1972 Stockholm Declaration decisions.
questions.statute_or_case: Article 253, Constitution of India / EPA 1986 Preamble

questions.question_text: In the landmark Oleum Gas Leak Case (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India AIR 1987 SC 1086), the Supreme Court laid down which strict legal doctrine replacing Rylands v. Fletcher?
options: The Doctrine of ABSOLUTE LIABILITY (an enterprise engaged in hazardous industry owes an absolute, non-delegable duty with no exceptions)
questions.explanation: M.C. Mehta (1987) established Absolute Liability for hazardous/inherently dangerous industries without any Rylands v. Fletcher exceptions.
questions.statute_or_case: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak 1987)

questions.question_text: In M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) 1 SCC 388, the Supreme Court enunciated which constitutional doctrine regarding natural resources like rivers, forests, and air?
options: The PUBLIC TRUST DOCTRINE (State is a trustee of all natural resources for the public and cannot convert them to private ownership)
questions.explanation: Kamal Nath (1997) held public trust doctrine is part of Indian environmental jurisprudence under Art 21.
questions.statute_or_case: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) 1 SCC 388

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Central Government (or delegated authority) has power to issue binding directions including:
options: Directing closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process, or stoppage/regulation of supply of electricity, water or other services
questions.explanation: Section 5 gives statutory power to issue direct closure and service disconnection orders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14A of The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (as substituted by the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023, w.e.f. 1 April 2024), contravention of Section 7 (excess emission/discharge) or Section 8 (unsafe handling of hazardous substances) now attracts a civil penalty of:
options: Not less than Rs. 1 lakh, extending up to Rs. 15 lakh per contravention, plus an additional Rs. 50,000 per day of continuing default
Imprisonment up to 5 years or fine up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both
questions.explanation: The Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 decriminalised the old Section 15 imprisonment for Section 7/8 contraventions; Section 14A now imposes a civil penalty of Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 15 lakh, with a further Rs. 50,000 per day of continuing default, imposed by an adjudicating officer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15F of The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (inserted by the 2023 Jan Vishwas amendment), a person who fails to pay a penalty imposed under Sections 14A, 14B, 15, 15A or 15B within ninety days of its imposition is liable to imprisonment which may extend to:
options: Three years, or fine up to twice the penalty amount, or both
questions.explanation: Section 15F retains a criminal consequence only for non-payment of the civil penalty itself: imprisonment up to three years or a fine up to twice the unpaid penalty, or both; the old Section 15(2) enhanced-imprisonment-for-continuing-default provision no longer exists in this form.

questions.question_text: In Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (Bichhri Case 1996) 3 SCC 212, the Supreme Court applied which environmental principle to compel chemical factories to pay costs of remediating toxic sludge?
options: The POLLUTER PAYS PRINCIPLE (financial cost of preventing/remediating damage lies on the polluting industry)
questions.explanation: Bichhri Case (1996) enforced Polluter Pays Principle making polluting industry liable for full environmental restoration costs.
questions.statute_or_case: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. UOI (1996)

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(b) of The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (Citizen Suit Provision), a private citizen can file a complaint in court after giving notice of how many days to the Central Government?
options: Sixty days in the prescribed manner
questions.explanation: Section 19(b) mandates 60 days prior statutory notice before filing private environmental complaints.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, which court's jurisdiction is barred in respect of any action taken by the Central Government under the Act?
questions.explanation: Section 22 explicitly bars Civil Court jurisdiction in EPA matters.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(a) of EPA 1986, 'environment' includes:
options: Water, air and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property
questions.explanation: Section 2(a) provides an all-encompassing definition of environment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b) of EPA 1986, 'environmental pollutant' means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be or tend to be:
questions.explanation: Section 2(b) defines environmental pollutant based on potential injury to environment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(e) of EPA 1986, 'hazardous substance' means any substance or preparation which, by reason of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling, is liable to cause harm to:
options: Human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism, property or the environment
questions.explanation: Section 2(e) defines hazardous substance broadly across living creatures, property, and environment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of EPA 1986, no person shall handle or cause to be handled any hazardous substance EXCEPT in accordance with:
options: Such procedural safeguards and rules as may be prescribed
questions.explanation: Section 8 mandates strict compliance with statutory procedural safeguards for handling hazardous substances.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10(1) of EPA 1986, any person empowered by Central Government has a right to enter and inspect any place at all reasonable times for the purpose of:
options: Performing any functions of Central Government under the Act or examining compliance with rules/notices
questions.explanation: Section 10(1) grants wide inspection and entry powers to statutory environmental officers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11(1) of EPA 1986, Central Government officers may take samples of air, water, soil or other substance from any factory for the purpose of:
questions.explanation: Section 11(1) empowers Central Government officers to take samples of air, water, soil or other substance for analysis at an environmental laboratory.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11(3) of EPA 1986, sample taken by an officer is split into how many parts in presence of occupier?
options: Two parts (each container placed in container sealed and marked)
questions.explanation: Section 11(3) requires the officer to divide the sample into two parts in the occupier's presence, each sealed, marked and signed by both.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12(1) of EPA 1986, Central Government may establish or recognize one or more:
options: Environmental Laboratories to carry out functions entrusted under the Act
questions.explanation: Section 12(1) lets the Central Government establish or recognise environmental laboratories to carry out functions under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15A of EPA 1986 (as substituted in 2024; Section 16 now deals with the Environmental Protection Fund), where a company contravenes the Act, who is liable to the penalty?
options: The company itself, liable to penalty of Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 15 lakh for each contravention
questions.explanation: The 2024 substitution moved corporate liability out of the old Section 16 into Section 15A, fixing a civil penalty directly on the company (Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 15 lakh, with a daily additional penalty for continuing default); Section 16 is now the Environmental Protection Fund provision.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15B of EPA 1986 (as substituted in 2024; the old Section 17 on this subject has been omitted), where a contravention is committed by a Government Department, who is liable to the penalty?
options: The Head of the Department, liable to a penalty equal to one month's basic salary, unless he proves the contravention occurred without his knowledge or instructions
questions.explanation: Section 15B fixes a civil penalty of one month's basic salary on the Head of the Department (or a negligent officer), subject to a due-diligence/no-knowledge defence; the old Section 17 provision was omitted in the 2024 restructuring.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of EPA 1986, no suit, prosecution or legal proceeding shall lie against Government or officers for:
options: Anything done or intended to be done in good faith in pursuance of the Act (Indemnity)
questions.explanation: Section 18 protects the Government and its officers/authorities from suit or prosecution for anything done or intended to be done in good faith under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of EPA 1986 (as substituted in 2024), the provisions of this Act and the rules or orders made thereunder shall have effect:
options: Only if the State Legislature consents
Notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in any other law for the time being in force
questions.explanation: Section 24, as substituted in 2024, is now a single overriding-effect clause; the earlier two-subsection provision on choosing between EPA and another Act's penalty no longer exists in this form.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) and Section 3(2)(v) of EPA 1986 (power to restrict areas where industries/processes may be carried on), the Central Government framed which major environmental notification regulating coastal areas?
questions.explanation: The CRZ Notification (currently CRZ Notification, 2019) is issued in exercise of powers under Section 3(1) and clause (v) of Section 3(2), which lets the Centre restrict where industries/processes may be carried on.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) and Section 3(2)(v) of EPA 1986, Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for major industrial and infrastructure projects is regulated by:
questions.explanation: The EIA Notification, 2006 is issued in exercise of powers under Section 3(1) and clause (v) of Section 3(2) of the EPA, restricting/regulating specified projects unless prior environmental clearance is obtained.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2)(b) of EPA 1986 (maximum allowable limits of concentration of pollutants, including noise, for different areas), restrictions on ambient noise levels in silence/residential/commercial zones are regulated by:
options: The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000
questions.explanation: The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 were made under Section 3(2)(ii), Section 6(2)(b) and Section 25 of the EPA, prescribing ambient noise standards for industrial, commercial, residential and silence zones.

questions.question_text: In T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1997) 2 SCC 267, the Supreme Court gave a broad meaning to 'Forest' under Forest Conservation Act to include:
options: All lands recorded as forest in government records regardless of ownership, as well as dictionary meaning of forest
questions.explanation: Godavarman held that "forest land" under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 covers the dictionary meaning of forest as well as any area recorded as forest in government records, irrespective of ownership.
questions.statute_or_case: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1997) 2 SCC 267

questions.question_text: In Taj Trapezium Case (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India 1997) 2 SCC 353, the Supreme Court ordered 292 polluting industries around Taj Mahal to:
options: Switch to natural gas (GAIL) or relocate outside Taj Trapezium Zone (TTZ) to prevent yellowing of Taj marble
questions.explanation: In the Taj Trapezium Case the Court, invoking the precautionary and polluter-pays principles, directed the identified industries to switch to natural gas or relocate outside the Taj Trapezium Zone to arrest damage to the Taj marble.
questions.statute_or_case: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997) 2 SCC 353

questions.question_text: In Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) 1 SCC 598, the Supreme Court held that Right to Life under Article 21 includes:
options: The right to enjoyment of pollution-free water and air for full enjoyment of life
questions.explanation: Subhash Kumar held that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to enjoyment of pollution-free water and air, enforceable through Article 32.
questions.statute_or_case: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) 1 SCC 598

questions.question_text: In Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand (1980) 4 SCC 162, the Supreme Court held that financial inability of a municipality:
options: Cannot be pleaded to escape mandatory duty to abate public nuisance under Section 133 CrPC / environmental laws
questions.explanation: Ratlam held that a local body cannot plead financial inability to escape its mandatory statutory duty to abate a public nuisance; Section 133 CrPC (now corresponding to Section 152, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) empowers a Magistrate to order abatement.
questions.statute_or_case: Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand (1980) 4 SCC 162

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of EPA 1986, carrying on any industry which discharges environmental pollutants in excess of prescribed standards is:
questions.explanation: Section 7 flatly prohibits discharging or emitting environmental pollutants in excess of prescribed standards; contravention now attracts a civil penalty under Section 14A.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(1) of EPA 1986, where discharge of excess pollutant occurs due to accident or unforeseen event, the person in charge is bound to:
options: Mitigate pollution and intimate prescribed authorities immediately
questions.explanation: Section 9(1) obliges the person in charge to prevent or mitigate the pollution and to immediately intimate the prescribed authorities of the occurrence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of EPA 1986, who appoints Government Analysts for analyzing samples of air, water, soil or other substances?
questions.explanation: Section 13 empowers the Central Government to appoint or recognise qualified persons as Government Analysts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of EPA 1986, the report of a Government Analyst may be used as evidence in:
questions.explanation: Section 14 lets a Government Analyst's report be used as evidence of the facts stated therein in any proceeding under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(a) of EPA 1986, a court can take cognizance of an offence on a complaint made by:
options: The Central Government or any authority authorized by that Government
questions.explanation: Section 19(a) lets a court take cognizance on a complaint by the Central Government or an authority/officer it authorises; clause (b) alternatively allows a private citizen to complain after 60 days' notice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2)(b) of EPA 1986, Central Government rules may prescribe the maximum allowable limits of concentration of:
options: Various environmental pollutants (including noise) for different areas
questions.explanation: Section 6(2)(b) specifically empowers rules prescribing maximum allowable pollutant concentration limits, including noise, for different areas.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2)(c) of EPA 1986, rules may prescribe the procedures and safeguards for handling:
questions.explanation: Section 6(2)(c) specifically empowers rules on procedures and safeguards for handling hazardous substances.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2)(e) of EPA 1986, rules may prescribe prohibition and restrictions on the location of industries in:
questions.explanation: Section 6(2)(e) specifically empowers rules restricting or prohibiting the location of industries and the carrying on of processes/operations in different areas.

questions.question_text: Under Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016 framed under EPA 1986, bio-medical waste from hospitals must be segregated into color-coded bags, namely:
questions.explanation: The Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (framed under Section 6/25 of the EPA) mandate segregation into Yellow, Red, White (translucent) and Blue category bags/containers.

questions.question_text: Under Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 framed under EPA 1986, single-use plastic items with low utility and high littering potential were banned in India from:
questions.explanation: The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2021 (under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, framed under the EPA) banned identified single-use plastic items with effect from 1 July 2022.
questions.statute_or_case: Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 (as amended 2021), under EPA, 1986

questions.question_text: Under E-Waste (Management) Rules framed under EPA 1986, electronics manufacturers are subjected to Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) requiring them to:
options: Collect and channelize end-of-life electronic equipment for safe recycling
questions.explanation: The E-Waste (Management) Rules, framed under the EPA, impose Extended Producer Responsibility obligations requiring producers to collect and channelize end-of-life electronic equipment for authorised recycling.

questions.question_text: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999:
options: Is Act No. 48 of 1999, came into force on 15 September 2003, and was enacted to comply with the TRIPS Agreement (Articles 22-24), India previously having no specific GI law
questions.explanation: Before this Act, GIs in India were protected only through passing-off actions and consumer-protection or trade-mark law; the first GI registered was Darjeeling Tea (2004).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(e) of the GI Act, 1999, a 'geographical indication' means an indication which identifies goods as:
options: Any goods that carry a place name

Agricultural, natural or manufactured goods originating (or manufactured) in a territory, region or locality, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin (and, for manufactured goods, one of the activities of production/processing/preparation takes place in that area)
Goods that are cheaper than others
questions.explanation: A GI covers agricultural, natural and manufactured goods, as well as handicrafts and industrial goods; the link between the product's qualities and its origin is essential.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of the GI Act, 1999, an application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by:
options: Any individual trader in the goods
Any association of persons or producers, or any organisation or authority established by or under any law, representing the interest of the producers of the goods concerned
questions.explanation: A GI is a collective right; it cannot be owned by a single producer. An individual producer may only be registered as an 'authorised user' under Section 17.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of the GI Act, 1999, the registration of a geographical indication is valid for:
options: Ten years, and may be renewed from time to time for further periods of ten years each (indefinitely) on payment of the renewal fee
questions.explanation: The registration of an authorised user is likewise for ten years or until the GI registration expires, whichever is earlier.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of the GI Act, 1999, the Register of Geographical Indications is maintained in two parts:
options: Part A for Indian GIs and Part B for foreign GIs
Part A, containing particulars of registered geographical indications; and Part B, containing particulars of registered authorised users
Part A for agricultural goods and Part B for manufactured goods
Part A for pending applications and Part B for granted registrations
questions.explanation: The GI Registry is located at Chennai; the Registrar of Geographical Indications is the Controller-General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of the GI Act, 1999, a geographical indication:
options: May be freely assigned like a trade mark
May be licensed to any producer for a fee
Is not a subject matter of assignment, transmission, licensing, pledge, mortgage or any such agreement (except on the death of an authorised user, when his right devolves on his successor in title)
May be mortgaged to a bank
questions.explanation: Because a GI belongs to the community of producers in the region, it cannot be transferred to a person outside that community.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the GI Act, 1999:
options: A GI may be registered as a trade mark by anyone
GIs and trade marks are governed by identical rules
There is no interaction between GI and trade mark law

The registration of a geographical indication as a trade mark is prohibited, and the Registrar of Trade Marks must refuse (or invalidate) a trade mark which contains or consists of a GI with respect to goods not originating in the territory indicated, if use of the mark would confuse or mislead the public as to the true origin
questions.explanation: Section 26 protects, for a limited class, trade marks containing a GI that were applied for or used in good faith before the commencement of the Act or before the GI was protected in its country of origin.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the GI Act, 1999, no person is entitled to institute a proceeding to prevent, or to recover damages for, the infringement of:
options: An UNREGISTERED geographical indication — but nothing in the Act affects the common-law right of action against any person for passing off goods as the goods of another, or the remedies for it
Any geographical indication, registered or not
questions.explanation: Registration is thus a pre-condition to a statutory infringement action; the passing-off remedy remains available for unregistered GIs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of the GI Act, 1999, infringement of a registered geographical indication occurs where a person, not being an authorised user, uses such geographical indication:
options: Only where the goods are physically identical

In a manner which indicates or suggests that the goods originate in a geographical area other than the true place of origin in a way that misleads the public; or which constitutes an act of unfair competition including passing off; or (for goods notified for additional protection) uses another GI even if the true origin is indicated or the GI is used in translation or accompanied by expressions such as 'kind', 'style' or 'imitation'
Only where the false GI is used in India
questions.explanation: Section 22(2) empowers the Central Government to notify certain goods for the higher (TRIPS Article 23-style) 'additional protection' that applies to wines and spirits internationally.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of the GI Act, 1999, a geographical indication shall NOT be registered if it:
options: Is applied for by a producers' association

Would deceive or cause confusion; is contrary to any law; comprises scandalous or obscene matter or matter hurting religious susceptibilities; would otherwise be disentitled to protection in a court; is determined to be a generic name or indication of goods; or falsely represents that the goods originate in another territory
questions.explanation: A 'generic' geographical name (one that has become the common name of a type of product) cannot be registered; the Explanation to Section 9 provides guidance on when a name is generic.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the GI Act, 1999, the rights conferred by registration are:
options: An exclusive right in the registered proprietor alone
No rights until an infringement occurs

The exclusive right of the registered proprietor and the authorised users to the use of the geographical indication in relation to the goods, and the right to obtain relief in respect of infringement — but the right of one authorised user is not exclusive as against another authorised user
questions.explanation: Only registered authorised users can exercise the right to use the GI; the registered proprietor holds the GI on behalf of the producers.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 39 and 40 of the GI Act, 1999, falsely applying a geographical indication to goods, or selling goods to which a false geographical indication is applied, is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for a term of not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees
questions.explanation: Section 41 provides enhanced punishment for a second or subsequent conviction; falsely representing a GI as registered (Section 42) was decriminalised by the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 and now attracts only a monetary penalty, while Sections 43 and 44 stand omitted since 1 August 2024.

questions.question_text: Under Section 66 of the GI Act, 1999, a suit for infringement of a registered geographical indication, or for passing off:
options: Must be filed before the Registrar
Must be instituted before a District Court having jurisdiction (a court not inferior to a District Court)
Lies only to the High Court
May be filed before any Magistrate
questions.explanation: Section 67 provides for reliefs including injunction and, at the plaintiff's option, damages or an account of profits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the GI Act, 1999, 'homonymous geographical indications' (identical or nearly identical GI names used for goods originating in different places):
options: Cannot both be registered under any circumstances
Are always registered on a first-come-first-served basis

May both be registered, if the Registrar is satisfied that the indications can be sufficiently differentiated in practice and equitable treatment of the producers and non-deception of consumers can be ensured
questions.explanation: Homonymous GIs (e.g. two regions in different countries sharing a place name) are handled by imposing conditions to distinguish them.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(f) of the GI Act, 1999, 'goods' means:
options: Any agricultural, natural or manufactured goods or any goods of handicraft or of industry, and includes food stuff
questions.explanation: The broad definition allows registration of handicrafts (Kanchipuram silk, Pashmina, Channapatna toys), foodstuffs (Rasgulla, Bikaneri Bhujia) and industrial goods.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of the GI Act, 1999, a person claiming to be a producer of goods in respect of which a geographical indication is registered:
options: May apply to the Registrar to be registered as an 'authorised user' of that geographical indication, jointly with the registered proprietor
Automatically becomes an authorised user on registration of the GI
May use the GI without any registration
questions.explanation: Only a registered authorised user has the right to use the GI and to sue for infringement; the application requires the registered proprietor's involvement.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the GI Act, 1999, a registered geographical indication or an authorised user may be removed from the register:
options: On the application of any person aggrieved, for contravention or failure to observe a condition of registration, or where the registration was made without sufficient cause or wrongly remains on the register, or for any error or defect in an entry
Only if the producers request it
questions.explanation: Rectification of the register is now sought before the High Court after the abolition of the IPAB by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(n) read with Section 11 of the GI Act, 1999, the 'registered proprietor' of a geographical indication is:
options: The Central Government in every case
The association of persons, producers, organisation or authority in whose name the geographical indication is registered — holding it for the benefit of the producers of the goods
The first producer to sell the goods
questions.explanation: The proprietor is a representative body; it cannot exploit the GI for its own private commercial benefit to the exclusion of the producers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22(2) and (3) of the GI Act, 1999, 'additional protection' (protection regardless of whether the public is misled) is available:
options: Never; India provides only the basic level of protection
For such goods or classes of goods as the Central Government may notify in the Official Gazette (used to give Indian GIs the higher level of protection that TRIPS mandates only for wines and spirits)
questions.explanation: Once goods are notified, use of the GI on goods not from the region is barred even if the true origin is disclosed or the GI is used with words like 'type' or 'style'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11(2) of the GI Act, 1999, an application for registration of a geographical indication must contain:
options: A statement of how the GI serves to designate the goods as originating from the territory/region/locality in respect of the quality, reputation or other characteristic attributable to the geographical environment; the class of goods; the geographical map of the territory; particulars of the appearance of the GI (words or figurative elements, or both); a statement of the producers proposed to be initially registered; and such other particulars as may be prescribed
Only the name of the GI
Only proof of the applicant's trade mark
Only a sample of the product
questions.explanation: This 'statement of case', setting out how the qualities are attributable to the geographical origin, is a central document in a GI application; further procedural particulars are prescribed under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Rules, 2002.

questions.question_text: A landmark international dispute concerning an Indian geographical indication was:
options: The 'Darjeeling' tea disputes, in which the Tea Board of India opposed foreign registrations of marks such as 'Darjeeling' and 'Darjeeling Lounge' to protect the reputation of the GI
A copyright case over Bollywood music
A trade-mark case over 'India Pale Ale'
questions.explanation: Darjeeling Tea was the first registered Indian GI (2004) and also received a certification mark; the Tea Board has pursued enforcement in several jurisdictions.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 56 and 70 of the GI Act, 1999, the Registrar and other officers of the Geographical Indications Registry:
options: May disclose confidential application details freely
