questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of HAMA 1956, the statutory presumption regarding registered adoption deeds is a:
options: Rebuttable presumption ('shall presume unless and until disproved')
questions.explanation: Section 16 creates a rebuttable statutory presumption of law which stands until disproved.

questions.question_text: Can a Hindu father by Will disinherit his minor children or aged parents from receiving maintenance under HAMA 1956?
options: No, statutory maintenance under Section 20/22 cannot be defeated by Will; dependants are entitled to maintenance out of estate
questions.explanation: Under Section 22, heirs and legatees taking estate under Will take it subject to maintenance of dependants.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21(iv) of HAMA 1956, a grandson (son of pre-deceased son) is a dependant so long as he is a minor, to the extent he is unable to obtain maintenance from:
questions.explanation: Section 21(iv) condition for grandson dependant is inability to get maintenance from parents' estate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21(v) of HAMA 1956, a grand-daughter (unmarried daughter of pre-deceased son) remains a dependant:
options: So long as she remains unmarried (and unable to obtain maintenance from parents' estate)
questions.explanation: Section 21(v) specifies grand-daughter is dependant as long as she remains unmarried.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(2)(d) of HAMA 1956, in fixing wife's maintenance, court MUST consider:
options: Value of claimant's property and any income derived therefrom or from her own earnings
questions.explanation: Section 23(2)(d) mandates considering claimant's independent income and property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(2)(c) of HAMA 1956, if wife is living separately from husband, court checks:
options: Whether the claimant is justified in doing so under Section 18(2)
Whether she has filed criminal FIR
Whether she lives in same town
questions.explanation: Section 23(2)(c) requires court to verify justification for separate residence under s. 18(2).

questions.question_text: Under HAMA 1956, if a married Hindu man adopts a child without obtaining consent of his living wife (who is of sound mind and not converted/renounced), the adoption is:
questions.explanation: Lack of mandatory wife's consent under Section 7 violates Section 6(i) making adoption void ab initio.

questions.question_text: Under HAMA 1956, does an adoptive mother become a Class I heir of her adopted son under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956?
options: No, she is Class II heir
Yes, under Section 12 HAMA read with HSA Schedule, adoptive mother has full status of mother in Class I
questions.explanation: Section 12 replaces ties in birth family with adoptive family for all purposes, making adoptive mother Class I heir.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(a) of HAMA 1956, a custom applicable to a family ceases to be recognized as law if it has been:
questions.explanation: Section 3(a) second proviso states family custom loses force of law if discontinued by family.

questions.question_text: What is the primary overarching object of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 as stated in its Preamble?
options: To amend and codify the law relating to adoptions and maintenance among Hindus
To enforce compulsory registration of marriages
questions.explanation: The Preamble states HAMA 1956 is 'An Act to amend and codify the law relating to adoptions and maintenance among Hindus'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a petition for divorce by mutual consent requires that the parties have been living separately for at least:
questions.explanation: Section 13B(1) requires that the husband and wife have been living separately for a period of one year or more before presenting a petition for divorce by mutual consent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus if neither party has a spouse living at the time of marriage. Violation of this condition makes the marriage:
questions.explanation: Section 11 renders bigamous marriages in violation of Section 5(i) null and void ab initio.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(iii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the bridegroom must have completed the age of 21 years and the bride must have completed the age of:
questions.explanation: Section 5(iii) prescribes minimum marriageable age as 21 years for male and 18 years for female.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, where a Hindu marriage is solemnized in accordance with customary rites including Saptapadi (taking of seven steps by bridegroom and bride jointly before sacred fire), the marriage becomes complete and binding when:
questions.explanation: Section 7(2) explicitly provides that marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, when either the husband or the wife has without reasonable excuse withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply for:
questions.explanation: Section 9 governs Restitution of Conjugal Rights (remedy upheld in Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar).

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, either party to a marriage may present a petition praying for a decree for Judicial Separation on any of the grounds specified in:
questions.explanation: Section 10(1) provides that Judicial Separation may be sought on any ground listed in Section 13(1).

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a marriage is voidable and may be annulled by a decree of nullity if:
options: The marriage has not been consummated owing to the impotence of the respondent
Consent was obtained by force or fraud
Respondent was pregnant by someone other than petitioner at time of marriage
questions.explanation: Section 12 specifies statutory grounds rendering a Hindu marriage voidable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(ib) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, divorce may be granted if the respondent has deserted the petitioner for a continuous period of not less than how many years immediately preceding presentation of petition?
questions.explanation: Section 13(1)(ib) mandates minimum continuous desertion of 2 years for divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, children born of void or voidable marriages are statutorily conferred the status of:
questions.explanation: Section 16 confers statutory legitimacy on children of void and voidable marriages, granting rights in parents' property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, where in any proceeding it appears to the court that either wife or husband has no independent income sufficient for support and necessary expenses of proceeding, court may order respondent to pay monthly maintenance:
questions.explanation: Section 24 provides for maintenance pendente lite and litigation expenses for either spouse.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, any court exercising jurisdiction under the Act may at the time of passing any decree or subsequent thereto, order the respondent to pay to the applicant permanent alimony and maintenance which shall be a charge on:
questions.explanation: Section 25 empowers courts to grant permanent alimony and maintenance, creating a charge on immovable property.

questions.question_text: In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017), the Supreme Court held that the 6-month statutory waiting period (cooling-off period) under Section 13B(2) for mutual consent divorce is:
options: Directory and can be waived by the court in exceptional circumstances
Mandatory and cannot be waived by any court
Applicable only if parties have children
Subject to High Court approval only
questions.explanation: Amardeep Singh (2017) held that the 6-month cooling-off period under Section 13B(2) is directory and waivable by court.

questions.question_text: In Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that it can grant divorce directly on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage in exercise of plenary powers under:
questions.explanation: Shilpa Sailesh (2023) held that the Supreme Court can grant divorce for irretrievable breakdown under Article 142 without waiting period.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, no petition for divorce shall be presented before the expiration of how long from the date of marriage, except in cases of exceptional hardship to petitioner or exceptional depravity on part of respondent?
questions.explanation: Section 14 bars filing for divorce within one year of marriage except in cases of exceptional hardship or depravity.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, when a marriage has been dissolved by a decree of divorce and either there is no right of appeal or time for appealing has expired without appeal being filed, it shall be lawful for either party to:
questions.explanation: Section 15 permits remarriage after dissolution of marriage once appeal periods have elapsed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Act applies to any person who is a Hindu by religion in any of its forms or developments, including Virashaiva, Lingayat, or follower of Brahmo, Prarthana, or Arya Samaj, and to any person who is:
options: Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(b) extends application of HMA to Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, nothing contained in the Act shall apply to the members of any:
options: Scheduled Tribe within the meaning of clause (25) of Article 366 of Constitution, unless Central Govt notifies
questions.explanation: Section 2(2) excludes Scheduled Tribes from operation of HMA unless notified by Central Government.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, "Custom" and "Usage" mean any rule which, having been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, has obtained the force of law among Hindus in any local area, tribe, community, group or family, provided the rule is:
options: Certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy
questions.explanation: Section 3(a) defines Custom requiring it to be ancient, continuous, certain, reasonable, and not opposed to public policy.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(c) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, two persons are said to be "Full Blood" when they are descended from a common ancestor by the same wife, and "Half Blood" when they are descended from a common ancestor by:
options: Same mother but different fathers (Uterine Blood)
questions.explanation: Section 3(c) defines Full Blood (same parents) and Half Blood (same father, different mothers).

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(d) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, two persons are said to be "Uterine Blood" when they are descended from a common ancestress by:
questions.explanation: Section 3(d) defines Uterine Blood as descent from common ancestress by different husbands.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(f) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, "Sapinda Relationship" with reference to any person extends as far as how many generations in line of ascent through mother, and how many generations in line of ascent through father?
options: 5 generations through mother, 7 generations through father
3 generations through mother, 5 generations through father
questions.explanation: Section 3(f)(i) defines Sapinda relationship: 3 generations through mother, 5 generations through father.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(v) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus if the parties are NOT Sapindas of each other, UNLESS:
options: The custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two
questions.explanation: Section 5(v) prohibits Sapinda marriages unless saved by customary usage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(iv) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus if the parties are NOT within degrees of prohibited relationship, UNLESS:
options: The custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two
questions.explanation: Section 5(iv) prohibits marriage within degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(ii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, at the time of marriage neither party must be incapable of giving valid consent in consequence of unsoundness of mind, or suffering from mental disorder rendering unfit for marriage and procreation, or subject to recurrent attacks of:
questions.explanation: Section 5(ii)(c) covers recurrent attacks of insanity (Epilepsy was deleted by Marriage Laws Amendment Act, 1999).

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, State Governments are empowered to make rules for Registration of Hindu Marriages. Failure to register a Hindu marriage under Section 8:
options: Shall NOT affect the validity of any Hindu marriage
questions.explanation: Section 8(5) explicitly enacts that non-registration does not affect validity of a Hindu marriage.

questions.question_text: In Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006), the Supreme Court held that registration of marriages of all persons who are citizens of India belonging to various religious denominations should be made:
questions.explanation: Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006) directed mandatory registration of all marriages across India regardless of religion.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, any marriage solemnized after commencement of Act shall be null and void ab initio and may on petition presented by either party be so declared by decree of nullity if it contravenes any of conditions specified in:
options: Clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of Section 5 (Bigamy, Prohibited Relationship, Sapinda)
questions.explanation: Section 11 renders marriages violating Section 5(i), (iv), or (v) void ab initio.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12(1)(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a marriage is voidable and may be annulled if marriage has not been consummated owing to the respondent's:
questions.explanation: Section 12(1)(a) makes non-consummation due to respondent's impotence a ground for voidable marriage annulment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12(1)(c) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a petition for annulment of voidable marriage on ground that consent of petitioner was obtained by force or fraud must be presented within how long after force ceased or fraud was discovered?
questions.explanation: Section 12(2)(a)(i) requires fraud/force annulment petition to be presented within one year.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12(1)(d) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a marriage is voidable if respondent was at time of marriage pregnant by some person other than petitioner, provided petitioner was at time of marriage ignorant of fact, proceedings are instituted within 1 year, and marital intercourse has NOT taken place with consent since discovery of:
questions.explanation: Section 12(1)(d) & 12(2)(b) set statutory conditions for pre-marital pregnancy annulment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, divorce may be granted if respondent has after solemnization of marriage had voluntary sexual intercourse with any person other than his/her spouse. This is the ground of:
questions.explanation: Section 13(1)(i) codifies Adultery as a ground for divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (inserted by 1976 Amendment), divorce may be granted if respondent has after solemnization of marriage treated petitioner with:
questions.explanation: Section 13(1)(ia) provides Cruelty (both physical and mental) as a ground for divorce.

questions.question_text: In Dastane v. Dastane (1975), the Supreme Court laid down that in assessing Mental Cruelty in matrimonial cases, the standard of proof required is:
options: Preponderance of probabilities (and not proof beyond reasonable doubt)
questions.explanation: Dastane v. Dastane (1975) established preponderance of probabilities as standard of proof for cruelty in HMA.

questions.question_text: In Samar Ghosh v. Jaya Ghosh (2007), the Supreme Court enumerated illustrative guidelines for determining Mental Cruelty, holding that long period of continuous separation and complete coldness of conduct amounts to:
questions.explanation: Samar Ghosh (2007) provided landmark parameters for evaluating mental cruelty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(ii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, divorce may be granted if respondent has ceased to be a Hindu by:
questions.explanation: Section 13(1)(ii) makes apostasy / religious conversion a ground for divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(iii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, divorce may be granted if respondent has been incurably of unsound mind, or has been suffering continuously or intermittently from mental disorder of such a kind that petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with respondent. "Mental disorder" includes:
questions.explanation: Section 13(1)(iii) Explanation defines mental disorder including schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the former clause (iv) allowed divorce where the respondent had been suffering from a virulent and incurable form of leprosy. Leprosy was DELETED as a ground for divorce by which Amendment Act?
questions.explanation: The Personal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 omitted clause (iv) of Section 13(1) (leprosy) as a ground for divorce under HMA and made corresponding changes in other family laws.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 13(1)(iv), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (omitted by the Personal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019)

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(vi) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, divorce may be granted if respondent has renounced the world by entering any:
questions.explanation: Section 13(1)(vi) makes renunciation of world (entering Sannyasa) a ground for divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(vii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, divorce may be granted if respondent has not been heard of as being alive for a period of how many years by those who would naturally have heard of him?
questions.explanation: Section 13(1)(vii) makes 7 years un-heard absence a ground for divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1A)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (inserted by 1964 Amendment), either party to a marriage may present a petition for divorce on ground that there has been no resumption of cohabitation between parties for a period of how long after passing of a decree for Judicial Separation?
questions.explanation: Section 13(1A)(i) permits divorce after 1 year of non-resumption of cohabitation following Judicial Separation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1A)(ii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, either party may present a petition for divorce on ground that there has been no restitution of conjugal rights between parties for a period of how long after passing of a decree for Restitution of Conjugal Rights under Section 9?
questions.explanation: Section 13(1A)(ii) permits divorce after 1 year of non-restitution of conjugal rights following Section 9 decree.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(2)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a WIFE may present a petition for divorce on ground that in case of marriage solemnized before commencement of Act, husband had married again before such commencement or that another wife solemnized before commencement was alive at time of marriage. This is special ground for wives in:
questions.explanation: Section 13(2)(i) gives special divorce ground to wives of pre-1955 polygamous marriages.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(2)(ii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a wife may present a petition for divorce on ground that husband has since solemnization of marriage been guilty of:
questions.explanation: Section 13(2)(ii) confers special divorce ground on wife if husband commits rape, sodomy or bestiality.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(2)(iii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (inserted by 1976 Amendment), a wife may seek divorce if in a suit under Section 18 Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act or Section 125 CrPC / 144 BNSS a decree/order for maintenance was passed against husband and cohabitation has NOT been resumed for how long?
questions.explanation: Section 13(2)(iii) permits wife to seek divorce after 1 year of non-cohabitation following maintenance order.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(2)(iv) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (Option of Puberty), a wife may seek divorce if her marriage was solemnized before she attained age of 15 years and she repudiated marriage after attaining 15 years BUT before attaining age of:
questions.explanation: Section 13(2)(iv) codifies Option of Puberty for female married under 15, repudiated between 15 and 18.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, on motion of both parties made not earlier than 6 months after date of presentation of petition and not later than how many months after said date, Court shall pass decree of divorce by mutual consent?
questions.explanation: Section 13B(2) prescribes 6 to 18 months window for second motion in mutual consent divorce.

questions.question_text: In Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section 9 (Restitution of Conjugal Rights), holding that Section 9 does NOT violate Article 21 or Article 14 of Constitution because:
options: Its object is to preserve marriage and prevent breakdown
questions.explanation: Saroj Rani (1984) upheld Section 9 HMA, overruling Andhra Pradesh High Court decision in T. Sareetha.

questions.question_text: In Bipinchandra Jaisinghbhai Shah v. Prabhavati (1956), the Supreme Court held that to establish Desertion as a ground for divorce, two essential elements must co-exist: (1) Factum of separation, and (2):
questions.explanation: Bipinchandra (1956) laid down that desertion requires both Factum Deserendi and Animus Deserendi.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (as interpreted in Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun, 2023 3-Judge Bench), children of void and voidable marriages are entitled to inherit property of:
options: Entire joint family property of relatives
Their parents (both self-acquired and coparcenary ancestral property share of parents)
questions.explanation: Revanasiddappa (2023 3-Judge Bench) affirmed children of void/voidable marriages inherit parents' share in ancestral & self-acquired property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, every petition under the Act shall be presented to the District Court within local limits of whose ordinary original civil jurisdiction the marriage was solemnized, or respondent resides, OR where:
options: The parties to marriage last resided together
The wife resides on date of presentation of petition
Petitioner resides where respondent resides outside India or not heard of for 7 yrs
questions.explanation: Section 19 lists statutory venues for filing matrimonial petitions under HMA.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, every petition presented under the Act shall state as distinctly as nature of case permits the facts on which claim is based and shall also state that there is no:
options: Collusion between petitioner and other party to marriage
questions.explanation: Section 20 requires verification stating absence of collusion in matrimonial petitions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, subject to other provisions of the Act and rules made by High Court, all proceedings under the Act shall be regulated as far as may be by the:
questions.explanation: Section 21 applies CPC 1908 to regulate proceedings under HMA.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (inserted by 1976 Amendment), every petition under the Act shall be tried as expeditiously as possible and endeavor shall be made to conclude trial within how many months from date of service of notice?
questions.explanation: Section 21B(2) mandates target trial disposal period of 6 months from notice service.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21B(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, every appeal under the Act shall be heard as expeditiously as possible and endeavor shall be made to conclude appeal within how many months from date of service of notice of appeal?
questions.explanation: Section 21B(3) sets target disposal period of 3 months for HMA appeals.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, every proceeding under the Act shall be conducted in camera UNLESS presiding judge orders otherwise, and printing or publishing any matter in relation to proceeding without prior permission of court is punishable with fine up to:
questions.explanation: Section 22 mandates in-camera proceedings and penalizes unauthorized publication with fine up to Rs 1,000.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(1)(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, before granting any relief under the Act, Court must be satisfied that ground for relief exists and petitioner is NOT in any way taking advantage of his/her own:
options: Wrong or disability for purpose of such relief
questions.explanation: Section 23(1)(a) enacts principle that no party shall take advantage of his own wrong (Nullus commodum capere potest de injuria sua propria).

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(1)(b) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, where ground of petition is adultery, Court must be satisfied that petitioner has NOT in any manner been accessory to or connived at or:
questions.explanation: Section 23(1)(b) bars relief if petitioner has condoned or connived at adultery.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, before proceeding to grant any relief under the Act, it shall be the duty of the Court in the first instance to make every endeavor to bring about a:
questions.explanation: Section 23(2) places statutory duty on Court to attempt matrimonial reconciliation in first instance.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23A of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (inserted by 1976 Amendment), in any proceeding for divorce or judicial separation or restitution of conjugal rights, respondent may not only oppose relief but may also claim any relief under Act on ground of petitioner's adultery, cruelty or desertion. This is:
options: Counter-claim for relief in matrimonial cause
questions.explanation: Section 23A permits respondent to file counter-claim for matrimonial relief.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Court may from time to time pass interim orders and provisions in decree with respect to custody, maintenance and education of:
questions.explanation: Section 26 empowers courts to pass orders regarding custody, maintenance and education of minor children.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Court may make such provisions in decree as it deems just and proper with respect to any property presented at or about time of marriage which may belong:
options: Jointly to both husband and wife (Stridhan / Joint property)
questions.explanation: Section 27 empowers courts to dispose of property presented jointly at marriage (including Stridhan).

questions.question_text: Under Section 28(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, all decrees made by Court in any proceeding under Act shall be appealable to Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from decisions of Court. Under Section 28(4), period of limitation for filing an appeal is:
options: 90 days from date of decree or order
questions.explanation: Section 28(4) (amended in 2003) prescribes 90 days limitation period for appeals under HMA.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, orders made by Court under Section 25 (permanent alimony) or Section 26 (custody) shall be appealable if they are not interim orders. Does an appeal lie against an order passed under Section 24 (maintenance pendente lite)?
options: No appeal lies against Section 24 interim maintenance order (only revision/writ)
questions.explanation: Section 28(2) bars appeals against interim orders under Section 24.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, any marriage between two Hindus solemnized after commencement of Act is void if at date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living, and provisions of Sections 494 and 495 IPC / 82 BNS shall apply. This penalizes:
questions.explanation: Section 17 penalizes Bigamy committed by Hindus.

questions.question_text: In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) and Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995), the Supreme Court held that a Hindu husband who converts to Islam and marries a second time without dissolving his first Hindu marriage is guilty of:
options: No offence because Islam permits polygamy
Bigamy under Section 17 HMA read with Section 494 IPC / 82 BNS
questions.explanation: Sarla Mudgal (1995) & Lily Thomas (2000) established that conversion to Islam does not dissolve first Hindu marriage; second marriage constitutes bigamy.
questions.statute_or_case: Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000)

questions.question_text: In Smt. Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v. Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988), the Supreme Court held that a woman marrying a Hindu man whose first marriage is subsisting (second wife of bigamous marriage) is NOT entitled to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC because:
options: Section 125 CrPC does not apply to Hindus
Her marriage is void ab initio under Section 11 read with Section 5(i) HMA
Second wives are excluded by statute
questions.explanation: Yamunabai (1988) held second wife of void bigamous marriage is not a legally wedded wife for Sec 125 CrPC (though later Badshah v. Urmila relaxed rule where husband concealed first marriage).

questions.question_text: In Badshah v. Urmila Badshah Godse (2014), the Supreme Court held that where a man marries a woman concealing his subsisting first marriage, he cannot take advantage of his own wrong, and the second wife IS entitled to maintenance under:
questions.explanation: Badshah (2014) protected second wives duped into bigamous marriages, granting maintenance under Sec 125 CrPC.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, every person who procures a marriage of himself or herself to be solemnized in contravention of Section 5(iii) (minimum age of 21 for male, 18 for female) shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine up to:
questions.explanation: Section 18(a) (amended by Child Marriage Restraint Amendment 2006) penalizes child marriage contravention with up to 2 yrs RI or fine up to Rs 1 Lakh.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18(b) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, contravention of Section 5(iv) (prohibited relationship) or Section 5(v) (Sapinda relationship) is punishable with simple imprisonment up to:
options: 1 month, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both
questions.explanation: Section 18(b) penalizes contravention of prohibited relationship or Sapinda rule with up to 1 month imprisonment or fine up to Rs 1,000.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, if Court is satisfied that party in whose favor permanent alimony/maintenance was granted under Section 25 has remarried, or if wife has not remained chaste, or if husband has had extramarital sexual intercourse, Court shall:
options: Vary, modify or rescind any such order
questions.explanation: Section 25(3) empowers Court to rescind or modify permanent alimony upon remarriage or unchastity.

questions.question_text: In Naveen Kohli v. Neelu Kohli (2006), the Supreme Court recommended to Central Government that "Irretrievable Breakdown of Marriage" should be incorporated as a statutory ground for divorce under:
questions.explanation: Naveen Kohli (2006) strongly recommended introducing Irretrievable Breakdown of Marriage as a statutory ground in HMA.

questions.question_text: In Rajnesh v. Neha (2020), the Supreme Court laid down comprehensive nationwide guidelines on payment of maintenance in matrimonial cases, mandating filing of a mandatory Affidavit of:
options: Assets and Liabilities by both parties
questions.explanation: Rajnesh v. Neha (2020) made filing Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities mandatory in all maintenance proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(1)(c) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, where ground of petition is cruelty, Court must be satisfied that petitioner has NOT in any manner:
questions.explanation: Section 23(1)(c) bars relief if petitioner has condoned cruelty (though resumption of cohabitation must show genuine forgiveness).

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(1)(d) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Court must be satisfied before granting decree that there is no unnecessary or improper:
questions.explanation: Section 23(1)(d) bars matrimonial relief if there is unexplained, improper or unnecessary delay in filing petition.

questions.question_text: In Pratibha Rani v. Suraj Kumar (1985), the Supreme Court held that Stridhan property of a Hindu married woman is her absolute property, and husband/in-laws retaining it after demand commit:
options: Criminal Breach of Trust under Section 406 IPC / 316 BNS
questions.explanation: Pratibha Rani (1985) declared Stridhan absolute property of wife, making retention Criminal Breach of Trust.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(e) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, "District Court" means Principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction in a district, and includes any other Civil Court specified by State Government by notification, as well as a:
options: Family Court established under Family Courts Act, 1984
questions.explanation: Section 3(e) read with Family Courts Act 1984 vests HMA jurisdiction in Family Courts where established.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(ib) Explanation of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, "Desertion" means desertion of petitioner by other party to marriage without reasonable cause and without consent or against wish of such party, and includes willful neglect of petitioner by other party. The burden of proving desertion lies on:
questions.explanation: Under Section 13(1)(ib) Explanation, burden of proving desertion rests on petitioner.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, notwithstanding that a marriage is null and void under Section 11, any child of such marriage who would have been legitimate if marriage had been valid shall be:
options: Legitimate whether such child is born before or after commencement of Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act 1976
questions.explanation: Section 16(1) confers retrospective & prospective statutory legitimacy on children of void marriages.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, where a decree of nullity is granted in respect of a voidable marriage under Section 12, any child begotten or conceived before decree is made shall be deemed to be their:
questions.explanation: Section 16(2) preserves legitimacy of children born of annulled voidable marriages.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, mutual consent divorce petition must state that parties have been living separately for 1 year or more, that they have NOT been able to live together, and that they have:
options: Mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved
questions.explanation: Section 13B(1) sets out 3 essential joint assertions required in mutual consent divorce petition.

questions.question_text: In Smt. Sureshta Devi v. Om Prakash (1991), the Supreme Court held that consent given by a party to a mutual consent divorce petition under Section 13B can be unilaterally withdrawn at any time before passing of decree. This was affirmed by 3-Judge Bench in:
questions.explanation: Smruti Pahariya (2009) affirmed Sureshta Devi, holding mutual consent must persist until decree is passed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21A of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (inserted by 1976 Amendment), where petitions under HMA are pending in different District Courts between same parties (e.g. one for RCR and another for divorce), petitions shall be transferred and heard together by the District Court in which the:
questions.explanation: Section 21A provides for consolidation of cross-petitions before District Court where earlier petition was filed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21C of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (inserted by 1976 Amendment), every document filed in proceedings under HMA shall be received in evidence without requirement of being stamped under Indian Stamp Act, 1899. This is exemption from:
options: Stamp Duty on documents filed in HMA proceedings
questions.explanation: Section 21C exempts documents filed in HMA proceedings from stamp duty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(1)(e) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Court must be satisfied before granting decree that there is no other legal ground why relief should not be granted. This is general residual condition of:
options: Absence of any legal bar to relief
questions.explanation: Section 23(1)(e) requires absence of any other legal bar before decree is granted.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, can permanent alimony and maintenance be ordered in favor of the HUSBAND against the wife if husband has no independent income?
options: No, maintenance is for wives only
Yes, Section 25 explicitly applies gender-neutrally to either husband or wife
questions.explanation: Section 25 (and Section 24) HMA are gender-neutral, allowing either husband or wife to claim maintenance.

questions.question_text: In Dr. N.G. Dastane v. Mrs. S. Dastane (1975), the Supreme Court held that acts of cruelty by one spouse are deemed CONDONED if the aggrieved spouse subsequently:
options: Resumes normal marital cohabitation with full knowledge and forgiveness
questions.explanation: Dastane (1975) established that voluntary resumption of cohabitation with forgiveness constitutes Condonation of cruelty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(1)(b) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, if cruelty has been condoned, can it be revived if respondent subsequently commits a fresh matrimonial offence (such as desertion or fresh cruelty)?
options: Only if criminal FIR is filed
Yes, condoned cruelty is revived by subsequent matrimonial wrong
questions.explanation: Condonation is conditional on future good behavior; subsequent matrimonial wrong revives condoned past cruelty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(i) read with Section 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, if a Hindu man marries a second wife while his first wife is alive, can the SECOND wife file a petition for declaration of nullity under Section 11?
options: Yes, either party to second marriage can file petition under Section 11
No, second wife has no standing
questions.explanation: Section 11 permits either party to the null marriage (including second wife) to file for declaration of nullity.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or custom in force immediately before commencement of Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in Act. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 4 enacts Overriding Effect of HMA over inconsistent ancient texts and customs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a marriage solemnized between Hindus before commencement of Act which is otherwise valid shall NOT be deemed to be invalid merely because parties belonged to different:
options: Castes or sub-castes or different subdivisions of same caste
questions.explanation: Section 29(1) validates pre-1955 inter-caste and inter-subcaste Hindu marriages.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, nothing contained in the Act shall affect any right recognized by custom or conferred by any special enactment to obtain the:
options: Dissolution of a Hindu marriage, whether solemnized before or after commencement of Act
questions.explanation: Section 29(2) saves customary modes of divorce (such as caste punchayat divorce where recognized by valid custom).

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Hindu Marriage Validity Act 1949 and Bombay Prevention of Hindu Bigamous Marriages Act were repealed by HMA. This section was formally repealed by:
questions.explanation: Section 30 (Repeals) was repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1960 as spent.

questions.question_text: In V. Bhagat v. D. Bhagat (1994), the Supreme Court held that making wild, reckless and unsubstantiated allegations of adultery or mental insanity in written statement against spouse amounts to:
options: Mental Cruelty entitling spouse to decree of divorce under Section 13(1)(ia)
questions.explanation: V. Bhagat (1994) held that false scandalous allegations in written statement constitute mental cruelty.

questions.question_text: In Manish Jain v. Akanksha Jain (2017), the Supreme Court held that court while exercising power under Section 24 HMA to grant maintenance pendente lite must consider status of parties and capacity of spouse to pay, and wife's mere higher educational qualification does NOT automatically disentitle her from claiming:
questions.explanation: Manish Jain (2017) affirmed educated wife unable to maintain herself is entitled to Section 24 maintenance.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, an application for payment of costs of proceeding and monthly maintenance pendente lite shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within how many days from date of service of notice on respondent?
questions.explanation: Section 24 proviso (inserted in 2001) mandates 60-day target for disposing interim maintenance applications.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1)(ib) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, does constructive desertion (where one spouse by intolerable conduct forces the other to leave home) constitute legal desertion by the fleeing spouse?
options: No, the spouse whose intolerable conduct forced the other to leave is guilty of Constructive Desertion
Fleeing spouse is guilty of desertion
questions.explanation: Constructive Desertion places fault on spouse whose unbearable behavior drove the other out of matrimonial home.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(iii) read with Child Marriage Restraint Act / Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006, a child marriage (where male is under 21 or female under 18) under Hindu Marriage Act is:
options: Void ab initio under HMA Sec 11
Neither void nor voidable under HMA Sec 11/12, but punishable under Sec 18 and voidable under PCMA 2006
Valid in all respects without penalty
questions.explanation: Child marriage is not listed in Sec 11 or 12 HMA (hence valid under HMA but punishable under Sec 18 & voidable under PCMA 2006).

questions.question_text: Under Section 10(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, where a decree for Judicial Separation has been passed, it shall no longer be obligatory for petitioner to cohabit with respondent. Court may, upon application by either party and on being satisfied of truth of statements, rescind decree of judicial separation if it considers it:
options: Just and reasonable to do so
questions.explanation: Section 10(2) empowers court to rescind judicial separation decree if just and reasonable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(1)(bb) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (inserted by 1976 Amendment), where a divorce is sought under Section 13B (mutual consent), Court must be satisfied that such consent has NOT been obtained by:
questions.explanation: Section 23(1)(bb) requires Court to satisfy itself that mutual consent was free from force, fraud or undue influence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Act extends to the whole of India, and applies also to Hindus domiciled in the territories to which this Act extends who are:
options: Outside the said territories (Extra-territorial application to domiciled Hindus)
questions.explanation: Section 1(2) gives extra-territorial application of HMA to Hindus domiciled in India residing abroad.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(a) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, who is the natural guardian of a Hindu minor boy or an unmarried girl?
options: The mother, and after her, the father
The father, and after him, the mother
Jointly father and mother in all cases
questions.explanation: Section 6(a) provides that the natural guardian of a Hindu minor boy or unmarried girl is the father, and after him, the mother.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, in the appointment or declaration of any person as guardian of a Hindu minor, what is the paramount consideration?
options: The financial status of the father
questions.explanation: Section 13 mandates that in appointing or declaring a guardian of a Hindu minor, the welfare of the minor shall be the paramount consideration.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(a) proviso of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, the custody of a minor who has not completed the age of how many years shall ordinarily be with the mother?
questions.explanation: Section 6(a) proviso explicitly enacts that custody of a minor under 5 years of age shall ordinarily be with the mother.

questions.question_text: In Githa Hariharan v. Reserve Bank of India (1999), the Supreme Court interpreted the phrase "after him" in Section 6(a) of HMGA 1956 to mean:
options: "In the absence of" (when father is non-functional, absent, negligent, or indifferent)
questions.explanation: Githa Hariharan (1999) held that "after him" means "in the absence of the father", granting equal guardianship status to mothers.
questions.statute_or_case: Githa Hariharan v. Reserve Bank of India (1999)

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(b) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, in the case of an ILLEGITIMATE minor boy or an illegitimate unmarried girl, who is the first natural guardian?
options: The father, and after him, the mother
The mother, and after her, the father
questions.explanation: Section 6(b) enacts that for an illegitimate minor, the mother is the primary natural guardian, and after her, the father.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(c) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, in the case of a married Hindu minor girl, who is the natural guardian?
questions.explanation: Section 6(c) provides that the husband is the natural guardian of a married minor girl.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 proviso of HMGA 1956, a person ceases to be entitled to act as natural guardian of a Hindu minor if he/she has ceased to be a Hindu OR has:
options: Completely and finally renounced the world by becoming a sannyasi
questions.explanation: Section 6 proviso disqualifies natural guardians who convert to another religion or renounce the world.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, a natural guardian shall NOT, without the prior permission of the Court, mortgage, charge, sale, gift, or exchange any part of the minor's:
questions.explanation: Section 8(2)(a) mandates prior court permission before a natural guardian can alienate minor's immovable property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2)(b) of HMGA 1956, a natural guardian cannot lease any part of minor's immovable property without court permission for a term exceeding how many years, or for a term extending more than one year beyond date of minor majority?
questions.explanation: Section 8(2)(b) restricts unapproved leases of minor's immovable property to a maximum of 5 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(3) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, any disposal of immovable property by a natural guardian in contravention of sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) is:
options: Voidable at the instance of the minor or any person claiming under him
questions.explanation: Section 8(3) enacts that unapproved alienation of minor's immovable property is voidable at minor's option.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, after commencement of Act, no de facto guardian shall be entitled to dispose of or deal with property of a Hindu minor merely on ground of being a de facto guardian. This creates an absolute bar against:
options: De facto guardians alienating minor's property
questions.explanation: Section 11 places an absolute statutory bar against de facto guardians disposing of minor's property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, where a minor has an undivided interest in joint family property and the property is under management of an adult member of family (Karta), NO guardian shall be appointed for the minor in respect of such undivided interest, EXCEPT by the:
options: High Court under its inherent jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Section 12 bars appointing guardians for undivided coparcenary interest, preserving Karta management and saving High Court inherent powers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(a) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, "Minor" means a person who has not completed the age of:
questions.explanation: Section 4(a) defines Minor as a person under 18 years of age.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(b) of HMGA 1956, "Guardian" means a person having the care of the person of a minor or of his property or of both, and includes:
options: A testamentary guardian appointed by Will of minor's father/mother
A guardian appointed or declared by Court
questions.explanation: Section 4(b) defines Guardian including natural, testamentary, and court-appointed guardians.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(1) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, a Hindu father entitled to act as natural guardian may by Will appoint a guardian for any of his minor legitimate children in respect of:
options: The minor's person or property (other than undivided joint family interest)
questions.explanation: Section 9(1) empowers Hindu father to appoint testamentary guardian for minor's person or separate property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(2) of HMGA 1956, an appointment of testamentary guardian made by father under sub-section (1) shall have NO effect if the father predeceases the mother, BUT shall revive if the mother:
options: Dies without appointing by Will any person as guardian
questions.explanation: Section 9(2) enacts that father's testamentary appointment lapses if mother survives, unless mother dies without appointing guardian by Will.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(3) of HMGA 1956, a Hindu mother entitled to act as natural guardian (where father is dead or disqualified) or a Hindu mother of an ILLEGITIMATE child under Section 9(4) may by Will appoint a guardian for:
questions.explanation: Section 9(3) & 9(4) empower Hindu mother to appoint testamentary guardian by Will.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(5) of HMGA 1956, a testamentary guardian has the right to act as the minor's guardian after the death of the father or mother and to exercise all the rights of a natural guardian under this Act, to such extent and subject to such restrictions, if any, as are specified in this Act and in the:
questions.explanation: Section 9(5) provides that the testamentary guardian exercises the rights of a natural guardian subject to the restrictions specified in the Act and in the will itself.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, a minor is statutorily INCOMPETENT to act as guardian of the:
questions.explanation: Section 10 renders a minor incompetent to act as guardian of the property of any minor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of HMGA 1956, the provisions of this Act shall be in addition to, and not, save as hereinafter expressly provided, in derogation of, the:
questions.explanation: Section 2 states HMGA is supplemental to and in addition to Guardians and Wards Act 1890.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of HMGA 1956, any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or custom in force before commencement of Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in Act. This is the:
questions.explanation: Section 5 enacts Overriding Effect of HMGA over inconsistent prior laws/customs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, the natural guardianship of an adopted son who is a minor passes, on adoption, to the:
options: Adoptive father, and after him, the adoptive mother
questions.explanation: Section 7 provides that natural guardianship of adopted minor passes to adoptive father and after him adoptive mother.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1) of HMGA 1956, the natural guardian of a Hindu minor has power, subject to this section, to do all acts which are necessary or reasonable and proper for the benefit of the minor or for the realization, protection or benefit of minor's estate. BUT the guardian can in no case bind the minor by a:
questions.explanation: Section 8(1) proviso enacts that natural guardian cannot bind minor by personal covenant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(5) of HMGA 1956, the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 shall apply to an application for obtaining permission of Court under sub-section (2) as if it were an application for permission under Section 29 of that Act. Application for permission under Sec 8(2) shall be made to District Court or Court under:
options: Section 4A of Guardians and Wards Act 1890 within whose jurisdiction property is situate
questions.explanation: Section 8(5) applies Guardians and Wards Act 1890 procedures for seeking court permission under Section 8(2).

questions.question_text: In ABC v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2015), the Supreme Court held that an unmarried Hindu mother can be appointed sole natural guardian of her child under Section 6(b) HMGA without:
options: Giving notice to or revealing identity of biological father
questions.explanation: ABC v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2015) affirmed that an unwed mother can obtain sole guardianship without notifying biological father.

questions.question_text: In Gaurav Nagpal v. Sumedha Nagpal (2009), the Supreme Court reiterated that in custody disputes between parents under Section 13 HMGA & Section 17 GWA, the paramount consideration is the welfare of child, and parental rights under statute are:
options: Subordinate to the welfare of the minor child
questions.explanation: Gaurav Nagpal (2009) established that statutory rights of parents yield to the paramount welfare of the minor.

questions.question_text: In Rosy Jacob v. Jacob A. Chakramakkal (1973), the Supreme Court held that in considering custody of minor children, the Controlling consideration is the welfare of minor, and orders regarding custody are:
options: Interlocutory orders subject to modification whenever child welfare requires
questions.explanation: Rosy Jacob (1973) held custody orders are temporary/interlocutory and open to alteration as child welfare demands.
questions.statute_or_case: Rosy Jacob v. Jacob A. Chakramakkal (1973)

questions.question_text: In Panni Lal v. Rajinder Singh (1993), the Supreme Court held that a sale of minor's immovable property by natural guardian without prior court permission under Section 8(2) HMGA can be set aside by minor by filing suit within how many years of attaining majority under Article 60 Limitation Act?
options: 3 years from date of attaining majority
questions.explanation: Panni Lal (1993) held minor must challenge unapproved Section 8(2) sale within 3 years of attaining majority.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(2) of HMGA 1956, no person shall be entitled to the guardianship of a Hindu minor by virtue of provisions of this Act or of any law relating to guardianship in marriage among Hindus, if Court is of opinion that his guardianship will NOT be for the:
questions.explanation: Section 13(2) disqualifies any person from guardianship if court finds it contrary to minor's welfare.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of HMGA 1956, the Act applies to any person who is a Hindu by religion in any of its forms, including Lingayat, Virashaiva, follower of Brahmo/Arya Samaj, and to any person who is:
options: Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(b) applies HMGA to Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) of HMGA 1956, the Act does NOT apply to members of any Scheduled Tribe unless Central Government by notification in Official Gazette otherwise directs. This mirrors Section 2(2) of:
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) HMGA mirrors Section 2(2) HMA excluding Scheduled Tribes unless notified.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 Explanation of HMGA 1956, the expressions "father" and "mother" do NOT include a:
questions.explanation: Section 6 Explanation excludes step-father and step-mother from natural guardianship.

questions.question_text: Since HMGA 1956 is supplemental to the general law (Section 2), a testamentary guardian appointed by the Will of a Hindu father or mother under Section 9 may be removed by the Court for the reasons set out in the:
questions.explanation: Section 2 keeps HMGA in addition to the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890; Section 39 of that Act allows the Court to remove a guardian appointed by will on grounds such as abuse of trust or neglect of duty.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2, HMGA 1956 read with Section 39, Guardians and Wards Act, 1890

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(6) of HMGA 1956, the right of a testamentary guardian of a minor girl ceases on her:
questions.explanation: Section 9(6) enacts that the right of a testamentary guardian, where the minor is a girl, ceases upon her marriage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(4) of HMGA 1956, no court shall grant permission to natural guardian under sub-section (2) to alienate minor's immovable property EXCEPT in case of:
options: Necessity or for an evident advantage to the minor
questions.explanation: Section 8(4) mandates that court shall grant Sec 8(2) permission only in case of necessity or evident advantage to minor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (read with Section 13 HMGA), in appointing a guardian, Court shall be guided by what is consistently with law for the welfare of minor, considering minor's age, sex, religion, character/capacity of proposed guardian, and if minor is old enough to form an intelligent preference, Court may consider minor's:
questions.explanation: Section 17 GWA requires court to consider intelligent preference of minor if old enough.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, where Court is satisfied that it is for welfare of minor that an order should be made appointing a guardian of his person or property, Court may make an order appointing a guardian or declaring a person to be guardian. Such order removes any:
options: Natural or testamentary guardian whose appointment is inconsistent with court order
questions.explanation: Section 7 GWA empowers Court to appoint guardian overriding prior inconsistent guardianships for child welfare.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, Court may make such interlocutory orders for temporary custody and protection of person or property of minor as it thinks proper. This power is exercised during pendency of:
questions.explanation: Section 12 GWA governs interim temporary custody orders during guardianship proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, if a ward leaves or is removed from custody of a guardian of his person, Court if of opinion that it will be for welfare of ward to return to custody of guardian, may make an order for his return and enforce it by:
options: Arrest or issuing warrant for production of ward
questions.explanation: Section 25 GWA empowers Court to order return of ward to guardian's custody for ward welfare.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (read with Section 8 HMGA), a court-appointed guardian shall not without previous permission of Court mortgage, charge, sell, gift or exchange minor's immovable property or lease it for more than:
questions.explanation: Section 29 GWA restricts alienation/lease of minor immovable property without court sanction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, Court may remove a guardian appointed by Will or Court for grounds including abuse of trust, continuous failure to perform duties, incapacity, ill-treatment of ward, or if guardian ceases to reside within jurisdiction or is convicted of an offence involving:
questions.explanation: Section 39 GWA lists statutory grounds for removal of guardians.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, the powers of a guardian of the person or property cease by his death, removal or discharge, OR by the ward attaining majority, OR in case of a female ward by her:
options: Marriage to a husband who is not unfit
questions.explanation: Section 41 GWA prescribes cessation of guardian powers upon ward majority or female ward marriage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 47 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, an appeal lies to the High Court from an order of District Court appointing or refusing to appoint a guardian, or declaring/refusing to declare guardian, or removing/refusing to remove guardian under Section 39. Period of limitation is governed by:
questions.explanation: Section 47 GWA provides statutory appeal to High Court against guardianship orders.

questions.question_text: Under Indian Majority Act, 1875 (as amended in 1999), every person domiciled in India attains majority on completing the age of 18 years. Does the former provision extending majority to 21 years when a guardian was appointed by court under GWA 1890 still exist after 1999 Amendment?
options: No, 1999 Amendment unified age of majority to 18 years for all persons
Yes, 21 years still applies if court guardian appointed
questions.explanation: Indian Majority (Amendment) Act 1999 abolished the 21-year majority exception, fixing 18 years uniformly.

questions.question_text: In Madhegowda v. Ankegowda (2002), the Supreme Court held that alienation of a Hindu minor's property by a de facto guardian is void ab initio under Section 11 HMGA and does NOT transfer any right, title or interest to the purchaser because Section 11 imposes an:
options: Absolute statutory prohibition against de facto guardians
questions.explanation: Madhegowda v. Ankegowda (2002) held that alienation by a de facto guardian in contravention of Section 11 is void ab initio, and the minor on attaining majority may repudiate it without filing a suit.

questions.question_text: In Perry Kansagra v. Smriti Madan Kansagra (2019), the Supreme Court held that in international child custody disputes involving NRI parents, the principle of comity of foreign courts must yield to the:
options: Paramount consideration of the welfare of the minor child
questions.explanation: Perry Kansagra (2019) held comity of foreign courts yields to paramount welfare of child in cross-border custody cases.
questions.statute_or_case: Perry Kansagra v. Smriti Madan Kansagra (2019)

questions.question_text: In Nithya Anand Raghavan v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2017), a 3-Judge Bench of Supreme Court held that in habeas corpus petitions for custody of minor children brought from foreign countries, the Indian court must conduct a:
options: Summary or elaborate inquiry focused strictly on welfare of minor child in India
questions.explanation: Nithya Anand Raghavan (2017) 3-Judge Bench held child welfare in India overrides automatic foreign return orders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1) of HMGA 1956, can a natural guardian purchase immovable property for benefit of minor without court permission?
options: Yes, purchasing immovable property for minor's benefit does NOT require court permission under Sec 8(2)
questions.explanation: Section 8(2) restricts alienation (mortgage, sale, gift, exchange, lease), NOT purchase of property for minor's benefit.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(3) of HMGA 1956, if a natural guardian sells minor's immovable property without court permission under Section 8(2), the transaction is voidable at minor's instance. Can the purchaser enforce such contract against the minor during minority?
options: No, purchaser CANNOT enforce unapproved contract of sale against minor
questions.explanation: Purchaser cannot enforce unapproved sale of minor immovable property against minor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(3) of HMGA 1956, if a minor challenges an unapproved alienation of immovable property made by natural guardian after attaining majority, the minor must restore to purchaser any benefit received by minor. This is the doctrine of:
options: Restitution of Benefit upon avoidance of voidable contract
questions.explanation: Under Sec 8(3) read with Specific Relief Act Sec 33, minor avoiding sale must restore benefits received.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of HMGA 1956, if a Hindu father converts to Islam, does he remain the natural guardian of his Hindu minor child?
options: Yes, father remains natural guardian regardless of conversion
No, under Section 6 proviso he ceases to be natural guardian upon ceasing to be a Hindu
questions.explanation: Section 6 proviso explicitly disqualifies a natural guardian who ceases to be a Hindu by conversion.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(b) of HMGA 1956, who is the natural guardian of an illegitimate Hindu minor child if the mother ceases to be a Hindu or dies?
questions.explanation: Section 6(b) states: in case of illegitimate minor, the mother, and after her, the father.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(c) of HMGA 1956, who becomes natural guardian of a Hindu minor girl upon her marriage?
questions.explanation: Section 6(c) explicitly provides that husband is natural guardian of a married minor girl.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(1) of HMGA 1956, can a Hindu father appoint a testamentary guardian for his minor child by Will if the mother is alive and entitled to act as natural guardian?
options: Yes, but appointment remains inoperative during lifetime of mother and revives only if mother dies without appointing guardian
questions.explanation: Section 9(2) provides father's testamentary appointment is inoperative while mother lives and revives if mother dies without appointing guardian by Will.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(4) of HMGA 1956, a Hindu mother of an illegitimate minor child may by Will appoint a testamentary guardian for the minor. Does the father have power to override mother's testamentary appointment for an illegitimate child?
options: No, mother's testamentary appointment for illegitimate child is absolute
questions.explanation: Under Sec 6(b) & 9(4), mother is primary natural guardian of illegitimate child and her testamentary appointment governs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of HMGA 1956, a minor is incompetent to act as guardian of property of another minor. Can a minor act as guardian of the PERSON of his own minor child?
options: Yes, Sec 10 bars minor from acting as guardian of PROPERTY, not person of his own child
No, minor cannot act as guardian of person or property
questions.explanation: Section 10 restricts incompetence strictly to acting as guardian of property of a minor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of HMGA 1956, a De Facto Guardian is a person who takes continuous interest in managing minor's person/property without legal authority. A sale of minor's land by de facto guardian is:
questions.explanation: Section 11 creates absolute prohibition; sales by de facto guardians are null and void ab initio.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of HMGA 1956, who manages a Hindu minor's undivided interest in coparcenary joint family property?
options: The Karta / adult member of joint family managing property
questions.explanation: Section 12 recognizes Karta management of minor's undivided coparcenary interest.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1) of HMGA 1956, in the appointment or declaration of any guardian by Court, welfare of minor shall be the paramount consideration. Welfare of minor includes:
options: Physical, moral, ethical, educational, financial and emotional well-being of minor
questions.explanation: Child welfare under Section 13 encompasses holistic physical, moral, educational and emotional well-being.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2) of HMGA 1956, if a natural guardian wants to mortgage minor's land to raise funds for minor's medical treatment, guardian MUST obtain prior permission from the:
options: District Court having jurisdiction over location of land
questions.explanation: Section 8(2) read with Section 8(5) requires prior permission of District Court before mortgaging minor land.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(4) of HMGA 1956, before granting permission under Sec 8(2), Court shall issue notice of application to be served on affected persons and may make inquiry. Court grants permission ONLY if transaction is for:
options: Necessity or evident advantage to minor
questions.explanation: Section 8(4) mandates court permission strictly for minor necessity or evident advantage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (read with HMGA 1956), if there is a conflict between HMGA 1956 and GWA 1890 on any specific provision covered by HMGA, which Act prevails?
questions.explanation: HMGA 1956 is a later special Act; its specific provisions override GWA 1890 where inconsistent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, Court is NOT authorized to appoint or declare a guardian of person of minor whose father is living and is not in opinion of court unfit to be guardian. In HMGA 1956, how does Section 13 modify this?
options: Section 13 HMGA makes welfare of minor paramount, overriding Sec 19 GWA fitness presumption if welfare requires mother guardianship
questions.explanation: Section 13 HMGA overrides Section 19 GWA, making child welfare paramount over father's natural rights.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, a guardian of person appointed by court shall not remove ward from limits of court jurisdiction without court leave, EXCEPT for temporary purpose. Violation of Sec 26 is punishable under Sec 44 GWA with:
options: Fine up to Rs. 1,000 or civil imprisonment
questions.explanation: Section 44 GWA penalizes unauthorized removal of ward from jurisdiction with fine/imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, a guardian of property of a ward is bound to deal with property as carefully as a man of ordinary prudence would deal with it if it were his own. This is the duty of:
questions.explanation: Section 27 GWA enacts standard of ordinary prudence for guardian managing ward property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, a guardian appointed by court may apply by petition to Court for opinion, advice or direction on any present question respecting management/administration of ward property. Action taken by guardian in good faith under court direction protects guardian from:
questions.explanation: Section 33 GWA protects court-appointed guardians acting in good faith under court advice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, Court may require a guardian of property to give a bond with sureties to accounting for ward property, submit accounts periodically, and pay balance into court. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 34 GWA governs guardianship bonds and financial accounting duties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, where a guardian fails to accounting or commits breach of duty, Court may assign guardianship bond to a person entitled to sue on bond for recovering damages for minor. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 35 GWA permits suit on assigned guardianship bond for breach of trust.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, Court may make an order regulating conduct or proceedings of any guardian appointed or declared by Court. Disobedience to court order under Sec 43 is punishable in same manner as:
options: Injunction breach under Order XXXIX Rule 2A CPC (civil prison / attachment)
questions.explanation: Section 43(4) GWA applies CPC Order XXXIX R2A penalties for disobeying guardianship conduct orders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 48 of Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, an order made under this Act shall be final and shall not be liable to be contested by suit between parties, EXCEPT as provided by Section 47 appeal. This is:
questions.explanation: Section 48 GWA enacts finality of guardianship orders barring separate suits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(c) of HMGA 1956, "Natural Guardian" means any of the guardians mentioned in Section 6. Natural guardianship is created by:
questions.explanation: Natural guardianship arises by operation of law from birth relationship.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(a) of HMGA 1956, if father and mother are living separate, can the mother claim natural guardianship of minor child above 5 years if father is unfit or neglects minor?
options: Yes, under Section 6(a) as interpreted in Githa Hariharan and Section 13 child welfare
Mother can claim only if divorced
questions.explanation: Child welfare under Sec 13 read with Githa Hariharan permits mother guardianship if father is unfit or negligent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1) of HMGA 1956, can a natural guardian borrow money on behalf of minor to pay minor's school fees?
options: Yes, borrowings for minor's necessity or evident advantage are valid provided no personal covenant binds minor
questions.explanation: Section 8(1) permits necessary borrowings for minor's education/necessity without personal covenant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2)(a) of HMGA 1956, does exchange of minor's plot of land for another plot of land require prior court permission?
options: Yes, exchange of minor's immovable property explicitly requires prior court permission under Sec 8(2)(a)
questions.explanation: Section 8(2)(a) lists mortgage, charge, sale, gift, exchange as requiring prior court sanction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(3) of HMGA 1956, if a natural guardian gifts minor's house to a relative without court permission, when does the limitation period for minor to set aside gift begin?
questions.explanation: Article 60 Limitation Act prescribes 3 years from date minor attains majority to avoid Sec 8(3) transaction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(1) of HMGA 1956, can a father appoint a testamentary guardian for his minor child's share in UNDIVIDED coparcenary joint family property?
options: No, father CANNOT appoint testamentary guardian for undivided coparcenary interest (Sec 9(1) excludes undivided interest)
Father can appoint with Karta consent
Father can appoint for sons only
questions.explanation: Section 9(1) explicitly excludes undivided interest in joint family property from testamentary appointment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(3) of HMGA 1956, if a Hindu mother appoints a testamentary guardian by Will for her separate property gifted to minor child, does her appointment take effect upon her death if father is dead?
options: Yes, mother's testamentary appointment takes effect upon her death
questions.explanation: Section 9(3) validates mother's testamentary appointment taking effect upon her death when father is dead/disqualified.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of HMGA 1956, if a de facto guardian sells minor's land to pay off minor's ancestral debt, is the sale valid?
options: No, sale by de facto guardian is void ab initio under Section 11 regardless of necessity
questions.explanation: Section 11 imposes absolute prohibition; de facto guardian sales are null and void ab initio even if for necessity.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of HMGA 1956, if a minor is sole surviving coparcener of a Hindu joint family, can a guardian be appointed for his property under HMGA?
options: Yes, because there is no other adult coparcener/Karta managing property
questions.explanation: Where minor is sole surviving coparcener, Sec 12 bar does not apply as no adult Karta exists.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1) of HMGA 1956, if a father claims custody of his 6-year-old child under Section 6(a), but court finds father lives in unhealthy environment and neglects child while maternal grandparents provide excellent care, court will:
options: Refuse custody to father based on paramount welfare of child under Section 13
Grant custody to father because he is legal natural guardian
questions.explanation: Section 13 child welfare paramountcy overrides natural guardian's legal claim under Section 6.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of HMGA 1956, does the Act apply to a minor child whose one parent is Hindu and the other is Christian, if the child is brought up as a Hindu?
options: No, applies only if both parents are Hindu
Yes, Section 3(1)(c) applies HMGA to any child brought up as a Hindu
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(c) explicitly extends HMGA to any child, one of whose parents is Hindu, brought up as a Hindu.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(a) of HMGA 1956, if father and mother die, who becomes natural guardian of a Hindu minor child under HMGA?
options: HMGA does NOT provide for natural guardians beyond father and mother; court appoints guardian under GWA 1890
questions.explanation: HMGA Section 6 lists father and mother only; upon death of both, court appoints guardian under GWA 1890.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1) of HMGA 1956, can a natural guardian sell minor's MOVABLE property (such as shares or vehicles) without court permission?
options: No, movables also require court permission
Yes, Sec 8(2) requirement for court permission applies strictly to IMMOVABLE property, not movables
questions.explanation: Section 8(2) court permission requirement is restricted to immovable property.
