questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2)(b) of HMGA 1956, if a natural guardian leases minor's shop for 3 years, does this lease require prior court permission?
options: No, lease up to 5 years does NOT require court permission under Sec 8(2)(b)
questions.explanation: Section 8(2)(b) permits leases up to 5 years without prior court permission.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(5) of HMGA 1956 read with Section 31 of Guardians and Wards Act 1890, court permission to sell minor's land must specify the order, public auction or private sale, and the:
options: Minimum price at which property shall be sold
questions.explanation: Section 31 GWA read with Sec 8(5) HMGA requires court sanction to fix minimum sale price.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(2) of HMGA 1956, if a father appoints a testamentary guardian by Will and dies, and mother survives and appoints another testamentary guardian by her Will, whose appointment governs after mother's death?
options: Mother's testamentary appointment governs (father's appointment lspes under Sec 9(2))
questions.explanation: Under Sec 9(2), father's appointment has no effect if mother survives and makes testamentary appointment by Will.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of HMGA 1956, in a custody contest between a wealthy father and a loving mother of modest means, can custody be denied to mother solely because father has superior financial resources?
options: Yes, wealthy parent always gets custody
No, financial superiority alone does NOT outweigh mother's maternal care; father can be ordered to pay child maintenance
questions.explanation: Courts hold financial adequacy of father is met by ordering maintenance; mother's custody is preserved for child welfare.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(a) proviso of HMGA 1956, if a child is 4 years old, can the father claim custody against the mother without proving mother is unfit?
options: No, custody of minor under 5 years ordinarily belongs to mother under Sec 6(a) proviso unless mother is proved unfit
Yes, father gets custody as primary natural guardian
Father gets custody on weekends only
questions.explanation: Section 6(a) proviso presumes tender years custody (under 5 yrs) belongs to mother unless unfitness is proved.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(3) of HMGA 1956, if a minor avoids an unapproved land sale made by natural guardian after attaining majority, who bears the burden of proving that sale was for minor's necessity or evident advantage?
questions.explanation: The purchaser buying minor property bears burden of establishing legal necessity or evident advantage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of HMGA 1956, who is a "De Facto Guardian"?
options: A person who takes continuous informal charge of minor person/property without legal appointment or natural status
questions.explanation: Section 11 refers to de facto guardians who manage minor affairs without statutory/testamentary authority.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of HMGA 1956, does the prohibition against appointing a guardian for minor's undivided interest in coparcenary property apply if ALL coparceners of joint family are MINORS?
options: No, if all coparceners are minors, guardian can be appointed for joint property
questions.explanation: Where all coparceners are minors, no adult Karta exists, enabling court appointment of guardian.

questions.question_text: In Tejaswini Gaud v. Shekhar Jagdish Prasad Tewari (2019), the Supreme Court held that a writ of habeas corpus for the custody of a minor child is maintainable, and that in deciding it the court's primary concern is:
options: The welfare of the child, not the strict legal right of the party claiming custody
The strict legal title of the guardian
The pecuniary jurisdiction of the court
questions.explanation: Tejaswini Gaud (2019) held that habeas corpus is an efficacious remedy in child custody disputes and that the welfare of the child remains the paramount consideration.
questions.statute_or_case: Tejaswini Gaud v. Shekhar Jagdish Prasad Tewari (2019)

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(b) of HMGA 1956, can a person empowered to act as guardian by or under any enactment relating to any Court of Wards be a statutory guardian under HMGA?
options: Yes, Section 4(b)(iv) explicitly includes Court of Wards statutory guardians
questions.explanation: Section 4(b)(iv) includes a person empowered to act as such under any enactment relating to any Court of Wards in the definition of Guardian.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1) of HMGA 1956, if a natural guardian enters into a contract for minor's benefit, does it create personal liability against the minor?
options: No, natural guardian CANNOT bind minor by personal covenant (minor is not personally liable)
questions.explanation: Section 8(1) proviso explicitly prohibits natural guardians from binding minor by personal covenant.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(5) of HMGA 1956, can a testamentary guardian alienate minor's immovable property without court permission if the Will explicitly authorizes him to sell?
options: No, court permission mandatory in all cases
Yes, testamentary guardian's powers are subject to terms of Will under Sec 9(5)
questions.explanation: Section 9(5) states testamentary guardian exercises powers subject to terms of Will and statutory provisions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1) of HMGA 1956, can a mother who remarries after husband's death lose natural guardianship of her minor child automatically?
options: No, remarriage does NOT automatically disqualify mother from natural guardianship unless court finds it contrary to minor welfare under Sec 13
Mother forfeits if second husband is non-Hindu
questions.explanation: Remarriage of mother does not automatically forfeit guardianship under HMGA 1956 unless minor welfare suffers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2) of HMGA 1956, if a natural guardian creates a CHARGE (e.g. security for loan) on minor's land without court permission, is the charge valid?
options: No, creating a charge on minor immovable property without court permission violates Sec 8(2)(a) and is voidable under Sec 8(3)
questions.explanation: Section 8(2)(a) explicitly includes creating a "charge" on minor immovable property as requiring prior court permission.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of HMGA 1956, HMGA applies to any child, legitimate or illegitimate, both of whose parents are Hindus, Buddhists, Jains or Sikhs by religion. Does HMGA apply to a child converted to Hinduism?
options: No, applies only to birth Hindus
Yes, Section 3(1)(a) applies to any person who is a Hindu by conversion or re-conversion
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(a) applies HMGA to converts and re-converts to Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism or Sikhism.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(5) of HMGA 1956, an appeal from an order of District Court granting or refusing permission under Section 8(2) to alienate minor property lies to the:
options: High Court under Section 47 of Guardians and Wards Act 1890
questions.explanation: Section 8(5) HMGA read with Section 47 GWA 1890 provides statutory appeal to High Court against Sec 8 court orders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1 of HMGA 1956, the Act extends to the whole of India, and applies also to Hindus domiciled in India who are:
options: Outside India (Extra-territorial operation to domiciled Hindus)
questions.explanation: Section 1(2) gives extra-territorial application of HMGA to Hindus domiciled in India residing abroad.

questions.question_text: Under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 amending Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a daughter of a coparcener:
options: Becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right in the same manner as the son
Cannot claim partition of ancestral property
Inherits only self-acquired property of father
questions.explanation: The 2005 Amendment to Section 6 conferred equal coparcenary rights on daughters by birth in joint Hindu family property (upheld in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma).
questions.statute_or_case: Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as amended in 2005)

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of the Act, shall be held by her as:
options: Full owner thereof and not as a limited owner
questions.explanation: Section 14(1) converted a female Hindu's limited estate into absolute full ownership of property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Act extends to:
options: The whole of India except the Scheduled Areas
Only the States and not the Union Territories
India and all Hindus domiciled anywhere in the world
questions.explanation: Section 1(2) provides that the Act extends to the whole of India. Unlike the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Hindu Succession Act contains no express extra-territorial application clause.

questions.question_text: According to Section 2(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Act applies to which of the following groups?
options: Virashaivas, Lingayats, and followers of Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj
Any person who is a convert or reconvert to the Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh religion
questions.explanation: Section 2(1) explicitly includes Virashaivas, Lingayats, Brahmo/Prarthana/Arya Samajists, Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs, and converts/reconverts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Act does NOT apply to members of which community unless directed by Central Government notification?
options: Scheduled Tribes within the meaning of Article 366(25) of the Constitution
questions.explanation: Section 2(2) creates a statutory exemption for Scheduled Tribes under Article 366(25) of the Constitution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, one person is said to be an 'agnate' of another if the two are related by blood or adoption:
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(a) defines an agnate as a relative related by blood or adoption wholly through males.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a person is said to be a 'cognate' of another if they are related by blood or adoption:
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(c) defines a cognate as a relative related by blood or adoption but not wholly through males.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(e)(i) of HSA 1956, two persons are related by 'full blood' when descended from a common ancestor by the same wife, and by 'half blood' when descended from:
options: A common ancestor but by different wives
A common ancestress but by different husbands
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(e)(i) defines full blood (same father & wife) and half blood (same father, different wives).

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(e)(ii) of HSA 1956, two persons are related by 'uterine blood' when they are descended from:
options: A common ancestor but by different wives
A common ancestress but by different husbands
The same father and same mother
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(e)(ii) defines uterine blood as descent from a common ancestress (mother) by different husbands.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(j) proviso of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, illegitimate children shall be deemed to be related to:
options: Their biological father in all cases
Their mother and to one another
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(j) proviso enacts that illegitimate children are related to their mother and to one another.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, any text, rule, custom or usage of Hindu law in force immediately before commencement shall:
options: Prevail over the provisions of the Act
Remain valid for agricultural land only
Cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in the Act
questions.explanation: Section 4 gives an overriding effect to HSA 1956 over prior inconsistent texts, rules, customs or usages.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(i) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Act does NOT apply to any property succession to which is regulated by:
options: The Indian Succession Act, 1925 by reason of Section 21 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954
questions.explanation: Section 5(i) excludes property succession regulated by Indian Succession Act 1925 pursuant to s. 21 of Special Marriage Act 1954.

questions.question_text: Which of the following properties is expressly exempted from the operation of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 under Section 5(iii)?
options: Valiamma Thampuran Kovilagam Estate and Palace Fund administered by Palace Administration Board
questions.explanation: Section 5(iii) expressly excludes the Valiamma Thampuran Kovilagam Estate and Palace Fund in Cochin.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1) proviso of HSA 1956 (as amended in 2005), coparcenary rights conferred on daughters do NOT affect or invalidate any disposition, alienation, or partition that took place before:
questions.explanation: Section 6(1) proviso protects alienations, dispositions or partitions effected prior to 20th December 2004.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2) of HSA 1956 (as amended in 2005), any property to which a female Hindu becomes entitled as a coparcener shall be held by her with:
options: Limited life estate only returning to brothers
Incidents of coparcenary ownership and capable of disposition by testamentary disposition
questions.explanation: Section 6(2) provides that a female coparcener holds the property with coparcenary incidents and testamentary disposal power.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3) of HSA 1956 (as amended in 2005), when a Hindu dies after 09.09.2005, his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property shall devolve by:
options: Testamentary or intestate succession under the Act, and NOT by survivorship
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) substituted devolution by survivorship with testamentary or intestate succession under the Act.

questions.question_text: For the purpose of calculating the interest of a Mitakshara coparcener under Section 6(3) Explanation, the coparcenary property shall be deemed to be divided:
options: As if a partition had taken place immediately before his death
When the court passes a final decree only
Equal to half of total estate
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) Explanation creates a statutory fiction of deemed partition immediately preceding death.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(4) of HSA 1956 (as amended in 2005), after 09.09.2005, no court shall recognize any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for recovery of father's debt solely on the ground of:
options: The rule of pious obligation under Hindu law
questions.explanation: Section 6(4) abolished the doctrine of pious obligation for debts contracted after the 2005 amendment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(5) Explanation of HSA 1956, 'partition' means any partition made by execution of a deed duly registered under the Registration Act 1908 or effected by:
options: An oral family arrangement witnessed by village head
questions.explanation: Section 6(5) Explanation defines partition strictly as registered partition deed or court decree.

questions.question_text: In the landmark 3-Judge Bench judgment Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that rights of a daughter under Section 6 are:
options: Conferred by birth, and the coparcener father need NOT be alive on 09.09.2005
Conditional upon father being alive on 09.09.2005
Available only to daughters born after 2005
questions.explanation: Vineeta Sharma (2020) settled that daughter's coparcenary right is by birth and father need not be alive on 09.09.2005.
questions.statute_or_case: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) 9 SCC 1

questions.question_text: Which earlier Supreme Court judgment regarding Section 6 daughter coparcenary rights was explicitly overruled in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020)?
questions.explanation: Vineeta Sharma overruled Prakash v. Phulavati (2016) which had held that coparcener father must be alive on 09.09.2005.

questions.question_text: In Ganduri Koteshwaramma v. Chakiri Yanadi (2011), the Supreme Court held that the benefit of the 2005 Amendment to Section 6 can be claimed by a daughter in a partition suit:
options: Only if preliminary decree was passed post-2005
At any stage before passing of the final decree, even if a preliminary decree was passed earlier
questions.explanation: Ganduri Koteshwaramma held that rights can be modified till final decree is passed in a partition suit.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the property of a male Hindu dying intestate devolves firstly upon:
options: Relatives specified in Class II of the Schedule
Relatives specified in Class I of the Schedule
questions.explanation: Section 8(a) lays down that intestate male property devolves firstly upon Class I heirs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of HSA 1956, if there is no Class I heir and no Class II heir, the property of an intestate male devolves thirdly upon:
questions.explanation: Section 8(c) provides that in absence of Class I and II heirs, property devolves upon agnates.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of HSA 1956, cognates succeed to the property of a male intestate:
options: Lastly, if there is no heir of Class I, Class II, or any agnate
questions.explanation: Section 8(d) provides that cognates inherit lastly when no Class I, Class II or agnate heir exists.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, among the heirs specified in the Schedule, Class I heirs take:
options: Simultaneously and to the exclusion of all other heirs
Subject to approval of Class II heirs
questions.explanation: Section 9 mandates that Class I heirs take simultaneously and exclude all Class II, agnate, and cognate heirs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of HSA 1956, among Class II heirs, the order of succession is determined such that:
options: Male relatives in Class II exclude female relatives
Those in the first entry are preferred to those in the second entry, and so on in succession
questions.explanation: Section 9 explicitly states entry I excludes entry II, entry II excludes entry III, and so on.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 Rule 1 of HSA 1956, how is the share distributed among widows if the intestate male left more than one widow?
options: All widows together take one share
Each widow takes one full separate share equal to a son
Widows get no share if sons exist
questions.explanation: Section 10 Rule 1 states that the intestate's widow, or if there are more widows than one, all widows together take one share.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 Rule 2 of HSA 1956, who among the following each take one share in Class I distribution?
options: Surviving sons, surviving daughters, and the mother
questions.explanation: Section 10 Rule 2 provides that surviving sons, daughters, and mother each take one share.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 Rule 3 & Rule 4 of HSA 1956, the heirs in the branch of a pre-deceased son or pre-deceased daughter take:
options: Equal per capita share with surviving sons
No share if mother is alive
Between them one share (per stirpes distribution)
questions.explanation: Section 10 Rules 3 & 4 provide for per stirpes distribution for branches of pre-deceased children.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property divided between heirs specified in ANY ONE entry in Class II of the Schedule is shared:
options: In 2:1 ratio between males and females
questions.explanation: Section 11 provides that heirs within the same entry of Class II share equally.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 Rule 1 of HSA 1956, in determining preference among agnates or cognates, which heir is preferred?
options: The one who has fewer or no degrees of ascent
The one who has more degrees of ascent
The male relative over female relative
questions.explanation: Section 12 Rule 1 lays down that heir with fewer or no degrees of ascent is preferred.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 Rule 2 of HSA 1956, where the number of degrees of ascent is the SAME between two agnates or cognates, preference goes to:
options: The heir who has more degrees of descent
The heir who has fewer or no degrees of descent
questions.explanation: Section 12 Rule 2 provides that when degrees of ascent are equal, fewer degrees of descent preferred.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, degrees of ascent and degrees of descent shall be computed:
questions.explanation: Section 13(2) states that degrees of ascent and descent are computed inclusive of the intestate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14(1) Explanation of HSA 1956, 'property' held by a female Hindu as full owner includes movable and immovable property acquired by her:
options: Only property purchased out of her own earnings
Only ancestral property received from father
Only dowry items listed at marriage
By inheritance, devise, partition, in lieu of maintenance, gift, purchase, prescription or stridhana
questions.explanation: Section 14(1) Explanation gives a wide definition covering all modes of property acquisition.

questions.question_text: Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 acts as an exception to Section 14(1). It applies to property acquired by gift, will, decree, or award where:
options: The terms of the gift, will, instrument, decree, or award prescribe a restricted estate in such property
The consideration was paid by husband
questions.explanation: Section 14(2) retains restricted estate if conferred as a new grant under written instrument/decree with express restriction.

questions.question_text: In the landmark Supreme Court decision V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977), it was held that if property is acquired by a female Hindu in lieu of maintenance under a instrument with restricted terms:
options: Section 14(2) applies and she gets only a life estate
Section 14(1) applies because maintenance is a pre-existing right, enlarging it into absolute ownership
The transaction is void ab initio
She holds property as trustee for male reversioners
questions.explanation: V. Tulasamma (1977) established that property given in lieu of pre-existing maintenance right becomes absolute under s. 14(1).
questions.statute_or_case: V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) 3 SCC 99

questions.question_text: In Jagannathan Pillai v. Kunjithapadam Pillai (1987), the Supreme Court interpreted Section 14(1) of HSA 1956 to hold that a female Hindu who re-acquires property after 1956:
options: Remains limited owner because she lost possession earlier
Must seek civil court permission for absolute title
Becomes absolute owner under Section 14(1) upon re-acquisition
questions.explanation: Jagannathan Pillai held that Section 14(1) applies whenever a female Hindu comes into possession of property after 1956.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the property of a female Hindu dying intestate devolves firstly upon:
options: Sons and daughters (including children of pre-deceased son/daughter) and the husband
questions.explanation: Section 15(1)(a) specifies that children (and issue of pre-deceased children) and husband are first heirs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(1) of HSA 1956, if a female Hindu dies intestate leaving NO children and NO husband, her property devolves secondly (clause b) upon:
questions.explanation: Section 15(1)(b) places 'heirs of the husband' second in order of general succession.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(1) of HSA 1956, thirdly (clause c) in order of succession to a female Hindu's property are:
questions.explanation: Section 15(1)(c) places mother and father third in order of general succession.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(2)(a) of HSA 1956, property inherited by a female Hindu from her father or mother shall, in absence of any son or daughter (or children of pre-deceased children), devolve upon:
questions.explanation: Section 15(2)(a) provides that property inherited from parents reverts to father's heirs if she dies childless.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(2)(b) of HSA 1956, property inherited by a female Hindu from her husband or father-in-law shall, in absence of any son or daughter (or children of pre-deceased children), devolve upon:
questions.explanation: Section 15(2)(b) provides that property inherited from husband or father-in-law reverts to husband's heirs if she dies childless.

questions.question_text: In Om Prakash v. Radha Charan (2009), a childless Hindu widow died intestate leaving self-acquired property. The Supreme Court held that her self-acquired property devolves under:
options: Section 15(1) upon husband's heirs, as Section 15(2) applies ONLY to property inherited from parents/husband
Equal split between parents and husband's heirs
questions.explanation: Om Prakash (2009) affirmed that self-acquired property of female Hindu is governed strictly by Section 15(1).
questions.statute_or_case: Om Prakash v. Radha Charan (2009) 15 SCC 66

questions.question_text: In Bhagat Ram v. Teja Singh (1999), the Supreme Court held that where a female Hindu inherits property from her mother and dies issue-less, under Section 15(2)(a) the property devolves upon:
questions.explanation: Bhagat Ram held that property inherited from mother goes to father's heirs under Section 15(2)(a) in absence of children.
questions.statute_or_case: Bhagat Ram v. Teja Singh, (2002) 1 SCC 210

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 Rule 1 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, among heirs specified in Section 15(1), those in one entry shall be preferred to those in any succeeding entry, and heirs in the same entry shall take:
questions.explanation: Section 16 Rule 1 states that heirs included in the same entry take simultaneously.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 Rule 3 of HSA 1956, devolution of property on heirs referred to in clauses (b), (d) and (e) of Section 15(1) shall take place as if:
options: The property belonged to the Central Government
The female intestate had never married
The heirs were Class I heirs under Section 8
The husband, father, or mother (as the case may be) had died intestate in respect thereof immediately after the intestate's death
questions.explanation: Section 16 Rule 3 creates a statutory fiction that husband/father/mother died intestate immediately after female Hindu.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, heirs related to an intestate by full blood shall be preferred to heirs related by half blood if:
options: The nature of the relationship is the same in every other respect
The half blood relative is younger
The full blood relative is male
questions.explanation: Section 18 grants preference to full blood over half blood when relationship nature is otherwise identical.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, if two or more heirs succeed together to the property of an intestate, they shall take the property:
options: Per capita and not per stirpes (save as otherwise expressly provided)
In equal shares between male and female branches
As joint tenants with right of survivorship
questions.explanation: Section 19(a) establishes per capita rule as default mode of succession unless expressly provided otherwise.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(b) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, two or more heirs succeeding together take property as:
options: Tenants-in-common and NOT as joint tenants
questions.explanation: Section 19(b) explicitly provides that co-heirs take as tenants-in-common.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a child who was in the womb at the time of the death of an intestate and who is subsequently born alive shall have:
options: No right to inherit unless born within 30 days
Half the share of a living child
The same right to inherit as if born before the death of the intestate, vesting from date of death
questions.explanation: Section 20 protects posthumous child born alive, vesting inheritance retroactively from intestate's death date.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, where two persons die in circumstances rendering it uncertain which survived the other (simultaneous death), it shall be presumed until contrary proved that:
options: Both died at the exact same instant without succession
questions.explanation: Section 21 establishes statutory presumption of commorientes: younger survived elder.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22(1) of HSA 1956, when an interest in immovable property or business of an intestate devolves upon two or more Class I heirs, and one proposes to transfer their interest:
options: The other heirs shall have a preferential right to acquire the interest proposed to be transferred
The State Government must be given first offer
Any stranger can buy at market price without restriction
questions.explanation: Section 22(1) confers a statutory right of pre-emption/preference on Class I co-heirs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22(2) of HSA 1956, if Class I heirs cannot agree on the consideration for transfer under preferential right, consideration shall be determined by:
options: The court on application being made to it in this behalf
questions.explanation: Section 22(2) empowers the court to fix consideration upon application.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22(3) of HSA 1956, if two or more Class I heirs propose to acquire the interest under preferential right, which heir shall be preferred?
options: The heir residing in the property
The heir who offers the highest consideration for the transfer
questions.explanation: Section 22(3) mandates preference to the co-heir offering highest consideration.

questions.question_text: Section 23 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (which restricted female heirs from claiming partition of a dwelling-house) was:
options: Omitted by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005
questions.explanation: Section 23 was omitted by 2005 Amendment Act, removing restriction on female heirs seeking partition of dwelling house.

questions.question_text: Section 24 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (which disqualified certain remarried widows from inheriting) was:
options: Omitted by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005
questions.explanation: Section 24 was omitted by 2005 Amendment Act; remarriage post-death does not disqualify widow heirs now.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a person who commits murder or abets the commission of murder is:
options: Disqualified only if convicted for life imprisonment
Disqualified from inheriting the property of the person murdered or any property in furtherance of succession to which murder was committed
Disqualified only if victim was father
questions.explanation: Section 25 imposes total statutory disqualification on murderers and abettors of murder.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, where a Hindu ceases to be Hindu by conversion to another religion, who is disqualified from inheriting property of Hindu relatives?
options: Children born to convert AFTER conversion and their descendants (unless Hindus when succession opens)
questions.explanation: Section 26 disqualifies children born after conversion and their descendants unless they are Hindus when succession opens.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, if any person is disqualified from inheriting any property under the Act, it shall devolve:
options: As if such disqualified person had died before the intestate
Upon the spouse of disqualified person
questions.explanation: Section 27 creates fiction that disqualified person predeceased the intestate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, no person shall be disqualified from succeeding to any property on the ground of:
questions.explanation: Section 28 abolishes disease, defect, or deformity as grounds of disqualification.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (Escheat), if an intestate leaves no heir qualified to succeed, the property devolves on the Government subject to:
options: All obligations and liabilities to which an heir would have been subject
questions.explanation: Section 29 enacts doctrine of escheat with Government taking property subject to all heir liabilities.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, any Hindu may dispose of by will or other testamentary disposition any property capable of being disposed of by him in accordance with:
questions.explanation: Section 30 recognizes testamentary succession governed by Indian Succession Act 1925.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 Explanation of HSA 1956, the interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property shall be deemed to be property:
options: Capable of being disposed of by him by will or testamentary disposition
Disposable only with consensus of all coparceners
questions.explanation: Section 30 Explanation empowered a Mitakshara coparcener to bequeath his coparcenary interest by Will.

questions.question_text: How many categories of heirs are currently listed in Class I of the Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (post 2005 amendment)?
questions.explanation: The 2005 amendment added 4 categories (daughters/sons of pre-deceased daughters etc.), bringing Class I heirs total to 16.

questions.question_text: Which of the following relatives is included in Class I of the Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956?
questions.explanation: Mother is a Class I heir under HSA 1956, while Father is in Class II Entry I.

questions.question_text: In Class II of the Schedule to HSA 1956, who constitutes Entry I?
questions.explanation: Entry I of Class II comprises solely the Father.

questions.question_text: Which relatives are included in Class II Entry II of the Schedule to HSA 1956?
options: (1) Son's daughter's son, (2) Son's daughter's daughter, (3) Brother, (4) Sister
questions.explanation: Class II Entry II consists of son's daughter's son, son's daughter's daughter, brother, and sister.

questions.question_text: Under the Schedule to HSA 1956 Explanation, references to a 'brother' or 'sister' in Class II do NOT include references to a brother or sister by:
questions.explanation: Schedule Explanation expressly provides that brother/sister in Class II excludes uterine brother/sister.

questions.question_text: In Arunachala Gounder v. P. Ponnusamy (2022), the Supreme Court held that self-acquired property of a male Hindu dying intestate prior to 1956:
options: Devolves by inheritance upon his daughter, rather than by survivorship to collateral agnates
questions.explanation: Arunachala Gounder (2022) affirmed daughter's right to inherit self-acquired property of father dying intestate even pre-1956.

questions.question_text: In Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978), the Supreme Court interpreted the deemed partition under Section 6 proviso (pre-2005) to hold that:
options: Deemed partition is an illusion without legal consequences
Widow gets no share in coparcenary
Partition takes effect 1 year after death
The share of the widow on deemed partition must be fixed crystallised share, not subject to further reduction
questions.explanation: Gurupad (1978) established that share allotted to widow on deemed partition is final and expanding.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(3) of HSA 1956, when a sthanamdar dies after the commencement of the Act, sthanam property held by him devolves upon family members:
options: Per capita as their separate property
Per stirpes as joint family property
questions.explanation: Section 7(3) provides that sthanam property devolves per capita as separate property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of HSA 1956, for persons governed by Marumakkattayam or Aliyasantana law, in Section 15(1) general succession of female Hindus, who is placed FIRST along with sons and daughters?
questions.explanation: Section 17(ii) modifies s. 15(1)(a) for matrilineal systems to include mother alongside sons and daughters.

questions.question_text: Where a Hindu male dies intestate leaving his Mother, Widow, Son, and Father, who amongst them will inherit his property under Section 8 & Schedule?
options: Mother, Widow, Son, and Father (all four sharing equally)
Mother, Widow, and Son (sharing equally in Class I), excluding Father
questions.explanation: Mother, Widow, and Son are Class I heirs taking simultaneously, while Father is in Class II and is excluded.

questions.question_text: Where a Hindu male dies intestate leaving Widow of pre-deceased son, Son of pre-deceased daughter, and Brother, how is property distributed?
options: Son of pre-deceased daughter takes all
Widow of pre-deceased son and Son of pre-deceased daughter share equally (Class I), excluding Brother (Class II)
questions.explanation: Both Widow of pre-deceased son and Son of pre-deceased daughter are Class I heirs, excluding Class II Brother.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14(1) of HSA 1956, property acquired by a female Hindu by her own skill or exertion or by purchase before or after the commencement of the Act is held as:
questions.explanation: Section 14(1) Explanation explicitly covers property acquired by own skill, exertion, or purchase as absolute property.

questions.question_text: What was the core effect of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 on Section 6 regarding coparcenary liabilities of a daughter?
options: Daughter is subject to the SAME liabilities in respect of coparcenary property as that of a son
Daughter is liable only for mother's debts
questions.explanation: Section 6(1)(c) explicitly enacts that a daughter is subject to the same liabilities in respect of coparcenary property as a son.

questions.question_text: Where an intestate Hindu female dies unmarried leaving her Mother, Father, and Brother, how does her property (self-acquired) devolve under Section 15(1)?
options: Mother and Father share equally (under entry c, as entry a & b have no living heirs)
questions.explanation: Under Section 15(1)(c), Mother and Father share equally when there are no children, issue of pre-deceased children, or husband/husband's heirs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(2)(a), if an unmarried female Hindu dies leaving property inherited from her father, and is survived by Mother and Father's Brother (Uncle), who inherits?
options: Equal split between Mother and Uncle
Mother inherits as heir of the father under Section 15(2)(a)
questions.explanation: Under S. 15(2)(a), property reverts to father's heirs. Mother is Class I heir of father, excluding father's brother (Class II).

questions.question_text: If a Hindu male dies intestate leaving two widows, W1 and W2, a Son, and a Daughter, into how many equal parts is his estate divided under Section 10?
options: 3 equal parts (W1 & W2 together get 1 part, Son gets 1 part, Daughter gets 1 part)
questions.explanation: Under Section 10 Rule 1 & 2, both widows together get 1 share, Son gets 1 share, Daughter gets 1 share (total 3 shares).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(3) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the expression 'Hindu' in any portion of the Act includes:
options: Only persons born in orthodox Hindu families
Any person who, though not a Hindu by religion, is nevertheless a person to whom the Act applies under Section 2
Persons domiciled in Uttar Pradesh only
questions.explanation: Section 2(3) defines 'Hindu' inclusively for all persons covered by the applicability section.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(d) of HSA 1956, a 'custom' or 'usage' must satisfy which of the following statutory requirements to have the force of law?
options: Approved by local High Court judge
Continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, certain, not unreasonable, and not opposed to public policy
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(d) lays down essential valid custom requirements: antiquity, uniformity, certainty, reasonableness, public policy.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(d) second proviso, in the case of a rule applicable ONLY to a family, custom ceases to have legal force if it has been:
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(d) second proviso states a family custom loses validity if discontinued by the family.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(i) of HSA 1956, 'Nambudri law' refers to the system of law applicable to persons governed by which enactments prior to 1956?
options: Madras Nambudri Act 1932, Cochin Nambudri Act, or Travancore Malayala Brahmin Act
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(i) defines Nambudri law with reference to specified Malabar/Cochin/Travancore Brahmin Acts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(4)(b) proviso of HSA 1956 (as amended in 2005), alienations made in respect of father's pre-2005 debt under pious obligation remain:
options: Enforceable in the same manner and to same extent as if 2005 Amendment had not been enacted
Subject to mandatory approval of District Judge
questions.explanation: Section 6(4)(b) proviso protects pre-2005 alienations under pious obligation rule.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 Rule 3 of HSA 1956, where neither agnate/cognate heir is entitled to preference under Rule 1 (ascent) or Rule 2 (descent), they take:
questions.explanation: Section 12 Rule 3 provides that when ascent and descent degrees are identical, agnates/cognates take simultaneously.

questions.question_text: In Class II of the Schedule to HSA 1956, which entry contains 'Brother's son, Sister's son, Brother's daughter, Sister's daughter'?
questions.explanation: Entry IV of Class II contains nephews and nieces (brother's/sister's sons and daughters).

questions.question_text: In Class II of the Schedule to HSA 1956, who constitutes Entry V?
questions.explanation: Entry V of Class II comprises paternal grandparents (Father's father and Father's mother).

questions.question_text: In Class II of the Schedule to HSA 1956, who constitutes Entry VI?
questions.explanation: Entry VI of Class II comprises Father's widow (stepmother) and Brother's widow.

questions.question_text: In Class II of the Schedule to HSA 1956, who constitutes Entry VII?
questions.explanation: Entry VII of Class II comprises paternal uncle and aunt (Father's brother and Father's sister).

questions.question_text: In Class II of the Schedule to HSA 1956, who constitutes Entry VIII?
questions.explanation: Entry VIII of Class II comprises maternal grandparents (Mother's father and Mother's mother).

questions.question_text: In Class II of the Schedule to HSA 1956, who constitutes Entry IX?
questions.explanation: Entry IX of Class II comprises maternal uncle and aunt (Mother's brother and Mother's sister).

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, unless the context otherwise requires, words importing the masculine gender shall:
options: NOT be taken to include females
Be interpreted according to General Clauses Act
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) explicitly provides that words importing masculine gender shall NOT be taken to include females.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(1) Explanation of HSA 1956, interest of a Hindu in tarwad/tavazhi/illom property is calculated on deemed partition based on:
options: Per stirpes share based on branches
Per capita share among all living members immediately before death
questions.explanation: Section 7(1) Explanation prescribes per capita share calculation for tarwad/tavazhi/illom deemed partition.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(3) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, for computing degrees of relationship, every generation constitutes:
options: A degree either ascending or descending
questions.explanation: Section 13(3) enacts that every generation constitutes a degree either ascending or descending.

questions.question_text: If a Hindu male dies intestate leaving his Son, Daughter, Mother, and Father's Brother, what share does Mother get?
options: 1/3rd share (sharing equally with Son and Daughter in Class I)
questions.explanation: Class I heirs are Son, Daughter, and Mother (3 heirs), sharing equally (1/3rd each). Father's brother is Class II and excluded.

questions.question_text: Under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, an adopted child in relation to intestate succession in the adoptive family has:
options: Half the share of a natural child
The exact same rights of inheritance as a natural-born legitimate child
No rights unless named in Will
questions.explanation: Under Section 3(1)(j) & HAMA 1956, an adopted child is treated on par with a natural child for succession.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of HSA 1956, if an intestate male leaves a full-blood brother and a half-blood brother (same father, different mothers):
options: The full-blood brother excludes the half-blood brother entirely
Half-blood brother takes precedence if older
questions.explanation: Section 18 mandates full blood preference over half blood when relationship nature is otherwise identical.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 Explanation of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, 'Court' for preferential right applications means:
options: High Court of the State exclusively
The court within the limits of whose jurisdiction the immovable property is situate or business is carried on
questions.explanation: Section 22 Explanation defines Court based on territorial jurisdiction over property or business.

questions.question_text: What is the primary overarching object of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 as stated in its Preamble?
options: To amend and codify the law relating to intestate succession among Hindus
To merge Hindu law with Indian Succession Act
To regulate solemnization of Hindu marriages
questions.explanation: The Preamble states HSA 1956 is 'An Act to amend and codify the law relating to intestate succession among Hindus'.

questions.question_text: In Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903), the Privy Council held that an agreement by a minor is:
options: Voidable at the option of the minor
Void ab initio (absolutely void), because under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 a minor is not competent to contract
Valid and binding on both parties
Voidable at the option of the other party
questions.explanation: A minor's agreement is a nullity from the beginning; there can be no ratification on majority, and the doctrine of estoppel does not apply against a minor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, consideration must move:
options: At the desire of the promisee only
From the promisee alone, never a third party
At the desire of the promisor (an act done at the desire of a third party or voluntarily is not consideration, as in Durga Prasad v. Baldeo)
Only in the form of money
questions.explanation: Under Indian law consideration may move from the promisee OR any other person, so a stranger to consideration can sue (Chinnaya v. Ramaya), but it must be at the promisor's desire.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the essential elements of a valid contract are:
options: A written and registered document in every case
Free consent of parties competent to contract, a lawful consideration and a lawful object, and the agreement is not expressly declared void
questions.explanation: Section 10 makes an agreement a contract only if all these elements are present; some contracts additionally require writing, registration or attestation by law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement made without consideration is void, EXCEPT where it:
options: Is in writing and registered and made out of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation; or is a promise to compensate a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor; or is a written promise to pay a time-barred debt
Is oral and made in the presence of witnesses
questions.explanation: Section 25 lists the three exceptions to the rule 'no consideration, no contract'; Explanation 2 adds that inadequacy of consideration does not by itself make a contract void.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 3 and 4 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the communication of an acceptance is complete:
options: Only when the proposer actually reads it
As against the proposer, when it is put in a course of transmission to him so as to be out of the power of the acceptor; and as against the acceptor, when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer
Only when the acceptor posts it, for both parties
When the acceptor decides to accept, in his own mind
questions.explanation: This gives rise to the 'postal rule' in India: the proposer is bound the moment the acceptance is posted, but the acceptor is bound only when it reaches the proposer, so the acceptor may revoke before then (Section 5).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(g) and Section 2(i) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the difference between a 'void agreement' and a 'voidable contract' is that:
options: A void agreement can be ratified but a voidable one cannot
A void agreement is not enforceable by law from the outset; a voidable contract is enforceable at the option of one party but not at the option of the other, until it is avoided
A voidable contract is one made by a minor
questions.explanation: Agreements hit by Sections 20, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30 and 56 are void; contracts vitiated by coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation (Sections 15-18) are voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused (Section 19/19A).

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract is said to be induced by 'undue influence' where:
options: One party threatens to commit a crime
One party makes a false statement of fact
Both parties are mistaken about a fact

One party is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage; and where such a person enters a transaction that appears unconscionable, the burden of proving that it was not induced by undue influence lies on the dominant party
questions.explanation: Section 16 gives examples of dominating relationships (real or apparent authority, fiduciary relation, mental distress caused by age, illness or bodily distress).

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, 'fraud' includes:
options: A false suggestion of a fact by one who does not believe it to be true, active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of it, a promise made without any intention of performing it, and any other act or omission specially declared fraudulent by law
Mere silence as to facts likely to affect willingness, in all cases
questions.explanation: The Explanation to Section 17 provides that mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence is equivalent to speech.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, where both parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement:
options: The agreement is voidable at the option of either party
The agreement is valid and enforceable
The agreement is voidable at the option of the mistaken party only
questions.explanation: Section 21 provides that a mistake as to a law in force in India does not make a contract voidable; Section 22 provides that a unilateral mistake of fact does not by itself make a contract voidable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the consideration or object of an agreement is unlawful where:
options: It is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy
questions.explanation: An agreement with an unlawful object or consideration is void; if the unlawful part can be severed, the lawful part may be enforced.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is:
options: Valid if the restraint is reasonable
Voidable at the option of the restrained party
Valid for a maximum of three years
Void to that extent (the only statutory exception being the sale of goodwill of a business, subject to reasonable local limits)
questions.explanation: Indian law does not, unlike English law, allow the courts to uphold 'reasonable' restraints of trade generally; a restraint operating during the term of employment is, however, not hit by Section 27 (Niranjan Shankar Golikari).

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement is void to the extent that it:
options: Absolutely restricts a party from enforcing his rights under a contract by the usual legal proceedings, or limits the time within which he may do so, or extinguishes the rights or discharges the liability on the expiry of a specified period
Names a particular court (out of two competent courts) as the forum for disputes
questions.explanation: Section 28 does not bar an ouster-of-jurisdiction clause choosing between courts that both have jurisdiction, nor a genuine arbitration agreement (which is expressly saved).

questions.question_text: In Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), the rule on remoteness of damages (codified in Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) is that the injured party may recover:
options: All losses actually suffered, however remote

Damages arising naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, and such damages as the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from its breach — but not damages for any remote or indirect loss
questions.explanation: Section 73 also provides that compensation is not given for remote or indirect loss, and that the party suffering the breach must take reasonable steps to mitigate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, where a contract names a sum to be paid on breach, or contains any other stipulation by way of penalty:
options: The exact sum named must always be paid
Nothing can be recovered unless actual loss is proved to the last rupee
The aggrieved party is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named (or the penalty stipulated), whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused
The court must award triple the named sum
questions.explanation: Indian law abolishes the English distinction between a penalty and liquidated damages; the named sum is the ceiling, and the court awards reasonable compensation (Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das; Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA, 2015).

questions.question_text: Under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the doctrine of frustration provides that:
options: A contract can be avoided merely because performance has become more expensive
Frustration is the same as breach and gives rise to damages
The doctrine applies only to contracts for the sale of goods

A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible or unlawful by reason of some event the promisor could not prevent, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful
questions.explanation: In India, frustration operates through the positive rule in Section 56 (not an implied term); Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur (1954) held that 'impossible' means impracticable or useless having regard to the object of the contract.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an offer of a reward for doing an act (a general offer to the world at large):
options: May be accepted by anyone who performs the act with knowledge of the offer, and the performance of the conditions of the proposal is an acceptance (as in Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.)
Cannot be accepted by an unknown person
Is not a valid offer at all
Requires a written acceptance communicated to the offeror before performance
questions.explanation: A general offer in the nature of a continuing offer can be accepted by anyone; a general offer for a reward is accepted by performance without prior communication.

questions.question_text: Under Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (novation, rescission and alteration):
options: A contract can never be varied once made
If the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for it, or to rescind or alter it, the original contract need not be performed
Only a court can rescind a contract
Alteration of a contract requires registration
questions.explanation: Section 63 further provides that a promisee may dispense with or remit performance wholly or in part, or extend the time, or accept any satisfaction he thinks fit — Indian law does not require fresh consideration for such an accord and satisfaction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the general position on 'time is of the essence of the contract' is that:
options: Time is always of the essence in every contract
Time is never of the essence

Whether time is of the essence is a question of the intention of the parties; in contracts for the sale of immovable property, time is presumed not to be of the essence unless the contract shows a contrary intention
Time is of the essence only in Government contracts
questions.explanation: Section 55 deals with the effect of failure to perform at a fixed time; where time is essential, failure makes the contract voidable at the option of the promisee, where it is not, the promisee is entitled to compensation for the delay.

questions.question_text: Under Section 124 and Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the difference between a 'contract of indemnity' and a 'contract of guarantee' is that:
options: An indemnity always requires consideration but a guarantee does not
A guarantee must always be in writing but an indemnity need not be
There is no difference under Indian law

In an indemnity there are two parties and the indemnifier undertakes to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the indemnifier himself or of any other person; in a guarantee there are three parties (creditor, principal debtor, surety) and the surety's liability is secondary, arising on the principal debtor's default
questions.explanation: The surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor unless otherwise provided (Section 128), and the surety is discharged in the circumstances in Sections 133-141.

questions.question_text: Under Section 148 and Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the difference between 'bailment' and 'pledge' is that:
options: A pledge (pawn) is a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise; a bailment is the wider concept of delivery of goods for a purpose, upon a contract that they be returned or dealt with according to the bailor's directions
A pledge transfers ownership of the goods
Only a bank can be a pawnee
questions.explanation: The pawnee has a right to retain the goods for the debt, interest and expenses (Section 173) and, on default, a right to sue or to sell after reasonable notice (Section 176).

questions.question_text: Under Section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an 'agent' is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealings with third persons, and:
options: Only a lawyer can act as an agent

Any person who is of the age of majority and of sound mind may employ an agent; but as between the principal and third persons, any person may become an agent (Section 184), though such an agent may not be liable to his principal
An agent must always be paid a commission
A minor can never be an agent for any purpose
questions.explanation: An agent's authority may be actual (express or implied) or apparent (ostensible); the principal is bound by acts within the agent's apparent authority (Section 237).

questions.question_text: Under Section 201 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agency is terminated by, among other modes:
options: Only by a written notice registered under the Registration Act

The principal revoking the agent's authority, the agent renouncing the business, the completion of the business, either party dying or becoming of unsound mind, or the principal being adjudicated an insolvent
Only on the expiry of one year
questions.explanation: An agency coupled with an interest cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest (Section 202); reasonable notice must be given of revocation or renunciation (Section 206).

questions.question_text: Under Section 68 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, if a person incapable of contracting (such as a minor or a lunatic), or anyone whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another with 'necessaries' suited to his condition in life:
options: The minor is personally liable to pay
The supplier has no remedy at all
The supplier is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person (a quasi-contractual claim, not a personal liability of the minor)
questions.explanation: Section 68 is one of the 'quasi-contracts' (Sections 68-72) or relations resembling contract; the claim lies only against the estate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, where a person lawfully does something for another, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and the other enjoys the benefit:
options: The latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered
No compensation is payable unless there was an express request
The benefit must be returned in specie only
The claim is barred as officious intermeddling in all cases
questions.explanation: Section 70 is a restitutionary obligation requiring (i) a lawful act done for another, (ii) not intended to be gratuitous, and (iii) actual enjoyment of the benefit.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(a)-(b) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an 'invitation to offer' (such as goods displayed with a price tag, an auction advertisement, or a tender notice) is:
options: A binding proposal the moment it is published
Not a proposal capable of acceptance; it merely invites the other party to make a proposal, which the inviter is then free to accept or reject
Enforceable by anyone who responds to it
questions.explanation: The distinction (Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v. Boots; Harvey v. Facey) determines who is the offeror and who the acceptor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an offer lapses or is revoked, among other ways:
options: It can never be revoked once made
Only by a written notice sent by registered post

By notice of revocation communicated before acceptance, by lapse of the time prescribed (or a reasonable time), by failure of the acceptor to fulfil a condition precedent, or by the death or insanity of the proposer if the fact comes to the acceptor's knowledge before acceptance
Only after 30 days in every case
questions.explanation: A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards (Section 5).

questions.question_text: Under Section 65 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when an agreement is discovered to be void, or a contract becomes void:
options: Each party keeps whatever it has received
The advantage must be paid to the Government
The section applies only to contracts void for fraud
Any person who has received any advantage under it is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it, to the person from whom he received it
questions.explanation: Section 65 provides restitution on a contract becoming void (e.g. by frustration under Section 56); it does not apply to an agreement void ab initio and known to be void, or to a minor's agreement.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when a promisee accepts performance of the promise from a third person:
options: He cannot afterwards enforce it against the promisor
He may still recover from the promisor
The contract is discharged only if the promisor consents
The third person becomes a party to the contract
questions.explanation: Acceptance of performance from a stranger discharges the promisor; Section 37 requires the parties to perform or offer to perform their respective promises unless performance is dispensed with or excused.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(d) and settled law, the doctrine of privity of contract in India means that:
options: Anyone who benefits from a contract can sue on it

Only a party to a contract can sue on it; a stranger to the contract cannot, though a stranger to the consideration can sue (subject to recognised exceptions such as a beneficiary under a trust, a family arrangement, or an assignee)
A stranger to consideration can never sue
Privity does not exist in Indian law
questions.explanation: The Indian Contract Act does not expressly bar a third-party beneficiary, but the Privy Council and the Supreme Court have applied the privity rule with exceptions (Jamna Das v. Ram Autar Pande; M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore).

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, 'coercion' is:
options: Any pressure of a commercial nature

The committing, or threatening to commit, any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code, or the unlawful detaining or threatening to detain any property, to the prejudice of any person, with the intention of causing him to enter into an agreement
The exercise of authority by a person in a fiduciary position
questions.explanation: A contract caused by coercion is voidable at the option of the coerced party (Section 19); the IPC need not be in force at the place where the coercion is employed (Explanation to Section 15).

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, agreements by way of wager are:
options: Voidable at the option of the loser
Void, and no suit can be brought for recovering anything alleged to be won on any wager, or entrusted to any person to abide the result of any game or other uncertain event on which any wager is made
questions.explanation: Section 30 makes wagering agreements void (not illegal); a subscription or contribution towards a prize of Rs 500 or more for the winner of a horse race is an exception.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (anticipatory breach), when a party has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety:
options: The other party may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified (by words or conduct) his acquiescence in its continuance
He must wait until the date of performance before doing anything
The contract is automatically at an end
He may only claim damages, never terminate
questions.explanation: On an anticipatory breach the injured party may sue at once or wait until the time for performance; if he waits, he keeps the contract alive for the benefit of both parties.

questions.question_text: The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 is:
questions.explanation: The Industrial Relations Code received assent on 28 September 2020 and is Act No. 35 of 2020.

questions.question_text: Under Section 104 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code subsumes and repeals which three earlier enactments?
options: The Factories Act, 1948; the Mines Act, 1952; and the Plantations Labour Act, 1951
The Payment of Wages Act, 1936; the Minimum Wages Act, 1948; and the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965
The Trade Unions Act, 1926; the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946; and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
The EPF Act, 1952; the ESI Act, 1948; and the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
questions.explanation: The IR Code consolidates the law on trade unions, standing orders and industrial disputes into a single statute.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a Works Committee must be constituted in an industrial establishment in which:
options: Twenty or more workers are employed
Ten or more workers are employed
Three hundred or more workers are employed
One hundred or more workers are employed, or were employed on any day in the preceding twelve months
questions.explanation: Section 3 retains the 100-worker threshold for a Works Committee (with equal employer and worker representatives) to promote amity in the establishment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a Grievance Redressal Committee must be set up in every industrial establishment employing:
options: Twenty or more workers, with a total membership not exceeding ten and adequate representation of women workers
questions.explanation: Section 4 requires a Grievance Redressal Committee for individual grievances in establishments with 20+ workers; an aggrieved worker may apply within one year of the cause of action.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, an application for registration of a Trade Union may be made by:
options: Any seven or more members, provided at least 10 per cent of the workers or 100 workers (whichever is less) of the establishment or industry are members
At least 30 per cent of the workforce
A majority of all workers in the industry
questions.explanation: Section 6 keeps the seven-member requirement for an application but adds a subsisting membership floor of 10% or 100 workers (whichever is less), subject to a minimum of seven, for continued registration.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a single trade union is recognised as the 'sole negotiating union' if it has:
options: At least 25 per cent of the workers as members
More members than any other single union
Fifty-one per cent or more of the workers on the muster roll of the establishment as its members
questions.explanation: Section 14 provides that a union with 51%+ membership is the sole negotiating union; where no union crosses 51%, a negotiating council is formed of unions each having at least 20% of the workers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, where no trade union has 51 per cent membership, a negotiating council is constituted of unions each having:
options: Not less than five per cent of the workers as members
At least forty per cent of the workers as members
Not less than twenty per cent of the workers as members, with one representative for every twenty per cent
questions.explanation: Section 14 sets the 20% threshold for a seat on the negotiating council, giving proportional representation to significant unions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, office-bearers and members of a registered Trade Union enjoy:
options: Immunity from civil suit in respect of any act done in contemplation or furtherance of an industrial dispute, where the act induces a breach of contract of employment or interferes with trade or business
Immunity only if the strike is legal
questions.explanation: Section 16 continues the civil immunity previously in the Trade Unions Act, 1926; Section 17 gives limited protection against a charge of criminal conspiracy for agreements to further legitimate union objects.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a person is disqualified from being an office-bearer of a registered Trade Union if:
options: He has not attained 18 years of age, or he has been convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude and sentenced to imprisonment (unless five years have elapsed since release)
He is over 60 years of age
He is employed in the same establishment
questions.explanation: Section 21 lists the disqualifications; a Minister or a person holding an office of profit under the Union or a State (other than employment in the connected industry) also cannot be an office-bearer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a dispute between two trade unions, or between a union and its members regarding registration or election of office-bearers, is adjudicated by:
options: The Registrar of Trade Unions with no appeal
The Industrial Tribunal having jurisdiction (no civil court other than the Tribunal may entertain such a dispute)
questions.explanation: Section 22 confers exclusive jurisdiction over internal trade-union disputes on the Industrial Tribunal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the chapter on standing orders applies to every industrial establishment wherein:
options: One hundred or more workers are employed
Fifty or more workers are employed
Twenty or more workers are employed
Three hundred or more workers are employed, or were employed on any day of the preceding twelve months
questions.explanation: The IR Code raises the standing-orders threshold from 100 (under the 1946 Act) to 300 workers, a significant relaxation for employers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, until an establishment's own standing orders are certified:
options: The model standing orders made by the Central Government are deemed to be adopted in that establishment
The establishment has no standing orders and none apply
The State labour department frames bespoke orders
The last settlement governs conditions of service
questions.explanation: Section 29 makes the Central Government's model standing orders the default; the employer must prepare draft standing orders within six months of the Code's commencement (Section 30).

questions.question_text: Under Section 38 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, disciplinary proceedings against a worker must ordinarily be completed within:
options: One year, with no subsistence allowance
Ninety days from the date of suspension, with the worker entitled to subsistence allowance during suspension
questions.explanation: Section 38 sets a 90-day time limit for disciplinary inquiries and prescribes subsistence allowance (50% of wages for the first 90 days, 75% thereafter) during suspension.

questions.question_text: Under Section 40 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, an employer proposing to effect a change in the conditions of service specified in the Third Schedule must give the affected workers:
options: Twenty-one days' notice of the change in the prescribed manner
questions.explanation: Section 40 requires 21 days' notice of change in respect of the matters listed in the Third Schedule (wages, hours, leave, etc.).

questions.question_text: Under Section 62 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a key change from the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is that:
options: Only unregistered unions may call a strike
Notice is required only for lock-outs, not strikes
The requirement of prior notice of strike or lock-out now applies to ALL industrial establishments, not only public utility services
questions.explanation: Section 62 extends the strike/lock-out notice regime, formerly confined to public utility services, to every industrial establishment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 62 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, no person employed in an industrial establishment may go on strike in breach of contract:
options: Without giving notice of strike within sixty days before striking, or within fourteen days of giving such notice, or during conciliation proceedings and seven days after, or during Tribunal proceedings and sixty days after
Without the written permission of the Central Government
Unless 90 per cent of the workers agree
At any time; there are no restrictions
questions.explanation: Section 62 prescribes the notice period and cooling-off restrictions; a strike or lock-out in contravention of Section 62 is 'illegal' under Section 63.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the definition of 'strike' now expressly includes:
options: A single worker's absence without leave
The concerted casual leave on a given day by fifty per cent or more of the workers employed in an industry
A go-slow by any number of workers
questions.explanation: The IR Code adds mass casual leave by 50%+ of workers to the definition of 'strike', closing a loophole used to circumvent strike-notice requirements.

questions.question_text: Under Section 64 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020:
options: Trade unions may fund any strike they choose
Employers may not fund any lock-out
No person shall knowingly spend or apply any money in direct furtherance or support of any illegal strike or lock-out
Only the Government may fund a strike
questions.explanation: Section 64 prohibits financial aid to illegal strikes or lock-outs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 70 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (Chapter IX), a worker who has been in continuous service for not less than one year cannot be retrenched unless:
options: The employer simply records the reason in a register
The Government issues a prior order in every case
He is given one month's written notice (or wages in lieu) and retrenchment compensation equivalent to fifteen days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service
questions.explanation: Section 70 preserves the retrenchment safeguards of the 1947 Act for establishments below the Chapter X threshold: notice/pay in lieu and 15 days' pay per completed year as compensation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 77 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, Chapter X (prior Government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure) applies to an industrial establishment (not seasonal or intermittent) in which:
options: Not less than three hundred workers were employed on an average per working day in the preceding twelve months (or such higher number as notified)
Not less than one hundred workers were employed
Not less than fifty workers were employed
Any number of workers is employed
questions.explanation: The IR Code raises the Chapter X threshold from 100 (under the 1947 Act) to 300 workers, and allows the appropriate Government to notify an even higher number.

questions.question_text: Under Section 78 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, an establishment to which Chapter X applies must obtain prior permission of the appropriate Government before:
options: Laying off a worker whose name is on the muster rolls (other than a badli or casual worker), except in cases of shortage of power or natural calamity
questions.explanation: Section 78 prohibits lay-off in large establishments without prior Government permission, subject to the stated exceptions; Sections 79 and 80 impose the same prior-permission requirement for retrenchment and closure.
