questions.question_text: Under Section 74 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, an employer intending to close down an undertaking must serve notice on the appropriate Government of:
options: At least sixty days before the intended date of closure
questions.explanation: Section 74 requires 60 days' prior notice of intended closure of an undertaking (Chapter IX); Section 75 provides closure compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year of continuous service.

questions.question_text: Section 83 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 introduces a new 'worker re-skilling fund' to which the employer must contribute, for each retrenched worker:
options: Nothing; the fund is entirely Government-financed
An amount equal to fifteen days' wages last drawn by the worker, to be credited to the worker's account within forty-five days of retrenchment
questions.explanation: Section 83 requires the employer to contribute 15 days' last-drawn wages per retrenched worker to the re-skilling fund, which is credited to the worker to support training.

questions.question_text: Under Section 44 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, an Industrial Tribunal now consists of:
options: Two members — one Judicial Member and one Administrative Member — appointed by the appropriate Government
A bench of High Court judges
questions.explanation: The IR Code replaces the single-member Industrial Tribunal of the 1947 Act with a two-member Tribunal (one Judicial, one Administrative); a National Industrial Tribunal is constituted by the Central Government under Section 46.

questions.question_text: Under Section 53 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, where conciliation of an industrial dispute fails:
options: Only the appropriate Government may refer the dispute for adjudication
The workman or employer may apply to the Industrial Tribunal within ninety days of the conciliation officer's failure report, without waiting for a Government reference
The matter must go to arbitration
questions.explanation: The IR Code lets the parties directly approach the Tribunal after a failed conciliation, reducing the earlier bottleneck of a discretionary Government reference.

questions.question_text: Under Section 42 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, parties to an industrial dispute may, before it is referred for adjudication, agree in writing to refer it to:
options: The High Court in its writ jurisdiction
Arbitration by a named arbitrator or arbitrators
A panel of the Bar Council
questions.explanation: Section 42 preserves voluntary reference to arbitration; on such a reference a strike or lock-out may be prohibited by notification and the arbitration award is published and enforced like a Tribunal award.

questions.question_text: Under Section 56 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, where a Tribunal or court proceeding results in reinstatement of a dismissed worker and the employer prefers an appeal:
options: The worker gets nothing until the appeal is decided
The employer may recover wages already paid
The employer must pay the worker full wages last drawn during the pendency of the proceedings in the higher court, if the worker was not employed elsewhere
questions.explanation: Section 56 continues the 'last drawn wages' protection (formerly Section 17B of the 1947 Act) for a reinstated worker during appellate proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 84 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the commission of an unfair labour practice specified in the Second Schedule:
options: Is prohibited for both employers and workers and their trade unions, and is an offence under the Code
Is prohibited only for trade unions
questions.explanation: Section 84 bars unfair labour practices (listed in the Second Schedule) by employers, workers and unions alike; Section 86 prescribes penalties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 86 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, an employer who contravenes the provisions on lay-off, retrenchment or closure requiring prior permission is punishable with:
options: Fine of one lakh rupees which may extend to ten lakh rupees
Fine not exceeding one thousand rupees
questions.explanation: Section 86 sets graded monetary penalties for contraventions; illegal lay-off/retrenchment/closure attracts a fine of Rs 1 lakh to Rs 10 lakh.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, an individual worker whose services are discharged, dismissed, retrenched or otherwise terminated (a dispute deemed to be an industrial dispute even if no union is a party):
options: May sue in the civil court at any time
Has no remedy under the Code

May apply directly to the Industrial Tribunal after the expiry of forty-five days from the date he applied to the conciliation officer, and in any case before the expiry of two years from the date of termination
Must first obtain the employer's consent
questions.explanation: Section 4(9) deems an individual discharge/dismissal/retrenchment/termination dispute to be an industrial dispute; Section 4(10)-(11) let the worker apply directly to the Tribunal after 45 days from his conciliation application, and within two years of the termination.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the definition of 'worker' excludes a person employed in a supervisory capacity drawing wages exceeding:
options: Eighteen thousand rupees per month, or an amount notified by the Central Government
questions.explanation: The IR Code raises the supervisory wage ceiling in the 'worker' definition from Rs 10,000 (under the 1947 Act) to Rs 18,000 per month (or a notified amount).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, 'fixed term employment' means:
options: The engagement of a worker on the basis of a written contract of employment for a fixed period, with the worker entitled to the same hours, wages, allowances and statutory benefits as a permanent worker, and gratuity on completion of one year
Employment for a maximum of thirty days only
questions.explanation: The IR Code formally recognises fixed-term employment, guaranteeing parity of service conditions with permanent workers and pro-rata gratuity even before five years of service.

questions.question_text: Under Section 55 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the award of a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal becomes enforceable:
options: On the expiry of thirty days from the date of its communication to the parties (subject to the Government's limited power to defer where it is inexpedient on grounds of national economy or social justice)
Only after confirmation by the High Court
questions.explanation: Section 55(3) provides that an award becomes enforceable on the expiry of thirty days from the date it is communicated to the parties, subject to the appropriate Government's power to declare that it will not become enforceable on that date.

questions.question_text: Under Section 97 and Section 98 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the jurisdiction of civil courts is:
options: Barred only for disputes above a monetary limit
Barred in respect of any matter which the Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal is empowered to decide under the Code
questions.explanation: Section 97 ousts civil-court jurisdiction over matters within the Tribunal's remit; Section 98 protects action taken in good faith.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, recognition of trade unions at Central and State level is:
options: Available only to unions with 90 per cent membership
Provided for, so that the Central or State Government may recognise a Trade Union as a Central or State Trade Union for consultation on national or State labour matters
questions.explanation: Section 27 gives statutory backing to recognition of central and state trade unions for tripartite consultation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23(2) of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, in a registered Trade Union (other than one in the unorganised sector), the number of office-bearers who may be 'outsiders' (not actually engaged or employed in the connected establishment or industry) must not exceed:
options: One-third of the total number of office-bearers, or five, whichever is less
There is no limit; all office-bearers may be outsiders
questions.explanation: Section 23(2) caps outsider office-bearers at one-third of the total or five, whichever is less (a retired or retrenched employee is not treated as an outsider). Section 23(1) separately requires at least half the office-bearers of an unorganised-sector union to be insiders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, an appeal against the Registrar's refusal to register a Trade Union or cancellation of its registration lies to:
questions.explanation: Section 10 provides an appeal to the Industrial Tribunal against non-registration or cancellation of a trade union's registration.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a person who has attained the age of fourteen years and is employed in a non-hazardous industry:
options: Cannot be a union member under any circumstances
May be an office-bearer of the union
May be a member of a registered Trade Union (subject to the rules of the union) and enjoy the rights of a member
May be a member only with a court order
questions.explanation: Section 20 permits union membership from age 14 (in a non-hazardous industry), while Section 21 sets 18 as the minimum age to be an office-bearer.

questions.question_text: The Information Technology Act, 2000:
options: Is Act No. 21 of 2000, came into force on 17 October 2000, and is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce, 1996
questions.explanation: The Act provides legal recognition for electronic transactions and digital/electronic signatures and addresses cybercrime; it was substantially amended in 2008.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(4) read with the First Schedule of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Act does NOT apply to:
options: A negotiable instrument (other than a cheque, or certain instruments issued to or endorsed by RBI-regulated entities); a power-of-attorney; a trust; and a will or any other testamentary disposition
Any contract for the sale or conveyance of immovable property
questions.explanation: These documents still require traditional paper form and signature. The First Schedule earlier also excluded contracts for the sale or conveyance of immovable property, but that entry was omitted by notification S.O. 4720(E) dated 26 September 2022, so such contracts are no longer excluded from the Act.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 1(4) and First Schedule, Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended by S.O. 4720(E), dated 26-9-2022)

questions.question_text: Under Section 3A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (inserted in 2008), an 'electronic signature':
options: Means only a scanned image of a handwritten signature
Can be used only by the Government

Is a technology-neutral concept — authentication of an electronic record by a subscriber by means of an electronic technique specified in the Second Schedule (which includes, but is not limited to, the asymmetric-cryptosystem 'digital signature' of Section 3)
questions.explanation: The 2008 amendment moved from the single 'digital signature' model to a broader 'electronic signature' regime while retaining the digital signature as one recognised method.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (inserted in 2008), a contract formed through electronic means:
options: Is not to be deemed unenforceable solely on the ground that electronic form or means was used for communicating proposals, acceptance, revocation and counter-proposals
Is valid only for goods, not services
questions.explanation: Section 10A gives statutory validity to click-wrap and e-mail contracts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, a person who, without permission of the owner, accesses a computer, downloads data, introduces a virus, damages data, disrupts a computer, or denies access to an authorised user, is liable:
options: To pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected (a civil wrong; since the 2008 amendment there is no statutory upper limit on the compensation)
To a fine not exceeding Rs 5,000
Only if the loss exceeds Rs 1 crore
questions.explanation: Section 43 covers ten enumerated acts of computer contravention; where the same acts are done dishonestly or fraudulently, they become the criminal offence in Section 66.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, a body corporate that is negligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices while handling sensitive personal data or information, thereby causing wrongful loss or gain:
options: Commits a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment
Is liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person affected (the 'reasonable security practices' being those in the SPDI Rules, 2011 or an agreed contract)
Is liable only to a Government penalty
questions.explanation: Section 43A is to be omitted once the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is fully brought into force, which will govern data-protection obligations instead.

questions.question_text: Under Section 46 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the adjudicating officer (an officer not below the rank of a Director to the Government of India or an equivalent State officer) adjudicates claims for damage where:
options: The claim does not exceed one lakh rupees
The claim is of any amount
There is no monetary limit at all
The claim for damage does not exceed five crore rupees; claims above that amount lie before the competent civil court
questions.explanation: The adjudicating officer must have legal and IT experience; an appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal (Section 57).

questions.question_text: Under Section 48 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, appeals against the orders of an adjudicating officer or the Controller lie to:
options: The Appellate Tribunal — the functions of the erstwhile Cyber Appellate Tribunal were merged into the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) by the Finance Act, 2017
questions.explanation: A further appeal from the Appellate Tribunal lies to the High Court within 60 days on a question of fact or law (Section 62).

questions.question_text: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (punishment for sending 'offensive' messages through a communication service) was:
options: Struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), for being vague, overbroad and a disproportionate restriction on the freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a)
Amended to make it clearer in 2018
questions.explanation: In the same judgment the Court upheld Section 69A (blocking) and read down Section 79(3)(b) (intermediary liability) to require a court order or Government notification for 'actual knowledge'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 66 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, where a person dishonestly or fraudulently does any act referred to in Section 43, he is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees, or with both
questions.explanation: 'Dishonestly' and 'fraudulently' take their meanings from Sections 24 and 25 of the Indian Penal Code (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023).

questions.question_text: Under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000, 'identity theft' — fraudulently or dishonestly making use of the electronic signature, password or any other unique identification feature of any other person — is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and also with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees
questions.explanation: Section 66D punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device with the same maximum imprisonment and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 66E of the Information Technology Act, 2000, whoever intentionally captures, publishes or transmits the image of a private area of any person without consent, under circumstances violating that person's privacy, is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine not exceeding two lakh rupees, or with both
questions.explanation: 'Private area' means the naked or undergarment-clad genitals, pubic area, buttocks or female breast.

questions.question_text: Under Section 66F of the Information Technology Act, 2000, 'cyber terrorism' — using a computer resource to threaten the unity, integrity, security or sovereignty of India, or to strike terror, by denial of access, unauthorised access to a protected system, or introducing a contaminant, likely to cause death, injury, damage to property or disruption of essential supplies/services — is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment which may extend to imprisonment for life
questions.explanation: Cyber terrorism is the most serious offence under the Act, carrying a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 67 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form is punishable, on first conviction, with:
options: Imprisonment which may extend to three years and fine which may extend to five lakh rupees (and, on a second or subsequent conviction, imprisonment up to five years and fine up to ten lakh rupees)
questions.explanation: Section 67A (sexually explicit material) and Section 67B (child sexually explicit material) carry higher punishments — up to five years and ten lakh rupees on first conviction.

questions.question_text: Under Section 69 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Central or State Government (or an authorised officer) may direct the interception, monitoring or decryption of information transmitted through any computer resource:
options: For any reason whatsoever, without safeguards
Only with the prior approval of a court

In the interest of the sovereignty or integrity of India, defence, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence, or for investigating an offence — subject to the safeguards in the rules
questions.explanation: Failure by an intermediary or a person in charge of a computer resource to assist the agency is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine (Section 69(4)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Central Government may issue directions for blocking public access to any information through any computer resource:
options: On the same grounds as Section 69 (except the 'investigation of an offence' ground), for reasons to be recorded in writing, following the procedure in the Blocking Rules, 2009 — a power upheld as constitutional in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
For any reason and without recording reasons
Only with a court order in every case
Only against websites hosted in India
questions.explanation: Non-compliance with a Section 69A blocking direction by an intermediary is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine.

questions.question_text: Under Section 70 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the appropriate Government may, by notification, declare any computer resource which directly or indirectly affects the facility of Critical Information Infrastructure to be a 'protected system'; securing unauthorised access to a protected system is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment of either description which may extend to ten years and also with fine
questions.explanation: Section 70A designates the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) as the national nodal agency; Section 70B establishes CERT-In.

questions.question_text: Under Section 72 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, breach of confidentiality and privacy — a person who, having secured access to any electronic record, book, register, correspondence, information, document or other material under the powers conferred by the Act, discloses it to any other person without consent — is now punishable with:
options: A civil penalty which may extend to five lakh rupees (imprisonment was omitted by the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023, with effect from 30 November 2023)
questions.explanation: Before the 2023 amendment, Section 72 carried imprisonment up to two years or fine up to one lakh rupees, or both; that criminal punishment has been decriminalised. Section 72A (disclosure of personal information in breach of a lawful contract) was similarly converted from imprisonment/fine into a civil penalty which may extend to twenty-five lakh rupees.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 72, Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended by Act 18 of 2023, w.e.f. 30-11-2023)

questions.question_text: Under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, an 'intermediary' (such as a network service provider, web host, search engine, online marketplace or social-media platform) is not liable for any third-party information, data or communication link made available or hosted by it, provided that:
options: It is always liable for all user content
It need do nothing to claim the exemption
The exemption applies only to Indian companies

Its function is limited to providing access to a communication system, or it does not initiate the transmission/select the receiver/modify the information; it observes due diligence and follows the Central Government's guidelines; and, on receiving actual knowledge (a court order or Government notification) that the material is being used to commit an unlawful act, it expeditiously removes or disables access to it
questions.explanation: The 'actual knowledge' requirement in Section 79(3)(b) was read down in Shreya Singhal to mean a court order or Government notification; the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 prescribe the due-diligence obligations.

questions.question_text: Under Section 65 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, knowingly or intentionally concealing, destroying or altering (or causing another to do so) any computer source code required to be kept or maintained by law, is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment up to three years, or with fine which may extend to two lakh rupees, or with both
questions.explanation: 'Computer source code' means the listing of programmes, computer commands, design and layout and programme analysis of computer resources in any form.

questions.question_text: Under Section 75 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Act applies to an offence or contravention committed outside India by any person, if:
options: The person is an Indian citizen only
The act or conduct constituting the offence or contravention involves a computer, computer system or computer network located in India
Never; the Act has no extra-territorial effect
The offence is also an offence in the country where committed
questions.explanation: Section 75 gives the Act extra-territorial operation based on the location of the affected computer resource.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, where any law requires that information or a matter be in writing, typewritten or printed form:
options: The requirement can never be satisfied electronically
Only Government records may be kept electronically
That requirement is deemed satisfied if the information or matter is rendered or made available in an electronic form and is accessible so as to be usable for a subsequent reference
A paper copy must always accompany the electronic record
questions.explanation: Section 4 is the core 'legal recognition of electronic records' provision; Section 5 similarly recognises electronic signatures.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, unless otherwise agreed, the despatch of an electronic record occurs when it:
options: Enters a computer resource outside the control of the originator; and receipt occurs when the electronic record enters the designated computer resource (or, if none is designated, when it is retrieved by the addressee)
questions.explanation: Section 13 also deems the place of despatch to be the originator's place of business and the place of receipt to be the addressee's place of business.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 and Section 21 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, digital/electronic signature certificates are issued by:
options: Certifying Authorities licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities (a subscriber generates a key pair, and the Certifying Authority certifies the public key)
questions.explanation: The Controller maintains the Repository of digital signature certificates and acts as the root certifying authority (RCAI).

questions.question_text: Under Section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (inserted in 2008), the Central Government may notify any department, body or agency as an 'Examiner of Electronic Evidence' for the purpose of:
options: Providing expert opinion on electronic form evidence before any court or other authority
questions.explanation: This complements Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (inserted by the IT Act) on the admissibility of electronic records, later interpreted in Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014) and Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020).

questions.question_text: Under Section 66B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, dishonestly receiving or retaining any stolen computer resource or communication device, knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen, is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment of either description which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees, or with both
questions.explanation: Section 66B is the cyber equivalent of receiving stolen property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 84B and Section 84C of the Information Technology Act, 2000, a person who abets or attempts to commit an offence under the Act:
options: Faces no liability unless the offence is completed
Is punished more severely than the principal offender
Is only liable to a civil penalty

Is punishable with the punishment provided for the offence (for abetment, if the offence is committed in consequence) or, for an attempt, with up to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence, or with the fine, or both
questions.explanation: These general provisions on abetment and attempt were added by the 2008 amendment; Section 85 deals with offences by companies.

questions.question_text: Under Section 87 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Central Government has framed the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, which:
options: Prescribe due-diligence obligations for intermediaries (including grievance officers, and additional obligations for 'significant social media intermediaries' such as a Chief Compliance Officer, a nodal contact person and enabling identification of the first originator of a message), and a code of ethics and grievance-redressal framework for digital news publishers and OTT platforms
questions.explanation: Parts of the 2021 Rules, particularly the 'traceability' requirement and the oversight mechanism for digital media, have been challenged in various High Courts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 61 of the Information Technology Act, 2000:
options: Civil courts have full concurrent jurisdiction

No civil court has jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which an adjudicating officer or the Appellate Tribunal is empowered to determine, and no injunction may be granted by any court in respect of any action taken (or to be taken) under the Act
Only the High Court is barred
Civil courts may grant injunctions freely
questions.explanation: Section 61 ousts civil-court jurisdiction over matters within the statutory adjudicatory scheme; Section 63 allows compounding of contraventions.

questions.question_text: The Information Technology Act, 2000, through its (First/Second) Schedule amendments, also amended:
options: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 only
The Indian Penal Code, the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (inserting Section 65B on electronic records), the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
questions.explanation: These consequential amendments integrated electronic records into the general law of crime and evidence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, in all questions regarding intestate succession, female special property, marriage, divorce, maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts, trusts, and wakfs, the rule of decision shall be:
options: The Muslim Personal Law (Shariat), notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary
questions.explanation: Section 2 mandates that Shariat shall apply to Muslims in specified personal law matters notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Central Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, which subject was EXCLUDED from mandatory Shariat application?
questions.explanation: Section 2 of the Central Act saved 'questions relating to agricultural land' from automatic Shariat application.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937

questions.question_text: Under the Kerala State Amendment to Section 2 of the Shariat Act (Kerala Act 42 of 1963), what was the major modification made?
options: Gifts were made subject to Registration Act
The words '(save questions relating to agricultural land)' were omitted, extending Shariat to agricultural land in Kerala
questions.explanation: Kerala State Amendment deleted the exception for agricultural land, applying Shariat to agricultural land as well.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of the Shariat Act, 1937, a Muslim competent to contract can make a declaration to obtain the benefit of Shariat for which additional subjects NOT covered in Section 2?
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) allows a declaration to voluntarily apply Shariat to Adoption, Wills, and Legacies.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 3(1), Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937

questions.question_text: Once a declaration is made by a Muslim under Section 3(1) of the Shariat Act, 1937, the provisions of Shariat apply to:
options: The declarant, all his minor children, and their descendants
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) provides that declaration binds the declarant, his minor children, and their descendants.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) of the Shariat Act, 1937, if the prescribed authority refuses to accept a declaration, the declarant may file an appeal to:
options: An officer appointed by the State Government by general or special order
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) provides an appeal to the State Government's designated officer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Shariat Act, 1937, who has the power to make rules prescribing the authority, form, and fees for declarations?
questions.explanation: Section 4 empowers the State Government to make rules carrying out the Act's purposes.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 4, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Shariat Act, 1937, customary laws enforcing provisions in which enactments were explicitly repealed in so far as inconsistent with the Act?
options: Bombay Regulation IV of 1827, Madras Civil Courts Act 1873, Punjab Laws Act 1872, Oudh Laws Act 1876, CP Laws Act 1875
questions.explanation: Section 6 repealed custom-enforcing provisions in colonial provincial regulations and acts.

questions.question_text: What are the four primary sources of Islamic Law (Shariat)?
options: Panchayat rules, Custom, Will, and Contract
Quran, Sunnah (Hadith), Ijma (Consensus), and Qiyas (Analogical Deduction)
Supreme Court judgments, High Court rulings, Statutes, and Ordinances
questions.explanation: The 4 primary sources of Sunni Islamic jurisprudence are Quran, Sunnah/Hadith, Ijma, and Qiyas.

questions.question_text: Under Islamic Law, what is 'Ijma'?
options: Analogical reasoning of an individual judge
Consensus of Islamic jurists (Mujtahids) of a particular age on a question of law
questions.explanation: Ijma means consensus of learned Islamic scholars/jurists on a legal issue.

questions.question_text: Under Islamic Law, what is 'Qiyas'?
options: Analogical deduction derived from the Quran and Sunnah for new legal problems
questions.explanation: Qiyas is reasoning by analogy applied to deduce legal rules from established textual sources.

questions.question_text: Which are the four major sub-schools of Sunni Islamic Jurisprudence?
questions.explanation: The 4 main orthodox Sunni schools of law are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali.

questions.question_text: The vast majority of Muslims in India belong to which school of Islamic jurisprudence?
questions.explanation: The majority of Indian Muslims are governed by the Hanafi school of Sunni law.

questions.question_text: What are the three essential elements of a valid Gift ('Hiba') under Muslim Law?
options: (1) Written deed, (2) Registration, and (3) Stamp duty
(1) Payment of consideration, (2) Court order, and (3) Witness
(1) Declaration of gift by donor (Ijab), (2) Acceptance of gift by donee (Qabul), and (3) Delivery of possession (Qabza)
questions.explanation: Valid Hiba requires declaration (Ijab), acceptance (Qabul), and delivery of possession (Qabza).
questions.statute_or_case: Muslim Law of Hiba / Hafeeza Bibi v. Shaikh Farid

questions.question_text: In Hafeeza Bibi v. Shaikh Farid (2011) 5 SCC 654, the Supreme Court held that an ORAL gift (Hiba) made by a Muslim:
options: Is void unless registered under Registration Act
Is voidable at option of Collector
Applies only to property below Rs. 100
Is valid, and writing/registration under Section 123 of Transfer of Property Act is NOT mandatory because of Section 129 TPA
questions.explanation: Hafeeza Bibi (2011) affirmed that oral Hiba is valid and exempted from TPA s. 123 registration by virtue of s. 129 TPA.
questions.statute_or_case: Hafeeza Bibi v. Shaikh Farid (2011) 5 SCC 654

questions.question_text: Under Section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the provisions of Chapter VII (Gifts requiring registered instrument) do NOT affect any rule of:
questions.explanation: Section 129 TPA explicitly exempts rules of Mohammedan Law from TPA gift registration requirements.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is a 'Hiba-bil-Iwad'?
options: A gift made under a Will
A gift for consideration; a transaction resembling a sale consisting of two acts: a gift followed by a return gift (Iwad)
questions.explanation: Hiba-bil-Iwad is a gift made for a return consideration, carrying incidents of a sale.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is an 'Ariyat'?
options: A grant of usufruct (right to use property or enjoy profits) without transfer of ownership, revocable at grantor's will
questions.explanation: Ariyat is the transfer of right to enjoy usufruct temporarily without transferring title.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is a 'Marz-ul-Mawt' gift?
options: A gift made to a mosque
A gift made by a person during death-illness under apprehension of imminent death
questions.explanation: Marz-ul-Mawt gift is a gift made during fatal illness under apprehension of death.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum limit of property that a Muslim can validly dispose of by 'Marz-ul-Mawt' gift OR by 'Wasiyat' (Will)?
options: One-third (1/3rd) of his net estate (after payment of funeral expenses and debts)
questions.explanation: Under Muslim law, both Will (Wasiyat) and Marz-ul-Mawt gifts are restricted to 1/3rd of net estate.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni (Hanafi) Law, can a Muslim make a bequest by Will of up to 1/3rd of his estate to one of his legal HEIRS without consent of other heirs?
options: Yes, 1/3rd bequest to an heir is valid without consent
No, under Sunni law a bequest to an heir is INVALID unless consented to by all other heirs AFTER testator's death
questions.explanation: Under Sunni law, bequest to an heir requires consent of co-heirs after death. Under Shia law, bequest to heir up to 1/3rd is valid without consent.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, is a bequest by Will of up to 1/3rd of estate in favour of one of the legal HEIRS valid without consent of other heirs?
options: Yes, under Shia law a bequest to an heir up to 1/3rd is VALID without consent of other heirs
questions.explanation: Shia law allows bequeathing up to 1/3rd to any heir without consent of other heirs.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni Law, a bequest by Will in favour of an UNBORN person is valid ONLY IF the child is born within:
options: Ten months from date of Will
Nine months from date of death
Six months from the date of execution of the Will
questions.explanation: Sunni law requires unborn beneficiary to be born within 6 months of Will date.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, a bequest in favour of an UNBORN person is valid if the child is born within:
options: Ten months from the date of execution of the Will
questions.explanation: Shia law extends the period for unborn beneficiary's birth to 10 months from Will date.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is a 'Wakf'?
options: The permanent dedication by a person professing Islam of any property for any purpose recognized by Muslim law as pious, religious or charitable
questions.explanation: Wakf is defined as permanent dedication of property for pious, religious, or charitable purposes.
questions.statute_or_case: Wakf Act, 1995 & Mussalman Wakf Validating Act 1913

questions.question_text: In whom does the ownership of property dedicated as a Wakf vest under Islamic Law?
questions.explanation: Ownership of Wakf property vests in God; Mutawalli is merely a manager (Vidya Varuthi Thirtha v. Balusami).
questions.statute_or_case: Vidya Varuthi Thirtha v. Balusami Ayyar (1921)

questions.question_text: What is the legal status/position of a 'Mutawalli' of a Wakf?
options: He is a manager or superintendent of the Wakf property, NOT a trustee in whom legal title vests
questions.explanation: Mutawalli manages Wakf affairs; property title does not vest in him.

questions.question_text: What is a 'Wakf-alal-Aulad'?
options: A Wakf created for the maintenance and support wholly or partially of the Wakif's family, children or descendants, with ultimate benefit reserved for charity
questions.explanation: Wakf-alal-Aulad is a family settlement wakf valid under Mussalman Wakf Validating Act 1913.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni (Hanafi) Law, who are the three principal classes of heirs in Intestate Succession?
options: Sharers (Zawul Furud), Residuaries (Asabah), and Distant Kindred (Zawul Arham)
Class I, Class II, and Class III
questions.explanation: Hanafi law classifies intestate heirs into Sharers (Quranic heirs), Residuaries, and Distant Kindred.

questions.question_text: How many 'Sharers' (Quranic Heirs or Zawul Furud) are specified under Hanafi Law of Intestate Succession?
questions.explanation: Hanafi law lists 12 Sharers: 4 males (father, true grandfather, uterine brother, husband) and 8 females (wife, mother, true grandmother, daughter, son's daughter, full sister, consanguine sister, uterine sister).

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, what is the share of a WIFE in her deceased husband's estate if he leaves a child or son's child?
questions.explanation: Wife gets 1/8th if deceased left children/grandchildren, and 1/4th if no children/grandchildren.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, what is the share of a WIFE in her deceased husband's estate if he leaves NO child or son's child?
questions.explanation: Wife gets 1/4th when deceased husband leaves no child or son's child.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, what is the share of a HUSBAND in his deceased wife's estate if she leaves NO child or son's child?
questions.explanation: Husband gets 1/2 share if deceased wife leaves no issue, and 1/4th if she leaves issue.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, what is the share of a HUSBAND in his deceased wife's estate if she leaves a child or son's child?
questions.explanation: Husband gets 1/4th share when deceased wife leaves children or grandchildren.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, what is the share of a SINGLE DAUGHTER when there is no son?
questions.explanation: Single daughter gets 1/2 share as a Sharer when there is no son.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, what is the collective share of TWO OR MORE DAUGHTERS when there is no son?
questions.explanation: Two or more daughters take 2/3rds collectively when there is no son.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, when a male Hindu/Muslim dies leaving a SON and a DAUGHTER, how do they inherit as Residuaries?
options: The son takes double the share of the daughter (2:1 ratio)
questions.explanation: When son and daughter inherit together as Residuaries, male gets double the female share (Quranic 2:1 rule).

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, what is the Doctrine of 'Aul' (Increase)?
options: Where estate remains after sharers, it returns to sharers
Where the sum total of fractional shares of Sharers exceeds unity (1), the fractional shares are proportionally reduced by increasing denominator
Where shares are doubled for sons
questions.explanation: Aul applies when total Sharer fractions > 1, reducing each share proportionally.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law, what is the Doctrine of 'Radd' (Return)?
options: Reduction of shares when estate is small
Where sum total of Sharer shares is less than unity (1) and there are NO Residuaries, the surplus returns proportionally to Sharers (except spouse traditionally)
questions.explanation: Radd returns leftover estate to Quranic sharers when no residuary heirs exist.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Law of Guardianship, what is 'Hizanat'?
options: The custody of the person of a minor child, which belongs primarily to the mother
questions.explanation: Hizanat refers specifically to the right of physical custody of a minor child.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni (Hanafi) Law, a mother is entitled to the custody (Hizanat) of her male child until he completes the age of:
questions.explanation: Under Hanafi law, mother gets custody of a boy until 7 years of age.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni (Hanafi) Law, a mother is entitled to the custody (Hizanat) of her female child until she completes the age of:
questions.explanation: Under Hanafi law, mother retains custody of a girl until she attains puberty (15 years).

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, a mother is entitled to the custody (Hizanat) of her male child until he completes the age of:
questions.explanation: Under Shia law, mother's custody of a boy ends at 2 years of age.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, a mother is entitled to the custody (Hizanat) of her female child until she completes the age of:
questions.explanation: Under Shia law, mother's custody of a girl ends at 7 years of age.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, who is the Natural Guardian of a minor child's person and property?
questions.explanation: Under Muslim law, the father is the sole natural legal guardian of minor child's property.

questions.question_text: Does a Muslim MOTHER have legal power to sell or mortgage her minor child's immovable property as a legal guardian?
options: No, mother is not a legal guardian of minor's property and any alienation of minor's property by her is void ab initio (Imambandi v. Mutsaddi)
questions.explanation: In Imambandi v. Mutsaddi (1918), Privy Council held mother is de facto guardian with no legal power to alienate minor's immovable property.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is 'Shufa' (Pre-emption)?
options: Right of minor to repudiate marriage
Right of Mutawalli to lease property
A right which the owner of a certain immovable property possesses to acquire by purchase another immovable property sold to a stranger
questions.explanation: Shufa (pre-emption) is the right of a neighboring property owner to substitute himself for a buyer.

questions.question_text: Who among the following has the TOP priority among pre-emptors (Shufa) under Hanafi Law?
questions.explanation: Shafi-i-Sharik (co-sharer) has first priority among pre-emptors.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, pre-emption (Shufa) is recognized ONLY between:
options: Two co-sharers in an undivided property (no pre-emption if co-sharers exceed two or for neighbors)
questions.explanation: Shia law restricts pre-emption strictly to cases where there are exactly two co-owners.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, can a gift of 'Mushaa' (undivided share in property capable of division) be validly made?
options: Valid in all cases under Sunni law
A gift of Mushaa in divisible property is invalid (Fasid) under Hanafi law until undivided share is separated and delivered, but valid under Shia law
questions.explanation: Doctrine of Mushaa under Hanafi law makes gift of undivided divisible share irregular until partitioned.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(1) of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, what is the exact short title of Act No. 26 of 1937?
options: The Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937
questions.explanation: Section 1(1) defines exact title of Act No. 26 of 1937.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(2) of the Shariat Act, 1937, the Act extends to:
questions.explanation: Section 1(2) extends the Act to the whole of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Shariat Act, 1937, which of the following is listed as a matter governed by Shariat?
options: Special property of females, including property inherited or obtained under contract or gift
questions.explanation: Section 2 explicitly includes female special property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Shariat Act, 1937, Wakfs governed by Shariat exclude:
options: Charities and charitable institutions and charitable and religious endowments
questions.explanation: Section 2 contains express parenthetical exception for charitable institutions/endowments.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(b) of the Shariat Act, 1937, to make a declaration applying Shariat to Wills and Adoption, the declarant must be competent to contract under:
options: Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(b) requires declarant to be competent to contract under Section 11 of Contract Act.

questions.question_text: Does Islamic Law recognize formal legal Adoption (like under Hindu law) as creating parent-child status for inheritance?
options: No, uncodified Islamic law does NOT recognize adoption as creating blood-heir status for inheritance
questions.explanation: Islamic law does not recognize adoption as conferring status of biological child for inheritance (though custody/guardianship under Juvenile Justice Act is permitted).
questions.statute_or_case: Shabnam Hashmi v. Union of India (2014) 4 SCC 1

questions.question_text: In Shabnam Hashmi v. Union of India (2014) 4 SCC 1, the Supreme Court held that a Muslim prospective adoptive parent:
options: Is strictly forbidden from adopting under any law
Can adopt a child under the secular Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, regardless of personal law constraints
Must seek permission of All India Muslim Personal Law Board
Can adopt only under Shariat Act
questions.explanation: Shabnam Hashmi (2014) affirmed that JJ Act is an enabling secular law available to all citizens including Muslims.
questions.statute_or_case: Shabnam Hashmi v. Union of India (2014) 4 SCC 1

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, can a Muslim make a Will (Wasiyat) ORALLY without writing?
options: No, Will must be registered under Registration Act
No, Will must be on Rs. 100 stamp paper
Yes, an oral Will is completely valid under Muslim law if intention is clear and proved
questions.explanation: Under Muslim personal law, a Will may be made orally or in writing; no writing is mandatory.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is the effect if a Muslim testator bequeaths MORE THAN 1/3rd of his estate by Will to a stranger without consent of heirs?
options: The bequest is valid UP TO 1/3rd, and void as to the excess over 1/3rd (unless heirs consent after death)
questions.explanation: Bequest exceeding 1/3rd is valid up to 1/3rd limit and void for excess unless heirs consent post-death.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni Law, when must the co-heirs give their consent to validate a bequest exceeding 1/3rd OR a bequest to an heir?
options: AFTER the death of the testator
questions.explanation: Under Sunni law, consent of heirs given during testator's lifetime is invalid; it must be given after testator's death.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, when can co-heirs give their consent to validate a bequest exceeding 1/3rd?
options: Either during the lifetime of the testator OR after his death
questions.explanation: Under Shia law, consent of heirs given during testator's lifetime or after death is valid.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, if a donor makes a Hiba of immovable property, delivery of possession (Qabza) can be:
options: Actual physical possession only in all cases
Actual delivery of physical possession OR constructive delivery of possession (e.g. delivering title deeds / rent collection direction)
questions.explanation: Delivery of possession can be actual or constructive depending on property nature and donor-donee relation.

questions.question_text: Where a Muslim parent makes a gift (Hiba) of property to his/her MINOR child who resides with them, is actual transfer of physical possession required?
options: Yes, physical delivery to minor is mandatory
Yes, property must be placed in court custody
No, actual physical delivery of possession is NOT required; declaration of gift by parent suffices
questions.explanation: Parent-to-minor-child living together exception dispenses with formal physical delivery of possession.

questions.question_text: Can a Muslim donor REVOKE a gift (Hiba) after delivery of possession under Sunni Law?
options: Yes, except when gift is made to blood relatives within prohibited degrees, or between spouses, or when donee is dead or property lost/sold
No, gift is irrevocable in all cases
questions.explanation: Under Sunni law, gift can be revoked before possession, or after possession by court decree except specified relations (spouses, prohibited blood relations etc.).

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, can a gift (Hiba) be revoked AFTER delivery of possession?
options: A gift to a blood relative (whether within prohibited degrees or not) cannot be revoked after delivery of possession
Cannot be revoked even before possession
questions.explanation: Under Shia law, gift to any blood relative becomes irrevocable once possession is delivered.

questions.question_text: What is the key statutory object of the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913?
options: To transfer wakfs to District Collector
To validate Wakf-alal-Aulad (family wakfs) which had been declared invalid by the Privy Council in Abul Fata Mahomed Ishak (1894)
To convert wakfs into commercial trusts
questions.explanation: The 1913 Act reversed the Privy Council decision in Abul Fata case, restoring validity of family wakfs.

questions.question_text: Under the Wakf Act, 1995, who exercises general superintendence over all Wakfs in a State?
options: The State Wakf Board established under Section 13
questions.explanation: State Wakf Board created under Wakf Act 1995 has general superintendence over wakfs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 83 of the Wakf Act, 1995, disputes relating to Wakf property or Mutawalli position are determined by:
options: The Wakf Tribunal constituted by the State Government
questions.explanation: Section 83 creates specialized Wakf Tribunals with exclusive jurisdiction over Wakf matters.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Intestate Succession, if a Muslim male dies leaving his FATHER and a SON, what share does Father get?
options: Father gets 1/6th as a Sharer, and Son gets remaining 5/6th as Residuary
questions.explanation: When son exists, Father's fixed Quranic share is 1/6th as a Sharer, and Son takes remainder as Residuary.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Intestate Succession, if a Muslim male dies leaving ONLY his MOTHER and FATHER (no children or brothers/sisters), how is property divided?
options: Mother gets 1/3rd as Sharer, and Father gets remaining 2/3rds as Residuary
questions.explanation: Mother gets 1/3rd when no children/siblings exist, and Father takes remaining 2/3rd as Residuary.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Intestate Succession, if a Muslim male dies leaving MOTHER, FATHER, and TWO BROTHERS, what is Mother's share?
options: Mother's share is reduced from 1/3rd to 1/6th because of presence of two brothers
questions.explanation: Presence of 2 or more brothers/sisters reduces Mother's share from 1/3rd to 1/6th.

questions.question_text: Under Hanafi Inheritance, what are 'Distant Kindred' (Zawul Arham)?
options: All blood relatives of deceased who are neither Sharers nor Residuaries (e.g. daughter's children, maternal uncle)
questions.explanation: Distant Kindred inherit thirdly when no Sharers (except spouse) or Residuaries exist.

questions.question_text: Does a Muslim wife lose her right to inherit from her husband if she is UNCHASTE?
options: No, unchastity does NOT disqualify a Muslim widow from inheriting under Muslim personal law
questions.explanation: Unlike traditional Hindu law pre-1956, unchastity does not disqualify a Muslim heir under Shariat.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni Law, what is the effect if an heir KILLS the deceased (homicide)?
options: The murderer heir is disqualified from inheriting, whether homicide was intentional or accidental
questions.explanation: Sunni law disqualifies murderer from inheriting whether homicide was intentional or accidental.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, an heir who causes death of the deceased is disqualified from inheritance ONLY IF the homicide was:
questions.explanation: Shia law restricts disqualification to intentional murder only.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law of Inheritance, how are heirs classified into three main Classes?
options: Class I (Parents & Children), Class II (Grandparents & Siblings), Class III (Uncles & Aunts)
questions.explanation: Shia law divides blood heirs into 3 distinct classes where Class I excludes Class II, and Class II excludes Class III.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law of Inheritance, does a childless widow inherit any share in her deceased husband's IMMOVABLE LAND?
options: No, a childless widow under Shia law takes no share in land/real estate, but gets 1/4th share in value of buildings and trees
questions.explanation: Shia law excludes childless widow from inheriting land itself, granting her 1/4th value of structures/trees.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, in the enumerated matters where the parties are Muslims, Shariat is the rule of decision:
options: only if no contrary custom or usage is proved
only where both parties consent in writing
notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary
subject to any local custom having the force of law
questions.explanation: The opening words of Section 2 — "Notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary" — displace custom in the listed matters such as succession, marriage, dissolution, maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts and wakfs.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Shariat Act, 1937, 'Wakfs' governed by Shariat include:
questions.explanation: Section 2 applies Shariat to Wakfs generally (saving public charities under state laws).

questions.question_text: Can a Muslim male appoint a FEMALE as a 'Mutawalli' of a Wakf?
options: Yes, a female can be validly appointed as Mutawalli unless the religious duties attached require a male (e.g. Imam/Khatib)
No, females can never be Mutawalli
questions.explanation: A woman can be Mutawalli if secular/administrative duties are involved.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, can a non-Muslim be appointed as a 'Mutawalli' of a Wakf?
options: No, non-Muslim can never be Mutawalli
Yes, a non-Muslim can be appointed if office duties are purely administrative and not religious
questions.explanation: Non-Muslim can be Mutawalli for secular administrative duties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of the Shariat Act, 1937, the declaration before prescribed authority is:
questions.explanation: Once declaration is made and accepted under Section 3, it permanently applies Section 2 rules to declarant and descendants.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is the legal effect of a gift (Hiba) made to take effect in FUTURE (contingent gift)?
options: A gift in futuro (contingent on future event) is VOID under Muslim law
questions.explanation: Hiba must take immediate effect; contingent gift in futuro is void.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is a 'Sadqah'?
options: A gift made with a religious or charitable motive to acquire spiritual merit (Thawab), irrevocable once possession is delivered
questions.explanation: Sadqah is a gift dedicated for religious/pious merit, irrevocable upon possession.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni Law, if a Muslim dies leaving a WIFE and a SON, how is the estate divided?
options: Wife gets 1/8th as Sharer, Son gets remaining 7/8th as Residuary
questions.explanation: Wife gets 1/8th (presence of child), Son takes remaining 7/8th as Residuary.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni Law, if a Muslim dies leaving HUSBAND and DAUGHTER, how is estate divided?
options: Husband gets 1/4th as Sharer, Daughter gets 1/2 as Sharer, and remaining 1/4th returns to Daughter under Radd
questions.explanation: Husband gets 1/4th, Daughter gets 1/2 (2/4th); remaining 1/4th returns to Daughter under Radd doctrine.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is the 'Rule of Exclusion' regarding grandfathers and brothers?
options: Father excludes true grandfather; Son excludes son's son
questions.explanation: Closer degree of blood relationship excludes distant degree of same line.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(4) of the Shariat Act, 1937 (inserted in 1983), every rule made by State Government under the Act shall be laid before:
questions.explanation: Section 4(4) mandates laying state rules before State Legislature.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Shariat Act, 1937, does Shariat apply to questions of GUARDIANSHIP of Muslim minors?
options: No, guardianship is governed exclusively by Guardians and Wards Act 1890
Yes, guardianship is explicitly enumerated in Section 2
questions.explanation: Section 2 explicitly includes guardianship among subjects governed by Shariat.

questions.question_text: In Ahmedabad Women Action Group (AWAG) v. Union of India (1997) 3 SCC 573, the Supreme Court held regarding writ petitions challenging personal laws:
options: Uniform Civil Code is declared immediately effective
The court will not entertain PILs seeking judicial codification or abolition of personal laws, as these are matters for legislature
All personal laws are criminal laws
questions.explanation: AWAG (1997) affirmed that reform/codification of personal laws lies within legislative domain.
questions.statute_or_case: AWAG v. Union of India (1997) 3 SCC 573

questions.question_text: Does the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 apply to the Renoncants of Pondicherry?
options: No, Pondicherry State Amendment proviso explicitly exempts the Renoncants
questions.explanation: Section 1 footnote/proviso exempts the Renoncants of Union Territory of Pondicherry.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, what is the effect if a donor makes a Hiba of a house to A for life, and after A's death to B?
options: Under Hanafi law, the life condition is void and A gets full absolute ownership (Hiba with derogating condition)
A gets life estate and B gets remainder
questions.explanation: Under Hanafi law, gift of corpus cannot be limited in duration; condition limiting duration is void, gift is absolute.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, can a valid life interest (Amra / Ruqba) be created in property?
options: No, invalid under Shia law too
Yes, Shia law recognizes creation of life interest (Amra) and limited time grant (Ruqba) as valid usufructuary grants
questions.explanation: Shia law recognizes life interest (Amra) as valid grant of usufruct.
questions.statute_or_case: Shia Law of Gifts & Life Estate

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Shariat Act, 1937, does Shariat apply to questions regarding MAINTENANCE and DOWER?
options: No, maintenance is governed by CrPC only
No, dower is governed by Contract Act only
Yes, maintenance and dower are explicitly enumerated in Section 2
questions.explanation: Section 2 explicitly includes maintenance and dower.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Law, can an illegitimate child inherit from his biological FATHER?
options: Yes, inherits equal share with legitimate son
No, an illegitimate child has no right of inheritance from biological father under either Sunni or Shia law
questions.explanation: Illegitimate child inherits only from mother and mother's relatives under Sunni law; under Shia law, inherits from neither.

questions.question_text: Under Sunni Law, does an illegitimate child inherit from his biological MOTHER?
options: Yes, under Sunni law an illegitimate child inherits from mother and her relatives
No, cannot inherit from mother either
questions.explanation: Sunni law recognizes reciprocal inheritance between illegitimate child and mother.

questions.question_text: Under Shia Law, does an illegitimate child (Walad-uz-Zina) inherit from his biological MOTHER?
options: No, under Shia law an illegitimate child inherits neither from father nor from mother
questions.explanation: Shia law severs inheritance tie of illegitimate child with both parents completely.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the Shariat Act, 1937, a declarant must be a RESIDENT of:
options: The territories to which the Act extends
State of Jammu and Kashmir only
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(c) requires residency in territories covered by the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Muslim Personal Law, if a Muslim dies leaving NO heirs (Sharers, Residuaries, or Distant Kindred), his property devolves by:
questions.explanation: Failure of all heirs results in escheat to State.

questions.question_text: What is the primary overarching object of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 as stated in its Preamble?
options: To make provision for the application of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) to Muslims
questions.explanation: The Preamble states the Act is 'An Act to make provision for the application of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) to Muslims'.
questions.statute_or_case: Preamble, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937

questions.question_text: Under Section 166 of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, an application for compensation arising out of a motor vehicle accident involving death or bodily injury may be made by:
options: The police officer on duty only
The person who has sustained the injury, or owner of damaged property, or legal representatives of the deceased
The driver who caused the accident
questions.explanation: Section 166 lists persons entitled to apply for compensation before MACT.

questions.question_text: In the landmark 5-Judge Constitution Bench decision National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680, the Supreme Court fixed the standard compensation amounts under conventional heads at:
options: Loss of Estate: Rs. 50,000, Consortium: Rs. 1 Lakh, Funeral: Rs. 50,000
Loss of Estate: Rs. 5,000, Consortium: Rs. 10,000, Funeral: Rs. 5,000
Loss of Estate: Rs. 15,000, Loss of Consortium: Rs. 40,000, and Funeral Expenses: Rs. 15,000
Fixed total of Rs. 1 Lakh across all heads
questions.explanation: Pranay Sethi (2017) standardized conventional heads (Estate 15k, Consortium 40k, Funeral 15k) with 10% enhancement every 3 years.
questions.statute_or_case: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680

questions.question_text: In Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation (2009) 6 SCC 121, the Supreme Court standardized the multiplier table based on age of deceased for calculating loss of dependency. For age group 21-25 years, the multiplier is:
questions.explanation: Sarla Verma (2009) fixed multiplier of 18 for age groups 15-20 and 21-25 years.
questions.statute_or_case: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation (2009)

questions.question_text: Under Section 185 of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, a person is deemed to drive under the influence of alcohol if breath analyser test detects alcohol exceeding:
questions.explanation: Section 185 sets statutory limit of 30 mg alcohol per 100 ml blood.

questions.question_text: Under Section 199A of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (inserted by 2019 Amendment Act), where an offence under the Act has been committed by a MINOR, who is held guilty?
options: The parent of the minor or the owner of the motor vehicle (deemed guilty and punishable with 3 years jail and Rs. 25,000 fine)
questions.explanation: Section 199A holds parent/guardian/owner vicariously liable with 3 years jail and Rs. 25,000 fine for minor driving offences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 164 of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended by 2019 Amendment Act), compensation on NO FAULT BASIS for death resulting from motor accident is fixed at:
options: Five Lakh rupees for death, and Two Lakh Fifty Thousand rupees for grievous hurt
questions.explanation: Section 164 (replacing old S. 140) fixed no-fault compensation at Rs. 5 Lakhs for death and Rs. 2.5 Lakhs for grievous hurt.

questions.question_text: Under Section 161 of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended by 2019 Amendment Act), compensation payable in case of HIT AND RUN motor accidents is fixed at:
options: Two Lakh rupees in case of death, and Fifty Thousand rupees in case of grievous hurt
questions.explanation: Section 161 enhanced Hit & Run scheme compensation to Rs. 2 Lakhs for death and Rs. 50,000 for grievous hurt.

questions.question_text: Under Section 146(1) of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, no person shall use a motor vehicle in a public place unless there is in force a policy of insurance complying with:
options: Chapter XI (Insurance against Third Party Risks)
questions.explanation: Section 146(1) mandates compulsory third party risk insurance for operating motor vehicles in public places.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, what is the minimum age for driving a motor vehicle in any public place?
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) mandates minimum age of 18 years for driving motor vehicles in public places (except 16 yrs for 50cc without gear under s. 4(2)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(2) of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, a person who has attained the age of SIXTEEN years may drive a motor cycle in a public place PROVIDED its engine capacity does not exceed:
questions.explanation: Section 4(2) allows 16-year-olds to drive motor cycles with engine capacity up to 50cc.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(3) of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, what is the minimum age required for driving a TRANSPORT VEHICLE in any public place?
questions.explanation: Section 4(3) mandates minimum age of 20 years for driving transport vehicles.

questions.question_text: Under Section 173(2) of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019), no appeal shall lie against any award of a Claims Tribunal if the amount in dispute in the appeal is less than:
questions.explanation: Section 173(2) raised the minimum appeal threshold to Rs. 1 Lakh.

questions.question_text: Under Section 173(1) of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, an appeal against an award of MACT must be filed in the High Court within how many days from the date of award?
questions.explanation: Section 173(1) sets a 90-day limitation period for appeals to High Court.

questions.question_text: In Mukund Dewangan v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. (2017) 14 SCC 663, the Supreme Court held that a driver holding a driving license for Light Motor Vehicle (LMV):
options: Can drive a transport vehicle of LMV class (gross vehicle weight under 7,500 kg) without requiring a separate endorsement to drive a transport vehicle
questions.explanation: Mukund Dewangan (2017) held LMV license holder can drive transport vehicle under 7,500 kg without separate endorsement.
questions.statute_or_case: Mukund Dewangan v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. (2017)

questions.question_text: Under Section 165(1) of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, State Governments constitute Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals (MACT) for adjudicating compensation claims in respect of accidents involving:
options: Death of, or bodily injury to, persons arising out of the use of motor vehicles, or damages to property of a third party, or both
questions.explanation: Section 165(1) defines MACT jurisdiction for death, injury, and property damage claims.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of MVA 1988, no person shall drive a motor vehicle in any public place unless he holds an effective:
options: Driving license authorizing him to drive the vehicle category
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) bars driving in a public place without an effective driving licence authorising the driver for that class of vehicle.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of MVA 1988, who has power to disqualify a person from holding a driving license or revoke it for misconduct/offences?
questions.explanation: Section 19 empowers the Licensing Authority to disqualify a person from holding a driving licence or to revoke it on stated grounds of misconduct or disqualifying offences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of MVA 1988, operating a motor vehicle in a public place without a valid Certificate of Registration is:
questions.explanation: Section 39 requires every motor vehicle to be registered before use in a public place; driving an unregistered vehicle is punishable under Section 192.

questions.question_text: Under Section 56 of MVA 1988, a transport vehicle shall not be deemed to be validly registered unless it carries a valid:
options: Certificate of Fitness issued by prescribed authority
questions.explanation: Section 56 requires every transport vehicle to carry a valid Certificate of Fitness issued by the prescribed testing authority.

questions.question_text: Under Section 66 of MVA 1988, no owner of a transport vehicle shall use it in a public place save in accordance with conditions of a:
options: Permit granted or countersigned by Transport Authority
questions.explanation: Section 66 bars use of a transport vehicle in a public place except in accordance with a permit granted or countersigned by a Regional/State Transport Authority.

questions.question_text: Under Section 128 of MVA 1988, no driver of a two-wheeled motorcycle shall carry more than:
options: One person in addition to himself (pillion rider)
questions.explanation: Section 128 restricts a two-wheeled motorcycle to carrying not more than one pillion rider in addition to the driver, seated securely.

questions.question_text: Under Section 129 of MVA 1988, every person above four years of age riding a motorcycle in a public place shall wear protective headgear (helmet) conforming to:
questions.explanation: Section 129 requires protective headgear conforming to standards prescribed by the Central Government (Bureau of Indian Standards), subject to the turban exemption for Sikhs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 130 of MVA 1988, the driver of a motor vehicle in a public place shall produce his driving license and documents on demand by any:
questions.explanation: Section 130 obliges the driver to produce his licence and registration certificate for examination on demand by a police officer in uniform.

questions.question_text: Under Section 134 of MVA 1988, what is the duty of driver in case of accident and injury to a person?
options: Secure medical attention for injured, report to nearest police station within 24 hours, and inform insurer
questions.explanation: Section 134 requires the driver to take reasonable steps to secure medical attention for the injured, report the accident to the nearest police station within twenty-four hours, and give notice to the insurer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 134A of MVA 1988 (inserted in 2019), a GOOD SAMARITAN who renders emergency medical or non-medical assistance to a victim of an accident shall:
options: Be forced to pay hospital bills
Not be liable for any civil or criminal action for injury or death of victim
questions.explanation: Section 134A protects a Good Samaritan acting in good faith from civil or criminal liability for any injury to, or death of, the accident victim.

questions.question_text: Under Section 147(1)(b) of MVA 1988, a third party insurance policy must insure against liability incurred in respect of:
options: Death or bodily injury to any person or damage to any property of a third party caused by or arising out of use of vehicle
questions.explanation: Section 147(1)(b) requires the policy to cover death of, or bodily injury to, any person or damage to third-party property arising out of the use of the vehicle.

questions.question_text: Under Section 149 of MVA 1988 (Section 150 as amended 2019), which of the following is a valid defence for an insurer to avoid liability to third party?
options: Vehicle driven by person not duly licensed or driven for purpose not allowed by permit
questions.explanation: The 2019 Amendment renumbered the old duty-of-insurer provision as Section 150; sub-section (2) lists breach of a permit or licensing condition as a valid statutory defence for the insurer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 168 of MVA 1988, the MACT after specifying amount of compensation shall direct payment of just compensation by:
options: The insurer, owner, or driver, as the case may be
questions.explanation: Section 168 empowers the Tribunal, on determining the just compensation, to direct payment by the insurer, owner or driver, as may be applicable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 171 of MVA 1988, MACT may direct that in addition to compensation, simple interest shall be paid at such rate from:
options: The date of making the claim petition
questions.explanation: Section 171 lets the Tribunal award simple interest from a date not earlier than the date of making the claim.

questions.question_text: Under Section 181 of MVA 1988 (as amended 2019), driving a motor vehicle without a valid driving license is punishable with fine of:
questions.explanation: Section 181, as amended in 2019, raised the fine for driving in contravention of Sections 3 or 4 (no valid licence/under age) to Rs. 5,000, with imprisonment up to three months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 182A of MVA 1988 (as amended 2019), manufacturing or selling motor vehicles in contravention of statutory safety standards is punishable with fine up to:
options: Rs. 1 Lakh per vehicle or imprisonment up to 1 year
questions.explanation: Section 182A(1) punishes a manufacturer, importer or dealer who sells/alters a vehicle in contravention of Chapter VII safety standards with a fine of Rs. 1 lakh per vehicle or imprisonment up to one year, or both.

questions.question_text: Under Section 183 of MVA 1988 (as amended 2019), driving at excessive speed (overspeeding) for light motor vehicle is punishable with fine between:
questions.explanation: Section 183(1)(i) fixes a fine of not less than Rs. 1,000 but up to Rs. 2,000 for overspeeding a light motor vehicle; medium/heavy vehicles attract Rs. 2,000-4,000.

questions.question_text: Under Section 184 of MVA 1988 (as amended 2019), driving dangerously (jumping red light, using handheld mobile phone while driving) is punishable for 1st offence with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine between:
questions.explanation: Section 184, for a first offence, prescribes imprisonment of six months to one year or a fine of Rs. 1,000 to Rs. 5,000, or both; a subsequent offence within three years attracts up to two years or a fine of Rs. 10,000.

questions.question_text: Under Section 194A of MVA 1988 (inserted 2019), carrying excess passengers in a transport vehicle is punishable with fine of:
options: Two hundred rupees per excess passenger
questions.explanation: Section 194A fixes the fine at Rs. 200 per excess passenger, and the vehicle cannot move until the excess passengers are off-loaded.

questions.question_text: Under Section 194B of MVA 1988 (inserted 2019), driving without wearing a seat belt or carrying child without seat belt is punishable with fine of:
questions.explanation: Section 194B fixes a fine of Rs. 1,000 for driving without a seat belt or for carrying a passenger, including a child, without one.

questions.question_text: Under Section 194D of MVA 1988 (inserted 2019), driving a motorcycle without wearing a protective helmet is punishable with fine of Rs. 1,000 AND:
options: Disqualification of license for three months
questions.explanation: Section 194D imposes a fine of Rs. 1,000 and disqualifies the offender from holding a licence for three months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 194E of MVA 1988 (inserted 2019), failure to draw to the side of the road to allow free passage to emergency vehicles (fire engine, ambulance) is punishable with fine up to:
questions.explanation: Section 194E punishes failure to give way to a fire service, ambulance, or other specified emergency vehicle with imprisonment up to six months or a fine of Rs. 10,000, or both.

questions.question_text: Under Section 199A(4) of MVA 1988, when a juvenile commits an offence driving a vehicle, the registration of the motor vehicle used shall be cancelled for a period of:
questions.explanation: Section 199A(4) mandates cancellation of the registration of the motor vehicle used in the offence for a period of twelve months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 199A(5) of MVA 1988, a minor who commits an offence by driving a motor vehicle shall NOT be eligible to obtain a driving license until he attains the age of:
