questions.explanation: Section/Precedent under Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: Under Section 199A(5) of MVA 1988, a minor who commits an offence by driving a motor vehicle shall NOT be eligible to obtain a driving license until he attains the age of:

questions.question_text: Under Section 200 of MVA 1988, specified compoundable traffic offences under the Act can be compounded by designated officers either:
options: Before or after the institution of prosecution
questions.explanation: Section 200(1) allows the listed offences to be compounded by notified officers or authorities either before or after institution of the prosecution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 206(4) of MVA 1988 (inserted 2019), a police officer who impounds a driving license for offences under Section 184/185/194D shall submit it to Licensing Authority for:
questions.explanation: Section 206(4) requires the seizing officer to forward the licence to the Licensing Authority for disqualification or revocation proceedings under Section 19.

questions.question_text: Under Section 207 of MVA 1988, a police officer can SEIZE and detain a motor vehicle if operated in public place without:
options: Registration certificate, permit, or driving license
questions.explanation: Section 207 allows a police officer to detain a vehicle used without a certificate of registration, permit, or in some cases a valid driving licence.

questions.question_text: In Sarla Verma (2009), what deduction for personal and living expenses of deceased is made when deceased was married with 2 to 3 dependent family members?
questions.explanation: Sarla Verma standardized the deduction for personal and living expenses of a married deceased at 1/3rd where there are 2 to 3 dependants.
questions.statute_or_case: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation (2009) 6 SCC 121

questions.question_text: In Sarla Verma (2009), what deduction for personal and living expenses is made when deceased was a BACHELOR?
questions.explanation: Sarla Verma held that where the deceased is a bachelor, 50% of the income is ordinarily treated as personal and living expenses and 50% as the contribution to the family.
questions.statute_or_case: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation (2009) 6 SCC 121

questions.question_text: In Sarla Verma (2009), what deduction for personal expenses is made when deceased had 4 to 6 dependent family members?
questions.explanation: Sarla Verma fixed the deduction for personal and living expenses at 1/4th where the deceased, being married, had 4 to 6 dependants.
questions.statute_or_case: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation (2009) 6 SCC 121

questions.question_text: In Pranay Sethi (2017), for a deceased self-employed person aged below 40 years, what percentage addition is made towards FUTURE PROSPECTS?
questions.explanation: Pranay Sethi fixed future-prospects addition at 40% of established income for a self-employed or fixed-salary deceased below 40 years.
questions.statute_or_case: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680

questions.question_text: In Pranay Sethi (2017), for a deceased person holding a permanent job aged below 40 years, what percentage addition is made towards FUTURE PROSPECTS?
questions.explanation: Pranay Sethi fixed future-prospects addition at 50% of established income for a permanently employed deceased below 40 years.
questions.statute_or_case: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680

questions.question_text: In Pranay Sethi (2017), for a deceased person holding a permanent job aged 40 to 50 years, what percentage addition is made towards FUTURE PROSPECTS?
questions.explanation: Pranay Sethi fixed future-prospects addition at 30% of established income for a permanently employed deceased aged 40 to 50 years.
questions.statute_or_case: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680

questions.question_text: In Pranay Sethi (2017), for a deceased person holding a permanent job aged 50 to 60 years, what percentage addition is made towards FUTURE PROSPECTS?
questions.explanation: Pranay Sethi fixed future-prospects addition at 15% of established income for a permanently employed deceased aged 50 to 60 years.
questions.statute_or_case: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680

questions.question_text: Under MVA 1988, does 'Third Party' include a passenger travelling in a private car or pillion rider on a two-wheeler under a Comprehensive / Package Policy?
options: No, third party means pedestrians only
Yes, as held in National Insurance Co. v. Balakrishnan (2013), comprehensive policy covers passengers/pillion riders
questions.explanation: In Balakrishnan the Supreme Court held that, unlike an Act-only policy, a Comprehensive/Package Policy also covers gratuitous passengers and pillion riders as third parties.
questions.statute_or_case: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Balakrishnan (2013) 1 SCC 731

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(a) of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, a divorced Muslim woman is entitled to a reasonable and fair provision and maintenance to be made and paid to her within:
options: The iddat period by her former husband
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(a) mandates that former husband must make and pay reasonable and fair provision & maintenance within the iddat period.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 3(1)(a), Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986

questions.question_text: In the landmark 5-Judge Constitution Bench judgment Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) 7 SCC 740, the Supreme Court interpreted Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act to mean that:
options: The husband is liable to pay maintenance ONLY for 3 months of iddat
The Act is unconstitutional and void
The husband's liability to MAKE a reasonable and fair provision WITHIN the iddat period extends FOR THE ENTIRE FUTURE LIFETIME of the divorced woman (until she remarries)
State Wakf Board is primarily liable
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi (2001) held that provision made within iddat must contemplate future needs of divorced woman for her entire life unless she remarries.
questions.statute_or_case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) 7 SCC 740

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(b) of the 1986 Act, where a divorced Muslim woman maintains children born to her before or after divorce, the former husband is liable to pay reasonable and fair provision and maintenance for the children for a period of:
options: Two years from the respective dates of birth of such children
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(b) specifies a 2-year maintenance period from child's birth date payable by former husband under this Act.

questions.question_text: In Noor Saba Khatoon v. Mohd. Quasim (1997) 6 SCC 233, the Supreme Court held regarding Section 3(1)(b) of the 1986 Act and Section 125 CrPC that:
options: Section 3(1)(b) does NOT abrogate the right of minor Muslim children to claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC until they attain majority (or marriage for daughters)
Muslim children get maintenance for 2 years only under all laws
Father is exempt from maintaining children post-divorce
questions.explanation: Noor Saba Khatoon (1997) held minor children's maintenance right under CrPC 125 till majority is independent and unaffected by S. 3(1)(b).
questions.statute_or_case: Noor Saba Khatoon v. Mohd. Quasim (1997) 6 SCC 233

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the 1986 Act, a divorced Muslim woman is entitled to receive from her former husband an amount equal to:
options: The sum of Mahr or dower agreed to be paid to her at marriage or thereafter according to Muslim law
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(c) guarantees prompt or deferred Mahr/dower payment upon divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(d) of the 1986 Act, a divorced woman is entitled to receive all properties given to her before, at, or after marriage by:
options: Her relatives, friends, husband, or husband's relatives or friends
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(d) covers all marriage gifts given to her by any side.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(a) of the 1986 Act, a 'divorced woman' is defined as a Muslim woman who was married according to Muslim law and:
options: Is separated by desertion without divorce
Is living separately with mutual consent
Has filed a suit for annulment in High Court
Has been divorced by, or has obtained divorce from, her husband in accordance with Muslim law
questions.explanation: Section 2(a) defines divorced woman as one divorced by or from husband under Muslim law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b)(i) of the 1986 Act, what is the 'iddat period' for a divorced woman subject to menstruation?
options: Three menstrual courses after the date of divorce
questions.explanation: Section 2(b)(i) defines iddat for menstruating woman as 3 menstrual courses.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b)(ii) of the 1986 Act, what is the 'iddat period' for a divorced woman who is NOT subject to menstruation?
options: Three lunar months after her divorce
questions.explanation: Section 2(b)(ii) defines iddat for non-menstruating woman as 3 lunar months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b)(iii) of the 1986 Act, if a woman is PREGNANT (enceinte) at the time of divorce, when does her iddat period terminate?
options: The period between divorce and delivery of child or termination of pregnancy, whichever is earlier
questions.explanation: Section 2(b)(iii) defines pregnant woman's iddat as lasting until delivery or pregnancy termination.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(c) of the 1986 Act, 'Magistrate' means a Magistrate of the First Class exercising jurisdiction under CrPC 1973 in the area where:
questions.explanation: Section 2(c) establishes territorial jurisdiction based on ordinary residence of the divorced woman.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(3) of the 1986 Act, when a divorced woman applies to a Magistrate for maintenance/Mahr/property delivery, within what period SHOULD the Magistrate dispose of the application?
options: Within one month of the date of filing of the application (unless recorded reasons for delay)
questions.explanation: Section 3(3) prescribes a speedy target period of 1 month for application disposal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(3) of the 1986 Act, in determining the quantum of provision and maintenance, the Magistrate shall have regard to:
options: Only income tax return of husband
Needs of divorced woman, standard of life enjoyed by her during marriage, and means of her former husband
questions.explanation: Section 3(3) lays down statutory criteria: needs, marital standard of life, and husband's means.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(4) of the 1986 Act, if a former husband fails without sufficient cause to comply with Magistrate's order, what sentence of imprisonment can be imposed?
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or until payment if sooner made
questions.explanation: Section 3(4) provides up to 1 year imprisonment (or until payment) for non-compliance.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced woman has NOT remarried and is unable to maintain herself AFTER the iddat period, who is primarily liable to maintain her?
options: Such of her relatives as would be entitled to inherit her property on her death according to Muslim law (in proportion to inheritance shares)
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) places post-iddat maintenance liability on her potential Muslim law inheritance heirs in proportion to their shares.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) First Proviso of the 1986 Act, if the divorced woman unable to maintain herself after iddat has CHILDREN, who must the Magistrate order to pay maintenance first?
options: Only such children (and if children unable, then her parents)
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) 1st proviso specifies children first, then parents if children lack means.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 4(1) proviso 1, Muslim Women Divorce Act, 1986

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(2) of the 1986 Act, when can a Magistrate direct the State WAKF BOARD to pay maintenance to a divorced Muslim woman?
options: In all cases immediately on divorce
Where she is unable to maintain herself and has NO relatives, or such relatives have NOT enough means to pay
questions.explanation: Section 4(2) places secondary statutory liability on State Wakf Board when no relatives exist or lack means.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 1986 Act, a divorced woman and her former husband can OPT IN to be governed by Sections 125 to 128 of CrPC 1973 IF they file a joint or separate declaration by affidavit on:
options: The date of the first hearing of the application under Section 3(2)
questions.explanation: Section 5 allows opting into CrPC 125-128 if declaration is filed on the date of first hearing.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 Explanation of the 1986 Act, 'date of the first hearing of the application' means:
options: The date when plaint is filed
The date when judgment is delivered
The date fixed in the summons for the attendance of the respondent to the application
questions.explanation: Section 5 Explanation defines first hearing date as the returnable date fixed in summons.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 5 Explanation, Muslim Women Divorce Act, 1986

questions.question_text: In Shabana Bano v. Imran Khan (2010) 1 SCC 666, the Supreme Court held regarding jurisdiction of Family Courts and Section 125 CrPC for divorced Muslim women:
options: A divorced Muslim woman can file an application under Section 125 CrPC before Family Court even after iddat period so long as she does not remarry
Family Court has no jurisdiction over Muslim women
Section 125 CrPC is repealed by 1986 Act
Application can be filed in Wakf Board only
questions.explanation: Shabana Bano (2010) affirmed that a divorced Muslim woman can maintain a S. 125 CrPC application before Family Court post-iddat.
questions.statute_or_case: Shabana Bano v. Imran Khan (2010) 1 SCC 666

questions.question_text: In Iqbal Bano v. State of U.P. (2007) 6 SCC 785, the Supreme Court held that proceedings under the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 are:
options: Civil in nature, and an application filed under Section 125 CrPC can be converted and treated as an application under the 1986 Act
questions.explanation: Iqbal Bano (2007) held 1986 Act proceedings are civil in nature and CrPC 125 petitions can be treated under 1986 Act.
questions.statute_or_case: Iqbal Bano v. State of U.P. (2007) 6 SCC 785

questions.question_text: In Shamima Farooqui v. Shahid Khan (2015) 5 SCC 705, the Supreme Court held regarding an able-bodied husband's duty to pay maintenance under Section 125 CrPC / 1986 Act:
options: Unemployed husband is exempt from paying maintenance
Husband pays only 10% of minimum wage
An able-bodied husband cannot escape liability to pay maintenance by pleading financial constraint or unemployment
questions.explanation: Shamima Farooqui (2015) held able-bodied husband has a moral and legal duty to earn and pay maintenance.
questions.statute_or_case: Shamima Farooqui v. Shahid Khan (2015) 5 SCC 705

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(1) of Act No. 25 of 1986, the short title of the Act is:
options: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
questions.explanation: Section 1(1) states exact short title.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1) of the 1986 Act, who has the power to make rules carrying out the purposes of the Act?
questions.explanation: Section 6(1) empowers Central Government to make rules.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3) of the 1986 Act, every rule made under the Act shall be laid before each House of Parliament for a total period of:
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) mandates laying rules before Parliament for 30 days.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of the 1986 Act (Transitional provisions), every Section 125 or 127 CrPC application by a divorced Muslim woman pending on commencement of the Act shall:
options: Be disposed of by the Magistrate in accordance with the provisions of the 1986 Act (subject to Section 5 option)
questions.explanation: Section 7 required pending CrPC 125 applications to be governed by 1986 Act provisions.

questions.question_text: What event catalyzed the enactment of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 by Parliament?
options: The Supreme Court judgment in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985)
questions.explanation: The 1986 Act was passed by Parliament following political controversy over the Shah Bano judgment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act, the phrase 'fair and reasonable provision' is distinct from 'maintenance'. What is the legal distinction affirmed in Danial Latifi?
options: 'Provision' means lump sum capital/asset or arrangement made for her future support, while 'maintenance' covers recurring living expenses during iddat
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi explained 'provision' contemplates long-term future support arrangement made during iddat.
questions.statute_or_case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the 1986 Act, if Mahr was agreed to be paid at marriage as 'Deferred Mahr', when must it be paid under the Act?
options: On divorce, as part of Section 3 entitlement
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(c) makes all unpaid Mahr (whether prompt or deferred) immediately payable on divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(d) of the 1986 Act, if husband refuses to deliver wedding gifts and furniture given to wife by her parents, what remedy does she have?
options: Application under Section 3(2) to Magistrate for an order directing delivery of properties
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) provides summary remedy before Magistrate to recover marriage properties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(4) of the 1986 Act, how is unpaid maintenance or Mahr recovered by the Magistrate if husband defaults?
options: By issuing a warrant for levying the amount in the manner provided for levying fines under CrPC
questions.explanation: Section 3(4) authorizes issuing distress warrant like levying criminal fine under CrPC.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, how are relative shares of maintenance calculated among heirs?
options: In the proportions in which they would inherit her property under Muslim law on her death
Equal division among all living relatives
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) specifies maintenance share is proportional to potential inheritance share.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) 2nd Proviso of the 1986 Act, if one parent is unable to pay their share of maintenance due to lack of means:
options: Magistrate may order that parent's share to be paid by other relatives who have means
questions.explanation: Proviso 2 allows redistributing share of needy parent onto other solvent inheriting relatives.

questions.question_text: If a divorced Muslim woman REMARRIES, what is the effect on her post-iddat maintenance under Section 4 of the 1986 Act?
options: Her maintenance from relatives/Wakf Board under Section 4 ceases upon remarriage
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) condition requires that woman 'has not re-married'. Remarriage terminates S. 4 maintenance.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 1986 Act, what is required to opt for CrPC Sections 125 to 128 instead of 1986 Act?
options: Joint or separate declaration by affidavit filed by divorced woman AND former husband on date of first hearing
questions.explanation: Section 5 requires BOTH divorced woman and former husband to declare preference by affidavit on first hearing date.

questions.question_text: If the former husband REFUSES to sign a Section 5 affidavit to opt for CrPC 125, how does the Magistrate dispose of the woman's Section 3 application?
options: Magistrate disposes of application under the provisions of the 1986 Act (applying Danial Latifi principles)
Magistrate transfers case to High Court
questions.explanation: Without mutual Section 5 affidavit, application proceeds under 1986 Act.

questions.question_text: Does the 1986 Act apply to a Muslim woman whose marriage was dissolved by KHULA or MUBARAT?
options: No, applies only to Talaq by husband
Yes, Section 2(a) covers any woman divorced by or who has OBTAINED divorce from husband under Muslim law (including Khula/Mubarat)
No, Khula waives all rights under 1986 Act
questions.explanation: Section 2(a) explicitly includes women who 'have obtained divorce from' husband under Muslim law.

questions.question_text: Does a divorced Muslim woman's application under Section 3 of the 1986 Act require payment of heavy ad valorem court fees?
options: Yes, court fee equal to Mahr value
No, applications under Section 3 are summary proceedings before Magistrate requiring nominal court fee
questions.explanation: Section 3 applications before Magistrate are summary quasi-criminal/civil proceedings with nominal fees.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(b) of the 1986 Act, if a child is born 1 month AFTER divorce, for how long must former husband pay maintenance for this child?
options: For 2 years from date of divorce
For a period of two years from the child's date of birth
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(b) specifies 2 years from child's respective date of birth.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(2) of the 1986 Act, which Wakf Board is ordered to pay maintenance?
options: The State Wakf Board functioning in the area in which the woman resides
Wakf Board of husband's native state
questions.explanation: Section 4(2) specifies State Wakf Board functioning in the area where woman resides.

questions.question_text: Can a divorced Muslim woman claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC if she filed her application BEFORE divorce occurred?
options: No, petition lapses immediately on divorce
Yes, as held in Shabana Bano, divorce during pendency of S. 125 CrPC petition does not oust jurisdiction
She must refile in High Court
questions.explanation: Shabana Bano (2010) affirmed S. 125 CrPC application remains maintainable post-divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act, does 'reasonable and fair provision' include housing/residence for the divorced woman?
options: Yes, reasonable provision includes arrangements for residence/housing as part of future life security
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi affirmed 'provision' encompasses living arrangements, food, clothes, and financial security.
questions.statute_or_case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

questions.question_text: In Danial Latifi (2001), the Constitution Bench upheld the 1986 Act against challenge under Articles 14 and 21 by construing Section 3(1)(a) such that:
options: It declared Wakf Board solely responsible
It made CrPC 125 unconstitutional for Muslims
It does NOT limit maintenance to iddat period, but requires provision to be PAID/MADE within iddat for woman's life post-iddat
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi harmonized the Act with Articles 14 & 21 by reading 'within iddat' as the timeline for making long-term provision.
questions.statute_or_case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(4) of the 1986 Act, before sentencing a defaulting husband to imprisonment for non-payment, the Magistrate MUST ensure that:
options: The person is heard in defence and sentence is imposed according to CrPC provisions
Wife gives written consent to jail him
questions.explanation: Section 3(4) requires hearing the defaulting person in defence before sentencing.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(4) of the 1986 Act, what is the maximum term of imprisonment for EACH month's default in paying maintenance?
options: Up to one year (or until payment if sooner made)
questions.explanation: Section 3(4) prescribes imprisonment up to 1 year or until payment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced Muslim woman has no children, no living parents, who among her relatives can be ordered to pay maintenance?
options: Her brothers, sisters, or other relatives who would inherit her property under Muslim law on her death
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) targets any Quranic heirs/residuaries who would inherit her estate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced woman has 2 brothers, B1 (inherits 2/3rd) and B2 (inherits 1/3rd), how is maintenance liability shared between them?
options: B1 pays 2/3rd and B2 pays 1/3rd of the ordered maintenance (proportional to inheritance share)
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) mandates maintenance liability in exact proportion to inheritance share.

questions.question_text: Can a former husband be ordered to pay maintenance under SECTION 4 of the 1986 Act?
options: No, Section 4 applies ONLY to relatives/Wakf Board post-iddat; husband's liability is under Section 3 during/within iddat
Yes, husband is primary under Section 4
Yes, joint liability with Wakf Board
questions.explanation: Section 4 excludes former husband; husband's liability is governed by Section 3.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the 1986 Act, if Mahr was fixed in gold coins at marriage, how is it paid on divorce?
options: An amount equal to the value of Mahr agreed upon according to Muslim law
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(c) requires payment of sum equal to agreed Mahr according to Muslim law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(d) of the 1986 Act, if husband's friend gifted a refrigerator to the bride at marriage, who owns it post-divorce?
options: The divorced woman, and husband/in-laws must deliver it to her under Section 3(1)(d)
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(d) explicitly includes gifts from husband's friends as property of divorced woman.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(2) of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, the Act extends to:
questions.explanation: Section 1(2) extends the Act to the whole of India.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b)(i) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced Muslim woman has 3 menstrual cycles within 75 days, when does her iddat end?
options: Upon completion of the 3rd menstrual course
questions.explanation: Section 2(b)(i) defines iddat as 3 menstrual courses (actual biological courses).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b)(ii) of the 1986 Act, if a menopausal divorced woman is not subject to menstruation, her iddat is:
questions.explanation: Section 2(b)(ii) specifies 3 lunar months for non-menstruating women.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) of the 1986 Act, who can file an application before Magistrate on behalf of divorced woman?
options: The divorced woman OR any person duly authorized by her
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) allows the woman or any person duly authorized by her to apply.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(3) proviso of the 1986 Act, if the Magistrate cannot dispose of the application within 1 month, he must:
options: Record reasons for the delay in writing
questions.explanation: Section 3(3) proviso requires recording reasons for exceeding 1 month timeline.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(4) of the 1986 Act, how is unpaid maintenance recovered if husband has no cash?
options: By attachment and sale of his movable/immovable property in the manner of levying criminal fine under CrPC
By attachment of Wakf Board funds
questions.explanation: CrPC fine recovery rules apply, including property attachment and sale.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, can a divorced Muslim woman claim maintenance from her MARRIED DAUGHTER who has independent income?
options: Yes, children (son or daughter) having means are first among relatives liable under Section 4(1) proviso 1
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) proviso 1 specifies 'children' (both sons and daughters having means).

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced woman has NO children, who is next liable before other relatives?
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) proviso 1 places parents immediately after children.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(2) of the 1986 Act, if State Wakf Board fails to comply with Magistrate's maintenance order, how is the order enforced?
options: Magistrate enforces order against Wakf Board as a civil court decree / fine recovery under CrPC
questions.explanation: Magistrate's order against Wakf Board is enforceable via standard judicial execution process.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 1986 Act, if husband and wife file an affidavit opting for CrPC 125-128, which court disposes of the application?
options: The Magistrate hearing the Section 3 application disposes of it under CrPC 125-128
questions.explanation: Section 5 directs the Magistrate hearing the application to dispose of it under CrPC 125-128.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2)(a) of the 1986 Act, Central Government rules may prescribe:
options: The form of affidavit or written declaration to be filed under Section 5
questions.explanation: Section 6(2)(a) specifies rule-making for Section 5 affidavit form.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2)(b) of the 1986 Act, rules may prescribe procedure for Magistrate in disposing of applications, including:
options: Serving notices to parties, hearing dates, and related matters
questions.explanation: Section 6(2)(b) covers procedural rules for serving notice and hearing applications.

questions.question_text: Under Danial Latifi (2001), does the 1986 Act violate Article 14 or Article 15 of the Constitution of India?
options: No, the Act is constitutionally valid and does not discriminate against Muslim women when interpreted properly
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi Constitution Bench upheld 1986 Act's constitutional validity under Art. 14, 15, and 21.
questions.statute_or_case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

questions.question_text: If a divorced Muslim woman has sufficient independent income/property to maintain herself comfortably post-iddat, can she claim maintenance under Section 4 of the 1986 Act?
options: No, Section 4 requires that she is 'not able to maintain herself'
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) condition precedent is that woman is unable to maintain herself.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act, if a husband pays maintenance ONLY for 3 months of iddat and refuses any future provision, what can the wife do?
options: Apply under Section 3(2) for 'reasonable and fair provision' for her future life as mandated by Danial Latifi
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi held provision made in iddat must cover post-iddat future life needs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(b) of the 1986 Act, does the father's liability to maintain children for 2 years apply to ILLEGITIMATE children born of the marriage?
options: Applies to male legitimate children only
Section 3(1)(b) specifies 'children born to her before or after her divorce'
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(b) uses broad wording 'children born to her before or after her divorce'.

questions.question_text: A Muslim father is directed to pay maintenance for his minor children for two years under Section 3(1)(b) of the 1986 Act. Independently of that provision, the minor children:
options: Are restricted to the 2-year provision under the 1986 Act
Can be maintained only by the mother
Must look to the State Wakf Board after two years
Can claim maintenance from the father under Section 125 CrPC until they attain majority (an unmarried daughter until she can maintain herself), this right being unaffected by Section 3(1)(b)
questions.explanation: Noor Saba Khatoon v. Mohd. Quasim (1997) held the minor children's right to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC is independent of and unaffected by the 2-year provision in Section 3(1)(b) of the 1986 Act.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 3(1)(b), Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986; Noor Saba Khatoon v. Mohd. Quasim (1997) 6 SCC 233

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the 1986 Act, if Mahr was NOT specified at the time of marriage (Unspecified/Proper Dower - Mahr-i-Misl):
options: Magistrate determines proper dower according to Muslim law status of woman's family
questions.explanation: Under Muslim law, proper dower (Mahr-i-Misl) is determined based on female relatives' status if unspecified.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(d) of the 1986 Act, stridhana/gifts received by the woman are returnable to her. If former husband sold her gold jewelry:
options: Husband gets 1 year jail without option to pay
Magistrate orders husband to pay monetary value of gold under Section 3(3)
questions.explanation: Section 3(3) empowers Magistrate to direct payment of equivalent monetary value or delivery.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced woman has 1 Son (inherits 2/3rd) and 1 Daughter (inherits 1/3rd), how is her Section 4 maintenance divided between them?
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) mandates division in exact proportion of inheritance shares (2:1).

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if children are MINORS having no property or income of their own:
options: Magistrate orders parents of divorced woman to pay maintenance under Section 4(1) proviso 1
questions.explanation: If children are unable (minors without means), Section 4(1) proviso 1 shifts liability to woman's parents.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(2) of the 1986 Act, can the State Wakf Board recover maintenance paid to a divorced woman from her former husband?
options: No, Wakf Board cannot recover from former husband under Section 4(2); husband's liability is settled under Section 3
Yes, husband pays Wakf Board double
questions.explanation: Section 4(2) Wakf Board liability is statutory social security when family heirs lack means; no recovery from husband.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 1986 Act, if affidavit is filed on date of first hearing opting for CrPC 125, can the husband LATER withdraw his consent during trial?
options: No, once valid Section 5 affidavit is filed on first hearing date, jurisdiction under CrPC 125 is irrevocably fixed for that application
questions.explanation: Section 5 option once exercised at first hearing binds proceedings under CrPC 125.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b) of the 1986 Act, if a marriage was NOT consummated before divorce, what is the iddat period?
options: No iddat period is required under Muslim law for unconsummated divorce
questions.explanation: Under Muslim law, no iddat is observed if marriage was unconsummated prior to divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced woman is pregnant at divorce, when is provision & maintenance payable?
options: During the entire pregnancy period until delivery (which constitutes her iddat period)
questions.explanation: Her iddat lasts until delivery under S. 2(b)(iii), so maintenance covers full pregnancy duration.

questions.question_text: In Danial Latifi (2001), the Supreme Court summarized the 1986 Act provisions to hold that a Muslim husband's liability under Section 3(1)(a) to pay maintenance:
options: Is NOT limited to the iddat period, but provision must be MADE within iddat for post-iddat period
Is limited strictly to 3 lunar months
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi held husband must make fair provision within iddat contemplating wife's long-term future.
questions.statute_or_case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the 1986 Act, if husband paid 50% Mahr during marriage, how much Mahr must he pay on divorce under Section 3?
options: The remaining unpaid 50% balance of Mahr
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(c) requires paying amount equal to unpaid dower due.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(4) of the 1986 Act, can a Magistrate sentence a defaulting husband to imprisonment if he genuinely lacks means due to permanent paralysis?
options: Sentence is mandatory regardless of cause
Section 3(4) states if he fails 'without sufficient cause'; physical incapacity may constitute sufficient cause
questions.explanation: Section 3(4) specifies non-compliance 'without sufficient cause'; genuine physical impossibility is sufficient cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, who determines the 'standard of life enjoyed by her during her marriage' when fixing maintenance against relatives?
options: The Judicial Magistrate First Class hearing the Section 4 application
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) empowers Judicial Magistrate First Class to determine maintenance having regard to marital standard of life.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, an offence under the Act is cognizable ONLY IF information is given to police by:
options: The married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced or any person related to her by blood or marriage
questions.explanation: Section 7(a) restricts cognizability to complaints by the aggrieved woman or her blood/marriage relatives.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(2) of the 1986 Act, if a State has no Wakf Board established, who pays maintenance under Section 4(2)?
options: Any Wakf Board functioning in the area in a State under any law for the time being in force
questions.explanation: Section 4(2) refers to State Wakf Board established under Wakf Act functioning in the area.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 1986 Act, can the wife ALONE file an affidavit opting for CrPC 125 if husband refuses?
options: Yes, wife's affidavit alone is sufficient
No, Section 5 requires declaration by divorced woman AND her former husband (either jointly or separately)
Yes, if she has minor children
questions.explanation: Section 5 requires BOTH parties to declare preference for CrPC 125-128.

questions.question_text: Does the 1986 Act apply to a Muslim woman whose marriage was dissolved by TALAQ-E-BIDDAT (instant triple talaq) prior to 2017?
options: Yes, Section 2(a) covers all women divorced in accordance with Muslim law
Only if approved by High Court
questions.explanation: Section 2(a) applied to all divorces under Muslim law prior to 2017 declaration.

questions.question_text: In Danial Latifi (2001), the Supreme Court held that the 1986 Act was enacted to:
options: Codify and regulate post-divorce entitlements of Muslim women while maintaining harmony with constitutional gender justice under Article 21
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi affirmed 1986 Act provides effective protection of rights of divorced Muslim women consistent with Art. 21.
questions.statute_or_case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced woman is NOT menstruating due to medical reasons (amenorrhea), her iddat is 3 lunar months under Section 2(b)(ii). Must husband pay provision within those 3 months?
options: Yes, within the 3 lunar months of iddat period
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(a) requires provision made and paid within her specific iddat period (3 lunar months).

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(d) of the 1986 Act, does 'properties' given at marriage include immovable property (e.g. house or plot) gifted to the bride?
options: Yes, all properties (movable or immovable) given before, at, or after marriage are covered
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(d) uses un-restricted term 'all the properties' covering movable and immovable assets.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(4) of the 1986 Act, can a Magistrate sentence a defaulting husband to imprisonment MORE than once for continuous default of different months?
options: No, 1 sentence covers all defaults forever
Yes, default in payment of maintenance for each month constitutes a fresh default for which warrant/sentence can be issued under CrPC rules
questions.explanation: Under CrPC fine levying rules applied by s. 3(4), each month's default is a distinct breach.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced woman has NO living children, parents, or other relatives with means, who pays her maintenance?
options: The State Wakf Board under Section 4(2)
questions.explanation: Section 4(2) mandates State Wakf Board payment when relatives are absent or lack means.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of the 1986 Act, what happened to CrPC Section 125 applications pending on 19th May 1986?
options: They were required to be disposed of in accordance with 1986 Act provisions (unless Section 5 option exercised)
They were transferred to Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Section 7 transitional provision mandated applying 1986 Act to all pending CrPC 125 cases.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) of the 1986 Act, where is the Section 3 application filed?
options: Before Family Court in state capital only
Before the Judicial Magistrate First Class having jurisdiction in the area where divorced woman resides
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) specifies filing before Magistrate having jurisdiction where woman resides.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(a) of the 1986 Act, if husband pays maintenance during iddat BUT makes NO provision for post-iddat life, can wife file application under Section 3(2)?
options: No, iddat maintenance fulfills all requirements
No, she must sue under Section 4 only
Yes, because Section 3(1)(a) requires BOTH 'provision' AND 'maintenance' to be made within iddat for future life
No, she must apply to Wakf Board
questions.explanation: Danial Latifi affirmed that failure to make 'provision' for future life gives right to Section 3(2) order.

questions.question_text: In Vijay Kumar Prasad v. State of Bihar (2004) 5 SCC 196, on a father's claim for maintenance from his son under Section 125 CrPC, the Supreme Court held on territorial jurisdiction under Section 126 CrPC that:
options: The petition may be filed wherever the claimant parent resides
Only a Family Court at the State capital has jurisdiction
The son may choose the forum
Jurisdiction is determined by the place where the person from whom maintenance is claimed resides, not by the claimant's residence
questions.explanation: The Court held that for a parent's claim the residence of the claimant does not confer jurisdiction; the proceeding lies where the respondent (son) is or resides under Section 126 CrPC.
questions.statute_or_case: Vijay Kumar Prasad v. State of Bihar (2004) 5 SCC 196

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(b) of the 1986 Act, if former husband is ordered to pay 2 years child maintenance, can mother claim HIGHER amount if child falls ill?
options: Yes, Magistrate determines 'reasonable and fair provision and maintenance' having regard to child's medical needs
No, fixed at Rs. 100 per month
No, father pays nothing for medical
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(b) specifies 'reasonable and fair provision and maintenance' taking into account actual needs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced Muslim woman has NO relatives capable of paying, and Wakf Board pays her maintenance under Section 4(2), does she forfeit her Wakf maintenance if she REMARRIES?
options: No, Wakf Board pays for life
Yes, remarriage terminates maintenance entitlement under Section 4
questions.explanation: Section 4 maintenance is conditional on non-remarriage; remarriage ends entitlement.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the 1986 Act, can former husband deduct past maintenance paid during marriage from Mahr payable on divorce?
options: No, Mahr is a distinct debt/consideration for marriage and cannot be reduced by maintenance paid during cohabitation
questions.explanation: Mahr is a separate debt; maintenance paid during marriage cannot be set off against Mahr due on divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1)(d) of the 1986 Act, if property given to wife at marriage is held by husband's brother, can Magistrate order husband's brother to deliver it to her?
options: No, only husband can be ordered
No, wife must file civil suit against brother
Yes, Section 3(1)(d) covers properties given by relatives/friends, and Section 3(3) directs delivery to divorced woman
questions.explanation: Section 3(3) authorizes order directing delivery of Section 3(1)(d) properties from whoever holds them.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 1986 Act, what form must the Section 5 option declaration take?
options: An affidavit or any other declaration in writing in such form as may be prescribed
questions.explanation: Section 5 specifies affidavit or written declaration in prescribed form.

questions.question_text: Does the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 apply to a married Muslim woman who has NOT been divorced?
options: Yes, applies to all Muslim wives
No, the 1986 Act applies ONLY to a 'divorced woman'; a non-divorced married Muslim woman claims maintenance under Section 125 CrPC / BNS
Applies if husband marries second wife
questions.explanation: The 1986 Act specifically protects 'divorced women'; existing wives claim maintenance under CrPC 125 / BNS.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(3) of the 1986 Act, if husband proves he paid full Mahr and made fair provision during iddat, what order does Magistrate pass?
options: Orders husband to pay double Mahr
Magistrate finds Section 3 application satisfied and rejects further claims against husband under Section 3
questions.explanation: If Section 3 obligations are fulfilled by husband, no further Section 3 order lies against him.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the 1986 Act, if a divorced woman's father is alive and wealthy, but her minor children have no income, who pays her Section 4 maintenance?
options: Her father pays, because minor children are unable to pay under Section 4(1) proviso 1
questions.explanation: Under Section 4(1) proviso 1, when children are unable to pay (minors), liability shifts to her parents (father).

questions.question_text: What is the primary overarching object of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 as stated in its Preamble?
options: To protect the rights of Muslim women who have been divorced by, or have obtained divorce from, their husbands and to provide for matters connected therewith
questions.explanation: The Preamble states the Act is 'An Act to protect the rights of Muslim women who have been divorced by, or have obtained divorce from, their husbands'.
questions.statute_or_case: Preamble, Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, any pronouncement of talaq by a Muslim husband upon his wife by spoken/written words or in electronic form is:
questions.explanation: Section 3 explicitly declares any pronouncement of instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) in any form to be void and illegal.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 3, Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, what is the maximum punishment prescribed for a Muslim husband who pronounces instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) upon his wife?
options: Imprisonment for one year without fine
Imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and fine
questions.explanation: Section 4 imposes imprisonment for up to 3 years and fine for pronouncing instant triple talaq.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(c) of the 2019 Act, 'talaq' is defined as:
options: Talaq-e-biddat or any other similar form of talaq having the effect of instantaneous and irrevocable divorce pronounced by a Muslim husband
questions.explanation: Section 2(c) specifically targets talaq-e-biddat and instantaneous irrevocable forms of talaq.

questions.question_text: In the landmark 5-Judge Constitution Bench judgment Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) 9 SCC 1, the Supreme Court declared Talaq-e-Biddat unconstitutional on the ground that:
options: It is manifestly arbitrary and violates Article 14 of the Constitution of India
It violates Article 25 freedom of religion
It violates Transfer of Property Act
questions.explanation: Shayara Bano (2017) struck down triple talaq by 3:2 majority as manifestly arbitrary under Article 14.
questions.statute_or_case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) 9 SCC 1

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, a married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced is entitled to receive from her husband:
options: Such amount of subsistence allowance for her and dependent children as determined by the Magistrate
No allowance since marriage is void
questions.explanation: Section 5 grants a right to subsistence allowance for woman and dependent children as determined by Magistrate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, in the event of pronouncement of talaq by her husband, who is entitled to custody of minor children?
options: The married Muslim woman, in such manner as determined by the Magistrate
questions.explanation: Section 6 explicitly vests custody of minor children in the married Muslim woman upon talaq pronouncement as determined by Magistrate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, an offence under the Act is COMPOUNDABLE:
options: At the instance of the married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced, with the permission of the Magistrate
By police officer at police station
questions.explanation: Section 7(b) allows compounding at victim's instance with Magistrate's permission on set terms.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, no person accused of an offence under the Act shall be released on BAIL unless the Magistrate satisfy which mandatory condition?
options: Accused pays Rs. 1 Lakh cash bail
After hearing the married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced, the Magistrate is satisfied there are reasonable grounds for granting bail
Bail is granted automatically in 24 hours
questions.explanation: Section 7(c) mandates hearing the wife before granting bail to the accused husband.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(3) of the 2019 Act, the Act was deemed to have come into force retrospectively on:
questions.explanation: Section 1(3) gave retrospective effect from 19th September 2018 (when first Ordinance was promulgated).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(a) of the 2019 Act, 'electronic form' adopts its definition from which act?
options: Section 2(1)(r) of the Information Technology Act, 2000
questions.explanation: Section 2(a) references IT Act 2000 Section 2(1)(r) for electronic form.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b) of the 2019 Act, 'Magistrate' means a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class exercising jurisdiction in the area where:
questions.explanation: Section 2(b) defines territorial jurisdiction based on wife's residence.

questions.question_text: If a Muslim husband pronounces instant triple talaq via a WhatsApp message or SMS text to his wife, does it fall under Section 3 of the 2019 Act?
options: Yes, Section 3 explicitly includes pronouncement 'by words, either spoken or written or in electronic form'
No, only oral pronouncement is illegal
Only if sent via speed post
questions.explanation: Section 3 expressly covers spoken, written, electronic (WhatsApp/SMS/email), or any other manner.

questions.question_text: What is the legal effect on the MARRIAGE STATUS when a husband pronounces instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) under Section 3 of the 2019 Act?
options: The marriage remains completely valid and intact because the pronouncement is void and illegal in law
questions.explanation: Because Section 3 declares pronouncement null and void, it has zero legal effect on marriage continuity.

questions.question_text: Does the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 apply to Talaq-us-Sunnah (Talaq Ahsan or Talaq Hasan)?
options: Yes, covers all forms of divorce
No, Section 2(c) restricts definition of talaq strictly to talaq-e-biddat or instantaneous irrevocable talaq
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act targets instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat), not revocable forms like Talaq Ahsan/Hasan.

questions.question_text: In Shamim Ara v. State of U.P. (2002) 7 SCC 518, the Supreme Court laid down that a valid talaq under Muslim law requires:
options: Proof of reasonable cause and preceding attempt at reconciliation by two arbitrators (one from husband's family and one from wife's family)
Pronouncement of word 'talaq' 3 times in 1 second
questions.explanation: Shamim Ara (2002) held talaq must be for reasonable cause preceded by reconciliation effort.
questions.statute_or_case: Shamim Ara v. State of U.P. (2002) 7 SCC 518

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the 2019 Act, which Ordinance was repealed upon enactment of Act No. 20 of 2019?
options: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Second Ordinance, 2019 (Ord. 4 of 2019)
questions.explanation: Section 8(1) repealed Ordinance 4 of 2019, saving actions taken thereunder.

questions.question_text: Under the 2019 Act, can a NEIGHBOR or UNRELATED stranger file an FIR against a husband for pronouncing triple talaq?
options: Yes, if neighbor is a lawyer
No, Section 7(a) restricts cognizability to information given by the wife or her blood/marriage relative
questions.explanation: Section 7(a) prevents stranger FIRs by confining complaint locus to wife or her relatives.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, is the subsistence allowance payable to the wife IN ADDITION TO maintenance under Section 125 CrPC / BNS?
options: No, wife must choose between S. 5 allowance and CrPC 125
S. 5 allowance is paid by State
Section 5 states 'Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in any other law for the time being in force'
questions.explanation: Section 5 non-obstante 'without prejudice' clause saves rights under other maintenance laws.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, who determines the terms and conditions for compounding the offence of pronouncing triple talaq?
questions.explanation: Section 7(b) specifies compounding is on terms and conditions determined by Magistrate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(2) of the 2019 Act, as extended post-30th October 2019, the Act applies to:
options: The whole of India, including Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir and Union Territory of Ladakh
questions.explanation: Vide Notification S.O. 3912(E) dated 30 Oct 2019, the Act extends to UT of J&K and UT of Ladakh.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, is the sentence of imprisonment for pronouncing triple talaq mandatory or discretionary?
options: Punished with imprisonment which MAY extend to three years, and shall ALSO be liable to fine (discretionary up to 3 years)
questions.explanation: Section 4 specifies imprisonment up to 3 years and fine.

questions.question_text: What is the primary overarching object of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 as stated in its Preamble?
options: To protect the rights of married Muslim women and to prohibit divorce by pronouncing talaq by their husbands
questions.explanation: Preamble states Act is 'An Act to protect the rights of married Muslim women and to prohibit divorce by pronouncing talaq by their husbands'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, does the father's natural guardianship under Guardians and Wards Act automatically override the mother's right to child custody upon triple talaq pronouncement?
options: No, Section 6 contains a non-obstante clause ('Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law') giving mother custody as determined by Magistrate
questions.explanation: Section 6 non-obstante clause overrides contrary provisions in Guardians & Wards Act.

questions.question_text: In Masroor Ahmed v. State (NCT of Delhi) 2008, the Delhi High Court analyzed Islamic divorce forms and held that Triple Talaq (Talaq-e-Biddat):
options: Was an innovation disapproved by Islamic jurisprudence which should be treated as a single revocable talaq (Talaq Ahsan)
Was a criminal offence under IPC
questions.explanation: Masroor Ahmed (2008) highlighted jurisprudential consensus treating biddat as single revocable talaq.
questions.statute_or_case: Masroor Ahmed v. State (NCT of Delhi) 2008

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a Muslim husband pronounces triple talaq in a FIT OF ANGER during a heated argument, what is the legal result?
options: The pronouncement is void and illegal, and husband remains liable under Section 4
questions.explanation: Section 3 applies to pronouncements 'in any other manner whatsoever' without exception for anger.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, if the Magistrate grants bail to an accused husband WITHOUT giving notice or hearing to the married woman upon whom talaq was pronounced:
options: Case is transferred to Supreme Court
The bail order is in violation of statutory requirement under Section 7(c)
questions.explanation: Section 7(c) explicitly conditions bail on hearing the woman upon whom talaq was pronounced.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, who determines the quantum of subsistence allowance for the woman and dependent children?
questions.explanation: Section 5 empowers Magistrate to determine the subsistence allowance amount.

questions.question_text: Can a Muslim husband who pronounces triple talaq avoid prosecution under Section 4 by offering to pay double Mahr?
options: Yes, Mahr payment grants complete immunity
No, criminal liability under Section 4 is independent of Mahr payment
Yes, if wife agrees in writing
questions.explanation: Section 4 penalizes the illegal act of pronouncement; paying Mahr does not wipe out the offence (though compounding under s. 7(b) is possible).

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, who among the following CAN legally file information/complaint to police to initiate investigation?
options: The wife's father, mother, brother, sister, or other blood/marriage relative
questions.explanation: Section 7(a) permits information from wife or any person related to her by blood or marriage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a husband pronounces triple talaq by sending a VIDEO RECORDING via email, is it covered?
options: No, only text messages are covered
Yes, Section 3 explicitly includes pronouncement 'in electronic form'
questions.explanation: Section 3 covers electronic forms under IT Act 2000, including video/audio recordings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, can an offence under the Act be compounded BEFORE the court without the wife's consent?
options: No, Section 7(b) strictly mandates compounding 'at the instance of the married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced'
Yes, Magistrate can compound over wife's objection
questions.explanation: Section 7(b) gives the wife sole veto/control over compounding.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(1) of Act No. 20 of 2019, the short title of the Act is:
options: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019
questions.explanation: Section 1(1) defines exact short title of Act No. 20 of 2019.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, in addition to imprisonment up to 3 years, the husband shall ALSO be liable to:
questions.explanation: Section 4 specifies punishment of imprisonment up to 3 years 'and shall also be liable to fine'.

questions.question_text: If a Muslim husband pronounces Talaq-e-Biddat, does the wife have to observe IDDAT under the 2019 Act?
options: No, because the pronouncement is void and illegal, so no divorce occurred and no iddat is triggered
questions.explanation: Since pronouncement is void in law, marriage continues uninterrupted without iddat.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, for whom can subsistence allowance be claimed?
options: For the married Muslim woman AND her dependent children
questions.explanation: Section 5 explicitly covers subsistence allowance 'for her and dependent children'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, who determines the MANNER of custody of minor children?
questions.explanation: Section 6 specifies custody in such manner 'as may be determined by the Magistrate'.

questions.question_text: Does the 2019 Act apply to Shia Muslims as well as Sunni Muslims in India?
options: Yes, the Act applies to any Muslim husband who pronounces instantaneous triple talaq / talaq-e-biddat
questions.explanation: The Act applies universally to all Muslim husbands in India regardless of sect.

questions.question_text: In Shayara Bano (2017), which judges delivered the majority ruling declaring Triple Talaq unconstitutional?
options: CJI J.S. Khehar and Justice Abdul Nazeer
Justice D.Y. Chandrachud and Justice Bobde
Justice Rohinton F. Nariman, Justice U.U. Lalit, and Justice Kurian Joseph
questions.explanation: Nariman & Lalit JJ (holding it manifestly arbitrary under Art. 14) and Kurian Joseph J (holding it against Quranic jurisprudence) formed 3:2 majority.
questions.statute_or_case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) 9 SCC 1

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, can an accused husband obtain ANTICIPATORY BAIL under Section 438 CrPC / Section 482 BNS?
options: Yes, provided the court hears the married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced before granting anticipatory bail
No, anticipatory bail is totally barred
questions.explanation: Supreme Court held anticipatory bail is maintainable under S. 438 CrPC provided statutory condition of hearing wife is complied with.
questions.statute_or_case: Rahna Jalal v. State of Kerala (2021) 1 SCC 733

questions.question_text: In Rahna Jalal v. State of Kerala (2021) 1 SCC 733, the Supreme Court held regarding anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC for offences under the 2019 Act:
options: There is no express bar on granting anticipatory bail under the 2019 Act, but Magistrate/Court must comply with Section 7(c) requirement of hearing the wife
questions.explanation: Rahna Jalal (2021) settled that S. 438 CrPC anticipatory bail is available subject to hearing the wife.
questions.statute_or_case: Rahna Jalal v. State of Kerala (2021) 1 SCC 733

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a husband pronounces triple talaq in writing on a piece of paper and hands it to his wife, what is the legal effect?
options: It is void and illegal, and husband commits an offence under Section 4
questions.explanation: Section 3 expressly covers written pronouncements.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, what does the phrase 'or in any other manner whatsoever' cover?
options: Any medium or mode of communication used to pronounce instantaneous triple talaq
questions.explanation: The omnibus phrase ensures no loophole allows escaping Section 3 prohibition.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, if a husband is convicted and sentenced to 2 years imprisonment, can the Magistrate ALSO direct him to pay subsistence allowance under Section 5?
options: Yes, criminal sentence under Section 4 does not affect wife's entitlement to subsistence allowance under Section 5
questions.explanation: Penal liability under Section 4 and civil protection rights under Section 5 operate concurrently.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, if the husband fails to pay the subsistence allowance ordered by Magistrate, how can the Magistrate enforce payment?
options: By issuing a warrant for levying the amount in the manner provided for levying fines under CrPC / BNS
questions.explanation: Standard CrPC fine recovery process applies for enforcing subsistence allowance orders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, up to what age of the child does the mother's custody protection apply?
questions.explanation: Section 6 specifies 'minor children' (under 18 years).

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, if a married Muslim woman's BROTHER gives information to the police station regarding triple talaq, can police register an FIR?
options: No, only wife herself must go
No, brother requires power of attorney
Yes, Section 7(a) explicitly includes information given by 'any person related to her by blood or marriage'
questions.explanation: Section 7(a) explicitly empowers blood or marriage relatives to inform police.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, if the wife agrees to forgive her husband and compound the offence, can the Magistrate refuse permission if terms are unfair?
options: Yes, Section 7(b) requires 'permission of the Magistrate, on such terms and conditions as he may determine'
No, Magistrate must allow compounding automatically
questions.explanation: Section 7(b) subjects compounding to judicial scrutiny and permission of Magistrate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, why does the Act mandate hearing the married Muslim woman before granting bail?
options: To ensure victim's safety, prevent coercion, and assess subsistence allowance and child custody needs
To transfer case to High Court
questions.explanation: Mandatory hearing protects victim's voice and safeguards her civil entitlements (allowance & custody).

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2) of the 2019 Act (Repeal and Savings), actions taken under the 2019 Second Ordinance prior to Act's passing are deemed to be:
options: Done or taken under the provisions of the 2019 Act
questions.explanation: Section 8(2) contains standard savings clause preserving acts done under Ordinance.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(3) of the 2019 Act, why was 19th September 2018 chosen as the enforcement date?
options: Because the first Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Ordinance was promulgated on 19th September 2018
questions.explanation: The Act replaced the succession of Ordinances starting from 19 Sept 2018.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a husband pronounces triple talaq verbally in private with no witnesses present, can he be prosecuted under Section 4?
options: Yes, if the wife or her relative proves the pronouncement beyond reasonable doubt
questions.explanation: Section 3 applies to any pronouncement; proof of pronouncement is a matter of evidence at trial.

questions.question_text: Does the 2019 Act prohibit a Muslim husband from seeking a lawful divorce under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 or by Talaq Ahsan?
options: No, the 2019 Act ONLY prohibits instantaneous irrevocable triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat)
Yes, requires converting to Hindu law
questions.explanation: Lawful, revocable, and judicial divorce modes remain entirely untouched by the 2019 Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, can a Magistrate order subsistence allowance if the husband is currently unemployed?
options: No, allowance is paid by State
Yes, as per Shamima Farooqui principles, an able-bodied husband is presumed capable of earning to pay subsistence allowance
questions.explanation: Able-bodied husband's duty to maintain/pay allowance is well-settled.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, if the husband attempts to forcibly snatch minor children after pronouncing triple talaq, what can Magistrate do?
options: Issue an order directing custody to the mother under Section 6 and direct police assistance for enforcement
questions.explanation: Section 6 empowers Magistrate to order and enforce minor children's custody to mother.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, if a wife's MARRIED SISTER gives information to police about triple talaq, is the FIR validly registered?
options: Yes, sister is a relative by blood under Section 7(a)
questions.explanation: Sister is a blood relative covered by Section 7(a).

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, if the case is compounded by permission of Magistrate, what is the legal effect on the accused husband?
options: Compounding has the effect of an ACQUITTAL of the accused under CrPC Section 320(8)
questions.explanation: Under CrPC 320(8), compounding an offence operates as an acquittal of the accused.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, who must file the bail application before the Magistrate?
options: The accused husband (or person acting on his behalf)
questions.explanation: Section 7(c) specifies 'on an application filed by the accused'.

questions.question_text: In Shayara Bano (2017), what was the minority view of CJI J.S. Khehar and Justice S. Abdul Nazeer?
options: Triple Talaq is illegal under Contract Act
Triple Talaq is a fundamental religious practice under Article 25, but directed Parliament to consider legislation
questions.explanation: Minority of 2 judges held it protected under Art. 25 but placed 6-month injunction directing Parliament to legislate.
questions.statute_or_case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) 9 SCC 1

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a husband pronounces triple talaq over a phone call (voice call), is it void and illegal?
options: Yes, spoken words transmitted via phone call fall under Section 3 ('words, either spoken... or in electronic form')
questions.explanation: Spoken words via telephonic/electronic medium are fully covered by Section 3.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, is the offence of pronouncing triple talaq bailable as a matter of right at the police station?
options: Yes, police officer must grant bail
No, Section 7(c) imposes strict statutory court bail conditions (hearing wife and satisfied on reasonable grounds), making it non-bailable at police station
questions.explanation: Section 7(c) conditions make it non-bailable at police station; bail is granted only by Magistrate after hearing wife.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, can a married Muslim woman claim subsistence allowance while she continues to reside in the matrimonial home?
options: Yes, entitlement to subsistence allowance arises upon pronouncement of talaq regardless of residence
No, allowance only if in hospital
questions.explanation: Section 5 creates an unconditional entitlement upon pronouncement of talaq.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, if the minor child is a 6-month-old infant, who gets custody?
options: The mother (married Muslim woman) under Section 6
questions.explanation: Section 6 entitles mother to custody of minor children upon triple talaq pronouncement.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, can a wife's FATHER-IN-LAW file information to police against his own son for pronouncing triple talaq?
options: Yes, father-in-law is a relative by marriage of the married Muslim woman
questions.explanation: Section 7(a) includes relatives by blood OR marriage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, if wife agrees to compound the offence on condition that husband pays Rs. 2 Lakhs subsistence allowance and returns gold jewelry, can Magistrate sanction compounding?
options: Yes, Magistrate may permit compounding on such terms and conditions as he may determine fit
questions.explanation: Section 7(b) gives Magistrate wide discretion to set terms and conditions for compounding.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(c) of the 2019 Act, 'talaq-e-biddat' refers to:
options: Pronouncing 3 talaqs at once (in a single breath/session) or irrevocable instantaneous divorce
questions.explanation: Talaq-e-biddat is the practice of triple talaq in one sentence or single sitting causing instant divorce.

questions.question_text: What constitutional entry in Schedule VII of the Constitution empowers Parliament to enact the 2019 Act?
options: List III (Concurrent List), Entry 5: Marriage and divorce; infants and minors; adoption; wills, intestacy and succession
questions.explanation: Entry 5 of Concurrent List covers marriage, divorce, and personal law matters.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a husband sends a email pronouncing triple talaq, and then claims he didn't mean it, is the pronouncement void and illegal?
options: Yes, the pronouncement itself is void and illegal in law under Section 3, regardless of secret intentions
questions.explanation: Section 3 attaches voidness to the act of pronouncement itself.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, what court tries the offence of pronouncing triple talaq?
options: Judicial Magistrate of the First Class (or Metropolitan Magistrate)
questions.explanation: Section 2(b) defines Magistrate as JMFC/MM having jurisdiction where woman resides.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, can subsistence allowance be determined for a minor child who is 15 years old?
questions.explanation: Section 5 covers dependent children without upper age restriction beyond dependency.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, if the Magistrate awards custody of minor children to the mother, can the husband be granted visitation rights?
options: Yes, custody is determined by Magistrate 'in such manner as may be determined by the Magistrate', which includes framing visitation terms
questions.explanation: Magistrate's broad discretion under Section 6 permits specifying fair visitation terms for father.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, if information is given to police by the wife's MATERNAL UNCLE, is it valid?
options: Yes, maternal uncle is a person related to her by blood
questions.explanation: Maternal uncle is a blood relative under Section 7(a).

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, if the married woman upon whom talaq was pronounced is served notice of bail application but chooses NOT to appear:
options: The Magistrate, after satisfying that she was heard/given opportunity of being heard, can proceed to decide bail on merits
questions.explanation: Giving reasonable opportunity of hearing satisfies procedural requirement of Section 7(c).

questions.question_text: What is the key statutory distinction between the 1986 Act and the 2019 Act?
options: The 1986 Act deals with rights and maintenance of DIVORCED Muslim women after a valid divorce, whereas the 2019 Act PROHIBITS instant triple talaq and penalizes it while preserving marriage
questions.explanation: 1986 Act applies post-valid divorce; 2019 Act renders instant triple talaq void and illegal ab initio.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a Muslim husband pronounces triple talaq through a public newspaper advertisement, is it void and illegal?
options: No, valid if 3 times in paper
Yes, Section 3 covers pronouncement 'in any other manner whatsoever'
questions.explanation: Section 3 covers any manner of pronouncement whatsoever.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, if a husband is convicted of pronouncing triple talaq, can he be awarded a sentence of 6 months imprisonment?
options: Yes, Section 4 prescribes imprisonment 'which may extend to three years' (giving court discretion from 1 day up to 3 years)
questions.explanation: Section 4 provides upper limit of 3 years; Magistrate can sentence for any period up to 3 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, can a Magistrate modify or increase the subsistence allowance later if circumstances change?
options: Yes, under standard CrPC 127 / BNS principles, Magistrate can alter/modify allowance on proof of changed circumstances
questions.explanation: Magistrate's ongoing jurisdiction under S. 5 allows altering allowance upon proof of changed circumstances.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, does mother's custody right apply if the minor child is 17 years old?
options: Yes, 'minor child' includes any child under 18 years of age under Majority Act
questions.explanation: Under Indian Majority Act, minority extends up to 18 years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, if police receive a phone call from an anonymous person reporting triple talaq in neighborhood, can police register FIR directly?
options: Yes, police can register on suspicion
No, Section 7(a) requires information from the aggrieved wife or her blood/marriage relative specifically
questions.explanation: Section 7(a) expressly conditions cognizability on information given by wife or her blood/marriage relatives.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, if husband and wife compound the offence before Magistrate, does the husband get a criminal record of conviction?
options: No, compounding operates as an ACQUITTAL, leaving no criminal conviction record
questions.explanation: Under CrPC 320(8), compounding results in complete acquittal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, what 'satisfaction' must Magistrate reach before granting bail to the accused husband?
options: That there are reasonable grounds for granting bail after hearing the married Muslim woman
That husband promises never to speak again
questions.explanation: Section 7(c) requires judicial satisfaction that reasonable grounds for bail exist post-hearing the wife.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a Muslim husband pronounces triple talaq in a foreign country (e.g. UAE or UK) to his wife residing in India, does the 2019 Act apply?
options: Yes; being a penal statute it can reach an Indian citizen who pronounces talaq abroad (extraterritorial operation under Section 4 IPC / Section 1(5) BNS), and the court where the wife resides in India has jurisdiction under Section 2(b)
questions.explanation: Penal statutes operate extraterritorially against Indian citizens abroad (Section 4 IPC / Section 1(5) BNS), and Section 2(b) fixes the forum where the married Muslim woman resides.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2(b), MWMA 2019; Section 4 IPC / Section 1(5) BNS

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, can a court impose BOTH imprisonment and fine on the convicted husband?
options: No, court must choose between jail OR fine
Yes, Section 4 specifies imprisonment up to 3 years 'AND shall also be liable to fine'
questions.explanation: Section 4 uses cumulative wording 'imprisonment... AND fine'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, what factors does Magistrate consider when fixing subsistence allowance?
options: Financial needs of woman & children, standard of living enjoyed during marriage, and financial capacity/income of husband
Fixed rate of Rs. 500 per day
questions.explanation: Standard maintenance criteria apply: needs, marital status, and husband's means.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, if the father is a wealthy businessman and mother is unemployed, does father automatically get child custody?
options: No, Section 6 gives primary custody entitlement to mother upon triple talaq pronouncement, taking welfare of child into account
questions.explanation: Section 6 explicitly prioritizes mother's custody entitlement post-triple talaq.
