questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, if police refuse to register FIR when wife approaches with triple talaq complaint, what remedy does she have?
options: Send complaint to Superintendent of Police under Section 154(3) CrPC / Section 173 BNS or file application under Section 156(3) CrPC before Magistrate
questions.explanation: Standard CrPC 154(3) / 156(3) remedies apply for police refusal to register cognizable FIR.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, can compounding happen during the POLICE INVESTIGATION stage before court filing?
options: Yes, police officer can compound FIR
No, Section 7(b) specifies compounding 'with the permission of the Magistrate', which requires judicial application before court
questions.explanation: Section 7(b) requires Magistrate permission for compounding.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, if accused husband applies for regular bail after arrest, must Magistrate issue notice to wife?
options: Yes, Section 7(c) explicitly requires hearing the married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced before granting bail
No, notice only if wife is in court
questions.explanation: Section 7(c) statutory mandate requires hearing the wife on bail application.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(1) of the 2019 Act, which Ordinance was repealed?
options: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Second Ordinance, 2019 (Ord. 4 of 2019)
questions.explanation: Section 8(1) explicitly repeals Ordinance 4 of 2019.

questions.question_text: If a Muslim husband pronounces Talaq-e-Biddat, can the wife ALSO file a complaint under Section 85 BNS 2023 (Section 498A IPC - Cruelty)?
options: Yes, if the harassment and illegal pronouncement form part of matrimonial cruelty under Section 85 BNS / 498A IPC
questions.explanation: Offence under 2019 Act can co-exist with cruelty prosecution under Section 85 BNS / 498A IPC.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the 2019 Act, if a husband pronounces triple talaq in a private handwritten letter posted to his wife's address, is it void?
options: No, letter must be published in news
Yes, Section 3 explicitly includes 'by words, either spoken or WRITTEN'
questions.explanation: Section 3 explicitly includes written pronouncements by words.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, what is the nature of the offence of pronouncing instant triple talaq?
options: A cognizable, non-bailable (at police station), and compoundable (with Magistrate permission at victim's instance) criminal offence
A strict liability contempt of court
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act defines it as a cognizable, compoundable (at victim's instance with Magistrate leave), and statutorily restricted bail offence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the 2019 Act, does the Magistrate's order for subsistence allowance require a separate civil suit?
options: No, Magistrate passes the subsistence allowance order in summary proceedings under Section 5 directly
questions.explanation: Section 5 provides summary statutory remedy directly before Magistrate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the 2019 Act, does the mother retain child custody even if she has no independent income?
options: No, custody given to rich father
Yes, mother's right to custody under Section 6 is not barred by her lack of financial income; father pays subsistence allowance for children under Section 5
No, custody given to Wakf Board
questions.explanation: Mother's custody right under S. 6 works in tandem with father's duty to pay child subsistence allowance under S. 5.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(a) of the 2019 Act, if a wife's MARRIED DAUGHTER gives information to police about triple talaq pronounced on her mother, is police information valid?
options: Yes, daughter is a relative by blood under Section 7(a)
questions.explanation: Daughter is a blood relative covered by Section 7(a).

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(b) of the 2019 Act, can police officers FORCE the wife to compound the offence?
options: No, Section 7(b) specifies compounding must be 'at the instance of the married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced'
questions.explanation: Compounding requires voluntary initiative of the victimized married woman.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(c) of the 2019 Act, what is the role of the married Muslim woman during the bail hearing?
options: She is entitled to be heard by the Magistrate before any decision on bail is made
questions.explanation: Section 7(c) guarantees her right of audience before bail is determined.

questions.question_text: If a Muslim husband pronounces triple talaq and is arrested, can he be released on bail by the Police Station Officer without going to Magistrate?
options: No, Section 7(c) explicitly requires a bail application filed before the MAGISTRATE and hearing the wife
questions.explanation: Bail jurisdiction under Section 7(c) is reserved for the Magistrate after hearing the wife.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the 2019 Act, when is the offence complete?
options: A mere verbal threat by the husband to pronounce triple talaq in future carries the full three-year term under Section 4
Neither a pronouncement nor a threat is penalised
Section 4 requires three separate pronouncements made on three different days
Only on the actual pronouncement of talaq as described in Section 3; a mere threat to pronounce it in future is not the completed Section 4 offence
questions.explanation: Section 4 punishes a husband "who pronounces talaq referred to in section 3"; the offence turns on an actual pronouncement, not on a threat to do so.
questions.statute_or_case: Sections 3 and 4, Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019

questions.question_text: What is the official Act number and year of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act?
questions.explanation: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act is Act No. 20 of 2019.

questions.question_text: The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 is:
questions.explanation: The NGT Act received assent on 2 June 2010 and is Act No. 19 of 2010; it was brought into force on 18 October 2010.

questions.question_text: The NGT Act, 2010 repealed and replaced which two earlier enactments?
options: The Water Act, 1974 and the Air Act, 1981
The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991
The National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 and the National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997
The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
questions.explanation: Section 38(1) repeals the National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 and the National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997; pending NEAA cases stand transferred to the NGT.

questions.question_text: The Preamble to the NGT Act, 2010 expressly refers to the decisions taken at which international conferences?
options: The Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015)
The Basel Convention (1989) and the Ramsar Convention (1971)
The Montreal Protocol (1987) and the Vienna Convention (1985)
The Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment (1972) and the Rio Conference on Environment and Development (1992)
questions.explanation: The Preamble records that India participated in the Stockholm Conference (June 1972) and the Rio Conference (June 1992), which called on States to provide effective access to environmental justice and to develop laws on liability and compensation.

questions.question_text: The Preamble to the NGT Act, 2010 notes that the right to a healthy environment has been construed as part of which fundamental right?
options: The right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution
The right to equality under Article 14
The right to freedom of trade under Article 19(1)(g)
The right against exploitation under Article 23
questions.explanation: The Preamble records that in Indian judicial pronouncements the right to a healthy environment has been read into the right to life under Article 21.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(c) of the NGT Act, 2010, 'environment' includes:
options: Water, air and land and the inter-relationship among water, air, land, human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property
Only land and its sub-soil resources
questions.explanation: The Section 2(1)(c) definition of 'environment' mirrors the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and covers the inter-relationship between the physical elements and living beings and property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(m) of the NGT Act, 2010, a 'substantial question relating to environment' includes a case where there is a direct violation of a specific statutory environmental obligation by which the community at large is affected, or:
options: Any private individual suffers minor inconvenience
A municipal bye-law is technically breached
The gravity of damage to the environment or property is substantial, or the damage to public health is broadly measurable
An environmental clearance application is merely delayed
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(m) requires either community-wide impact, substantial gravity of damage, broadly measurable public-health damage, or consequences relating to a specific activity or point source of pollution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(j) of the NGT Act, 2010, the definition of 'person' includes:
options: Only the Central and State Governments
An individual, a Hindu undivided family, a company, a firm, an association of persons, a trustee, a local authority and every artificial juridical person
questions.explanation: Section 2(1)(j) gives 'person' an inclusive, wide meaning so that a broad range of entities can be made liable or can approach the Tribunal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the NGT Act, 2010, the National Green Tribunal is established by:
options: The Supreme Court of India by judicial order
Each State Government within its territory
The Ministry of Law and Justice by executive circular
questions.explanation: Section 3 empowers the Central Government, by notification, to establish the Tribunal with effect from a specified date to exercise the jurisdiction conferred by the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal consists of a full-time Chairperson and:
options: Exactly five Judicial Members and five Expert Members
Not less than ten but not more than twenty full-time Judicial Members, and not less than ten but not more than twenty full-time Expert Members
Any number of part-time members the Chairperson chooses
Only Expert Members, with no Judicial Members
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) fixes the sanctioned strength between 10 and 20 Judicial Members and between 10 and 20 Expert Members, as the Central Government notifies from time to time.

questions.question_text: Under the proviso to Section 4(4)(c) of the NGT Act, 2010, when a Bench hears an application or appeal, the number of Expert Members must be:
options: Always one, regardless of the number of Judicial Members
At least twice the number of Judicial Members
Equal to the number of Judicial Members hearing that application or appeal
Determined afresh by the Central Government for each case
questions.explanation: The proviso to Section 4(4)(c) requires parity: Expert Members on a Bench must equal the Judicial Members, reflecting the multi-disciplinary character of environmental adjudication.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(2) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Chairperson may, if considered necessary:
options: Appoint additional permanent members without Central Government approval
Transfer the case to a High Court
Refer the matter to the Law Commission
Invite one or more persons having specialised knowledge and experience in a particular case to assist the Tribunal in that case
questions.explanation: Section 4(2) allows the Chairperson to co-opt subject experts to assist the Tribunal in a particular case.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(1) of the NGT Act, 2010, a person is qualified for appointment as Chairperson or Judicial Member only if he is or has been:
options: A Judge of the Supreme Court of India or a Chief Justice of a High Court (a Judge of a High Court is also qualified to be a Judicial Member)
A District Judge with ten years' service
A member of the Central Administrative Tribunal
questions.explanation: Section 5(1) restricts Chairperson/Judicial Member to former Supreme Court Judges or High Court Chief Justices; the proviso adds that a sitting or former High Court Judge is qualified to be a Judicial Member.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(2) of the NGT Act, 2010, a person qualified for appointment as an Expert Member must have, among other things:
options: Only a bachelor's degree in any discipline

A prescribed science/engineering qualification with fifteen years' experience including five years' practical experience in environment and forests, OR fifteen years' administrative experience including five years in environmental matters
Ten years' practice as an advocate in a High Court
Membership of a State Pollution Control Board for two years
questions.explanation: Section 5(2) prescribes either a high scientific/technical qualification plus 15 years' experience (with 5 years in environment/forests) or 15 years' administrative experience (with 5 years in environmental matters).

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Chairperson of the Tribunal is appointed by the Central Government:
options: On the sole recommendation of the Environment Minister
After approval by both Houses of Parliament
In consultation with the Chief Justice of India
By the President in his individual discretion
questions.explanation: Section 6(2) requires the Central Government to consult the Chief Justice of India before appointing the Chairperson; Judicial and Expert Members are appointed on the recommendation of a Selection Committee.

questions.question_text: Section 7 of the NGT Act, 2010, as originally enacted, fixes the term of office of the Chairperson, Judicial Member and Expert Member at:
options: Until the age of 62 with no fixed term
Five years from the date they enter office, with no eligibility for re-appointment
questions.explanation: Section 7 originally provided a non-renewable five-year term subject to age ceilings. Section 10A (inserted 2017) now subjects members appointed after the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 to Chapter II of that Act.

questions.question_text: Under the provisos to Section 7 of the NGT Act, 2010, an Expert Member of the Tribunal shall not hold office after attaining the age of:
questions.explanation: The last proviso to Section 7 sets the age ceiling for an Expert Member at 65; a former Supreme Court Judge serving as Chairperson/Judicial Member may serve up to 70.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10(1) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Chairperson or a Judicial Member may be removed by the Central Government only in consultation with the Chief Justice of India and, under Section 10(2), only after an inquiry by:
options: A committee of the Bar Council of India
A Judge of the Supreme Court in which the member has been informed of the charges and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard
questions.explanation: Section 10(2) protects tenure by requiring a Supreme Court Judge's inquiry with due process before removal of the Chairperson or a Judicial Member.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of the NGT Act, 2010, when a vacancy arises in the office of Chairperson by death, resignation or otherwise, the functions are discharged by:
options: A retired Chief Justice nominated by the Bar
The Judicial Member of the Tribunal whom the Central Government authorises by notification, until a new Chairperson is appointed
questions.explanation: Section 11 lets the Central Government authorise a Judicial Member to act as Chairperson during a vacancy.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14(1) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal has jurisdiction over all civil cases where a substantial question relating to environment is involved and the question arises out of the implementation of the enactments specified in:
options: the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure
questions.explanation: Section 14 links the Tribunal's original jurisdiction to the seven environmental statutes listed in Schedule I.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14(3) of the NGT Act, 2010, an application for adjudication of a dispute must ordinarily be made within:
options: Six months from the date on which the cause of action first arose (extendable by a further 60 days for sufficient cause)
Thirty days, with no power to condone delay
Three years, as under the Limitation Act
Twelve years, as for suits relating to immovable property
questions.explanation: Section 14(3) prescribes a six-month limitation for dispute applications, with a further 60 days condonable on sufficient cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(1) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal may by order provide for:
options: Relief and compensation to victims of pollution and environmental damage, restitution of damaged property, and restitution of the environment
Only issuing advisory guidelines to Pollution Control Boards
questions.explanation: Section 15(1) empowers the Tribunal to award compensation, property restitution and environmental restitution; under Section 15(2) this is in addition to relief under the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(3) of the NGT Act, 2010, an application for compensation, relief or restitution must be made within:
options: One year from the date of the accident
Five years from the date the cause for compensation first arose (extendable by a further 60 days for sufficient cause)
Ten years from the date of knowledge
questions.explanation: Section 15(3) fixes a five-year outer limit for compensation claims, with a further 60 days condonable for sufficient cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the NGT Act, 2010, an appeal to the Tribunal must be preferred within:
options: Ninety days, with no power of condonation
Sixty days, extendable by six months
Thirty days from communication of the order, decision or direction (extendable by a further 60 days for sufficient cause)
questions.explanation: Section 16 gives a 30-day appeal period against the listed authority orders, with a further 60 days condonable for sufficient cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal exercises appellate jurisdiction over orders such as those under Section 28 of the Water Act, 1974, Section 31 of the Air Act, 1981 and:
options: Directions issued under Section 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and orders granting or refusing environmental clearance
Orders of criminal courts under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
Assessment orders under the Income-tax Act, 1961
Land acquisition awards under the Right to Fair Compensation Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Section 16 lists appealable orders under the Water Act, Water Cess Act, Forest (Conservation) Act, Air Act, Environment (Protection) Act (including environmental clearance decisions) and the Biological Diversity Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17(3) of the NGT Act, 2010, in the case of an accident the Tribunal applies:
options: The principle of volenti non fit injuria
questions.explanation: Section 17(3) codifies no-fault liability for accidents while handling hazardous substances, so the claimant need not prove negligence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17(2) of the NGT Act, 2010, where damage cannot be attributed to a single activity but is the combined effect of several, the Tribunal may:
options: Dismiss the claim for want of a single identifiable polluter
Direct the State Government to bear the entire liability
Apportion the liability for relief or compensation among those responsible on an equitable basis
Refer the question of apportionment to arbitration
questions.explanation: Section 17(2) allows equitable apportionment of liability among multiple contributors to environmental damage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18(2) of the NGT Act, 2010, an application to the Tribunal may be made by, among others:
options: Only the person who has personally sustained physical injury
Only registered environmental NGOs with FCRA clearance
Any aggrieved person, including a representative body or organisation, and specified public authorities such as Pollution Control Boards
questions.explanation: Section 18(2) adopts a liberal standing rule, allowing aggrieved persons, representative bodies, legal representatives of the deceased and government/statutory authorities to apply.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18(3) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal shall endeavour to dispose of an application or appeal finally within:
options: Six months from the date of filing, after giving the parties an opportunity to be heard
One year from the date of filing
Ninety days from the first hearing
Two years from the date of filing
questions.explanation: Section 18(3) sets a six-month endeavour timeline for final disposal, reflecting the Act's object of expeditious environmental adjudication.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(1) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal is not bound by the procedure in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 but is:
options: Bound by the Code of Criminal Procedure instead
Guided by the principles of natural justice
Bound by the rules of the High Court where it sits
Free to ignore natural justice in urgent cases
questions.explanation: Section 19(1) frees the Tribunal from CPC procedure but requires adherence to natural justice; Section 19(2) lets it regulate its own procedure.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(3) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal is:
options: Strictly bound by the Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Bound only by the hearsay rule
Not bound by the rules of evidence in the Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Required to apply the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891
questions.explanation: Section 19(3) exempts the Tribunal from the technical rules of evidence, though Section 19(4) gives it civil-court powers such as summoning witnesses and requiring production of documents.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(4) of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal has the same powers as a civil court under the CPC in respect of matters such as summoning witnesses, requiring discovery of documents, and:
options: Passing interim orders including injunction or stay, and ordering a person to cease and desist from violating a Schedule I enactment
questions.explanation: Section 19(4) lists civil-court powers including interim orders and cease-and-desist orders; Section 19(5) deems Tribunal proceedings to be judicial proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the NGT Act, 2010, while passing any order, decision or award the Tribunal shall apply:
options: The principle of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle
Only the principle of strict liability
questions.explanation: Section 20 statutorily mandates the three core principles of environmental jurisprudence recognised in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996).

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the NGT Act, 2010, the decision of the Tribunal is:
options: Always unanimous, or the case is dismissed
By majority of the Members; if opinion is equally divided, the Chairperson (if he has not heard the matter) hears and decides it
Taken only by the senior-most Judicial Member
Referred to the Supreme Court whenever members disagree
questions.explanation: Section 21 provides for majority decisions and a mechanism for resolving an equal division of opinion.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of the NGT Act, 2010, an appeal against an award, decision or order of the Tribunal lies to:
options: The jurisdictional High Court, within thirty days, on any ground
The Central Government, within sixty days
The Supreme Court, within ninety days of communication, on any of the grounds specified in Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
A larger Bench of the Tribunal itself
questions.explanation: Section 22 provides a direct statutory appeal to the Supreme Court within 90 days, limited to substantial questions of law of the kind in Section 100 CPC; the Supreme Court may condone delay for sufficient cause.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of the NGT Act, 2010, an amount ordered by way of compensation or relief for damage to the environment is remitted to:
options: The Prime Minister's National Relief Fund
The general revenue account of the State concerned
The Environmental Relief Fund established under Section 7A of the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991
questions.explanation: Section 24 channels environmental-damage compensation into the Environmental Relief Fund for use on environment-related purposes as prescribed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the NGT Act, 2010, an award, order or decision of the Tribunal:
options: Is executable by the Tribunal as a decree of a civil court, and unpaid amounts are recoverable as arrears of land revenue
Can be enforced only by a fresh civil suit
Is merely recommendatory and not enforceable
Requires confirmation by the High Court before execution
questions.explanation: Section 25 gives Tribunal orders the force of a civil-court decree; the Tribunal may also transmit the order to a civil court for execution, and dues are recoverable as arrears of land revenue.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26(1) of the NGT Act, 2010, an individual who fails to comply with an order, award or decision of the Tribunal is punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or fine which may extend to:
options: Ten crore rupees, or with both
One crore rupees, or with both
questions.explanation: Section 26(1) prescribes up to 3 years' imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs 10 crore for an individual, with an additional fine up to Rs 25,000 per day for continuing default.

questions.question_text: Under the proviso to Section 26(1) of the NGT Act, 2010, a company that fails to comply with a Tribunal order is punishable with fine which may extend to:
options: Ten crore rupees, with no additional daily fine
Twenty-five crore rupees, with an additional fine up to one lakh rupees per day of continuing default
questions.explanation: The proviso to Section 26(1) enhances the fine for companies to up to Rs 25 crore, plus up to Rs 1 lakh per day for continuing default.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26(2) of the NGT Act, 2010, every offence under the Act is:
options: Triable only by the Court of Session
Compoundable by the Pollution Control Board
Deemed to be non-cognizable, notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure
questions.explanation: Section 26(2) makes NGT offences non-cognizable; under Section 30 no court inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate First Class may try them.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the NGT Act, 2010, where a Government Department fails to comply with a Tribunal order:
options: The Head of the Department is deemed guilty unless he proves the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence
No prosecution is possible because of sovereign immunity
Only the concerned clerk is liable
The matter is closed after an internal departmental inquiry
questions.explanation: Section 28 fixes vicarious criminal liability on the Head of the Department, with a due-diligence defence, and also on other officers whose consent, connivance or neglect is proved.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the NGT Act, 2010, with effect from the establishment of the Tribunal:
options: Civil courts retain concurrent jurisdiction with the Tribunal
No civil court has jurisdiction to entertain appeals or settle disputes or claims that the Tribunal is empowered to determine, and no civil court may grant an injunction in such matters
Only High Courts lose jurisdiction, not subordinate courts
Civil courts may still grant interim injunctions pending Tribunal proceedings
questions.explanation: Section 29 bars civil-court jurisdiction over matters within the Tribunal's remit; the constitutional writ jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court is not ousted.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the NGT Act, 2010, a court may take cognizance of an offence under the Act only on a complaint made by the Central Government or its authorised officer, or by:
options: Any person, without any prior notice
The registrar of the Tribunal suo motu
A person who has given not less than sixty days' notice of the alleged offence and of the intention to complain
A State Pollution Control Board, without notice
questions.explanation: Section 30 restricts who may set the criminal law in motion and requires a citizen complainant to give 60 days' prior notice, mirroring Section 19 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the NGT Act, 2010, the Chairperson, Members, officers and other employees of the Tribunal are deemed to be:
options: Judicial officers of the High Court
Employees of the Ministry of Environment
Public servants within the meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code
questions.explanation: Section 31 gives Tribunal personnel public-servant status; Section 32 protects action taken in good faith under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33 of the NGT Act, 2010:
options: The provisions of the Act have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent in any other law for the time being in force
The Act yields to any inconsistent State law
The Act applies only where no other environmental law applies
The Act overrides the Constitution to the extent of inconsistency
questions.explanation: Section 33 is a non-obstante clause giving the NGT Act overriding effect over inconsistent laws and instruments.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34 of the NGT Act, 2010, Schedule I may be amended by:
options: The Tribunal itself by a full-court resolution
The Central Government by notification, with every such notification laid in draft before both Houses of Parliament for thirty days
Any State Government for its own territory
The Supreme Court while deciding an appeal
questions.explanation: Section 34 allows the Central Government to add or omit environmental enactments in Schedule I, subject to prior draft placement before Parliament.

questions.question_text: Schedule I to the NGT Act, 2010 lists how many environmental enactments over which the Tribunal has jurisdiction?
questions.explanation: Schedule I lists seven statutes: the Water Act 1974, Water Cess Act 1977, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Air Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 and Biological Diversity Act 2002.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statutes is NOT included in Schedule I to the NGT Act, 2010?
options: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
questions.explanation: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Indian Forest Act, 1927 are not in Schedule I, so the NGT has no jurisdiction over disputes arising purely under those Acts.

questions.question_text: Schedule II to the NGT Act, 2010 specifies:
options: The heads under which compensation or relief for damage may be claimed (such as death, disability, loss of wages, medical expenses, damage to property, flora and fauna, and environmental restoration)
The composition and salaries of Tribunal members
The list of environmental enactments within jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Schedule II (referred to in Sections 15(4) and 17(1)) enumerates the specific heads of compensation the Tribunal may award.

questions.question_text: The Principal Bench of the National Green Tribunal is located at:
options: New Delhi, with Zonal Benches at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai
Nagpur, with Zonal Benches at Delhi and Chennai
Bengaluru, with Zonal Benches at Delhi and Kolkata
questions.explanation: Under the notification made pursuant to Section 4(3), the Principal Bench sits at New Delhi and the four Zonal Benches sit at Bhopal (Central), Pune (Western), Kolkata (Eastern) and Chennai (Southern); Circuit Benches are also held.

questions.question_text: In Bhopal Gas Peedith Mahila Udyog Sangathan v. Union of India (2012), the Supreme Court held that environmental matters falling within the NGT Act, 2010:
options: Can only be heard by the Supreme Court
Must always be filed as civil suits in district courts
Should ordinarily be instituted before and adjudicated by the NGT, which has exclusive jurisdiction over Schedule I environmental disputes
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court directed that cases involving substantial environmental questions under the Schedule I enactments be transferred to and dealt with by the NGT.
questions.statute_or_case: Bhopal Gas Peedith Mahila Udyog Sangathan v. Union of India (2012) 8 SCC 326

questions.question_text: In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996), the Supreme Court held that the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle:
options: Have no place in Indian law without express legislation
Apply only to Central Government projects
Were rejected as contrary to the right to trade
Are part of the environmental law of India and essential features of sustainable development
questions.explanation: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum recognised sustainable development, the precautionary principle and polluter pays as part of Indian law; Section 20 of the NGT Act later codified them.
questions.statute_or_case: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647

questions.question_text: In Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha (2021), the Supreme Court held that the NGT:
options: Has the power to take suo motu cognizance of environmental issues
Can act only on a formal application or appeal by a party
Cannot pass any order without the Central Government's sanction
Is barred from issuing directions to statutory authorities
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court affirmed that, given its sui generis role and the Act's beneficial object, the NGT is not powerless to act suo motu on environmental exigencies.
questions.statute_or_case: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha, 2021 INSC 624

questions.question_text: The right of the NGT to be guided by the polluter pays principle traces to the Supreme Court's decision in:
options: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) (Bichhri case)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
questions.explanation: In the Bichhri case the Supreme Court applied the polluter pays principle, holding that the financial cost of remedying environmental damage falls on the industry that caused it.
questions.statute_or_case: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) 3 SCC 212

questions.question_text: The absolute liability standard often applied by the NGT in hazardous-activity accident claims originates in:
options: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), as adopted without change in India
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) (Oleum Gas Leak case)
Ryland's rule as limited by the Bhopal settlement
questions.explanation: In the Oleum Gas Leak case the Supreme Court evolved the rule of absolute liability for enterprises engaged in hazardous activities, without the exceptions to the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher.
questions.statute_or_case: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, AIR 1987 SC 1086

questions.question_text: Under Section 32 of the NGT Act, 2010, protection from suit or legal proceeding is available for:
options: Any act, whether in good faith or not, by a Tribunal Member
Only acts of the Central Government, not State Governments
Only acts done after prior sanction of the Supreme Court
Anything done or intended to be done in good faith in pursuance of the Act or any rule or order made under it
questions.explanation: Section 32 gives good-faith immunity to Government and statutory-authority employees and to the Chairperson and Members for acts done under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of the NGT Act, 2010, where the Tribunal holds a claim to be false or vexatious:
options: It may, after recording reasons, award costs, including lost benefits due to any interim injunction
It must impose a mandatory minimum penalty of Rs 1 lakh
It has no power to award costs at all
It must refer the claimant for prosecution
questions.explanation: Section 23 gives the Tribunal a general power as to costs and a specific power to award costs against false or vexatious claims.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(5) of the NGT Act, 2010, all proceedings before the Tribunal are deemed to be:
options: Judicial proceedings, and the Tribunal is deemed to be a civil court for specified purposes of the criminal procedure law
Arbitral proceedings under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
questions.explanation: Section 19(5) deems Tribunal proceedings judicial (for the offences of giving false evidence etc.) and deems the Tribunal a civil court for the purposes of Section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the criminal procedure code.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38(3) and (5) of the NGT Act, 2010, on the establishment of the NGT, the National Environment Appellate Authority:
options: Continues to function alongside the NGT
Is converted into a Zonal Bench of the NGT
Stands dissolved, and its pending cases stand transferred to the NGT
Becomes an advisory body to the Central Government
questions.explanation: Section 38(3)-(5) dissolves the NEAA and transfers its pending cases to the NGT, to be disposed of as if filed under the NEAA Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a 'negotiable instrument' means:
options: Any document of title to goods
A promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer
Any written agreement to pay money
questions.explanation: Section 13 recognises only three instruments as negotiable by statute — promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques — though custom may make other instruments negotiable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a 'promissory note' is:
options: An order by one person to another to pay money
An instrument always drawn on a banker

An instrument in writing (not being a bank-note or a currency-note) containing an unconditional undertaking, signed by the maker, to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person, or to the bearer of the instrument
questions.explanation: A promissory note has two parties (maker and payee) and contains an unconditional promise to pay; a currency note is expressly excluded.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a 'bill of exchange' is:
options: An unconditional promise by the maker to pay
An instrument that can never be payable to bearer
A document that must be attested by two witnesses

An instrument in writing containing an unconditional order, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person, or to the bearer of the instrument
questions.explanation: A bill of exchange has three parties — drawer, drawee and payee — and contains an order (not a promise) to pay.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a 'cheque' is:
options: A bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand, and includes the electronic image of a truncated cheque and a cheque in electronic form
Any order to pay money on demand
A promissory note payable at a bank
An instrument payable only after a fixed period
questions.explanation: A cheque is always drawn on a banker and always payable on demand; the definition was expanded to cover truncated and electronic cheques.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the 'holder' of a negotiable instrument is:
options: Any person who physically possesses the instrument
Any person entitled in his own name to the possession of the instrument and to receive or recover the amount due thereon from the parties liable
questions.explanation: Section 8 requires both a right to possession and an entitlement to recover; a finder or thief in possession is not a 'holder'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a 'holder in due course' is a person who:
options: For consideration became the possessor of the instrument (or the payee/indorsee) before it was overdue, without notice that the title of the transferor was defective
Is merely named as payee, without consideration
questions.explanation: A holder in due course takes the instrument free of prior defects of title and can enforce it against all prior parties (Sections 36 and 53).

questions.question_text: Under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the law raises certain presumptions until the contrary is proved, including that:
options: The holder is always a thief
Every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that it was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration
questions.explanation: Section 118 presumes consideration, date, time of acceptance and transfer, order of indorsements, stamping, and that the holder is a holder in due course.

questions.question_text: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds is an offence punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both
questions.explanation: Section 138 (inserted in 1988) criminalises cheque dishonour where the cheque was issued to discharge a legally enforceable debt or liability and is returned unpaid for insufficiency of funds or because it exceeds the arrangement.

questions.question_text: Under the provisos to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, prosecution for cheque dishonour is possible only if:
options: The cheque is presented within one year and notice is given within one year

The cheque is presented within its validity period (generally three months), the payee gives a written demand notice within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour, and the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receipt of the notice
No notice is required at all
The drawer is given 90 days to pay
questions.explanation: The cause of action under Section 138 arises only on the drawer's failure to pay within 15 days of the demand notice; the complaint must then be filed within one month (Section 142).

questions.question_text: Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, in a prosecution under Section 138:
options: The complainant must prove the existence of the debt beyond reasonable doubt
There is no presumption in favour of the holder
It is presumed, until the contrary is proved, that the holder of the cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a debt or other liability
The accused is presumed innocent of the debt
questions.explanation: Section 139 raises a rebuttable presumption of a legally enforceable debt in favour of the cheque holder; the accused must raise a probable defence to rebut it (Rangappa v. Sri Mohan, 2010).

questions.question_text: Under Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a complaint for an offence under Section 138:
options: May be filed by any member of the public
Is triable only by the Court of Session

Must be made in writing by the payee or holder in due course, within one month of the date the cause of action arises, and is triable only by a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class (delay may be condoned for sufficient cause)
questions.explanation: Section 142 makes the offence non-cognizable and complaint-based; Section 142A and Section 142(2) deal with the place of trial (where the payee's bank branch is situated).

questions.question_text: Under Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (inserted in 2018), the court trying a Section 138 offence may:
options: Direct the drawer to pay interim compensation of up to twenty per cent of the cheque amount to the complainant, even before conviction
Award the complainant the full cheque amount as a matter of course
Do nothing until the trial concludes
questions.explanation: Section 143A allows interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount; Section 148 allows an appellate court to order deposit of at least 20% of the fine or compensation as a condition of suspending the sentence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 118(g) and Section 138 jurisprudence, the offence of cheque bouncing is committed by:
options: The payee who presented the cheque
The drawer of the cheque (the account holder who issued it), and, where the drawer is a company, the persons in charge of and responsible to the company under Section 141
The bank that dishonoured the cheque
questions.explanation: Section 141 extends liability for company cheques to directors and officers in charge of the business, subject to a due-diligence defence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, 'indorsement' means:
options: Only a signature on the face of the instrument
The act of the drawee accepting a bill
When the maker or holder of a negotiable instrument signs it (otherwise than as such maker) on the face or back, or on a slip of paper annexed to it (an allonge), for the purpose of negotiation
questions.explanation: An indorsement 'in blank' (Section 16) specifies no indorsee and makes the instrument payable to bearer; an indorsement 'in full' names the indorsee.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a banker who, having sufficient funds of the customer, wrongfully dishonours the customer's cheque:
options: Has no liability to the drawer
Is liable only to the payee
Commits a criminal offence under Section 138
Is liable to compensate the drawer for any loss or damage caused by such default
questions.explanation: Section 31 imposes a statutory duty on the drawee banker to honour the customer's cheque where duly required and funds are available.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 123 to 126 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a cheque crossed 'account payee' or 'not negotiable':
options: Must be paid only into a bank account (a crossed cheque cannot be paid over the counter), and 'not negotiable' crossing means the transferee gets no better title than the transferor
May be encashed over the counter by anyone
Is payable only to the drawer
questions.explanation: A general crossing (Section 123) directs payment only through a banker; a special crossing (Section 124) names a specific banker; 'not negotiable' (Section 130) destroys negotiability (Great Western Railway v. London and County Banking Co.).

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the 'drawer' and 'drawee' of a bill of exchange are:
options: The drawer is the person who pays and the drawee is the person who receives payment
The drawer is the maker of the bill; the drawee is the person directed to pay; and when the drawee accepts the bill he is called the 'acceptor'
Interchangeable terms for the same person
questions.explanation: Section 7 also defines 'payee' (the person named to receive payment) and 'drawee in case of need'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, 'days of grace' allowed on an instrument payable at a fixed period after date or sight (not payable on demand) are:
options: No days of grace are allowed
questions.explanation: Section 22 adds three days of grace to the nominal maturity date of a time instrument; a cheque and any instrument payable on demand carry no days of grace.

questions.question_text: Under Section 85 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, where a cheque payable to order purports to be indorsed by or on behalf of the payee, the drawee banker who pays it in due course:
options: Remains fully liable for the forged indorsement
Must reimburse the true owner personally
Is discharged, even though the indorsement is later found to have been forged or made without authority
questions.explanation: Sections 85 and 85A protect a paying banker who pays an order cheque or a bank draft on an apparently regular indorsement in due course; Section 131 protects a collecting banker acting in good faith and without negligence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, 'payment in due course' means payment:
options: In accordance with the apparent tenor of the instrument, in good faith and without negligence, to a person in possession of the instrument, under circumstances not affording reasonable ground to believe that he is not entitled to receive the amount
Any payment made by a banker
Payment made only to the original payee
Payment after obtaining a court order
questions.explanation: 'Payment in due course' discharges the party paying and is a precondition for the banker protections in Sections 85, 85A, 89 and 128.

questions.question_text: Under Section 87 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a material alteration of a negotiable instrument, made without the consent of the parties liable:
options: Has no effect on the instrument

Renders the instrument void as against anyone who was a party to it at the time of the alteration and who did not consent to it (a holder in due course who is not a party to the alteration may still enforce it according to its original tenor if the alteration is not apparent)
Makes the instrument payable to bearer
questions.explanation: Changing the date, sum payable, time or place of payment, or the parties, is a material alteration; crossing an uncrossed cheque and filling blanks are permitted (Sections 49 and 125).

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, where the amount stated in an instrument differs in figures and in words:
options: The instrument is void for uncertainty
The amount stated in words is the amount undertaken or ordered to be paid
The lower of the two amounts is payable
questions.explanation: Section 18 resolves the conflict in favour of the words.

questions.question_text: Under Section 46 and Section 48 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, 'negotiation' of a negotiable instrument payable to order is effected by:
options: A written assignment attested by two witnesses
questions.explanation: An order instrument is negotiated by indorsement and delivery; a bearer instrument is negotiated by delivery alone (Section 47).

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the liability of the drawer of a bill of exchange or cheque is that:
options: In case of dishonour by the drawee or acceptor, he is bound to compensate the holder, provided due notice of dishonour has been given to or received by him
He is not liable once he has drawn the instrument
He is liable only if he is also the acceptor
He is primarily liable before the acceptor
questions.explanation: The drawer's liability is secondary and conditional on dishonour and notice; the acceptor of a bill (Section 32) and the maker of a note are primarily liable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 99 and Section 100 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, 'noting' and 'protest' are:
options: Steps required for every dishonoured cheque
A formal record by a notary public of the dishonour of a bill (noting) and a formal certificate of dishonour (protest), which are compulsory only for foreign bills
questions.explanation: Noting and protest authenticate the fact of dishonour; while optional for inland bills, they are compulsory for a foreign bill if required by the law of the place where it was drawn.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and settled law, the maker of a promissory note and the acceptor of a bill of exchange are:
options: Not liable unless a notice of dishonour is served
Primarily and absolutely liable on the instrument
Liable only to the immediate party
questions.explanation: Primary liability rests on the maker of a note and the acceptor of a bill; drawers and indorsers are secondarily (conditionally) liable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted or indorsed without consideration:
options: Creates no obligation of payment between the parties to the transaction, but if any party has transferred it to a holder for consideration, such holder and every subsequent holder deriving title from him may recover on it
questions.explanation: Section 43 preserves the rights of a holder for consideration even though the instrument originated without consideration (an accommodation instrument).

questions.question_text: Under Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (inserted in 2002), an offence under the Act is:
options: Triable only by the High Court
questions.explanation: Section 147 makes every offence under the Act compoundable, notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure; the Supreme Court has issued guidelines encouraging early compounding (Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H., 2010).

questions.question_text: Under Section 46 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the making, acceptance or indorsement of a negotiable instrument is completed by:
questions.explanation: Section 46 makes delivery essential to complete every negotiable act; until delivery the instrument is inchoate.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, where one person signs and delivers to another a stamped but otherwise incomplete instrument ('inchoate instrument'):
options: The holder may not fill in any details
He authorises the holder to complete it for any amount not exceeding the amount covered by the stamp, and the instrument so completed is enforceable by a holder in due course
Only the signer may complete it
questions.explanation: Section 20 protects a holder in due course of a completed inchoate instrument even if it was completed for more than the person intended, up to the stamp value.

questions.question_text: The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 is:
questions.explanation: The OSH Code received assent on 28 September 2020 and is Act No. 37 of 2020.

questions.question_text: The OSH Code, 2020 amalgamates and repeals how many earlier central labour enactments?
options: Thirteen (including the Factories Act 1948, Mines Act 1952, Contract Labour Act 1970, Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979, Building and Other Construction Workers Act 1996 and Plantations Labour Act 1951)
questions.explanation: Section 143 repeals thirteen enactments relating to safety, health and working conditions across factories, mines, docks, plantations, construction, contract labour, migrant workers, transport, beedi, journalism, cinema and sales promotion.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(4) read with Section 3 of the OSH Code, 2020, the Code generally applies to every establishment in which:
options: Twenty or more workers are employed
One hundred or more workers are employed
Any number of workers is employed
Ten or more workers are employed, or were employed on any day of the preceding twelve months
questions.explanation: The general applicability threshold is 10 workers; the Code does not apply to offices of the Central or State Government or to a ship of war, though it applies to contract labour engaged in Government offices.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1) of the OSH Code, 2020, 'factory' means premises where a manufacturing process is carried on with the aid of power and employing:
options: Twenty or more workers (or forty or more workers where the manufacturing process is carried on without the aid of power)
Ten or more workers with power, twenty without power
Fifty or more workers in every case
questions.explanation: The OSH Code raises the Factories Act thresholds from 10/20 to 20 (with power) / 40 (without power), taking many small units out of the 'factory' regime.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the OSH Code, 2020, every employer must issue to every employee:
options: An appointment letter in the prescribed form (and to existing employees within three months of the commencement of the relevant provision)
A appointment letter only if the employee asks
questions.explanation: Section 6(1)(f) makes a formal appointment letter mandatory for the first time across all covered establishments, formalising employment relationships.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the OSH Code, 2020, every employer must also ensure that every employee is:
options: Provided a free annual (or as prescribed) medical examination, for such classes of establishments and workers above a prescribed age as may be notified
questions.explanation: Section 6 requires free periodical medical examination for prescribed categories of workers, along with maintenance of a safe workplace, safe plant and systems of work.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the OSH Code, 2020, the maximum daily working hours for a worker (subject to the appropriate Government's power to prescribe) is:
questions.explanation: Section 25 fixes the normal working day at 8 hours; the appropriate Government prescribes weekly hours, spread-over and the number of overtime hours (subject to worker consent).

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the OSH Code, 2020, where a worker works overtime, he must be paid wages at:
options: Twice the ordinary rate of wages
One and a half times the ordinary rate
questions.explanation: Section 27 fixes the overtime rate at double the ordinary rate of wages, consistent with the Factories Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 32 of the OSH Code, 2020, an adult worker who has worked 180 days or more in a calendar year is entitled to annual leave with wages at the rate of:
options: One day for every ten days of work
One day of leave for every twenty days of work (one day for every fifteen days for an adolescent worker or a worker in an underground mine)
One month's leave regardless of days worked
No annual leave; only casual leave
questions.explanation: Section 32 continues the Factories Act formula: adults earn leave at 1:20, adolescents and underground-mine workers at 1:15, after 180 qualifying days.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43 of the OSH Code, 2020, the employment of women:
options: Is prohibited between 7 p.m. and 6 a.m. in every case
Is permitted in all establishments for all types of work, including before 6 a.m. and beyond 7 p.m., subject to the woman's consent and to prescribed conditions of safety, holidays and working hours
Is permitted only with the husband's consent
questions.explanation: Section 43 removes the blanket bar on night work by women and on their employment in certain operations, replacing it with a consent-plus-safeguards model; Section 44 requires adequate safety before deploying women in hazardous operations.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45 of the OSH Code, 2020, the provisions on contract labour apply to every establishment or contractor in which:
options: Twenty or more contract labour are employed
Ten or more contract labour are employed
One hundred or more contract labour are employed
Fifty or more contract labour are employed, or were employed on any day of the preceding twelve months
questions.explanation: The OSH Code raises the contract-labour threshold from 20 (under the Contract Labour Act, 1970) to 50, and requires the contractor to obtain a licence valid for five years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 57 of the OSH Code, 2020, the employment of contract labour:
options: Is prohibited in the 'core activities' of an establishment (with specified exceptions such as sanitation, security, canteen, and activities where the need is intermittent or of a sporadic nature)
Is permitted in every activity without restriction
Is permitted only in Government establishments
questions.explanation: Section 57 introduces a statutory bar on contract labour in core activities, with an enumerated list of activities not regarded as core.

questions.question_text: Under Section 55 of the OSH Code, 2020, if a contractor fails to pay wages to contract labour:
options: The contract labour has no remedy
The principal employer is liable to pay the wages due and may recover the amount from the contractor
Only the State Government is liable
questions.explanation: Section 55 continues the principal employer's secondary liability for wages of contract labour engaged through the contractor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 59 of the OSH Code, 2020 (Part on inter-State migrant workers), the provisions apply to every establishment in which:
options: Five or more inter-State migrant workers are employed
Twenty or more inter-State migrant workers are employed
Ten or more inter-State migrant workers are employed, or were employed on any day of the preceding twelve months
Any number of inter-State migrant workers is employed
questions.explanation: The OSH Code covers establishments with 10+ inter-State migrant workers and, significantly, allows a migrant worker to register himself on the portal (self-registration), not only through a contractor.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 60 to 63 of the OSH Code, 2020, inter-State migrant workers are entitled to:
options: A one-time cash grant of Rs 50,000
A journey (travelling) allowance for the to-and-fro journey home, portability of ration (public distribution system) benefits and building-worker welfare benefits, and access to a toll-free helpline
questions.explanation: The OSH Code adds journey allowance (payable annually by the employer), PDS portability and helpline access to the protections for inter-State migrant workers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the OSH Code, 2020, every employee at the workplace has a duty to:
options: Take reasonable care for his own health and safety and that of others, comply with safety and health requirements, and not do anything wilfully or negligently that may endanger himself or others
Ignore safety rules if they slow down work
Report only accidents that cause death
Do nothing; all duties are on the employer
questions.explanation: Section 13 imposes safety duties on employees; Section 15 bars any person from wilfully or recklessly interfering with or misusing anything provided for safety, health or welfare.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the OSH Code, 2020, every employee in an establishment has the right to:
options: Obtain from the employer information relating to safety and health standards, and to represent to the employer or Inspector-cum-Facilitator about inadequate safety arrangements
questions.explanation: Section 14 gives workers a right to information about safety and health; Section 89 gives workers in factories the right to warn about imminent danger and to stop work if the employer does not act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of the OSH Code, 2020, a Safety Committee (with equal representation of employers and workers) and safety officers must be provided:
options: In every establishment with 5 or more workers
In such establishments or class of establishments as the appropriate Government may require by order or notification
questions.explanation: Section 22 empowers the appropriate Government to mandate Safety Committees and the appointment of safety officers for notified establishments (typically large factories, mines, construction sites and hazardous units).

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of the OSH Code, 2020, welfare facilities to be provided by the employer include:
options: Drinking water, latrines and urinals, washing facilities, first-aid boxes, and a canteen in establishments employing one hundred or more workers
questions.explanation: Section 24 lists the welfare facilities; the canteen obligation attaches at 100+ workers, and creche facilities are provided as prescribed by the Central Government.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the OSH Code, 2020, where an accident in an establishment causes death or bodily injury preventing the injured person from working for more than 48 hours, the employer must:
options: Give notice of the accident to the specified authority in the prescribed form and manner
questions.explanation: Sections 10-12 require notice of prescribed accidents, dangerous occurrences and notifiable occupational diseases to the specified authority.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34 of the OSH Code, 2020, the officer who enforces the Code is designated the:
options: Inspector-cum-Facilitator, appointed by the appropriate Government, with both facilitation and inspection functions under a web-based inspection scheme
questions.explanation: Section 34 replaces the various inspectorates (Factories, Mines, etc.) with a common 'Inspector-cum-Facilitator' operating under a technology-enabled, randomised inspection scheme.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of the OSH Code, 2020, occupational safety and health standards are declared by:
options: Each employer for its own establishment
The Central Government by notification, on the recommendation of the National Occupational Safety and Health Advisory Board
questions.explanation: Section 18 read with Section 16 provides for the National Occupational Safety and Health Advisory Board to advise on standards, which the Central Government then notifies.

questions.question_text: Under Section 94 of the OSH Code, 2020, the general penalty for a contravention of the Code (not otherwise specifically provided for) is:
options: Imprisonment for not less than one year in every case
A penalty of not less than two lakh rupees, which may extend to three lakh rupees, with a further penalty of up to two thousand rupees per day of continued contravention after conviction
questions.explanation: Section 94 sets the residual monetary penalty; the Code favours monetary penalties over imprisonment for routine contraventions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 103 of the OSH Code, 2020, where a contravention of a safety provision results in an accident causing the death of an employee, the offender is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment up to two years, or a fine of not less than five lakh rupees, or both (and the court may direct at least half the fine to be paid to the victim's legal heirs)
questions.explanation: Section 103 provides enhanced punishment where a safety contravention causes death or serious bodily injury, with a portion of the fine going to the victim or heirs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 114 of the OSH Code, 2020, most offences under the Code (other than those causing death or serious bodily injury) may be:
options: Compounded, on payment of a sum in the prescribed manner, before or after the institution of prosecution
Compounded only by the High Court
Compounded only if the worker consents
questions.explanation: Section 114 allows compounding of most offences; Section 111 lets officers of the appropriate Government impose monetary penalties for certain contraventions instead of prosecution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 110(3) of the OSH Code, 2020, no court inferior to that of a:
options: Court of Session shall try an offence
District Judge shall try an offence
Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class shall try an offence punishable under the Code
High Court shall try an offence
questions.explanation: Section 110(3) fixes the trial forum; Section 110(2) requires the complaint (made by the Inspector-cum-Facilitator) to be filed within six months of the offence coming to his knowledge (Section 112 only deems the place of the establishment to be the place where the offence was committed).

questions.question_text: Under Section 117 of the OSH Code, 2020, where the age of a person is in question in a proceeding under the Code:
options: Age is presumed to be 25 in all cases
No proof of age is ever required

The onus of proving that the person is not a child or adolescent, or is above a specified age, lies on the person alleging it (with the employer bearing the onus in disputes about employing young persons)
questions.explanation: Section 117 places the burden regarding age; Section 118 places on the employer the onus of proving the limits of what was 'practicable' in respect of safety obligations.

questions.question_text: Under the OSH Code, 2020, Chapter XI contains special provisions relating to 'dangerous operations' and hazardous processes, largely retaining the post-Bhopal safeguards of the Factories Act, including:
options: Compulsory disclosure of information by the occupier, a site appraisal committee, emergency standards, permissible limits of exposure to chemicals, and the workers' right to warn about imminent danger
A blanket ban on all chemical industry
Immunity for occupiers of hazardous units
questions.explanation: Sections 82-90 carry forward the special hazardous-process regime introduced into the Factories Act after the 1984 Bhopal gas disaster.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of the OSH Code, 2020, every worker is entitled to:
options: At least one day of rest (weekly holiday) in a week, and a compensatory holiday if required to work on a rest day
Two days off every week without exception
A holiday only on national festivals
questions.explanation: Section 26 guarantees a weekly holiday and compensatory holidays for work done on rest days.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the OSH Code, 2020:
options: A worker may work in up to three factories a day
No worker shall be required or allowed to work in any establishment on a day on which he has already been working in another establishment (a bar on double employment in a factory or mine)
The bar applies only to Government employees
questions.explanation: Section 30 restricts double employment on the same day in a factory or mine, and Section 29 prohibits overlapping shifts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 37 of the OSH Code, 2020, the appropriate Government may provide for:
options: Third-party audit and certification of compliance with the Code by such persons and in such manner as may be prescribed
questions.explanation: Section 37 introduces third-party safety audits as a supplement to inspection.

questions.question_text: Under Section 66 of the OSH Code, 2020, an audio-visual (cine) worker:
options: Cannot be employed without a written agreement, a copy of which is provided to the worker
Need not have any written contract
Is excluded from the Code entirely
questions.explanation: Section 66 requires a written agreement for engagement of audio-visual workers, absorbing the Cine Workers and Cinema Theatre Workers Act, 1981 into the Code.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the OSH Code, 2020, one of the general duties of every employer is to ensure:
options: A workplace free from hazards that cause or are likely to cause injury or occupational disease, and disposal of hazardous and toxic waste including e-waste
That workers sign a waiver of all claims
questions.explanation: Section 6 codifies broad employer duties: safe workplace, safe plant and systems, information and training, and safe handling and disposal of hazardous waste.

questions.question_text: Under Section 120 of the OSH Code, 2020:
options: The Code yields to any collective agreement
The Code applies only where an employer opts in
The provisions of the Code have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in any other law or in the terms of any award, agreement or contract of service
State safety laws override the Code
questions.explanation: Section 120 gives the Code overriding effect, while preserving more favourable rights or privileges an employee may have under any other agreement or arrangement.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1) of the OSH Code, 2020, an 'adult' means a person who has completed:
questions.explanation: Section 2 defines 'adult' as one who has completed 18 years; 'adolescent' takes the meaning in the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the OSH Code, 2020, an appeal against an order of the registering officer refusing or cancelling registration of an establishment must be filed within:
questions.explanation: Section 4 provides a 30-day appeal against a Section 3 registration order to the appellate authority notified by the appropriate Government.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(j) of the Patents Act, 1970, an 'invention' means:
options: Any new idea, whether or not it can be made or used
A new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application
A discovery of a scientific principle
An improvement to an existing product, even if obvious
questions.explanation: All three ingredients — novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability — must be present; Section 2(1)(ja) defines 'inventive step' as a feature involving technical advance or economic significance (or both) that is not obvious to a person skilled in the art.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970, the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance is NOT an invention:
options: Only if the substance is a chemical

Unless it results in the enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance (and salts, esters, polymorphs, etc. of a known substance are deemed the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy)
questions.explanation: Section 3(d), the anti-'evergreening' provision, was interpreted in Novartis AG v. Union of India (2013), where the Supreme Court held that 'efficacy' means therapeutic efficacy and denied a patent for the beta-crystalline form of imatinib mesylate (Glivec).

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the Patents Act, 1970, which of the following is NOT patentable?
options: A new chemical compound with an inventive step

A method of medical, surgical, curative or diagnostic treatment of human beings or animals; a mathematical or business method; a computer programme per se; an algorithm; plants and animals in whole or any part thereof (other than micro-organisms)
questions.explanation: Section 3 lists what are not inventions; Section 4 additionally bars patents for inventions relating to atomic energy.

questions.question_text: Under Section 53 of the Patents Act, 1970, the term of every patent is:
options: Twenty years from the date of filing of the application (or, for a PCT national-phase application, from the international filing date)
The life of the inventor plus sixty years
questions.explanation: India moved to a uniform 20-year term (from filing) for all fields of technology in the 2002 amendment, in line with TRIPS; renewal fees must be paid to keep the patent in force.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11A of the Patents Act, 1970, a patent application is ordinarily published:
options: On the expiry of eighteen months from the date of filing (or the priority date, whichever is earlier), unless an early-publication request is made or the application is withdrawn
Only after the patent is granted
questions.explanation: From the date of publication until grant, the applicant has like privileges and rights as if a patent had been granted, but cannot institute infringement proceedings until the patent is actually granted (Section 11A(7)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 11B of the Patents Act, 1970, a patent application is examined:
options: Only after the patent term expires
Only when a request for examination is filed within the prescribed period (48 months from the priority/filing date); if no such request is made, the application is deemed to have been withdrawn
Only if a third party files an opposition
questions.explanation: India follows a 'request for examination' system; failure to request within the time limit results in deemed withdrawal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Patents Act, 1970, opposition to a patent may be filed:
options: Only after grant, within ten years
Before grant (pre-grant opposition, by any person, after publication), and after grant (post-grant opposition, by any person interested, within one year of the date of publication of the grant)
questions.explanation: The grounds for opposition include wrongful obtaining, prior publication, prior claiming, prior public knowledge or use, obviousness, non-patentable subject matter, insufficiency, and non-disclosure or wrong mention of the source/geographical origin of biological material.

questions.question_text: Under Section 84 of the Patents Act, 1970, any person interested may apply for a compulsory licence after the expiry of three years from the grant of the patent, on the ground that:
options: The reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied; or the patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price; or the patented invention is not worked in the territory of India
The patentee is a foreign company
The patent is more than five years old
A competitor wishes to make the product
questions.explanation: India's first compulsory licence was granted in Bayer Corporation v. Natco Pharma (2012) for the anti-cancer drug sorafenib tosylate (Nexavar), on all three grounds.

questions.question_text: Under Section 92A of the Patents Act, 1970, a compulsory licence is available for:
options: The export of any patented product to any country

The manufacture and export of patented pharmaceutical products to any country having insufficient or no manufacturing capacity to address public health problems, provided that country has granted a compulsory licence or notified/allowed importation
The import of patented products for personal use
questions.explanation: Section 92A implements the WTO Doha Declaration / Paragraph 6 mechanism on TRIPS and public health.

questions.question_text: Under Section 48 of the Patents Act, 1970, the exclusive rights conferred by a product patent are the right to prevent third parties, without consent, from:
options: Making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the patented product in India
questions.explanation: For a process patent, the right is to prevent unauthorised use of the process and the use, sale, offer for sale or import of a product obtained directly by that process.

questions.question_text: Under Section 107A of the Patents Act, 1970, which of the following does NOT constitute infringement?
options: Manufacturing the product for commercial sale during the patent term
Selling the patented product without licence
Exporting the patented product for profit
