Making, using or importing a patented invention solely for uses reasonably related to the development and submission of information required under law (the 'Bolar' or regulatory-review exemption); and importation of a patented product by any person from another person who is duly authorised under the law to produce and sell or distribute that product (parallel imports)
questions.explanation: Section 107A permits generic manufacturers to conduct trials and prepare regulatory dossiers before patent expiry, and permits parallel importation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 104 of the Patents Act, 1970, a suit for infringement of a patent must be instituted in:
options: A District Court having jurisdiction, but where the defendant makes a counter-claim for revocation of the patent, the suit and the counter-claim are transferred to the High Court
Any civil court, regardless of value
questions.explanation: After the abolition of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, appeals and revocation petitions lie to the High Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Patents Act, 1970, an application for a patent may be made by:
options: The true and first inventor, or his assignee, or the legal representative of a deceased person who was entitled to make the application
Any person who first files, regardless of who invented it
questions.explanation: India follows a 'first-to-file' system among competing applicants, but only a person deriving title from the true and first inventor may apply; the person importing an invention from abroad is not the 'true and first inventor'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Patents Act, 1970, an applicant who has also filed for the same or substantially the same invention in a country outside India must:
options: Do nothing; foreign filings are irrelevant

Furnish to the Controller a statement of particulars of every such foreign application and keep the Controller informed of its subsequent progress, and file details of foreign search/examination results as required
Assign the Indian application to the Government
questions.explanation: Failure to comply with the Section 8 disclosure obligation is a ground for revocation under Section 64(1)(m).

questions.question_text: Under Section 25(1)(k) and Section 10(4)(ii)(D) of the Patents Act, 1970, where an invention uses biological material, the applicant must:
options: Deposit the material with a foreign depository only
Disclose the source and geographical origin of the biological material in the specification, and obtain permission from the National Biodiversity Authority where required
questions.explanation: Non-disclosure or wrongful mention of the source or geographical origin of biological material, and anticipation by traditional knowledge, are grounds of opposition and revocation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 100 of the Patents Act, 1970, the Central Government and any person authorised by it may use a patented invention:
options: For the purposes of the Government (including Government use for public health), on such terms as may be agreed or, failing agreement, as determined by the High Court
For any purpose whatsoever, free of charge
Only with the patentee's prior written consent in every case
questions.explanation: Sections 99-103 permit Government use and acquisition of patents; Section 47 makes every grant subject to conditions permitting Government use and import.

questions.question_text: Under Section 146 of the Patents Act, 1970 read with the Rules, a patentee and every licensee must:
options: Furnish to the Controller a statement (Form 27) as to the extent to which the patented invention has been worked on a commercial scale in India, at prescribed intervals
Renew the patent every year in person
Report only if the Controller asks
questions.explanation: The 'statement of working' provides data used, among other things, in compulsory-licence proceedings; false statements are an offence under Section 122.

questions.question_text: Under Section 64 of the Patents Act, 1970, a granted patent may be revoked by the High Court on a petition by any person interested (or by the Central Government), on grounds including:
options: The patentee earning too much profit

Lack of novelty or inventive step, insufficiency of description, the invention not being patentable, wrongful obtaining, non-disclosure under Section 8, and the complete specification not sufficiently and fairly describing the invention
The patent being more than three years old
questions.explanation: Revocation may also be raised as a counter-claim in an infringement suit (Section 64 read with Section 104).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(l) of the Patents Act, 1970 and Section 13, 'new invention' / novelty means the invention:
options: Merely has not been patented before in India
Is unknown to the applicant's competitors

Has not been anticipated by publication in any document or used in the country or elsewhere in the world before the date of filing, i.e. the subject matter has not fallen into the public domain or formed part of the state of the art (absolute novelty)
questions.explanation: India applies a standard of absolute (worldwide) novelty; anticipation by prior publication, prior claim, prior public knowledge or use, and prior grant are examined.

questions.question_text: Following the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023, which of the following remains a criminal offence (imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both) under the Patents Act, 1970, rather than a civil penalty imposed by the Controller?
options: Contravention of a secrecy direction under Section 35, or making a foreign-filing application in contravention of Section 39, punishable under Section 118
Falsely representing that an article is patented (Section 120) — now only a monetary penalty adjudicated under Section 124A
Refusal or failure to furnish information required under Section 100(5) or Section 146 (Section 122) — now only a monetary penalty
Practice by a non-registered patent agent in contravention of Section 129 (Section 123) — now only a monetary penalty
questions.explanation: The 2023 Jan Vishwas Act converted the penalties under Sections 120, 122 and 123 from imprisonment/fine to civil monetary penalties adjudicated by the Controller (Section 124A, with appeal under Section 124B), and omitted Section 121 (wrongful use of the words 'patent office') altogether; Section 118 (secrecy/foreign-filing violations) remains a true criminal offence.
questions.statute_or_case: Sections 118, 120-124B, Patents Act, 1970, as amended by the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023

questions.question_text: The Patents Act, 1970 became fully TRIPS-compliant with the Patents (Amendment) Act, 2005, which:
options: Introduced product patents for pharmaceuticals, agro-chemicals and food, deleted the exclusive marketing rights (EMR) regime and the 'mailbox' provision, and added the pre-grant opposition and Section 3(d)
Reduced the patent term to ten years
questions.explanation: Before 2005, India granted only process patents in the pharmaceutical and chemical fields (a policy dating from the 1970 Act, based on the Ayyangar Committee report).

questions.question_text: Under Section 54 to 56 of the Patents Act, 1970, a 'patent of addition' is:
options: A second independent patent for the same invention
A patent that adds ten years to the term

A patent granted for an improvement in or modification of an invention for which the applicant already has a patent (or has applied), which is co-terminous with the main patent and for which no separate renewal fee is payable while the main patent remains in force
A patent granted in a foreign country
questions.explanation: A patent of addition cannot be independently challenged for lack of inventive step over the parent invention.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 57 and 58 of the Patents Act, 1970, amendment of a patent application or specification:
options: May freely broaden the scope of the claims
Can be made only by the Controller, not the applicant
Is permitted only by way of disclaimer, correction or explanation, and only if the amended claims fall wholly within the scope of the claims before amendment (no addition of new matter)
questions.explanation: Section 59 restricts post-filing amendments so that a patentee cannot enlarge the monopoly beyond what was originally disclosed and claimed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 47 of the Patents Act, 1970, the grant of a patent is subject to the condition that:
options: The Government may import or make the patented article for its own use, and any person may make, use or import the patented invention merely for experiment or research (including imparting instruction to pupils), and a patented medicine may be imported by the Government for its own dispensaries and hospitals
The patentee must sell the product at cost price
The patent is void if not worked within one year
Only Indian companies may be licensed
questions.explanation: Section 47 embodies the research/experimental-use exception and limited Government-use rights that attach automatically to every patent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(b) and Sections 73-74 of the Patents Act, 1970, the head of the Indian patent administration is:
options: The Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, who is the Controller of Patents for the purposes of the Act; the head office of the Patent Office is at Kolkata, with branch offices at Delhi, Mumbai and Chennai
questions.explanation: India recognises four territorial jurisdictions for patent filing based on the applicant's place of residence, business or origin of the invention.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(ac) of the Patents Act, 1970, 'capable of industrial application' in relation to an invention means:
options: That the invention will be commercially successful
That the invention has already been marketed
That the invention is capable of being made or used in an industry
That the invention is limited to manufacturing industry
questions.explanation: Industrial applicability (utility) is one of the three statutory requirements; a perpetual-motion machine, for example, would fail this test.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 68 and 69 of the Patents Act, 1970, an assignment, mortgage or licence of a patent:
options: Need not be registered at all
Is valid only if approved by the Central Government

Is not valid unless it is in writing and the agreement between the parties is reduced to the form of a document embodying all the terms and conditions governing their rights and obligations, and the application for registration of the title is filed with the Controller
questions.explanation: An unregistered document is generally not admitted in evidence to prove title in infringement proceedings (Section 69(5)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 108 of the Patents Act, 1970, the reliefs a court may grant in a suit for infringement of a patent include:
options: An injunction, and at the option of the plaintiff either damages or an account of profits, and an order that the infringing goods be seized, forfeited or destroyed
Only a fine payable to the Government
questions.explanation: A court may refuse damages or an account of profits for infringement occurring before the defendant was aware, or had reasonable grounds to be aware, of the patent (Section 111).

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, 1970, which of the following is NOT an invention?
options: A genetically engineered micro-organism with an inventive step

Plants and animals in whole or any part thereof (other than micro-organisms), including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes for the production or propagation of plants and animals
questions.explanation: Plant varieties are protected instead under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001; micro-organisms (if novel, non-obvious and not merely discovered from nature) may be patented.

questions.question_text: Under Section 117A of the Patents Act, 1970 and the scheme of the Act, appeals from the orders of the Controller now lie to:
options: The IPAB, which continues to function
The High Court, following the abolition of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021
questions.explanation: Until 2021, appeals lay to the IPAB; the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 abolished the IPAB and transferred its functions to the High Courts.
questions.statute_or_case: Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 (amending the Patents Act, 1970)

questions.question_text: The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 was enacted primarily to:
options: Bring plant varieties within the Patents Act, 1970

Give effect to Article 27(3)(b) of the TRIPS Agreement by providing a sui generis system for protecting plant varieties, while also recognising the rights of farmers and breeders and encouraging the development of new varieties
questions.explanation: India chose a sui generis regime rather than plant patents; Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, 1970 expressly excludes plants and plant varieties from patentability.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, a NEW variety is registrable only if it conforms to the criteria of:
questions.explanation: An 'extant variety' (already available in India) need only satisfy distinctiveness, uniformity and stability (DUS); a farmers' variety is registrable on the farmer's declaration.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, an application for registration may be filed in respect of:
options: Only new varieties bred by companies
A variety of a genus/species notified under Section 29(2) (a 'new variety'), an extant variety, or a farmers' variety — an essentially derived variety is registered separately, under Section 23
questions.explanation: The Central Government notifies the genera and species eligible for registration; the National Register of Plant Varieties is maintained under Section 13.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the certificate of registration of a plant variety is initially valid for:
options: Nine years in the case of trees and vines, and six years in the case of other crops, renewable so that the total period does not exceed eighteen years (trees and vines), fifteen years (extant varieties, from notification) or fifteen years (other cases, from registration)
questions.explanation: Section 35 requires payment of annual fees to keep the registration in force, failing which the registration is forfeited.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, a farmer:
options: May not save or re-use any seed of a protected variety

Is entitled to save, use, sow, re-sow, exchange, share or sell his farm produce including seed of a variety protected under the Act, in the same manner as before the Act — but not to sell branded seed of a protected variety
Must pay a royalty for every re-use of protected seed
Has no rights over protected varieties at all
questions.explanation: This 'farmers' privilege' is a defining feature of the Indian sui generis regime; 'branded seed' means seed put in a package or container and labelled to indicate it is of a protected variety.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39(2) of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, if a protected variety fails to perform in the manner claimed by the breeder under the given conditions:
options: The farmer must sue in a civil court only
A farmer who has been affected may claim compensation from the breeder before the Authority
The breeder's registration is automatically cancelled
questions.explanation: This is a unique 'reverse' liability provision protecting farmers against exaggerated performance claims.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the 'researcher's right' provides that:
options: No one but the breeder may use the variety for any purpose
Research use requires a compulsory licence
Researchers must pay a royalty for every use

Any person may use a registered variety for conducting experiments or research, and as an initial source of variety for the purpose of creating other varieties (but repeated use as a parental line for commercial production requires the authorisation of the breeder)
questions.explanation: The breeder's exemption ensures that plant-variety protection does not stifle further breeding.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(b) of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, 'benefit sharing' means:
options: The proportion of the benefit accruing to a breeder from a registered variety (or from his agent or licensee) to which a claimant is entitled, as determined by the Authority under Section 26 after inviting claims by public notice, from any person or group of persons or any governmental or non-governmental organisation who has contributed genetic material used in developing the variety
Distribution of the breeder's profits to shareholders
Sharing of seeds among farmers only
questions.explanation: Claims for benefit sharing are invited when an application is accepted; the amounts determined under Section 26 are deposited in the National Gene Fund (Section 45).

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the 'rights of communities' allow:
options: Communities to prohibit registration of any variety

Any person, group of persons or governmental/non-governmental organisation, on behalf of a village or local community, to file a claim before the Authority for the contribution of that community in the evolution of a variety, and the Authority may grant compensation, deposited in the Gene Fund
Communities to own all registered varieties
questions.explanation: Community rights recognise the collective, informal role of communities in conserving and improving plant genetic resources.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(i) of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, an 'essentially derived variety' (EDV):
options: Is a completely independent new variety

Is predominantly derived from an initial variety (or from a variety itself predominantly derived from the initial variety), retains the essential characteristics resulting from the genotype of the initial variety, and is clearly distinguishable from it — and, under Section 23(6), its commercial exploitation requires the authorisation of the breeder of the initial variety
Belongs to the farmer who grows it
questions.explanation: The EDV concept (from the UPOV framework) prevents 'cosmetic' modifications of a protected variety from escaping the breeder's rights.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the certificate of registration confers on the breeder (or his successor, agent or licensee) an exclusive right to:
options: Only sell the variety within India
Only license others to grow the variety
Prevent all research on the variety
Produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the variety
questions.explanation: Registration of an EDV or a farmers' variety confers the same rights, subject to the farmers' and researchers' rights.

questions.question_text: Under Section 47 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, a compulsory licence in respect of a registered variety may be granted:
options: After the expiry of three years from the date of issue of the certificate, on an application alleging that the reasonable requirements of the public for seeds or other propagating material have not been satisfied, or that the seed is not available to the public at a reasonable price
At any time, for any reason
questions.explanation: The Authority settles the terms and the duration of a compulsory licence (which is generally the remaining protection period), and may revoke or modify it (Sections 50-53).

questions.question_text: Under Section 34 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the protection granted to a breeder may be revoked on grounds including:
options: That the grant was based on incorrect information furnished by the applicant, or the certificate was granted to a person not eligible for protection, or the breeder has not provided the Registrar with information/documents/material required, or has failed to comply with directions, or the grant is not in the public interest
The passage of two years without commercial use
questions.explanation: Revocation is ordered by the Authority (or the Registrar on its direction) after notice and an opportunity to be heard.

questions.question_text: Under Section 64 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, infringement of the rights in a registered variety occurs where a person, without authorisation:
options: Grows the variety for personal consumption

Sells, exports, imports or produces the variety or its essentially derived variety, or uses, sells, exports, imports or produces any other variety giving its denomination identical or deceptively similar to that of a registered variety in a manner likely to confuse the public
Saves seed of the variety as a farmer
questions.explanation: A suit for infringement lies in a District Court (Section 65); relief includes injunction and, at the plaintiff's option, damages or an account of profits (Section 66).

questions.question_text: Under Section 42 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, a farmer who at the time of infringement was not aware and had no reasonable grounds to believe that the variety was registered:
options: Is liable to the full penalty regardless
Is barred from farming for one year
Is not liable to punishment under the Act (protection of innocent infringement)
questions.explanation: Section 39(2) separately requires the breeder to disclose the expected performance of the variety, and Section 44 exempts farmers from paying fees in proceedings before the Authority, the Registrar or the High Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the body established to administer the Act is:
options: The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority (headquartered in New Delhi), with a Chairperson and a Registrar-General/Registrar
The Seeds Committee under the Seeds Act, 1966
questions.explanation: The Authority also promotes public awareness, documents farmers' varieties and manages the National Gene Fund.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the National Gene Fund receives:
options: Benefit-sharing amounts, annual fees payable by way of royalty, compensation deposited under Section 41(4), and contributions from national and international organisations — and is applied for benefit sharing, compensation to communities and support for in-situ and ex-situ conservation
The registration fees paid by breeders only
Nothing; there is no such fund
questions.explanation: The Gene Fund is the financial mechanism for realising farmers' and community rights.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, registration is excluded where the prevention of commercial exploitation of a variety is necessary to protect:
options: The commercial interests of existing seed companies

Public order or public morality, human, animal and plant life and health, or to avoid serious prejudice to the environment (and no variety involving a 'terminator' gene-use restriction technology may be registered)
questions.explanation: Section 18(1)(c) requires a declaration that the variety does not contain a Genetic Use Restriction Technology or terminator technology.

questions.question_text: Under Section 56 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001 (as amended following the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021), an appeal against an order of the Authority or the Registrar lies to:
options: The High Court (the appeals earlier lay to the Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Tribunal / IPAB)
questions.explanation: An appeal must be filed within the prescribed period; the High Court endeavours to dispose of it expeditiously.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, an application for registration must be accompanied by, among other things:
options: An affidavit that the variety does not contain any gene or gene sequence involving terminator technology, a statement about the use of genetic material conserved by any tribal or rural family, and a complete passport data of the parental lines with the geographical location in India and all such information relating to the contribution of any farmer/village community in breeding the variety
Only a sample of the seed
questions.explanation: The disclosure of the source of germplasm and of any farmer/community contribution is central to the Act's benefit-sharing scheme; a false statement can lead to revocation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 (compulsory denomination) read with Section 15(4) of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, every application for registration must contain a 'variety denomination', which:
options: May be any word the breeder chooses, including a registered trade mark

Must enable the variety to be identified, must not be liable to mislead or cause confusion, must not consist solely of figures, and must be different from the denomination of any existing variety of the same or a closely related species (and it cannot itself be registered as a trade mark under the Trade Marks Act, 1999)
questions.explanation: Section 15(4) bars registration where the proposed denomination fails these tests, and Section 17(4) bars registering that denomination as a trade mark; the denomination is the generic designation of the variety and must remain usable by everyone even after protection expires.

questions.question_text: Under the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the 'novelty' requirement for a new variety is satisfied if, at the date of filing, propagating or harvested material of the variety has not been sold or otherwise disposed of by or with the consent of the breeder:
options: In India, earlier than one year before the date of filing; and outside India, earlier than six years (trees and vines) or four years (in any other case) before the date of filing
Only in the breeder's home country
questions.explanation: A commercial 'grace period' allows breeders to test-market a variety without destroying its novelty, within the stated windows.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, an application for registration of a variety may be made by:
options: Any person claiming to be the breeder; any successor of the breeder; any person being the assignee of the breeder; any farmer or group of farmers or community of farmers claiming to be the breeder of a variety; any university or publicly funded agricultural institution; or any person authorised to make an application on behalf of a breeder
questions.explanation: The wide list of eligible applicants reflects the Act's inclusion of farmers and public institutions as breeders.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 and Section 22 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, after an application is accepted it is advertised and any person may oppose registration within the prescribed time on grounds including:
options: That the applicant is not entitled to registration; that the variety is not registrable; that the grant may not be in the public interest; or that the variety may have an adverse effect on the environment
That the opponent simply wants to use the variety
That the application fee was too low
That the breeder is a small company
questions.explanation: The Registrar hears both parties and decides whether the variety is to be registered.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, a breeder in respect of whose variety a certificate of registration has been issued must:
options: Deposit such quantity of seeds or propagating material (including parental line seeds) of the registered variety in the National Gene Bank specified by the Authority, at his own expense, for reproduction purposes
Sell all his seed stock to the Government
questions.explanation: The deposit is made to the National Gene Bank, not to the Authority itself; it preserves reproducible material of every registered variety.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, an 'extant variety' includes:
options: A variety notified under Section 5 of the Seeds Act, 1966; a farmers' variety; a variety about which there is common knowledge; and any other variety in the public domain
questions.explanation: Extant varieties can be registered on satisfying only distinctiveness, uniformity and stability (not novelty), within a period specified by the Authority.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 70 to 73 of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, the penalty for falsely applying the denomination of a registered variety, or selling varieties to which a false denomination is applied, is:
options: Imprisonment for a term of not less than three months but which may extend to two years, or fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to five lakh rupees, or both (with enhanced punishment for a subsequent offence)
questions.explanation: Falsely representing a variety as registered (Section 72) is also an offence.

questions.question_text: A landmark dispute under the PPV&FR Act, 2001 concerned:
options: PepsiCo's registration of a potato variety (FL 2027 / FC5) used for Lay's chips, which the PPV&FR Authority revoked in December 2021 for procedural defects — incorrect information on the date of first sale and a defective assignment deed — a revocation the Delhi High Court upheld in 2023
A patent claim over basmati rice
A trademark dispute over a wheat brand
A geographical indication for Alphonso mango
questions.explanation: The Delhi High Court (Justice Navin Chawla, 5 July 2023) upheld the revocation on procedural infirmities in the application, though it noted that PepsiCo's exercise of its rights could not itself be called against the public interest.

questions.question_text: The PPV&FR Act, 2001 seeks to balance breeders' rights with farmers' rights; which international convention did India choose NOT to accede to, preferring its own model?
options: The UPOV Convention (International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants), because UPOV 1991 restricts the farmers' privilege to save and exchange seed
questions.explanation: India's sui generis regime under Article 27(3)(b) of TRIPS deliberately provides stronger farmers' rights than the UPOV framework.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24(5) and (6) of the PPV&FR Act, 2001, once a certificate of registration is issued, the Act provides that:
options: The certificate is valid only in the State where the breeder resides and lapses on any abusive third-party act
The certificate is valid worldwide and needs no renewal

The Registrar may issue directions to protect the breeder against any abusive act by a third party between filing and the Authority's decision, and the certificate — valid for nine years (trees/vines) or six years (other crops) — may be reviewed and renewed up to the maximum periods laid down (18 years for trees/vines, 15 years otherwise)
Renewal is barred once the initial term expires
questions.explanation: A single registration protects the variety throughout India for the applicable term, subject to timely payment of the annual fee under Section 35.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, when a marriage is intended to be solemnized under the Act, the parties shall give notice in writing to the Marriage Officer of the district in which at least one of the parties has resided for a period of not less than:
options: Thirty days immediately preceding the date on which such notice is given
questions.explanation: Section 5 mandates 30 days prior residence in the district before giving notice of intended marriage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(c) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, what are the minimum age requirements for the male and female parties at the time of solemnization?
options: Male has completed twenty-one years and Female has completed eighteen years
questions.explanation: Section 4(c) specifies male must be 21 and female must be 18.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7(1) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, any person may object to the intended marriage on the ground that it would violate Section 4 conditions within what period from the publication of notice?
options: Thirty days from the date of publication of notice
questions.explanation: Section 7(1) allows 30 days for filing objections following public notice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, if an intended marriage is NOT solemnized within how many months from the date of notice, the notice lapses and a fresh notice must be given?
options: Three months from the date of notice
questions.explanation: Section 14 provides that a notice lapses if marriage is not solemnized within 3 months.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 and 12 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, how many WITNESSES are required to sign the declaration and be present at the solemnization of the marriage in the presence of the Marriage Officer?
questions.explanation: Sections 11 & 12 mandate signature and presence of 3 witnesses.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, what is the legal effect of solemnization of marriage under SMA on a member of an undivided Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, or Jain family?
options: It converts the family into a trust
It has no effect on Hindu Undivided Family status
It shall be deemed to effect his severance from such undivided family
questions.explanation: Section 19 provides that marriage under SMA effects severance from the undivided family (subject to Section 21A exception).

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, succession to the property of any person married under the Act (and their children) shall be governed by which law?
questions.explanation: Section 21 applies the Indian Succession Act, 1925 to property succession (subject to Section 21A).

questions.question_text: Under Section 21A of The Special Marriage Act, 1954 (inserted by Amendment Act 68 of 1976), if BOTH parties to the marriage profess the Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, or Jain religion:
options: Sections 19 and 21 do NOT apply, and their property succession continues to be governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
They are severed from HUF automatically
Their marriage is registered under HMA
questions.explanation: Section 21A exempts couples where BOTH parties are Hindus/Buddhists/Sikhs/Jains from Sections 19 & 21, retaining Hindu Succession Act applicability.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, what is the mandatory waiting period for filing a joint petition for Divorce by Mutual Consent?
options: Parties must have been living separately for a period of ONE YEAR or more
questions.explanation: Section 28(1) requires living separately for at least 1 year before filing joint mutual consent divorce petition.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28(2) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, after filing a mutual consent divorce petition, between what timeline must the second motion be made by both parties?
options: Not earlier than six months after petition date and not later than eighteen months after said date
questions.explanation: Section 28(2) sets the second motion window between 6 months and 18 months from petition filing.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, no petition for divorce can be presented to the District Court unless at the date of presentation:
options: One year has elapsed since the date of solemnization of marriage (except in cases of exceptional hardship/depravity)
questions.explanation: Section 29 imposes a 1-year restriction bar on divorce petitions post-marriage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24(1) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, a marriage solemnized under the Act is VOID if:
options: Any of the conditions specified in Section 4 (monogamy, age, mental capacity, prohibited degrees) has not been fulfilled
Notice was published on a Sunday
questions.explanation: Section 24(1) declares marriage void if any core Section 4 condition is breached or respondent is impotent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, a marriage is VOIDABLE and may be annulled by a decree of nullity if:
options: The marriage has not been consummated owing to respondent's wilful refusal, or wife was pregnant by stranger at marriage, or consent obtained by coercion/fraud
questions.explanation: Section 25 lists grounds for voidable marriage: wilful refusal to consummate, pre-marriage pregnancy by stranger, fraud/coercion.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, what is the legal status of children born of void or voidable marriages?
options: Legitimate only if court issues certificate
They are deemed to be LEGITIMATE children of their parents in all respects
questions.explanation: Section 26 confers full statutory legitimacy on children of void and voidable SMA marriages.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1)(b) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, desertion by the respondent without reasonable cause is a ground for divorce if continued for a period of not less than:
options: Two years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition
questions.explanation: Section 27(1)(b) specifies min 2 years continuous desertion.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1A) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, a WIFE may present a petition for divorce on which additional grounds?
options: That her husband has been guilty of rape, sodomy, or bestiality since solemnization of marriage
questions.explanation: Section 27(1A) provides special extra grounds for wife: rape, sodomy, or bestiality.

questions.question_text: In Lata Singh v. State of U.P. (2006) 5 SCC 475, the Supreme Court held regarding inter-caste and inter-religious marriages under the Special Marriage Act that:
options: Adults have an absolute right to marry a person of their choice, and administration/police must protect inter-caste/inter-religious couples from harassment or violence
State Govt must approve inter-faith marriages
Panchayat has power to annul SMA marriage
questions.explanation: Lata Singh (2006) established right of adults to marry across caste/religion and mandated police protection.
questions.statute_or_case: Lata Singh v. State of U.P. (2006) 5 SCC 475

questions.question_text: In Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (Hadiya Case 2018) 16 SCC 368, the Supreme Court affirmed that the right to marry a person of one's choice is an integral part of:
options: Article 21 of the Constitution of India (Right to Life and Personal Liberty)
questions.explanation: Shafin Jahan (2018) recognized choice of marriage partner as a fundamental right under Article 21.
questions.statute_or_case: Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (2018) 16 SCC 368

questions.question_text: Under Section 36 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, how fast should an application for Alimony Pendente Lite (interim maintenance) be disposed of by the court?
options: Within sixty days from the date of service of notice on the respondent
questions.explanation: Section 36 proviso mandates target disposal within 60 days of notice service.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39(4) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, what is the limitation period for filing an APPEAL against any decree or order passed by District Court under the Act?
options: Ninety days from the date of the decree or order
questions.explanation: Section 39(4) sets a 90-day limitation period for appeals under SMA.

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, can an existing religious or customary marriage (e.g. Hindu or Muslim marriage) be REGISTERED under SMA?
options: No, SMA registration applies only to new marriages

Yes, if a ceremony was performed and the parties have lived together since, neither has more than one spouse living, neither is an idiot or lunatic, both have completed 21 years, they are not within prohibited degrees, and they have resided in the district for 30 days
Only if parties convert to Christianity
questions.explanation: Chapter III (Section 15) provides for registration of pre-existing religious marriages under SMA.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, what is the effect of registering a pre-existing marriage under Section 15?
options: The marriage is deemed to be a marriage solemnized under SMA from the date of registration, and children deemed legitimate
questions.explanation: Section 18 deems registered marriage to be solemnized under SMA, bringing it under civil law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 44 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, every person married under this Act who during the lifetime of his/her spouse contracts another marriage is punishable under:
options: Sections 494 and 495 of IPC / Section 82 of BNS 2023 (Bigamy)
questions.explanation: Section 44 applies penal provisions for bigamy (IPC 494/495 / BNS 82).

questions.question_text: Under Section 45 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, any person making, signing, or attesting a declaration or certificate containing a statement which is FALSE and which he knows to be false is punishable with imprisonment up to:
options: Three years, and shall also be liable to fine
questions.explanation: Section 45 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment and fine for false declarations.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8(2) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, if the Marriage Officer upholds an objection and refuses to solemnize marriage, an appeal lies within 30 days to:
options: The District Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the Marriage Officer has his office
questions.explanation: Section 8(2) provides appeal to District Court against Marriage Officer's refusal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(2) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, if an objection to an intended marriage is made unreasonably or maliciously, the Marriage Officer may award costs/compensation against objector up to:
questions.explanation: Section 9(2) allows Marriage Officer to award up to Rs. 1,000 as compensation for frivolous objections.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(2) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, what is the evidentiary value of a Certificate of Marriage entered in the Marriage Certificate Book?
options: Conclusive evidence of the fact that a marriage under this Act has been solemnized
questions.explanation: Section 13(2) declares Marriage Certificate to be conclusive evidence of solemnization.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, a petition for Restitution of Conjugal Rights may be filed when either spouse has:
options: Without reasonable excuse withdrawn from the society of the other
Taken up employment in another city
questions.explanation: Section 22 provides RCR remedy when a spouse withdraws from society without reasonable excuse.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, Judicial Separation may be decreed on any of the grounds specified in Section 27 OR on the ground of:
options: Failure to comply with a decree for restitution of conjugal rights
questions.explanation: Section 23 allows judicial separation on divorce grounds or non-compliance with RCR decree.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1)(a) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, voluntary sexual intercourse with any person other than his/her spouse (Adultery) is a ground for:
questions.explanation: Section 27(1)(a) lists post-marriage adultery as a fault ground for divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1)(h) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, a party can seek divorce if the respondent has not been heard of as being alive for a period of:
options: Seven years or more by those who would naturally have heard of him/her
questions.explanation: Section 27(1)(h) adopts standard 7-year presumption of death as a divorce ground.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(2)(i) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, failure to resume cohabitation for how long AFTER a decree of Judicial Separation provides ground for divorce?
questions.explanation: Section 27(2)(i) makes non-resumption of cohabitation for one year or upwards after a decree of judicial separation a ground for divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31(1) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, every petition under Chapter V or VI shall be presented to the District Court within local limits of whose jurisdiction:
options: The marriage was solemnized, or respondent resides, or parties last resided together, or wife resides (if petitioner/respondent resides outside India)
questions.explanation: Section 31(1) defines territorial jurisdiction for SMA matrimonial petitions.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, proceedings under the Act shall be conducted:
options: In camera if either party so desires or if court thinks fit, and shall not be printed or published without court permission
questions.explanation: Section 33 mandates in camera trial options and bans unauthorized printing/publication.

questions.question_text: Under Section 37 of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, permanent alimony ordered by court terminates upon:
options: The remarriage of the recipient spouse (or if recipient fails to remain chaste/chaste conduct)
questions.explanation: Section 37(3) specifies permanent alimony can be varied/rescinded upon remarriage or unchastity.

questions.question_text: In Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty v. Union of India (2023), the 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held regarding reading same-sex marriage into the Special Marriage Act, 1954 that:
options: The Court cannot rewrite SMA to include same-sex marriage; gender neutrality or inclusion of queer marriages is a policy matter for Legislature
High Court can alter SMA text
questions.explanation: Supriyo (2023) held amending SMA to cover same-sex marriage falls exclusively within legislative domain.
questions.statute_or_case: Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty v. Union of India (2023)

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(d) of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, parties within degrees of prohibited relationship CAN solemnize marriage under SMA IF:
options: Both parties pay fine to Marriage Officer
A custom governing at least one of the parties permits a marriage between them
questions.explanation: Section 4(d) proviso permits prohibited degree marriage if custom governing at least one party allows it.

questions.question_text: Under First Schedule of The Special Marriage Act, 1954, degrees of prohibited relationship include:
options: Mother, daughter, sister, grandmother, aunt, niece, father's wife, son's wife (and corresponding male relations)
questions.explanation: First Schedule Parts I & II enumerate detailed prohibited relationships.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 Explanation I of SMA 1954, 'relationship' includes relationship by:
options: Full blood, half blood, uterine blood, illegitimate blood, as well as by adoption
questions.explanation: Explanation I defines relationship comprehensively including half/uterine/illegitimate blood and adoption.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 Explanation II of SMA 1954, two persons are related by 'FULL BLOOD' when they are descended from:
options: A common ancestor by the same wife
A common ancestor by different wives
A common ancestress by different husbands
questions.explanation: Explanation II defines full blood: common ancestor by same wife.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 Explanation II of SMA 1954, two persons are related by 'HALF BLOOD' when they are descended from:
options: A common ancestress by different husbands
A common ancestor but by different wives
questions.explanation: Explanation II defines half blood: common ancestor by different wives.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 Explanation III of SMA 1954, two persons are related by 'UTERINE BLOOD' when they are descended from:
options: A common ancestor by different wives
A common ancestress but by different husbands
questions.explanation: Explanation III defines uterine blood: common ancestress by different husbands.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(2) of SMA 1954, where does the Marriage Officer publish a copy of the notice of intended marriage?
options: By affixing a copy to some conspicuous place in his office
questions.explanation: Section 6(2) mandates affixing notice in a conspicuous place in Marriage Officer's office.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(3) of SMA 1954, if one party to intended marriage does NOT reside in Marriage Officer's district, what must Marriage Officer do?
options: Send a copy of notice to Marriage Officer of district where that party resides to be affixed in his office
questions.explanation: Section 6(3) requires transmitting copy to other district's Marriage Officer for local publication.

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of SMA 1954, if an objection is received by a Marriage Officer in a specified area and the Officer entertains a doubt about it, what is the procedure?
options: He decides on spot without appeal
He transmits objection to Central Government, which decides after inquiry whether marriage should be solemnized
questions.explanation: Section 10 requires Marriage Officer abroad to refer objections to Central Government.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12(1) of SMA 1954, the marriage solemnization may take place at office of Marriage Officer OR at such other place within reasonable distance as parties desire, subject to:
questions.explanation: Section 12(1) permits solemnization outside the office upon payment of the prescribed additional fee.

questions.question_text: Under the proviso to Section 12(2) of SMA 1954, what is the mandatory verbal formula that each party must utter to the other in solemnization?
options: 'I, (A), take thee (B), to be my lawful wife (or husband)' in presence of Marriage Officer and 3 witnesses
questions.explanation: The proviso to Section 12(2) prescribes the exact mandatory declaration formula, in any language understood by the parties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of SMA 1954, when an application for REGISTRATION of an existing marriage is made under Section 15, what notice period is given for public objections?
questions.explanation: Section 16 requires 30 days public notice before registering an existing marriage under SMA.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of SMA 1954, if Marriage Officer refuses to register an existing marriage under Section 16, an appeal lies within 30 days to:
questions.explanation: Section 17 provides appeal to District Court against registration refusal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of SMA 1954, subject to Section 19 severance rules, any person married under SMA has:
options: The same rights and disabilities as a person not married under this Act regarding succession/rights not specified
questions.explanation: Section 20 preserves general civil rights and disabilities except as expressly modified by the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(1) of Act No. 43 of 1954, the short title is:
questions.explanation: Section 1(1) defines exact title.

questions.question_text: Under Section 1(2) of SMA 1954, the Act extends to the whole of India and applies also to:
options: Citizens of India domiciled in India who are abroad
questions.explanation: Section 1(2) extends extraterritorially to Indian citizens domiciled in covered territories.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(1) of SMA 1954, who appoints Marriage Officers for districts in a State?
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) empowers State Government to appoint Marriage Officers.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3(2) of SMA 1954, who appoints Marriage Officers for citizens of India abroad?
questions.explanation: Section 3(2) empowers Central Government to appoint Marriage Officers abroad.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(a) of SMA 1954, what is the monogamy requirement?
options: Neither party has a spouse living at the time of solemnization
questions.explanation: Section 4(a) mandates absolute monogamy for both parties.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(b) of SMA 1954, regarding mental capacity, a marriage cannot be solemnized if either party is:
options: Incapable of giving valid consent due to unsoundness of mind, or suffering from mental disorder rendering unfit for marriage/procreation, or subject to recurrent attacks of insanity
questions.explanation: Section 4(b) details three mental health disqualifications for valid marriage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(1) of SMA 1954, where does the Marriage Officer keep all notices of intended marriage?
options: Bound with the records of his office and entered in the 'Marriage Notice Book'
questions.explanation: Section 6(1) mandates maintaining records in Marriage Notice Book open for inspection.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9(1) of SMA 1954, for the purpose of inquiring into objections, the Marriage Officer has all the powers of a:
options: Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (summoning witnesses, examining on oath, compelling document production)
questions.explanation: Section 9(1) equips Marriage Officer with CPC Civil Court powers for conducting inquiries.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of SMA 1954, before marriage is solemnized, the parties and 3 witnesses must sign a declaration in the form specified in which Schedule?
questions.explanation: Section 11 specifies the Third Schedule form for the declaration by the parties and witnesses.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1) of SMA 1954, the Certificate of Marriage is entered in the Marriage Certificate Book in the form specified in which Schedule?
questions.explanation: Section 13(1) specifies the Fourth Schedule form for the Certificate of Marriage on solemnization (the Fifth Schedule form is for registration of an existing marriage under Section 16).

questions.question_text: Under Section 15(f) of SMA 1954, for registration of an existing marriage, the parties must have resided in the district of Marriage Officer for not less than:
questions.explanation: Section 15(f) requires 30 days residence in the district immediately preceding the registration application.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1)(e) of SMA 1954, unsoundness of mind / mental disorder is a ground for divorce. What is the statutory test?
options: The disorder must have subsisted for at least six months
The disorder must have subsisted for at least one year

That the respondent has been incurably of unsound mind, or has suffered continuously or intermittently from mental disorder of such a kind and to such an extent that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent (no fixed period is prescribed)
The disorder must have subsisted for at least three years
questions.explanation: Section 27(1)(e) prescribes no minimum duration; the test is whether the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1)(c) of SMA 1954, a spouse can seek divorce if the respondent is undergoing a sentence of imprisonment for an offence as defined in the Indian Penal Code / BNS of:
questions.explanation: Section 27(1)(c) makes a sentence of imprisonment for seven years or more a ground for divorce.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27A of SMA 1954 (inserted by 1976 Amendment), in any proceeding for divorce, if ground is established, the court may in its discretion pass a decree for:
options: Judicial Separation instead of divorce (alternative relief)
questions.explanation: Section 27A enables court to grant alternative relief of judicial separation in divorce suits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of SMA 1954, when a marriage is dissolved by divorce decree and no appeal is filed within limitation period (or appeal dismissed), can either party remarry?
options: Yes, it shall be lawful for either party to marry again
questions.explanation: Section 30 clarifies right of divorced persons to remarry once decree becomes final.

questions.question_text: Under Section 32 of SMA 1954, every petition for matrimonial relief shall state that there is no COLLUSION between petitioner and respondent, and must be:
options: Verified in the manner required by law for verification of plaints
questions.explanation: Section 32 requires verification of non-collusion in plaints manner.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34(1)(e) of SMA 1954, before granting a decree for divorce or judicial separation, the court must satisfy itself that there has not been any unnecessary or improper:
questions.explanation: Section 34(1)(e) requires the court to check against any unnecessary or improper delay in instituting the proceeding.

questions.question_text: Under Section 35 of SMA 1954, in any proceeding for divorce/judicial separation, if respondent opposes petition and charges petitioner with adultery, cruelty, or desertion:
options: The court may give to respondent the same relief as if respondent had presented a petition seeking such relief
questions.explanation: Section 35 provides counter-claim relief for respondent in matrimonial suits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38 of SMA 1954, regarding custody, maintenance, and education of minor children during or after matrimonial proceedings:
options: The court may pass interim orders and provisions in decree as it deems just and proper, and may alter/revoke them from time to time
questions.explanation: Section 38 gives court broad ongoing jurisdiction over child welfare, custody, and education.

questions.question_text: Under Section 40A of SMA 1954 (inserted in 1976), if two petitions for judicial separation/divorce between same parties are pending in different district courts:
options: The petition presented later in time shall be transferred to the District Court where earlier petition is pending
questions.explanation: Section 40A avoids multiplicity of proceedings by consolidating later petition into earlier court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 40B of SMA 1954, trial of petitions under the Act shall be conducted as expeditiously as possible, and trial should be concluded within:
options: Six months from the date of service of notice of petition on respondent
questions.explanation: Section 40B(2) sets target trial conclusion within 6 months of notice service.

questions.question_text: Under Section 46 of SMA 1954, if a Marriage Officer knowingly and wilfully solemnizes a marriage in violation of Section 4 or without publishing notice:
options: He shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or fine, or both
questions.explanation: Section 46 penalizes Marriage Officers for wrongful official action with up to 1 year jail.

questions.question_text: Under Section 47 of SMA 1954, the Marriage Certificate Book kept by the Marriage Officer shall be:
options: Open at all reasonable times for inspection without fee by any person desiring to inspect the same
Accessible to High Court judges only
questions.explanation: Section 47 ensures Marriage Certificate Book is a public record open for inspection.

questions.question_text: Under Section 50 of SMA 1954, who has rule-making power to prescribe fees, Marriage Notice Book forms, and procedures?
options: The State Government (or Central Government for Marriage Officers abroad)
questions.explanation: Section 50 empowers State Government (and Central Govt for abroad officers) to make rules.

questions.question_text: Can a Muslim male and a Hindu female solemnize a valid marriage under The Special Marriage Act, 1954 WITHOUT converting to each other's religion?
options: No, conversion is mandatory under SMA
No, only permitted if both are Christians
Yes, SMA 1954 is a secular civil law created specifically for inter-religious and inter-caste marriages without religious conversion
questions.explanation: SMA 1954 enables inter-religious civil marriage with zero requirement of religious conversion.

questions.question_text: If a Hindu male marries a Christian female under SMA 1954, which law governs the succession to their property upon death?
options: The Indian Succession Act, 1925 (under Section 21 of SMA 1954)
questions.explanation: Because parties belong to different religions, Section 21 applies Indian Succession Act 1925 (Section 21A exception does not apply).

questions.question_text: If a Hindu male marries a Hindu female under SMA 1954, which law governs the succession to their property upon death?
options: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (by virtue of Section 21A inserted in 1976)
questions.explanation: Section 21A retains Hindu Succession Act governance when BOTH parties are Hindus/Buddhists/Sikhs/Jains.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1)(d) of SMA 1954, treating the petitioner with CRUELTY is a ground for divorce. In Joydeep Majumdar v. Bharti Jaiswal Majumdar (2021) 3 SCC 742, the Supreme Court held that mental cruelty includes:
options: Sustained false, defamatory, and malicious complaints against spouse to military/employer authorities damaging career and reputation
questions.explanation: Joydeep Majumdar (2021) affirmed malicious defamatory complaints damaging career amount to severe mental cruelty.
questions.statute_or_case: Joydeep Majumdar v. Bharti Jaiswal Majumdar (2021)

questions.question_text: Section 27(1)(g) of SMA 1954 made virulent and incurable leprosy a ground for divorce. What did the Personal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 do to it?
options: Yes, the Personal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 deleted leprosy as a ground across personal laws including SMA
questions.explanation: The Personal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 (Act 6 of 2019) repealed leprosy grounds to end discrimination.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of SMA 1954, notice of intended marriage must be given in the form specified in which Schedule?
questions.explanation: Section 5 specifies the Second Schedule form for the notice of intended marriage (the First Schedule lists the degrees of prohibited relationship).

questions.question_text: Under Section 13(1) of SMA 1954, when the marriage is solemnized, the Marriage Officer enters a certificate in the Marriage Certificate Book which is signed by:
options: The parties and Marriage Officer only
The parties to the marriage, three witnesses, and the Marriage Officer
questions.explanation: Section 13(1) mandates signature of parties, 3 witnesses, and Marriage Officer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1)(f) of SMA 1954, suffering from venereal disease in a communicable form is a ground for divorce. What minimum duration must the disease have subsisted?
options: No minimum period is prescribed by the clause as it now stands
questions.explanation: As substituted by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976, Section 27(1)(f) simply requires that the respondent "has been suffering from venereal disease in a communicable form"; no fixed period is stipulated.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28(2) of SMA 1954, if parties file a mutual consent divorce petition but do NOT make the second motion within 18 months:
options: The petition shall stand dismissed / withdrawn
questions.explanation: Failure to move second motion within 18 months results in petition lapse/dismissal.

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 proviso of SMA 1954, when can a District Court grant leave to present a divorce petition BEFORE expiry of 1 year from marriage?
options: On application showing exceptional hardship suffered by petitioner or exceptional depravity on part of respondent
If parties belong to different states
questions.explanation: Section 29 proviso permits early filing in cases of exceptional hardship or depravity.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31(2) of SMA 1954, if the respondent is residing OUTSIDE the territories to which the Act extends or has not been heard of for 7 years, where can wife file petition?
options: In the District Court within local limits of whose jurisdiction she resides at date of presentation
questions.explanation: Section 31(2) enables wife to file where she resides if husband is abroad or untraceable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 36 of SMA 1954, to whom can Alimony Pendente Lite (interim maintenance) be granted during pending proceedings?
options: To wife exclusively in all cases
To the wife or husband who has no independent income sufficient for support and necessary expenses of proceeding
questions.explanation: Section 36 uses gender-neutral language allowing either wife or husband lacking income to claim interim alimony.

questions.question_text: Under Section 37(1) of SMA 1954, court may order the husband to pay permanent alimony/maintenance to wife. Can court ALSO order WIFE to pay permanent maintenance to husband under SMA?
options: Yes, wife pays in all cases
Section 37 specifies court ordering 'the husband to pay to the wife'
questions.explanation: Unlike HMA Section 25, Section 37 SMA specifies husband paying permanent alimony to wife (though S. 36 interim alimony is gender-neutral).

questions.question_text: Under Section 43 of SMA 1954, if a person who is ALREADY MARRIED solemnizes a second marriage under SMA, he is guilty of bigamy AND:
options: The marriage solemnized under SMA is VOID
questions.explanation: Section 43 & Section 24(1) make bigamous SMA marriage void and criminally punishable under IPC 494 / BNS 82.

questions.question_text: Under Section 48 of SMA 1954, Marriage Officers send periodic certified copies of entries in Marriage Certificate Book to:
options: The Registrar-General of Births, Deaths and Marriages of the State
questions.explanation: Section 48 mandates transmitting copies to Registrar-General.

questions.question_text: Under Section 49 of SMA 1954, if a Marriage Officer discovers an error in form or substance of an entry in Marriage Certificate Book, how can he correct it?
options: By erasing original entry with ink
Within one month of discovery, in presence of parties (or 2 witnesses), by entry in margin without altering original entry
questions.explanation: Section 49 sets out marginal correction procedure within 1 month of discovery.

questions.question_text: Under Section 51 of SMA 1954, which colonial enactment was repealed upon passing of the Special Marriage Act, 1954?
questions.explanation: Section 51 explicitly repealed the earlier Special Marriage Act, 1872.

questions.question_text: What Schedule of SMA 1954 contains the form of Certificate of Marriage for registered existing marriages under Section 15?
questions.explanation: Section 16 & Fifth Schedule specify registration certificate form.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(b)(ii) of SMA 1954, even if a party is capable of giving valid consent, marriage is invalid if suffering from mental disorder of such kind as to render person unfit for:
options: Marriage and the procreation of children
questions.explanation: Section 4(b)(ii) specifies mental disorder rendering unfit for marriage and procreation.

questions.question_text: If a Hindu male marries a Muslim female under SMA 1954, does the Hindu male get severed from his HUF under Section 19?
options: Yes, because Section 21A exception applies ONLY when BOTH parties are Hindus/Buddhists/Sikhs/Jains; inter-faith marriage results in Section 19 HUF severance
questions.explanation: Since one party is non-Hindu, Section 21A exception does not apply, so Section 19 HUF severance occurs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25(i) of SMA 1954, non-consummation of marriage owing to respondent's wilful refusal makes marriage voidable. Within what time must a petition be filed on the ground of fraud or coercion under Section 25(iii)?
options: Within one year after coercion ceased or fraud discovered
questions.explanation: Section 25 proviso requires fraud/coercion petition within 1 year of discovery/cessation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(1)(d) of SMA 1954, can cruelty be physical OR mental?
options: Yes, 'has treated the petitioner with cruelty' encompasses physical violence as well as mental torture
questions.explanation: Cruelty under SMA includes physical and mental cruelty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28(3) of SMA 1954, on passing a decree for divorce by mutual consent, the court declares the marriage dissolved with effect from:
questions.explanation: Section 28(3) specifies dissolution takes effect from decree date.

questions.question_text: Under Section 34(1)(b) of SMA 1954, before granting divorce on ground of adultery, court must satisfy itself that petitioner has NOT in any manner:
options: Been accessory to or connived at or condoned the adultery
questions.explanation: Section 34(1)(b) bars relief if petitioner connived at or condoned adultery.

questions.question_text: Under Section 40B(1) of SMA 1954, trial of petition under SMA shall be conducted from day to day until its conclusion UNLESS court finds adjournment necessary beyond following day for:
questions.explanation: Section 40B(1) mandates day-to-day trial subject to recorded reasons for adjournment.

questions.question_text: What is the primary overarching object of The Special Marriage Act, 1954 as stated in its Preamble?
options: To provide a special form of marriage in certain cases, for the registration of such and certain other marriages and for divorce
questions.explanation: Preamble states SMA 1954 is 'An Act to provide a special form of marriage in certain cases, for the registration of such and certain other marriages and for divorce'.

questions.question_text: The Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
options: Repealed the Indian Contract Act, 1872 entirely
Was originally Chapter VII of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (sections 76 to 123), which was repealed and re-enacted as a separate Act
questions.explanation: Sections 76-123 of the Contract Act, 1872 were repealed and the law of sale of movable goods was consolidated in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act 3 of 1930), which came into force on 1 July 1930.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the difference between a 'sale' and an 'agreement to sell' is that:
options: A sale must be in writing and an agreement to sell may be oral
A sale relates to existing goods and an agreement to sell to services
In a sale the property in the goods is transferred to the buyer at the time of contract; in an agreement to sell the transfer of property is to take place at a future time or subject to a condition
questions.explanation: Section 4(3)-(4): where transfer of property is immediate it is a sale; where it is to occur later or on a condition it is an agreement to sell, which becomes a sale when the time elapses or the condition is fulfilled.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(7) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, 'goods' means:
options: Every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money, and includes stock and shares, growing crops, grass, and things attached to or forming part of the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale
questions.explanation: Section 2(7) defines 'goods' to cover movable property, expressly excluding money and actionable claims but including severable things attached to land.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, if in a contract for the sale of specific goods the goods have, without the seller's knowledge, perished at the time the contract was made:
options: The contract is voidable at the buyer's option
The seller must supply substitute goods
The buyer must still pay the price
questions.explanation: Section 6 applies the rule of res extincta (as in Couturier v. Hastie): a contract for goods that have already perished, unknown to the seller, is void.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the distinction between a 'condition' and a 'warranty' is that:
options: A condition is written and a warranty is oral

A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, breach of which gives a right to repudiate; a warranty is collateral to the main purpose, breach of which gives only a right to claim damages
A condition applies to price and a warranty to quality
questions.explanation: Section 12 defines the terms; whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends on the construction of the contract, not merely on the word used.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, a buyer may elect (or be compelled) to treat the breach of a condition as a breach of warranty where:
options: The goods are of small value
The buyer has accepted the goods or part of them, or the contract is indivisible and the buyer has accepted the whole (the buyer then cannot reject the goods but may only claim damages)
questions.explanation: Section 13 converts a right of repudiation into a right to damages once the goods are accepted, or the buyer may voluntarily waive the condition.

questions.question_text: Under Section 14 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, there is an implied condition on the part of the seller that:
options: The buyer will resell at a profit
The price is the market price
In the case of a sale, he has a right to sell the goods, and in the case of an agreement to sell he will have such a right at the time the property is to pass
questions.explanation: Section 14 implies a condition as to title and warranties as to quiet possession and freedom from encumbrances (as in Rowland v. Divall).

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, in a contract for sale of goods by description:
options: There is an implied condition that the goods shall correspond with the description (and, if the sale is by sample as well as by description, with both the sample and the description)
The buyer bears all risk of non-correspondence
questions.explanation: Section 15 codifies the rule in Varley v. Whipp; correspondence with description is a condition.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the general rule is caveat emptor, but an implied condition as to quality or fitness for purpose arises where:
options: The buyer expressly or by implication makes known to the seller the particular purpose for which the goods are required, so as to show that he relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description which it is in the course of the seller's business to supply
questions.explanation: Section 16(1) is the fitness-for-purpose exception (Priest v. Last); Section 16(2) implies a condition of merchantable quality where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in such goods.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 read with Section 19 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, in a sale of unascertained goods:
options: Property passes immediately on contract in every case
No property in the goods is transferred to the buyer unless and until the goods are ascertained; where goods are ascertained or specific, property passes when the parties intend it to pass
questions.explanation: Section 18 bars passing of property in unascertained goods before ascertainment; Section 19 makes intention the governing test for specific or ascertained goods, with Sections 20-24 laying down rules for ascertaining intention.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, in an unconditional contract for the sale of specific goods in a deliverable state:
options: The property passes only on delivery
The property passes only on payment
The property never passes without registration
The property passes to the buyer when the contract is made, and it is immaterial whether the time of payment or delivery, or both, is postponed
questions.explanation: Section 20 is the first rule for ascertaining intention: property in specific goods in a deliverable state passes at the time of the contract.

questions.question_text: The maxim 'res perit domino' as reflected in Section 26 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 means:
options: Unless otherwise agreed, risk passes with property — the goods remain at the seller's risk until property is transferred, after which they are at the buyer's risk, whether delivery has been made or not
Risk always remains with the seller until delivery
Risk always remains with the buyer from the date of contract
questions.explanation: Section 26 links risk to property, not possession, subject to a contrary agreement and to the proviso on delay by a party's fault.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the general rule 'nemo dat quod non habet' means:
options: A buyer in good faith always gets good title
Where goods are sold by a person who is not their owner and who does not sell them under the authority or with the consent of the owner, the buyer acquires no better title than the seller had
Only registered dealers can pass title
questions.explanation: Section 27 states the rule, and Sections 27-30 (mercantile agent, sale by joint owner, voidable title, seller/buyer in possession) contain the exceptions protecting bona fide purchasers for value.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where a person who has sold goods continues in possession of them and delivers them to a bona fide second buyer:
options: The second buyer gets no title
The first buyer's title always prevails
The delivery is as effective as if expressly authorised by the owner, and the second buyer who takes in good faith and without notice of the earlier sale gets a good title
questions.explanation: Section 30(1) (seller in possession) and Section 30(2) (buyer in possession) are exceptions to nemo dat protecting later bona fide purchasers.

questions.question_text: Under Sections 45 to 49 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, an 'unpaid seller' who has parted with possession of the goods may exercise the right of:
options: Refusing to deliver goods already delivered
Stoppage in transit — resuming possession of the goods while they are in course of transit, if the buyer becomes insolvent, and retaining them until payment or tender of the price
questions.explanation: An unpaid seller in possession has a lien (Sections 47-49); one who has parted with possession has the right of stoppage in transit on the buyer's insolvency (Sections 50-52) and a right of resale (Section 54).

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(11) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, a 'property' in goods means:
options: The general property in the goods (ownership), and not merely a special property (such as that of a pledgee or bailee)
The right to use the goods
The market value of the goods
questions.explanation: The Act distinguishes the 'general property' (ownership, which the Act is concerned with transferring) from a 'special property' such as a lien or pledge.

questions.question_text: Under Section 55 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where property in the goods has passed to the buyer and he wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay:
options: The seller can only sue for damages for non-acceptance
The seller may sue him for the price of the goods
The seller must take the goods back
questions.explanation: Section 55 gives a suit for price where property has passed; Section 56 gives a suit for damages for non-acceptance where property has not passed or where the price is payable on a day certain irrespective of delivery.
