questions.question_text: Under Section 57 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver the goods to the buyer:
options: The buyer must accept substitute goods
The buyer's only remedy is to rescind
The buyer may sue the seller for damages for non-delivery
The buyer forfeits any advance paid
questions.explanation: Section 57 gives the buyer a damages action for non-delivery; Section 58 allows a suit for specific performance of a contract to deliver specific or ascertained goods.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, in a contract for sale by sample there is an implied condition that:
options: Only the price shall match the sample
The sample is merely a guide with no legal effect
The buyer must accept the bulk without inspection

The bulk shall correspond with the sample in quality, the buyer shall have a reasonable opportunity of comparing the bulk with the sample, and the goods shall be free from any defect rendering them unmerchantable that would not be apparent on reasonable examination of the sample
questions.explanation: Section 17(2) lists the three implied conditions in a sale by sample.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(9) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, a 'mercantile agent' is:
options: An agent having in the customary course of business as such agent authority either to sell goods, or to consign goods for sale, or to buy goods, or to raise money on the security of goods
A commission agent for immovable property
questions.explanation: Section 27's first proviso protects a buyer who buys in good faith from a mercantile agent in possession of the goods with the owner's consent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, it is the duty of the seller to deliver the goods and of the buyer to accept and pay for them:
options: In accordance with the terms of the contract of sale, and (unless otherwise agreed) delivery and payment are concurrent conditions
The buyer must collect the goods within 24 hours
questions.explanation: Section 32 makes delivery and payment concurrent conditions unless otherwise agreed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where the seller is authorised or required to send the goods to the buyer, delivery of the goods to a carrier for transmission to the buyer is:
options: Never a delivery to the buyer
A delivery only if the carrier is nominated by the buyer
Prima facie deemed to be a delivery of the goods to the buyer
A delivery only on the carrier's arrival
questions.explanation: Section 39 makes handing over to a carrier prima facie delivery to the buyer; the seller must make a reasonable contract with the carrier or the buyer may decline to treat it as delivery.

questions.question_text: Under Section 64 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, in a sale by auction:
options: All lots form a single contract
The sale is complete when the auctioneer opens the bidding
Bids cannot be retracted at any stage
Each lot is prima facie the subject of a separate contract; the sale is complete when the auctioneer announces its completion by the fall of the hammer; and until then a bidder may retract his bid
questions.explanation: Section 64 also provides that the seller may notify a reserve price and, if he reserves a right to bid, may bid himself; but secret bidding by or on behalf of the seller makes the sale voidable at the buyer's option.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(6) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, 'future goods' means:
options: Goods to be manufactured or produced or acquired by the seller after the making of the contract of sale
Goods owned by a third party
questions.explanation: A contract for the sale of future goods operates as an agreement to sell (Section 6(3)), since the seller does not yet own the goods.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 and Section 10 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, if the price of goods is not determined by the contract:
options: The contract is void for uncertainty
The buyer must pay a reasonable price, which is a question of fact depending on the circumstances of each case
The seller may charge any price he wishes
The market price on the date of suit applies
questions.explanation: Section 9 allows the price to be fixed by the contract, in a manner agreed, or by the course of dealing; failing that, Section 9(2) requires a reasonable price.

questions.question_text: Under Section 42 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the buyer is deemed to have accepted the goods when:
options: He pays any part of the price
He intimates acceptance to the seller, or does an act in relation to the goods inconsistent with the seller's ownership, or retains the goods beyond a reasonable time without intimating rejection
questions.explanation: Section 41 gives the buyer a right to examine the goods before acceptance; Section 42 defines the acts amounting to acceptance, after which the buyer loses the right to reject.

questions.question_text: Under Section 62 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the implied conditions and warranties under the Act:
options: Cannot be excluded under any circumstances
Are mandatory and override the contract
May be negatived or varied by express agreement, by the course of dealing between the parties, or by usage of trade
questions.explanation: Section 62 makes the statutory implied terms default rules that yield to a contrary contract, course of dealing or trade usage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4(1) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, a contract of sale of goods is:
options: A contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price, and there may be a contract of sale between one part-owner and another
A contract for the exchange of goods for goods (barter)
A contract for the hire of goods
A contract that must always be in writing and registered
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) requires a money consideration ('price'); an exchange of goods for goods is a barter, not a sale, and a gift is not a sale.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, in a contract for sale of unascertained or future goods by description, property passes to the buyer when:
options: Goods of that description and in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract, either by the seller with the buyer's assent or by the buyer with the seller's assent
The seller identifies the goods in his own mind
questions.explanation: Section 23 requires unconditional appropriation with assent; delivery to a carrier without reserving the right of disposal is deemed such an appropriation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where the seller reserves the right of disposal of the goods until certain conditions are fulfilled:
options: Property passes immediately on delivery regardless
The property in the goods does not pass to the buyer until those conditions are fulfilled, notwithstanding delivery of the goods to the buyer or to a carrier
The buyer may waive the conditions unilaterally
questions.explanation: Section 25 allows a seller (typically in documentary sales) to retain the right of disposal, so that property passes only on payment or acceptance of a bill of exchange.

questions.question_text: The Specific Relief Act, 1963 is:
options: Act No. 47 of 1963, which came into force on 1 March 1964
questions.explanation: The Act received assent on 13 December 1963 and was brought into force on 1 March 1964; it defines and amends the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief.

questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific relief can be granted:
options: For enforcing both civil rights and penal laws
Only where the Central Government permits
Only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights, and not for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law
Only in commercial disputes above a prescribed value
questions.explanation: Section 4 confines specific relief to the enforcement of individual civil rights and bars its use to enforce penal laws.

questions.question_text: A suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 by a person dispossessed of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law must be brought:
options: Within three years, and it may be brought against the Government
Within thirty days, with no exception
Within six months from the date of dispossession, and not against the Government
questions.explanation: Section 6(2) bars a suit brought after six months from dispossession or against the Government; Section 6(3) bars any appeal or review of a decree passed in such a suit.

questions.question_text: The essential distinction between a suit under Section 5 and a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is that:
options: A Section 5 suit is based on title, whereas a Section 6 suit is a summary possessory remedy based only on prior possession and dispossession without due process
A Section 5 suit is only for movable property and Section 6 only for immovable property
A Section 6 suit can be filed only by the Government
There is no difference; the sections are identical
questions.explanation: Section 5 enforces the right of a person entitled to possession (title); Section 6 protects settled possession against forcible dispossession, and even a trespasser in prior possession can sue the true owner who dispossesses him without recourse to law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6(4) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a decree in a Section 6 suit:
options: Conclusively decides the question of title between the parties
Does not bar the dispossessed party or the other party from later suing to establish title and recover possession
Bars any further litigation about the property forever
Can be appealed to the High Court within 90 days
questions.explanation: Section 6(4) preserves the right to a regular title suit; the Section 6 decree only restores possession and does not decide title.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a person in possession or control of a specific article of movable property, who is not its owner, may be compelled to deliver it to the person entitled to immediate possession when, among other cases:
options: The plaintiff simply prefers the article back
The article is worth less than Rs 1,000
The thing is held by the defendant as agent or trustee of the plaintiff, or compensation in money would not afford adequate relief, or it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage
The defendant refuses to sell the article
questions.explanation: Section 8 lists the situations (agency/trust, inadequacy of money compensation, difficulty of ascertaining damage, wrongful transfer) where delivery of the specific movable, rather than damages, may be ordered.

questions.question_text: After the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018, Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides that specific performance of a contract:
options: May be granted purely in the discretion of the court, as an exceptional remedy
Can never be granted where damages are claimable
Is available only for contracts relating to immovable property
Shall be enforced by the court, subject only to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16
questions.explanation: The 2018 amendment replaced the discretionary regime: specific performance is now the general rule and the court 'shall' enforce it, subject to the stated exceptions, doing away with the old requirement that damages be an inadequate remedy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following was REMOVED as a bar to specific performance by the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018?
options: That there exists an adequate alternative remedy in damages / compensation in money is adequate relief
That the contract is determinable in nature
That the contract involves a continuous duty the court cannot supervise
That the contract is dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties
questions.explanation: The old Section 14(1)(a) barred specific performance where compensation in money was an adequate relief. The 2018 substitution of Section 14 dropped that bar, consistent with making specific performance the norm.

questions.question_text: Under the substituted Section 14 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, which of the following contracts CANNOT be specifically enforced?
options: A contract for sale of immovable property

A contract which is in its nature determinable, or one whose performance involves a continuous duty the court cannot supervise, or one so dependent on personal qualifications that the court cannot enforce it, or one where substituted performance has been obtained under Section 20
A contract to execute a mortgage
A family settlement of doubtful rights
questions.explanation: Section 14 (as substituted in 2018) lists four categories of non-enforceable contracts: substituted performance obtained, continuous-duty contracts, personal-qualification contracts, and determinable contracts.

questions.question_text: Section 14A of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, inserted by the 2018 amendment, empowers the court to:
options: Award punitive damages of up to three times the contract value
Refer the dispute to compulsory arbitration
Engage one or more experts to report on any specific issue in a suit under the Act, whose opinion forms part of the record
Appoint a receiver in every specific-performance suit
questions.explanation: Section 14A allows the court to engage experts, direct persons to give information or produce documents to the expert, and examine the expert in open court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (as amended in 2018), a plaintiff seeking specific performance:
options: Need not show readiness and willingness if the contract is in writing
Must only aver, but not prove, readiness and willingness
Is presumed ready and willing unless the defendant disproves it
Must prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract to be performed by him
questions.explanation: Section 16(c) requires continuous readiness and willingness; the 2018 amendment changed 'aver and prove' to 'prove', so the burden of proof of readiness and willingness rests squarely on the plaintiff.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the general rule regarding specific performance of a part of a contract is that:
options: The court shall not direct specific performance of part of a contract, except where the unperformed part is small in proportion and admits of compensation in money
The court must always order performance of whatever part is possible
Part performance is never permitted in any circumstances
The plaintiff alone decides which part is to be performed
questions.explanation: Section 12(1) states the general prohibition; Section 12(2)-(3) provide the limited exceptions where the deficiency is minor and compensable, or the parts stand on independent footing.

questions.question_text: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (as substituted in 2018) introduced the concept of:
options: Automatic rescission of every breached contract
Substituted performance of contract, allowing the party suffering a breach to get the contract performed by a third party or by his own agency and recover the costs from the party in breach
A statutory penalty of 10% of contract value for every breach
questions.explanation: Section 20 gives the aggrieved party the option of substituted performance after at least 30 days' written notice to the party in breach.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20(2) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, before undertaking substituted performance the party suffering the breach must give the party in breach a written notice of not less than:
questions.explanation: Section 20(2) requires a minimum 30-day written notice calling upon the party in breach to perform; expenses can be recovered only if the contract is actually got performed through a third party or own agency.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a party who has got the contract performed through a third party or his own agency after notice:
options: May still obtain specific performance in addition
Loses all remedies against the party in breach
Shall not be entitled to claim the relief of specific performance against the party in breach, but may still claim compensation
questions.explanation: Section 20(3) bars specific performance once substituted performance is availed, but Section 20(4) preserves the right to claim compensation from the party in breach.

questions.question_text: Section 20A of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, inserted in 2018, provides that in a suit involving a contract relating to an infrastructure project specified in the Schedule:
options: No injunction shall be granted where granting it would cause impediment or delay in the progress or completion of the project
Only the Supreme Court may grant an injunction
Injunctions may be granted freely as in other suits
The project must be suspended pending the suit
questions.explanation: Section 20A protects notified infrastructure projects from injunctions that would delay them; Section 41(ha) is the corresponding bar in the injunction chapter.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20B of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, Special Courts to try suits relating to infrastructure-project contracts are designated by:
options: The State Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court
questions.explanation: Section 20B requires the State Government to designate one or more Civil Courts as Special Courts in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20C of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a suit filed under the Act must ordinarily be disposed of within:
options: Three years, as under the Limitation Act
Twelve months from the date of service of summons on the defendant, extendable by up to a further six months for reasons recorded in writing
questions.explanation: Section 20C (inserted 2018) sets a 12-month disposal timeline, extendable by a maximum aggregate of six months after recording reasons.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (as amended in 2018), in a suit for specific performance the plaintiff may claim compensation for breach:
options: Only in substitution for specific performance
Only if the contract is for immovable property
Only after the suit for specific performance is dismissed
In addition to specific performance (the option to claim compensation 'in substitution of' performance was deleted in 2018)
questions.explanation: Section 21(1) now permits compensation only 'in addition to' specific performance; under Section 21(4) the compensation is assessed on the principles of Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and under Section 21(5) it must be claimed in the plaint (which the court may allow to be amended).

questions.question_text: Under Section 24 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the dismissal of a suit for specific performance of a contract:
options: Bars the plaintiff's right to sue for compensation for breach of that contract, but not his right to sue for any other relief to which he may be entitled
Has no effect on any future suit
Bars every future suit relating to the property
Automatically entitles the defendant to damages
questions.explanation: Section 24 creates a bar (in the nature of res judicata / election of remedies) against a later compensation suit for breach after an SP suit is dismissed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 26 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, an instrument in writing may be rectified where, through:
options: A unilateral mistake of one party only
Fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, the instrument does not express their real intention
A change in market conditions after execution
The death of one of the parties
questions.explanation: Section 26 permits rectification for fraud or mutual mistake, without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value; rectification must be specifically claimed in the pleadings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, rescission of a contract may be adjudged where:
options: The plaintiff has simply changed his mind
The contract has become commercially disadvantageous
The contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff, or the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff
One party is dissatisfied with performance
questions.explanation: Section 27(1) sets the grounds for rescission; Section 27(2) lists when the court may refuse it (ratification, impossibility of restitution, third-party rights, non-severable part).

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, where a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property has been passed and the purchaser fails to pay the price within the time allowed, the vendor:
options: Must file a fresh suit for rescission
Loses all remedies and must convey the property
May forfeit the entire price paid without any court order
May apply in the same suit in which the decree was made to have the contract rescinded
questions.explanation: Section 28 allows the vendor to move the executing court in the same suit for rescission where the decree-holder purchaser defaults in payment, avoiding multiplicity of proceedings.

questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a written instrument may be ordered to be delivered up and cancelled at the suit of:
options: A person against whom the instrument is void or voidable and who has a reasonable apprehension that, if left outstanding, it may cause him serious injury
Only the person who executed the instrument
Only a registered owner of immovable property
questions.explanation: Section 31 provides the remedy of cancellation; if the instrument was registered, Section 31(2) requires the court to send a copy of its decree to the registering officer, who notes the cancellation.

questions.question_text: Under the proviso to Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a court shall not make a declaratory decree where the plaintiff:
options: Being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so
Is not in possession of the property
Has filed the suit after one year
questions.explanation: The proviso to Section 34 bars a bare declaration where consequential relief is available and not claimed; a declaration under Section 35 binds only the parties and those claiming through them.

questions.question_text: Under Section 36 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, preventive relief is granted:
options: As of right whenever a breach is threatened
Only by way of monetary compensation
At the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual
questions.explanation: Section 36 makes injunctive (preventive) relief discretionary; Section 37 explains that temporary injunctions are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure and perpetual injunctions are granted only by decree at the hearing on the merits.

questions.question_text: Under Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the invasion of the plaintiff's right to property where, among other cases:
options: The defendant is a Government body
There is no standard for ascertaining the actual damage, or compensation in money would not afford adequate relief, or the injunction is necessary to prevent multiplicity of judicial proceedings
questions.explanation: Section 38(3) lists the property-invasion cases; Section 38(1) more generally allows a perpetual injunction to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in the plaintiff's favour.

questions.question_text: Under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a mandatory injunction:
options: Compels the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, to prevent the breach of an obligation
Is the same as a temporary injunction
Can only restrain a person from acting, never compel action
Is available only in criminal proceedings
questions.explanation: Section 39 empowers the court, in its discretion, to grant a mandatory injunction requiring positive acts to prevent or undo a breach of obligation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, an injunction cannot be granted to:
options: Prevent a trespass on the plaintiff's land

Restrain a person from prosecuting a judicial proceeding pending at the institution of the suit (unless necessary to prevent multiplicity), or from instituting proceedings in a court not subordinate to that from which the injunction is sought, or from prosecuting a criminal matter
Prevent a nuisance that is reasonably clear
Restrain a breach of a registered covenant
questions.explanation: Section 41 enumerates the situations where an injunction is refused, including the 2018-inserted clause (ha) barring injunctions that would impede or delay an infrastructure project.

questions.question_text: Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits the court to grant an injunction to perform a negative agreement even though it cannot compel specific performance of the coupled affirmative agreement, provided that:
options: The contract relates to immovable property
The defendant consents to the injunction
The plaintiff has not failed to perform the contract so far as it is binding on him
questions.explanation: Section 42 is the statutory basis for enforcing negative covenants (e.g. exclusive-service clauses); the proviso conditions relief on the plaintiff's own performance.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the provisions of the specific-performance chapter apply to:
options: Only decrees of the Supreme Court
Awards to which the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 does not apply, and to directions in a will or codicil to execute a particular settlement
questions.explanation: Section 25 extends the specific-performance rules to certain non-1996-Act awards and to testamentary directions to execute settlements.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced against:
options: A transferee for value who has paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract
The legal representatives of a deceased party
A company that arises out of amalgamation of a contracting company
questions.explanation: Section 19 makes specific performance enforceable against a party and those claiming under him, but protects a bona fide transferee for value without notice of the earlier contract.

questions.question_text: In Katta Sujatha Reddy v. Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (2022), the Supreme Court held that the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018:
options: Is fully retrospective and reopens concluded matters
Is prospective and does not apply to transactions or suits that took place before 1 October 2018
Repealed the Specific Relief Act, 1963 in its entirety
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court held that the 2018 amendments, being substantive, operate prospectively from the notified date of 1 October 2018.
questions.statute_or_case: Katta Sujatha Reddy v. Siddamsetty Infra Projects (2022)

questions.question_text: The requirement of 'continuous readiness and willingness' as an essential condition for a decree of specific performance was emphasised by the Supreme Court in:
options: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao (1995)
questions.explanation: In N.P. Thirugnanam the Supreme Court held that the plaintiff must prove readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract throughout, from the date of the contract until the hearing.
questions.statute_or_case: N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao (1995)

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, in a suit for relief based on a contract, the person against whom relief is claimed:
options: Cannot raise any defence once the contract is proved
May only plead limitation as a defence
May plead by way of defence any ground available to him under any law relating to contracts
questions.explanation: Section 9 preserves all contract-law defences (e.g. want of consideration, coercion, misrepresentation) to a claimant for specific relief on a contract.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(a) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (as amended in 2018), specific performance cannot be enforced in favour of a person who:
options: Has obtained substituted performance of the contract under Section 20
Has not registered the agreement to sell
questions.explanation: Section 16(a) (substituted in 2018) bars specific performance for a person who has already availed substituted performance under Section 20, dovetailing with Section 14(a).

questions.question_text: Under Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, which of the following may obtain specific performance of a contract?
options: Only the party who drafted the contract
Any party to the contract, and (subject to the proviso) the representative in interest or the principal of any party
Only a party who has fully performed
Any member of the public affected by the contract
questions.explanation: Section 15 identifies the persons entitled to sue for specific performance, including parties, representatives in interest, beneficiaries of marriage settlements or family compromises, and amalgamated companies or LLPs.

questions.question_text: Under Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a person suing for specific performance of a contract for transfer of immovable property who also wants possession, partition or refund of earnest money:
options: Gets such relief automatically with the decree for specific performance
Must file a separate suit for it
Must specifically claim such relief in the plaint (the court may allow the plaint to be amended at any stage to include it)
Can never claim refund of earnest money
questions.explanation: Section 22 requires the additional relief to be specifically pleaded, but liberally permits amendment; the power to grant relief under clause (b) is without prejudice to the compensation power under Section 21.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, where a contract names a sum to be paid in case of breach, specific performance:
options: Is always barred, because the parties have fixed damages
Can be granted only with the defendant's consent
Is converted automatically into a money decree
May still be enforced if the court is satisfied the sum was named only to secure performance and not to give an option of paying money in lieu of performance
questions.explanation: Section 23 clarifies that a liquidated-damages clause is not, by itself, a bar to specific performance; and when performance is decreed, the court does not also decree the named sum.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, where a person contracts to sell immovable property in which he has no title or only an imperfect title, and later acquires an interest, the purchaser:
options: May compel him to make good the contract out of the interest subsequently acquired
Must wait until the seller acquires full title
questions.explanation: Section 13(1)(a) allows the purchaser or lessee to compel the seller to make good the contract from any interest acquired after the contract; the section also applies to sale or hire of movable property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 40 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a plaintiff suing for a perpetual or mandatory injunction:
options: May claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, the injunction, but only if such relief is claimed in the plaint
Automatically receives damages with the injunction
Must elect between the injunction and damages before filing
questions.explanation: Section 40 allows damages alongside or instead of an injunction, subject to the pleading requirement; dismissal of the injunction suit bars a later damages suit for the same breach.

questions.question_text: Sections 43 and 44 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (which dealt with certain declaratory and other reliefs) are:
options: Still in force and frequently invoked
Applicable only to Jammu and Kashmir
questions.explanation: Sections 43 and 44 were repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1974.

questions.question_text: The Schedule to the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (referred to in Sections 20A and 41(ha)) lists categories of 'infrastructure project' such as:
options: Only projects funded by the World Bank
Transport, Energy, Water and Sanitation, Communication, and Social and Commercial Infrastructure
questions.explanation: The Schedule, inserted in 2018, groups infrastructure sub-sectors under five broad categories; the Central Government may amend it by notification laid before Parliament.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, words and expressions used but not defined in the Act, and defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
options: Have the meanings assigned to them in the Indian Contract Act, 1872
Are to be given their ordinary dictionary meaning
Are defined by the court in each case
questions.explanation: Section 2(e) incorporates the definitions of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 into the Specific Relief Act for undefined terms; 'obligation' is defined to include every duty enforceable by law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11(2) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a contract made by a trustee:
options: In excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced
Can be enforced only against the beneficiary
questions.explanation: While Section 11(1) allows specific performance of a contract that performs a trust, Section 11(2) carves out contracts a trustee makes beyond his powers or in breach of trust.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, on adjudging the rescission of a contract, the court may:
options: Order the defaulting party to pay exemplary damages
Direct criminal prosecution of the party at fault
Require the party to whom relief is granted to restore any benefit received from the other party and to make any compensation that justice may require
questions.explanation: Section 30 embodies the equitable principle that a party seeking rescission must do equity by restoring benefits and compensating the other side as justice requires.

questions.question_text: The Code on Social Security, 2020 is:
questions.explanation: The Code on Social Security received assent on 28 September 2020 and is Act No. 36 of 2020.

questions.question_text: The Code on Social Security, 2020 amalgamates and repeals how many earlier central labour enactments?
options: Nine (including the EPF & MP Act 1952, ESI Act 1948, Maternity Benefit Act 1961, Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, and Employees' Compensation Act 1923)
questions.explanation: Section 164 repeals nine enactments, including the EPF & MP Act, ESI Act, Maternity Benefit Act, Payment of Gratuity Act, Employees' Compensation Act, Employment Exchanges Act, BOCW Welfare Cess Act, Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act and Cine Workers Welfare Fund Act.

questions.question_text: Under the First Schedule to the Code on Social Security, 2020, the Employees' Provident Fund provisions (Chapter III) apply to every establishment in which:
options: Ten or more employees are employed
Fifty or more employees are employed
One hundred or more employees are employed
Twenty or more employees are employed
questions.explanation: The EPF threshold of 20 employees is carried over from the EPF & MP Act, 1952; once the Chapter applies it continues to apply even if the number later falls below the threshold.
questions.statute_or_case: Chapter III / First Schedule, Code on Social Security, 2020

questions.question_text: Under the First Schedule to the Code on Social Security, 2020, the Employees' State Insurance provisions (Chapter IV) apply to every establishment in which:
options: Ten or more employees are employed (and, for a hazardous or life-endangering occupation notified by the Central Government, even one employee)
Twenty or more employees are employed
Fifty or more employees are employed
questions.explanation: The ESI threshold is 10 employees generally; the Code allows coverage of hazardous establishments with even a single employee, and provides for voluntary ESI coverage.
questions.statute_or_case: Chapter IV / First Schedule, Code on Social Security, 2020

questions.question_text: A major expansion made by the Code on Social Security, 2020 is that it:
options: Brings gig workers, platform workers and unorganised workers within the social-security framework for the first time
Removes maternity benefit for all women
questions.explanation: Chapters IX, and the definitions of 'gig worker' (Section 2(35)), 'platform worker' (Section 2(61)) and 'aggregator' (Section 2(2)), extend social security to the platform and unorganised economy.
questions.statute_or_case: Sections 2 and 114, Code on Social Security, 2020

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(35) of the Code on Social Security, 2020, a 'gig worker' is:
options: A permanent employee of a factory
A person who performs work or participates in a work arrangement and earns from such activities outside a traditional employer-employee relationship
questions.explanation: The gig-worker definition captures those engaged in work outside the conventional employment relationship; a 'platform worker' (Section 2(61)) accesses work through an online platform provided by an aggregator.

questions.question_text: Under Section 114 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the contribution payable by an aggregator to social-security schemes for gig and platform workers is:
options: A flat ten per cent of turnover
Nil; the schemes are entirely Government-funded
At a rate between one and two per cent of the aggregator's annual turnover, but not exceeding five per cent of the amount paid or payable by the aggregator to gig and platform workers
questions.explanation: Section 114 read with Section 141 sets the aggregator contribution at 1-2% of annual turnover, capped at 5% of amounts paid/payable to gig and platform workers; the categories of aggregators are in the Seventh Schedule.

questions.question_text: Under Section 53 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, gratuity is payable to an employee on termination of employment after continuous service of not less than:
options: Five years (not required in the case of death or disablement, or on expiry of a fixed-term contract)
questions.explanation: Section 53 retains the five-year qualifying period for gratuity but expressly dispenses with it for fixed-term employees on expiry of their term, and for death or disablement.

questions.question_text: Under the first proviso to Section 53(1) of the Code on Social Security, 2020, for a working journalist the qualifying period of 'five years' for gratuity is read as:
questions.explanation: The Code reduces the gratuity qualifying service for working journalists (as defined in the Working Journalists Act, 1955) to three years.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 53(1) proviso, Code on Social Security, 2020

questions.question_text: Under Section 53(2) of the Code on Social Security, 2020, gratuity is calculated at the rate of:
options: One month's wages for every year of service
Seven days' wages for every year of service
Fifteen days' wages (based on the rate of wages last drawn) for every completed year of service or part thereof in excess of six months
questions.explanation: Section 53(2) continues the 15-days-per-year formula of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972; for seasonal establishments the rate is seven days' wages per season (Section 56 deals with the application for, and determination of, the amount).

questions.question_text: Under Section 57 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, every employer (other than the Government) must:
options: Deposit the entire projected gratuity liability with the Central Government
Pay gratuity only if it earns a profit
Obtain compulsory insurance for its liability to pay gratuity, from LIC or another notified insurer
questions.explanation: Section 57 makes gratuity liability insurance compulsory (subject to exemptions for employers with an approved gratuity fund).

questions.question_text: Under Section 60 read with Section 59 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the maximum period of maternity benefit to which a woman is entitled is:
options: Twenty-six weeks (of which not more than eight may precede the expected date of delivery)
questions.explanation: The Code carries forward the enhanced 26-week maternity benefit introduced by the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017; for a woman with two or more surviving children it is 12 weeks.

questions.question_text: Under Section 60 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, a woman is entitled to maternity benefit only if she has actually worked for the employer for not less than:
options: Eighty days in the twelve months immediately preceding the expected date of delivery
questions.explanation: Section 60 retains the 80-day qualifying-work requirement of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.

questions.question_text: Under Section 64 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, a woman is entitled to a medical bonus in addition to maternity benefit where:
options: She has more than two children
No pre-natal confinement and post-natal care is provided free of charge by the employer
Her wages exceed Rs 21,000 per month
questions.explanation: Section 64 continues the medical bonus (a prescribed sum) payable when free medical care is not provided by the employer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 67 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, a creche facility must be provided in every establishment in which:
options: Ten or more employees are employed
Thirty or more women are employed
One hundred or more employees are employed
Fifty or more employees are employed
questions.explanation: Section 67 requires a creche within a prescribed distance in establishments with 50+ employees, and permits mothers up to four visits a day including rest intervals.

questions.question_text: Under Section 68 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the dismissal of a woman during or on account of her absence on maternity leave is:
options: Unlawful; she cannot be discharged or dismissed during such absence, nor can her conditions of service be varied to her disadvantage
questions.explanation: Section 68 protects a woman against dismissal during maternity absence; deprivation of maternity benefit or bonus is permitted only for gross misconduct after due notice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 74 of the Code on Social Security, 2020 (Chapter VII, employees' compensation), an employer is liable to pay compensation where:
options: Personal injury is caused to an employee by an accident arising out of and in the course of his employment
An employee is injured off duty at home
An employee is dismissed for misconduct
questions.explanation: Section 74 continues the core rule of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923; liability is excluded for injury not resulting in three days' disablement, or (except for death) where the accident was due to intoxication, wilful disobedience of safety rules, or wilful removal of safety devices.

questions.question_text: Under Section 77 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, compensation for an employee's injury must be paid:
options: Within one year, with no interest
Only after a civil suit is decreed

As soon as it falls due, and if not paid within one month the competent authority may direct interest at the rate prescribed by the Central Government plus, if the delay is unjustified, damages of up to 50 per cent of the arrears
questions.explanation: Section 77 imposes interest and a default penalty to deter delayed payment of employees' compensation.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the National Social Security Board is constituted to:
options: Recommend and monitor schemes for unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers, and advise the Central Government
questions.explanation: Section 6 establishes the National Social Security Board (term three years) for the unorganised, gig and platform workforce; State Governments constitute State Unorganised Workers' Boards.

questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, an appeal against an order determining and assessing provident-fund dues (Section 125) or levying damages (Section 128) in respect of Chapter III lies to:
options: The Tribunal constituted by the Central Government (the Industrial Tribunal), and no such appeal by the employer against an assessment is entertained unless he deposits 25 per cent of the amount due
The civil court, without any pre-deposit
questions.explanation: Section 23(1) provides an appeal to the Tribunal against assessment of PF dues (Section 125) and levy of damages (Section 128); Section 23(3) requires a 25% pre-deposit for an employer's appeal against an assessment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 48 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, disputes relating to Employees' State Insurance are decided by:
options: The Employees' Insurance Court constituted by the State Government (with an appeal to the High Court on a substantial question of law)
questions.explanation: Section 48-52 continue the Employees' Insurance Court machinery of the ESI Act, 1948; a claim must ordinarily be filed within three years of the cause of action.

questions.question_text: Under Section 133 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, an employer who deducts an employee's contribution from wages but fails to pay it to the Provident Fund or ESI Corporation is punishable with:
options: A warning for the first offence
Imprisonment for a term of one to three years and a fine of one lakh rupees
questions.explanation: Section 133 prescribes the highest penalties for non-payment of deducted employee contributions (1-3 years' imprisonment and a Rs 1 lakh fine); failure to pay the employer's own contribution attracts a lower penalty.

questions.question_text: Under Section 137 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, before prosecuting an employer for certain offences the Inspector-cum-Facilitator must:
options: Obtain the sanction of the Supreme Court
Give the employer an opportunity to comply within a specified period (not available for a repeat of the same offence within five years)
questions.explanation: Section 137 embodies the facilitative-enforcement approach: a compliance opportunity before prosecution for first-time offences.

questions.question_text: Under Section 138 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, a first-time offence punishable with fine only may be compounded on payment of:
options: Half of the maximum fine provided for that offence
The full maximum fine plus costs
Twenty per cent of the maximum fine
questions.explanation: Section 138(1): a first-time offence punishable with fine only may be compounded for half the maximum fine, and an offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year and also with fine for three-fourths of the maximum fine; compounding is barred where a similar offence was compounded or a conviction was recorded within the preceding three years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 142 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, an employee, unorganised worker or other person:
options: Cannot be asked for any identity document
May be required to establish his identity, or the identity of family members, through Aadhaar for registration, for receiving benefits, or for withdrawal of benefits
questions.explanation: Section 142 mandates Aadhaar-based identification for availing social-security benefits and services under the Code.

questions.question_text: Under Section 141 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, a 'Social Security Fund' is established for:
options: The social security and welfare of unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers, funded from contributions (including aggregator contributions), grants and penalties
questions.explanation: Section 141 creates a dedicated Social Security Fund; amounts received from composition of offences and from aggregator contributions are credited to it.

questions.question_text: Under Section 113 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, an unorganised worker, gig worker or platform worker becomes eligible for the benefit of schemes on:
options: Payment of a registration fee of Rs 1,000
Self-registration on the specified portal, on the basis of self-declaration and Aadhaar, subject to being 16 years or older (or a notified age)
questions.explanation: Section 113 provides for portal-based self-registration of unorganised, gig and platform workers so that they can access welfare schemes.

questions.question_text: Under Section 100 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the cess for the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Fund is levied at a rate:
options: Not exceeding two per cent, but not less than one per cent, of the cost of construction incurred by an employer
A flat five per cent of construction cost
Ten per cent of the contract value
questions.explanation: Section 100 continues the BOCW welfare cess of 1-2% of construction cost; Section 103 provides for self-assessment of the cess.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the amount of provident-fund contributions due from an employer:
options: Ranks last among the employer's debts
Has priority over all other debts in the distribution of the employer's property in insolvency or on winding up
Is extinguished on the employer's insolvency
Is payable only after secured creditors are fully paid
questions.explanation: Section 19 (and Section 47 for ESI) gives statutory priority to provident-fund and insurance contributions over other debts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 124 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, an employer:
options: May reduce wages to offset the contribution
May recover the employer's share of contribution from the employee
Must not, by reason only of his liability to pay any contribution under the Code, reduce (directly or indirectly) the wages of any employee
Must double the wages of every employee
questions.explanation: Section 124 prohibits the employer from passing on its statutory contribution burden to employees through wage cuts.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the age of superannuation for the purposes of the Employees' Provident Fund (Chapter III) is:
questions.explanation: The proviso to the definition of 'superannuation' in Section 2(82) fixes 58 years for Chapter III (EPF) purposes.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2(82) proviso, Code on Social Security, 2020

questions.question_text: Under Section 109 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the Central Government's welfare schemes for unorganised workers may cover matters relating to:
options: Life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection, education, and any other benefit determined by the Central Government
questions.explanation: Section 109(1) lists the fields of welfare for the Central Government's unorganised-worker schemes; funding may come from the Centre, the States, beneficiaries or employers, or CSR funds.

questions.question_text: Under Section 145 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, where an establishment is transferred, the transferor and transferee are:
options: Both fully discharged from all past liability
Jointly and severally liable to pay the contributions and other amounts due under the Code up to the date of transfer (the transferee's liability being limited to the assets obtained)
Liable only if the transfer deed says so
questions.explanation: Section 145 preserves accrued social-security dues on transfer of an establishment, capping the transferee's liability at the value of assets acquired.

questions.question_text: Under Section 133 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, a person who dishonestly makes a false return, report, statement or information required to be submitted under the Code:
options: Merely has to refund the amount
Is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to fifty thousand rupees, or both
Is barred from employment for life
questions.explanation: Section 133 clause (o), read with clause (iii) of the penalty provision, punishes dishonestly making a false return, report, statement or information with imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to Rs 50,000, or both (Section 148 separately empowers the Government to withdraw benefits for misuse).

questions.question_text: Under Section 161 of the Code on Social Security, 2020:
options: The Code yields to any private contract of service
The Code applies only where no other welfare law applies
State laws prevail over the Code
The Code has effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in any other law, or in the terms of any award, agreement or contract of service, whether made before or after the Code
questions.explanation: Section 161 is the non-obstante clause; however, more favourable benefits under a contract or scheme are preserved.

questions.question_text: Under Section 139 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, every establishment must report vacancies to:
options: Career centres, in the manner prescribed (replacing the compulsory notification of vacancies to employment exchanges)
questions.explanation: Section 139 modernises the Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act, 1959 by requiring reporting of vacancies to 'career centres'.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, for the purposes of Chapters III and IV the term 'employee' generally means a person drawing wages:
options: Of any amount, without a ceiling
Less than or equal to the wage ceiling notified by the Central Government
questions.explanation: A notified wage ceiling determines mandatory coverage under the EPF and ESI chapters, though higher-paid employees can be covered by agreement or option.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2(26) proviso, Code on Social Security, 2020

questions.question_text: Under Chapter III of the Code on Social Security, 2020, the standard employer and employee contribution to the Employees' Provident Fund is:
options: Twenty-five per cent by the employer only
One per cent by the employee only
Ten per cent (or twelve per cent as notified) of wages by each of the employer and the employee
questions.explanation: The Code retains the EPF contribution structure (statutory 10%, notified 12%) payable by both employer and employee on 'wages' as defined in the Code.
questions.statute_or_case: Chapter III, Code on Social Security, 2020

questions.question_text: The Trade Marks Act, 1999:
options: Is Act No. 47 of 1999, came into force on 15 September 2003, and repealed and replaced the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958
questions.explanation: The 1999 Act was enacted to make Indian trade mark law TRIPS-compliant, introducing service marks, well-known marks, a single register, and a ten-year registration term.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a 'trade mark' means a mark capable of being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, and may include:
options: The shape of goods, their packaging, and combination of colours
questions.explanation: The 1999 Act broadened the definition to cover shape marks, packaging (trade dress), colour combinations and service marks.

questions.question_text: Under Section 9 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the 'absolute grounds' for refusal of registration include that the mark:
options: Is identical to an earlier registered mark
Is similar to a well-known mark
Was applied for in bad faith by a former agent

Is devoid of any distinctive character; or consists exclusively of marks/indications which designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, values or geographical origin of the goods/services; or has become customary in the current language or bona fide trade practice — unless it has acquired a distinctive character through use before the date of application
questions.explanation: Section 9 also bars marks that deceive or cause confusion, hurt religious sentiments, are scandalous or obscene, or are prohibited under the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950; and shapes resulting from the nature of goods, needed to obtain a technical result, or giving substantial value to the goods.

questions.question_text: Under Section 11 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the 'relative grounds' for refusal of registration are that, because of identity/similarity with an earlier mark and identity/similarity of goods or services:
options: There exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, which includes the likelihood of association with the earlier mark; and a mark identical or similar to a well-known mark may be refused even for dissimilar goods where use would take unfair advantage of, or be detrimental to, the well-known mark
The mark is not represented graphically
The applicant is a foreign national
questions.explanation: A relative-grounds objection can be waived if the proprietor of the earlier mark consents; the Registrar also considers whether the earlier mark is a well-known mark.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(zg) read with Section 11(6)-(9) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a 'well-known trade mark' is:
options: Any mark that has been registered for more than ten years

A mark which has become so to the substantial segment of the public which uses the goods/services that its use on other goods/services would be likely to be taken as indicating a connection with the proprietor — and the Registrar cannot require, as a condition, that the mark has been used or registered in India, or is well-known to the public at large in India
Only a mark owned by a multinational company
A mark that has won an award
questions.explanation: Once a mark is determined to be well-known, it is protected across all classes of goods and services; the Registrar maintains a list of well-known marks (Rule 124).

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a registered trade mark is valid for:
options: Seven years, renewable for fourteen years
Ten years from the date of registration, and may be renewed for successive periods of ten years indefinitely on payment of the renewal fee
questions.explanation: The 1999 Act extended the term from 7 years (under the 1958 Act) to 10 years; a mark removed for non-renewal may be restored within one year on payment of a surcharge.

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, registration of a trade mark gives the registered proprietor:
options: A right that can never be challenged
A right to use the mark for any goods whatsoever
The exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and the right to obtain relief in respect of infringement
questions.explanation: Where two persons are registered proprietors of identical or nearly resembling marks, neither has exclusive rights against the other, but each has rights against third parties (Section 28(3)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 29 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, infringement of a registered trade mark occurs when a person, not being the proprietor or a permitted user, uses in the course of trade a mark which:
options: Is identical with, or deceptively similar to, the registered mark in relation to identical or similar goods/services so as to cause a likelihood of confusion; and (for a mark with a reputation in India) using an identical/similar mark even on dissimilar goods so as to take unfair advantage of or be detrimental to its distinctive character or repute
Is merely similar in some respect
Is used with the proprietor's consent
questions.explanation: Section 29(5) treats use of the mark as a trade name or part of a business name as infringement; Section 29(8) covers infringing use in advertising; Section 29(9) covers spoken use of words.

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(2) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the common-law action of 'passing off' is preserved, so that:
options: Nothing in the Act affects the right of action against any person for passing off goods or services as the goods or services of another, or the remedies in respect thereof — this protects unregistered marks with goodwill
Passing off applies only to identical marks
questions.explanation: The classic 'trinity' for passing off — goodwill/reputation, misrepresentation, and damage — was stated in Reckitt & Colman v. Borden (Jif Lemon) and applied in India in Cadila Health Care v. Cadila Pharmaceuticals (2001).

questions.question_text: Under Section 47 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a registered trade mark may be taken off the register on the ground of non-use where:
options: The mark has not been used for one year
A competitor wishes to use the mark

There has been no bona fide use of the mark for a continuous period of five years and three months up to the date of the application for removal, and there was no bona fide intention to use it when it was registered
The proprietor has changed its business
questions.explanation: Removal for non-use may be refused where the non-use was due to special circumstances in the trade and not to an intention to abandon or not to use the mark.

questions.question_text: Under Section 30 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, use of a registered mark is NOT an infringement where it is:
options: Used to trade on the proprietor's reputation

Used in accordance with honest practices to indicate the kind, quality, intended purpose or other characteristics of goods/services; or used to indicate the intended purpose of goods (e.g. accessories or spare parts); or where the goods bearing the mark were put on the market by the proprietor and are lawfully acquired (principle of exhaustion)
questions.explanation: Section 30(3)-(4) embody the principle of exhaustion of rights; Indian courts have held this to include international exhaustion (Kapil Wadhwa v. Samsung, 2012).

questions.question_text: Under Sections 18 to 23 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the registration procedure involves:
options: Filing an application, examination by the Registrar, advertisement of the accepted application in the Trade Marks Journal, a four-month period for filing opposition, hearing of any opposition, and registration with effect from the date of application
questions.explanation: An opposition under Section 21 must be filed within four months of advertisement; the registration, once granted, dates back to the filing date (Section 23(1)).

questions.question_text: Under Section 57 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, 'rectification' of the register (cancellation or variation of a registration, or removal of an entry made without sufficient cause or wrongly remaining) may be sought by:
options: Any person aggrieved, by application to the Registrar or (now) the High Court
Any member of the public without any grievance
questions.explanation: After the abolition of the IPAB by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, rectification applications and appeals lie to the High Court.

questions.question_text: Under Section 103 and Section 104 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, applying a false trade mark or false trade description, or selling goods to which a false trade mark is applied, is punishable with:
options: Imprisonment for a term of not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees
questions.explanation: The court may impose a lesser sentence for adequate and special reasons recorded in the judgment; Section 115 requires the opinion of the Registrar before a prosecution for certain offences and makes such offences cognizable.

questions.question_text: Under Section 134 read with Section 135 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a suit for infringement or passing off:
options: May be filed only where the defendant resides
Must be filed in the High Court in every case
Can be filed in any Magistrate's court

Must be instituted in a District Court (or a court not inferior to it) having jurisdiction; for infringement of a registered mark (but not for a pure passing-off action, which is governed by the ordinary rules of jurisdiction), Section 134(2) additionally allows the suit where the plaintiff actually and voluntarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain
questions.explanation: Section 134(2), by its own terms, extends the plaintiff's-forum benefit only to clauses (a) and (b) of Section 134(1) (infringement and other rights in a registered mark), not to clause (c) (passing off); the Supreme Court in IPRS v. Sanjay Dalia (2015) clarified its interaction with Section 20 CPC.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(h) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, 'deceptively similar' means:
options: A mark so nearly resembling another mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion
A mark that is identical in every respect
A mark used on different goods
A mark registered in a different country
questions.explanation: The test of deceptive similarity considers the nature of the marks, the degree of resemblance (phonetic, visual, conceptual), the nature of the goods, the class of purchasers and the surrounding circumstances (Amritdhara Pharmacy v. Satya Deo Gupta).

questions.question_text: The 'transborder' or 'spillover' reputation of a mark — a concept developed through case law rather than a term defined in the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — means that such reputation:
options: Is not recognised in Indian law

Is recognised in Indian passing-off and well-known-mark jurisprudence — a mark used abroad but not in India can be protected in India if its reputation has spilled over into India through advertising, media and travellers (N.R. Dongre v. Whirlpool Corp., 1996)
questions.explanation: Indian courts have protected foreign marks with a transborder reputation even in the absence of local use or registration; Toyota v. Prius Auto (2018) later cautioned that the reputation must exist in India at the relevant date.
questions.statute_or_case: N.R. Dongre v. Whirlpool Corporation, (1996) 5 SCC 714; Sections 11 and 27, Trade Marks Act, 1999

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(m) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a 'mark' includes:
options: Only a word or a logo
A device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral, shape of goods, packaging or combination of colours or any combination thereof
Only the name of a company
questions.explanation: This inclusive definition, together with the definition of 'trade mark', determines what can be registered.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(e) read with Section 70 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a 'certification trade mark' is a mark:
options: Owned by a group of traders for their own use
The same as a collective mark
A mark that certifies the proprietor's own goods

Indicating that the goods or services are certified by the proprietor in respect of origin, material, mode of manufacture, quality, accuracy or other characteristics — and the proprietor must not himself carry on a trade in those goods/services
questions.explanation: A 'collective mark' (Section 2(1)(g)) belongs to an association and distinguishes the goods/services of its members; examples of certification marks include 'AGMARK', 'ISI' and 'Woolmark'.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 2(1)(e) and Section 70, Trade Marks Act, 1999

questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, in legal proceedings the registration of a trade mark is:
options: Prima facie evidence of the validity of the original registration and of all subsequent assignments and transmissions; and it shall not be held invalid for want of distinctiveness under Section 9 for lack of evidence of distinctiveness before the Registrar, if the mark is shown to have in fact become distinctive by the date of registration through use by the proprietor or his predecessor in title
Conclusive evidence of validity for all time
No evidence of validity at all
questions.explanation: Section 32 separately provides that a mark registered in breach of Section 9(1) shall not be declared invalid if, after registration and before the challenge, it has acquired a distinctive character through use; unlike the repealed Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, the 1999 Act does not give registration conclusive validity after any fixed number of years.

questions.question_text: Under Section 12 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the Registrar may permit the registration of identical or similar marks by more than one proprietor:
options: Only if the marks are used in different States
In the case of honest concurrent use, or of other special circumstances, subject to such conditions and limitations as the Registrar thinks fit
Only with the consent of the Central Government
questions.explanation: 'Honest concurrent use' allows a later user who adopted the mark independently and in good faith to obtain registration despite an earlier identical or similar mark.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(r) and Section 48 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a 'registered user' / 'permitted use':
options: Requires no consent from the proprietor
Cannot be recorded on the register

Is use of a registered mark by a person other than the proprietor, in relation to goods/services with which he is connected in the course of trade, with the consent of the proprietor and subject to conditions, and such use is deemed to be use by the proprietor
questions.explanation: The 1999 Act relaxed the old requirement of recording all registered users, recognising unrecorded 'permitted use' by written consent of the proprietor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, an opposition to the registration of a trade mark:
options: May be filed only by the proprietor of an earlier registered mark
May be filed within one year of registration
May be filed by any person within four months of the advertisement or re-advertisement of the application in the Trade Marks Journal
questions.explanation: The Registrar serves the notice of opposition on the applicant, who files a counter-statement within two months, failing which the application is deemed abandoned.

questions.question_text: Under Section 124 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, where in an infringement suit the defendant pleads that the plaintiff's registration is invalid, and a rectification proceeding is pending or the court is satisfied the plea is prima facie tenable:
options: The court stays the infringement suit pending the final disposal of the rectification proceedings
The court dismisses the infringement suit
The court ignores the invalidity plea
The court itself cancels the registration
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court in Patel Field Marshal Agencies v. P.M. Diesels (2018) held that if a party does not file for rectification within the time permitted after the court finds the plea prima facie tenable, it loses the right to challenge validity.

questions.question_text: Under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, India is a member of the Madrid Protocol (since 2013), which allows:
options: Automatic worldwide protection with no filing

An applicant to file a single international application, based on a home application or registration, designating multiple member countries, administered by WIPO (given effect in India by Chapter IVA and Section 36A onwards)
questions.explanation: Chapter IVA (Sections 36A-36G) was inserted to implement the Madrid Protocol; the Registrar acts as the office of origin and the office of a designated Contracting Party.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 (which defines 'trade mark' by reference to both goods and services, unlike the goods-only definition in the repealed Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958), the 1999 Act for the first time expressly protected:
options: Service marks (marks used in relation to services, not merely goods) — with services classified in Classes 35-45 of the NICE Classification
questions.explanation: The recognition of service marks was a major reform, bringing banks, hotels, airlines, insurers and IT companies within trade-mark protection.

questions.question_text: Under Section 7 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 (read with the Fourth Schedule to the Trade Marks Rules, 2017), goods and services are classified according to:
options: A unique Indian classification of 20 classes
The Harmonised System of customs tariffs
The International Classification of Goods and Services (the NICE Classification), presently comprising 45 classes (34 for goods, 11 for services)
questions.explanation: An application may now be filed as a multi-class application covering several classes; the Registrar's classification decision under Section 7(2) is final.
questions.statute_or_case: Section 7, Trade Marks Act, 1999 and the Fourth Schedule to the Trade Marks Rules, 2017

questions.question_text: Under Sections 38 and 42 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the assignment of a registered trade mark:
options: May be with or without the goodwill of the business, in respect of all or some of the goods/services (assignment without goodwill requires advertisement as directed by the Registrar), and unregistered marks may also be assigned with or without goodwill
Can only be with the goodwill of the business
questions.explanation: This liberalised the older law, which restricted assignment of marks in gross; restrictions remain to prevent the creation of multiple exclusive rights likely to deceive.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(2)(b)-(c) read with Section 29 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, 'use' of a mark:
options: Means only physical application of the mark to goods

Includes use in printed or other visual representation, and in relation to services, use in any statement about the availability, provision or performance of services — actual physical use on goods is not always necessary
Requires the mark to be sold
questions.explanation: The broad definition of 'use' is important both for establishing prior rights and for showing infringing use.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(1)(zb) proviso and Section 9(3) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a mark shall not be registered as a trade mark if it consists exclusively of:
options: The shape of goods which results from the nature of the goods themselves; the shape necessary to obtain a technical result; or the shape which gives substantial value to the goods
questions.explanation: These functionality exclusions prevent trade-mark law from being used to obtain a perpetual monopoly over functional or aesthetic features that belong in patent or design law.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, 'transfer of property' means an act by which a living person conveys property, in present or in future, to:
options: Only to another individual human being
One or more other living persons, or to himself, or to himself and one or more other living persons ('living person' includes a company, association or body of individuals)
questions.explanation: Section 5 confines the Act to inter vivos transfers; testamentary succession and transfers by operation of law (inheritance, forfeiture, insolvency, court sale) are outside it.

questions.question_text: Under Section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which of the following CANNOT be transferred?
options: The chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate (spes successionis), a mere right of re-entry, an easement apart from the dominant heritage, and a mere right to sue
questions.explanation: Section 6 lists the non-transferable interests, including spes successionis (clause a), easements apart from the dominant heritage (clause c), a restricted interest personal to the owner (clause d), and a mere right to sue (clause e).

questions.question_text: Under Section 10 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a condition absolutely restraining the transferee from parting with or disposing of his interest in the property is:
options: Void (except in the case of a lease where the condition is for the benefit of the lessor, and except a transfer to or for the benefit of a woman not being a Hindu, Muhammadan or Buddhist, restraining anticipation)
questions.explanation: Section 10 embodies the rule against absolute restraints on alienation; a partial restraint may be valid if reasonable.

questions.question_text: The rule against perpetuities in Section 14 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that a transfer cannot create an interest that is to take effect after:
options: The lifetime of one or more persons living at the date of the transfer, and the minority of some person who is to be in existence at the expiration of that period (to whom the interest is to belong on attaining full age)
questions.explanation: Section 14 limits the postponement of vesting to lives in being plus the minority of an unborn person; Section 13 governs transfers for the benefit of an unborn person, who must take the whole remaining interest.

questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, where an interest is created for the benefit of an unborn person:
options: The unborn person may be given a life estate

The interest must be preceded by a prior life interest, and the unborn person must, on coming into existence, take the whole of the remaining interest of the transferor (no life estate can be given to an unborn person)
The transfer directly to an unborn person is fully valid
The prior interest must always be to the transferor himself
questions.explanation: An unborn person cannot be given a limited (life) interest; the entire residue must vest in him absolutely, else the transfer fails.

questions.question_text: Under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a person is said to have 'notice' of a fact where:
options: He has been formally served with a written notice only
The fact is published in a newspaper

He actually knows it, or would have known it but for wilful abstention from an inquiry or search which he ought to have made, or gross negligence — and registration of a document operates as constructive notice of it
A third party told him about it
questions.explanation: The Explanations to Section 3 treat registration, actual possession by a person, and notice to an agent as constructive notice.

questions.question_text: The doctrine of 'feeding the grant by estoppel' in Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that where a person fraudulently or erroneously represents that he is authorised to transfer certain immovable property and does so for consideration:
options: The transfer is void from the start
The transferee can only claim damages
The transferor keeps any after-acquired interest
