The transfer shall, at the option of the transferee, operate on any interest which the transferor may acquire in the property at any time during which the contract of transfer subsists
questions.explanation: Section 43 protects a bona fide transferee for value; it does not apply against a subsequent transferee for value in good faith without notice.

questions.question_text: The doctrine of 'lis pendens' in Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 means:
options: During the pendency of a suit in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred by any party so as to affect the rights of any other party under any decree that may be made in the suit, except with the court's authority
A suit cannot be filed about property that is subject to a transfer
The property must be sold to satisfy the decree
Any transfer during a suit is absolutely void
questions.explanation: Section 52 does not make a pendente lite transfer void; the transferee simply takes subject to the outcome of the suit.

questions.question_text: The doctrine of 'part performance' in Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 allows a transferee who has taken possession under a written contract of transfer of immovable property for consideration, and has performed or is willing to perform his part, to:
options: Compel the transferor to execute the sale deed
Defend his possession against the transferor and persons claiming under him, even though the transfer has not been completed by a registered instrument as required by law
Claim ownership of the property outright
Sell the property to a third party
questions.explanation: Section 53A is a shield, not a sword; after the 2001 amendment, the contract must be registered for Section 53A to be invoked.

questions.question_text: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a 'sale' of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards can be made only by:
options: An oral agreement plus delivery of possession
An entry in the municipal records
questions.explanation: Section 54 also provides that a contract for sale ('agreement to sell') does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on the property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 58(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a 'mortgage' is:
options: The absolute transfer of ownership of property
A lease for more than one year
A gift with a condition of repayment

The transfer of an interest in specific immovable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced (or to be advanced) by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement giving rise to a pecuniary liability
questions.explanation: Section 58 defines the six kinds of mortgage: simple, by conditional sale, usufructuary, English, by deposit of title-deeds (equitable), and anomalous.

questions.question_text: Under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds (an equitable mortgage) can be created:
options: By a person in certain notified towns delivering to a creditor documents of title to immovable property, with intent to create a security thereon (no registered instrument is required if there is no separate memorandum of deposit constituting the bargain)
Only by a registered mortgage deed
Only in favour of a scheduled bank
questions.explanation: An equitable mortgage arises from the act of deposit with the requisite intention; it is available in the towns specified by the State Government.

questions.question_text: The doctrine 'once a mortgage always a mortgage' and the mortgagor's 'right of redemption' are contained in Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which provides that:
options: The right of redemption ends on the due date of the loan

At any time after the principal money has become due, the mortgagor has a right, on payment of the mortgage money, to require the mortgagee to reconvey the property and deliver documents; and any clause that clogs or fetters this equity of redemption is void
The mortgagee may keep the property if the loan is not repaid on time
questions.explanation: A 'clog on the equity of redemption' is void; the right is extinguished only by the act of the parties or by a decree of the court (Section 60).

questions.question_text: Under Section 67 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the mortgagee's remedy of 'foreclosure' (absolute vesting of the property, extinguishing the mortgagor's right of redemption) is available in the case of:
options: A mortgage by conditional sale and an anomalous mortgage so providing — but NOT a simple mortgage or an English mortgage, where the remedy is sale
Only where the loan exceeds Rs 1 lakh
questions.explanation: Foreclosure suits lie for mortgages by conditional sale and anomalous mortgages; a simple, English or equitable mortgagee sues for sale of the property (Section 67).

questions.question_text: Under Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a 'lease' of immovable property is:
options: A transfer of ownership of the property
A licence to enter the property

A transfer of a right to enjoy such property, made for a certain time (or in perpetuity), in consideration of a price paid or promised, or of money, a share of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically or on specified occasions
questions.explanation: A lease transfers an interest in the property (a leasehold estate); a licence (Section 52, Indian Easements Act) creates only a personal permission to do something that would otherwise be unlawful.

questions.question_text: Under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent:
options: Can be made only by a registered instrument; all other leases may be made either by a registered instrument or by oral agreement accompanied by delivery of possession
Requires the sanction of the Collector
questions.explanation: Section 107 sets the formalities; a lease and a counterpart, where a registered instrument is used, must be executed by both lessor and lessee.

questions.question_text: Under Section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, a lessee is entitled to:
options: Retain all fixtures he has installed
Remove, before the lease ends (or within a reasonable time after), all things which he has attached to the earth, provided he leaves the property in the state in which he received it
Assign the lease without any restriction, even if the lease bars assignment
Refuse to pay rent if the property is damaged by a third party
questions.explanation: Section 108 sets out the rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee, including the lessee's right to remove fixtures and to deduct the cost of repairs the lessor fails to make.

questions.question_text: Under Section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease of immovable property determines by, among other modes:
options: Only on the death of the lessee

Efflux of time, happening of a specified event, merger, express surrender, implied surrender, forfeiture (for breach of an express condition or denial of the lessor's title), and expiry of a notice to quit
questions.explanation: Section 111 enumerates the modes of determination; Section 106 provides for notice to quit (default 6 months for immovable property leased for agricultural or manufacturing purposes; 15 days otherwise, though the notice need not now end with the tenancy month after the 2002 amendment).

questions.question_text: Under Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a 'gift' is the transfer of certain existing movable or immovable property, made voluntarily and without consideration, by a donor to a donee, and accepted:
options: At any time, even after the donor's death
Only if the donee pays a nominal sum
By or on behalf of the donee during the lifetime of the donor and while he is still capable of giving; if the donee dies before acceptance, the gift is void
questions.explanation: Section 123 requires a gift of immovable property to be made by a registered instrument attested by two witnesses; a gift of movable property may be by registered instrument or by delivery.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (transfer by ostensible owner), where a person is by the consent (express or implied) of the persons interested the ostensible owner of property and transfers it for consideration:
options: The transfer is not voidable on the ground that the transferor was not authorised to make it, provided the transferee, after taking reasonable care to ascertain that the transferor had power to transfer, acted in good faith
The real owner can recover the property in every case
The transferee gets no protection at all
questions.explanation: Section 41 protects a bona fide purchaser for value from an ostensible owner who took reasonable care (Ramcoomar Koondoo v. McQueen).

questions.question_text: The doctrine of election in Section 35 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that a person who takes a benefit under an instrument that also purports to transfer his own property to another:
options: May keep both the benefit and his own property
Must elect either to confirm the whole instrument (transferring his own property) or to dissent from it (in which case he must relinquish the benefit conferred, which reverts to the transferor)
questions.explanation: Election rests on the principle that one who accepts a benefit under a deed must give full effect to that deed.

questions.question_text: Under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (fraudulent transfer), every transfer of immovable property made with intent to defeat or delay the creditors of the transferor is:
options: Voidable at the option of any creditor so defeated or delayed (but this does not affect the rights of a transferee in good faith and for consideration)
Void only if the transferor is later declared insolvent
questions.explanation: Section 53(2) also makes a gratuitous transfer made with intent to defraud a subsequent transferee voidable at the option of that transferee.

questions.question_text: Under Section 55 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the seller of immovable property is bound to:
options: Guarantee that the buyer will make a profit

Disclose material defects in the property or in his title of which the buyer is not aware, produce title deeds for examination, answer questions as to title, execute a proper conveyance, and take reasonable care of the property between contract and delivery
questions.explanation: Section 55 also gives the seller a statutory charge on the property for unpaid purchase money and gives the buyer a charge for pre-paid price if delivery is refused.

questions.question_text: The rule in Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, protecting a transferee who makes improvements believing in good faith that he is absolutely entitled to the property, provides that when he is subsequently evicted by a person with a better title:
options: He is entitled to require the person causing the eviction either to pay the value of the improvement, or to sell his interest in the property to the transferee at the then market value irrespective of the improvement
He must remove the improvements at his own cost
He gets nothing for the improvements
He becomes the owner of the property
questions.explanation: Section 51 embodies the equitable principle that a bona fide improver of another's land should not be left uncompensated.

questions.question_text: Under Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a 'charge' on immovable property:
options: Is the same as a mortgage in all respects

Arises where property is made security for the payment of money and the transaction does not amount to a mortgage; the charge-holder has the same rights as a simple mortgagee (right to sale, not foreclosure), but a charge cannot be enforced against a bona fide transferee for value without notice
Can only be created by a court
questions.explanation: A charge may arise by act of parties or by operation of law; unlike a mortgage it does not transfer any interest in the property.

questions.question_text: Under Section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, unless a different intention is expressed or necessarily implied, a transfer of property passes to the transferee:
options: Only the physical possession of the property

All the interest which the transferor is then capable of passing in the property and in its legal incidents (including, for land, rents and profits accruing after the transfer, and things attached to the earth)
questions.explanation: Section 8 is the 'passing of interest' provision; the transferee takes the property with all its legal incidents unless the deed says otherwise.

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a transfer of property may be made subject to a condition, but a transfer is void if:
options: The condition is subsequent rather than precedent
The condition precedent is impossible, forbidden by law, fraudulent, involves injury to another's person or property, or is immoral or opposed to public policy
questions.explanation: Section 25 mirrors the tests for lawful object/consideration in the Contract Act; Section 26 requires only substantial compliance with a condition precedent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, an 'exchange' is a transaction where:
options: Two persons mutually transfer the ownership of one thing for the ownership of another, neither thing (or both things) being money only
One person transfers property for money
A person gifts property to another
A person leases property to another
questions.explanation: An exchange is effected in the same manner as a sale; each party has the rights and liabilities of a seller as to that which he gives and of a buyer as to that which he takes (Section 120).

questions.question_text: Under Section 130 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the transfer of an 'actionable claim' (an unsecured debt or a beneficial interest in movable property not in possession):
options: Can be effected only by an instrument in writing signed by the transferor (or his agent), and is complete and effectual upon the execution of such instrument (notice to the debtor is not necessary to complete the transfer, but binds the debtor only from the date of notice)
questions.explanation: Section 130 deals with assignment of debts and other actionable claims; the assignee takes subject to all equities available against the assignor.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, an interest is 'vested' when:
options: It depends on an uncertain future event

It is created in favour of a person without specifying the time when it is to take effect, or in terms specifying that it is to take effect forthwith or on the happening of an event which must happen — a vested interest is not defeated by the death of the transferee before he obtains possession and passes to his heirs
It always takes effect only on the transferor's death
questions.explanation: Section 21 defines a 'contingent interest' as one that takes effect only on the happening (or not happening) of a specified uncertain event; a contingent interest lapses if the transferee dies before it vests.
questions.statute_or_case: Sections 19 and 21, Transfer of Property Act, 1882

questions.question_text: Under Section 105 and settled law, the essential distinction between a lease and a licence is that:
options: A lease is always oral and a licence always written
A licence lasts longer than a lease
A lease creates an interest in the property and transfers exclusive possession; a licence is a bare personal permission to use the property without any transfer of interest or exclusive possession
questions.explanation: The test is the intention of the parties and whether exclusive possession was granted (Associated Hotels of India v. R.N. Kapoor, 1959).

questions.question_text: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 does NOT apply to:
options: Transfers by operation of law, such as by sale in execution of a decree, forfeiture, insolvency or intestate/testamentary succession
questions.explanation: Section 2 preserves the operation of the law of insolvency and Muslim law; Section 5 confines the Act to inter vivos transfers.
questions.statute_or_case: Sections 2 and 5, Transfer of Property Act, 1882

questions.question_text: Under Sections 3 and 4 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCB) are constituted for:
options: Preventing and controlling water pollution and maintaining or restoring wholesomeness of water
questions.explanation: The Water Act 1974 established CPCB and SPCBs to prevent and control water pollution and maintain water wholesomeness.

questions.question_text: Under what constitutional provision was the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 enacted by Parliament?
options: Article 252 of the Constitution of India (passed upon resolutions by State Legislatures)
questions.explanation: The Water Act 1974 was enacted under Article 252 after resolutions were passed by state legislatures.
questions.statute_or_case: Preamble & Article 252, Constitution of India / Water Act 1974

questions.question_text: Under Section 25 of the Water Act, 1974, no person shall, without the previous CONSENT of the State Board, establish or take any steps to establish any industry, operation or process which is likely to:
options: Discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream or well or sewer or on land
questions.explanation: Section 25 mandates prior Consent to Establish/Operate (CTE/CTO) from SPCB before discharging trade effluent.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33A of the Water Act, 1974 (inserted by 1988 Amendment), the Board has power to issue binding directions including:
options: The closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process, or stoppage/regulation of electricity, water or other service
questions.explanation: Section 33A equips Boards with direct power to issue closure orders and order disconnection of electricity/water supplies.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45E of the Water Act, 1974 (as substituted in 2024), whoever fails to comply with the consent requirements of Section 25 or Section 26 (discharging effluent without SPCB consent) is punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than:
options: One year and six months, but which may extend to six years and with fine
questions.explanation: Section 45E (inserted by the 2024 amendment, replacing the erstwhile Section 44) prescribes a minimum of 1 year 6 months imprisonment extending to 6 years and fine for failure to comply with Section 25/26 consent requirements; the renumbered Section 44 now deals only with tampering with monitoring devices, punishable by a civil penalty.

questions.question_text: In the landmark Kanpur Tanneries Case (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India AIR 1988 SC 1037), the Supreme Court ordered the closure of polluting tanneries discharging untreated effluent into River Ganga on the ground that:
options: Financial capacity of industries is irrelevant when weighed against public health and preservation of river environment
questions.explanation: M.C. Mehta (1988) held environmental protection and public health override financial stringency arguments of polluting industries.
questions.statute_or_case: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1988) 1 SCC 471

questions.question_text: Under Section 21 of the Water Act, 1974, when a sample of effluent is taken by a Board officer for analysis, into how many containers must the sample be divided in the presence of the occupier?
options: Two parts (or containers), each placed in a container sealed and marked by both officer and occupier
questions.explanation: Section 21 specifies sample splitting into 2 parts (one for State Water Lab and one for Central Water Lab if requested).

questions.question_text: Under Section 28 of the Water Act, 1974, any person aggrieved by an order made by the State Board under Section 25, 26, or 27 may prefer an appeal within 30 days to:
options: The Appellate Authority constituted by the State Government
questions.explanation: Section 28 provides for an appeal within 30 days to an Appellate Authority constituted by the State Government, consisting of a single person or three persons as the State Government thinks fit.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45E(4) of the Water Act, 1974 (the erstwhile Section 47 on offences by companies having been omitted in 2024), where an offence of failing to comply with Section 25/26 consent has been committed by a COMPANY, who shall be deemed guilty of the offence?
options: Every person who at the time the offence was committed was directly in charge of, and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business, as well as the company
questions.explanation: The 2024 amendment omitted Section 47 and relocated corporate vicarious liability, for the imprisonable offence under Section 45E, to Section 45E(4), fixing liability on persons directly in charge of the company's business as well as the company itself.

questions.question_text: Under Section 49(1)(b) of the Water Act, 1974 (Citizen Suit Provision), a court can take cognizance of an offence on a complaint made by any person who has given notice of at least:
options: Sixty days in the prescribed manner of the alleged offence and intention to make a complaint to the Board
questions.explanation: Section 49(1)(b) enables citizen suits after 60 days statutory notice to the Pollution Board.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(e) of the Water Act, 1974, 'pollution' means such contamination or alteration of physical, chemical, or biological properties of water as is likely to create a nuisance or render such water harmful to:
options: Public health or safety, or to domestic, commercial, industrial, agricultural or other legitimate uses, or to flora and fauna
questions.explanation: Section 2(e) provides a broad statutory definition of water pollution covering human health, usages, flora and fauna.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(g) of the Water Act, 1974, 'sewage effluent' means effluent from any sewage system or sewage disposal works and includes:
questions.explanation: Section 2(g) defines sewage effluent including sullage.

questions.question_text: Under Section 2(k) of the Water Act, 1974, 'trade effluent' includes any liquid, gaseous or solid substance which is discharged from any premises used for carrying on any:
options: Industry, operation or process, or treatment and disposal system, other than domestic sewage
questions.explanation: Section 2(k) defines trade effluent as non-domestic industrial/commercial discharge.

questions.question_text: Under Section 5(1) of the Water Act, 1974, what is the term of office of a member of a Pollution Control Board (other than an ex officio member)?
options: Three years from date of nomination
questions.explanation: Section 5(1) specifies 3 years term for nominated board members.

questions.question_text: Under Section 16(1) of the Water Act, 1974, the main function of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) is to:
options: Promote cleanliness of streams and wells in different areas of the States
questions.explanation: Section 16(1) specifies CPCB's primary duty: promoting cleanliness of streams and wells nationwide.

questions.question_text: Under Section 19 of Water Act 1974, the State Government after consultation with SPCB may declare any area as a:
questions.explanation: Section 19 lets the State Government, after consulting the State Board, restrict the Act to specified areas which are declared a water pollution, prevention and control area.

questions.question_text: Under Section 24(1)(a) of Water Act 1974, no person shall knowingly cause or permit to enter into any stream or well any poisonous, noxious or polluting matter exceeding:
options: Standards laid down by the State Board
questions.explanation: Section 24(1)(a) prohibits entry of poisonous, noxious or polluting matter into a stream, well, sewer or land beyond the standards laid down by the State Board.

questions.question_text: Under Section 32(1) of Water Act 1974, where emergency measures are required due to accidental pollution of a stream, who may take emergency remedial action?
questions.explanation: Section 32(1) empowers the State Board itself to carry out emergency removal or remedial operations where polluting matter has entered a stream or well due to an accident.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33(1) of Water Act 1974, a SPCB can apply to which court for an injunction restraining apprehended water pollution?
options: Courts not inferior to a Judicial Magistrate First Class or Metropolitan Magistrate
questions.explanation: Section 33(1) allows a Board to apply to a court not inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class for an order restraining apprehended pollution.

questions.question_text: Under Section 41A of the Water Act, 1974 (as substituted in 2024), failure to comply with a direction issued under Section 32 or Section 33A attracts:
options: A civil penalty of not less than Rs. 10,000, extending up to Rs. 15 lakh, with an additional penalty of Rs. 10,000 per day of continuing default
questions.explanation: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Amendment Act, 2024 decriminalised this default under Section 41A, replacing imprisonment with a monetary penalty imposed by the adjudicating officer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 42(1) of Water Act 1974 (as substituted in 2024), pulling down, damaging or defacing any notice or post put up by a Pollution Control Board attracts:
options: A civil penalty of not less than Rs. 10,000, extending up to Rs. 15 lakh
Imprisonment up to three months or fine up to Rs. 10,000 or both
questions.explanation: The 2024 amendment decriminalised the acts listed in Section 42(1), replacing imprisonment/fine with a civil penalty of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh imposed by the adjudicating officer.

questions.question_text: Under Section 48 of Water Act 1974 (as substituted in 2024), where a contravention under the Act is committed by a Government Department, who is liable to pay the penalty?
options: The Head of the Department, liable to a penalty equal to one month's basic salary, unless he proves the contravention occurred without his knowledge or instructions
questions.explanation: Section 48(1), as substituted in 2024, fixes liability on the Head of the Department for a penalty equal to one month's basic salary, subject to the due-diligence/no-knowledge defence.

questions.question_text: Under Section 58 of Water Act 1974, no Civil Court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which:
options: An Appellate Authority constituted under this Act is empowered to determine
questions.explanation: Section 58 bars civil courts from entertaining matters that an Appellate Authority under the Act is empowered to determine, and bars injunctions against action taken under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 60 of Water Act 1974, the provisions of the Water Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in:
questions.explanation: Section 60 gives the Water Act an overriding effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent in any other enactment.

questions.question_text: Under Section 17(1)(f) of Water Act 1974, one of the functions of a State Board is to inspect sewage or trade effluents, works and treatment plants:
options: Periodically, and to review plans/specifications relating to such plants
questions.explanation: Section 17(1)(f) empowers/obliges the State Board to inspect sewage and trade effluent treatment plants and review their plans and specifications; the Act does not fix a rigid daily or decade-long schedule.

questions.question_text: Under Section 20(3) of Water Act 1974, a State Board may direct a person in charge of an establishment discharging sewage/effluent to furnish information regarding:
options: Construction, installation or operation of the establishment or disposal system
questions.explanation: Section 20(3) empowers the Board to direct any person in charge of an establishment to furnish particulars of the construction, installation or operation of its disposal system.

questions.question_text: Under Section 54 of Water Act 1974, a document purporting to be a report signed by a Government analyst or Board analyst may be used in any proceeding under the Act as:
options: Evidence of the facts stated therein
questions.explanation: Section 54 makes the analyst's report usable as evidence of the facts stated in it, dispensing with the need to call the analyst as a witness.

questions.question_text: Under Section 51 of Water Act 1974, the Central Government may establish or specify a Central Water Laboratory to:
options: Analyze samples of water, sewage or trade effluent
questions.explanation: Section 51 lets the Central Government establish or specify a Central Water Laboratory, which analyses samples of water, sewage or trade effluent sent to it.

questions.question_text: Under Section 53 of Water Act 1974, who appoints the Government Analyst for analyzing water/effluent samples?
options: The State Government or Central Government
questions.explanation: Section 53 empowers the Central Government and State Government to each appoint qualified persons as Government analysts for samples sent to their respective laboratories.

questions.question_text: In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647, the Supreme Court declared that 'Precautionary Principle' and 'Polluter Pays Principle' are essential features of:
options: Sustainable Development and Article 21 Right to Life
questions.explanation: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum held that the Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle are part of Indian environmental law and essential features of sustainable development under Article 21.
questions.statute_or_case: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647

questions.question_text: In S. Jagannath v. Union of India (Shrimp Culture Case 1997) 2 SCC 87, the Supreme Court ordered closure of intensive shrimp aquaculture farms within Coastal Regulation Zone for violating:
options: Water Act 1974 and Environment Protection Act 1986
questions.explanation: In S. Jagannath the Court found unlicensed intensive/semi-intensive shrimp farms in the Coastal Regulation Zone operated without the consents required by the Water Act, 1974 and in violation of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the CRZ Notification.
questions.statute_or_case: S. Jagannath v. Union of India (1997) 2 SCC 87

questions.question_text: Under Section 27(2) of Water Act 1974, can a State Board review or revoke any condition of consent granted under Section 25?
options: Yes, SPCB may review any condition of consent and vary or revoke it
No, consent is irrevocable once given
questions.explanation: Section 27(2) empowers the State Board to review, from time to time, any condition of a Section 25/26 consent and to vary or revoke it by notice.

questions.question_text: Under Section 33A of Water Act 1974, who can be issued directions by the Board?
options: Any person, officer, or authority (including closure of industry or stopping power/water supply)
questions.explanation: Section 33A lets a Board issue binding written directions to any person, officer or authority, including closure of an industry or stoppage of electricity/water supply.

questions.question_text: Under Section 43 of Water Act 1974 (as substituted in 2024), whoever contravenes Section 24 (prohibition on polluting streams) is now liable to:
options: A civil penalty of not less than Rs. 10,000, extending up to Rs. 15 lakh, with an additional daily penalty for continuing contravention
1 year and 6 months extending to 6 years imprisonment and fine
questions.explanation: The 2024 amendment decriminalised contravention of Section 24, substituting the earlier imprisonment with a civil penalty of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh plus a daily penalty for continuing default.

questions.question_text: Under Section 45A of Water Act 1974 (as substituted in 2024), the penalty for contravention of a provision or direction for which no specific penalty is otherwise provided is:
options: Not less than Rs. 10,000, extending up to Rs. 15 lakh, with an additional daily penalty for continuing default
questions.explanation: Section 45A, as substituted in 2024, sets a residuary civil penalty of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh, with an additional daily penalty of up to Rs. 10,000 for continuing contravention.

questions.question_text: Under Section 49(1) of Water Act 1974, no court inferior to which magistrate shall try any offence under the Act?
options: Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate First Class
questions.explanation: The concluding part of Section 49(1) bars any court inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class from trying an offence under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under Section 50 of Water Act 1974, members, officers and servants of a Pollution Control Board are deemed to be:
options: Public servants within the meaning of Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code (corresponding to Section 2(28), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023)
questions.explanation: Section 50 deems Board members, officers and servants to be public servants within the meaning of Section 21 IPC; Section 59 of the Act deals separately with protection of action taken in good faith.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18(2) of Water Act 1974, where a State Board defaults in complying with a direction of the Central Board and a grave emergency results, the Central Government may direct that:
options: The Central Board may perform the functions of the State Board for that area
questions.explanation: Section 18(2) lets the Central Government direct the Central Board to step in and perform a defaulting State Board's functions during a grave emergency; Section 64 in fact deals with the State Government's rule-making power.

questions.question_text: Under Section 18 of Water Act 1974, in performance of its functions, every State Board is bound by directions issued by:
options: The Central Board and the State Government
questions.explanation: Section 18(1)(b) binds every State Board by written directions of the Central Board or the State Government, with disputes between the two referred to the Central Government.

questions.question_text: What is the primary statutory purpose of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977?
options: To levy a cess on water consumed by specified industries and local authorities to augment resources for Pollution Boards
questions.explanation: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 levies a cess on water consumption by specified industries and local authorities to raise funds for the Pollution Control Boards, supplementing the parent 1974 Act.
questions.statute_or_case: Preamble, Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977
